# Sūrah al-Baqarah (Chapter 2) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:1

> Alif-Lãm-Mĩm.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Twenty-Nine Openings of One Kind**

Al-Baqarah begins with three letters of the Arabic alphabet standing alone. Twenty-nine of the Qur'an's 114 sūrahs open the same way, with single letters or short groups of them, and the group *alif lām mīm* opens six: this sūrah, Āl ʿImrān, and the four sūrahs of the sequence al-ʿAnkabūt, al-Rūm, Luqmān and al-Sajdah. In recitation the letters are spoken by name, so the verse is heard as *alif lām mīm*, not as a string of sounds.

The practice is ancient and unexplained in the text itself, and Muslim scholarship has treated it as one of the deliberate silences of the Book. What can be said without speculation is structural: the letters are not part of the Arabic sentence that follows, they carry no grammatical role in it, and they are recited as verses. A reader who treats them as an ornament to be skipped is reading something other than what the Book contains.

**Fourteen Letters Out of Twenty-Eight**

The letters used in these openings come from exactly half the alphabet. Fourteen distinct letters appear across the twenty-nine sūrahs, in groups ranging from one letter to five, and the groupings repeat with variation: *alif lām mīm* at the head of six sūrahs, *ḥā mīm* at the head of seven, *alif lām rā* at the head of five. Arabic's twenty-eight letters are divided down the middle, and the chosen half is spread across the places of articulation, from the throat to the lips.

That balance is the kind of pattern the Book uses elsewhere in its signs, and it has attracted two kinds of reader. Some have treated the selection as evidence of a design that no human composition reproduces. Others have treated it as a threshold, a signal that what follows is of a different order from ordinary speech and should be approached with attention. Both readings assume the same thing: the letters are not noise inserted before the message.

**A Book Made of Letters Its Audience Owns**

Read beside the sentence that follows, the letters make a plain rhetorical point. The revelation is built from the same twenty-eight letters the Arabs spoke in the market, and it is arranged in a way they could not match. Three other sūrahs make the same move with the same vocabulary: *“Alif-Lãm-Ra. These are the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom”* (10:1), and again *“These are the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom”* (31:2).

The pattern is letters, then book, then guidance, and the order is not accidental. The letters are the raw material; the Book is what they became; guidance is what the Book does. Sūrah 2 will shortly describe itself as a guide, and its opening line names the alphabet that carries the claim. The audience is invited to consider that the difference between its own speech and this revelation lies not in the material but in the arrangement of the material.

**The Debate Over Meaning and the Position Worth Holding**

Commentators have offered many readings. One makes the letters abbreviations for names — *alif* for Allāh, *lām* for Jibrīl, *mīm* for Muḥammad — so that the opening of al-Baqarah would state the route of revelation from God through the angel to the prophet. Another gives them numerical values, since every Arabic letter has a number, and reads the combinations through the science called *al-jafr*. A third leaves the meaning with God alone.

Al-Rāzī took a middle course, comparing these letters to acts of worship whose wisdom is not disclosed, such as parts of the pilgrimage: performed faithfully, accepted without a visible reason. The objection to leaving them unexplained is that the Book calls itself clear, and the Qur'an answers the objection itself by classifying its verses: *“some verses are precise—they are the foundation of the Book—while others are elusive”* (3:7). A Book that says of itself that it contains both needs no apology for an element that resists paraphrase.

**What the Letters Ask of a Reader**

Whatever position a commentator takes on their meaning, the letters impose a behaviour. They stop the reciter before the first statement of the sūrah and require him to recite something he cannot explain. The effect is a small discipline at the threshold: the reader receives before he understands, and he continues reciting through a passage that offers his intellect nothing to complete.

Islamic practice treats the whole Fātiḥah, and passages like this one, as recited in that manner — words whose presence is acknowledged and whose full sense may lie beyond the reciter. The letters are therefore not a puzzle left unsolved by accident; they are the first test of the attitude the sūrah goes on to describe. The verses that follow will divide humanity into those who accept a guidance they cannot see the end of and those who withhold acceptance until every question is answered.

**What Follows the Three Letters**

Al-Baqarah is the longest sūrah of the Qur'an, 286 verses revealed in Madinah after the migration, and it opens by naming its readers. Its first twenty verses sort humanity into three groups in order: those who take the Book as guidance, those who reject it outright, and those who live among the believers while denying them in private. The sūrah that will contain the longest verse of the Book and its most detailed legal teaching begins with three uninterpreted letters.

The placement reads as deliberate. A book that will spend hundreds of verses establishing law, history and argument opens with a piece of language that no legal reasoning explains. Nothing in the sūrah's authority depends on the reader's ability to account for that opening, and the reader who continues past it has already accepted a revelation on its own terms rather than on his.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:2

> This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺,

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Claim Made Before Any Argument**

The sūrah's first sentence after the letters is a verdict about itself. The Arabic's demonstrative points to the revelation in front of the reader, and the noun is definite: not *a book* but *the* Book, a title rather than a category, as the Qur'an also uses the Criterion and the Reminder as titles. Some readers took the demonstrative as "that", which would point either to the Book on the Preserved Tablet or to the portion already revealed before this sūrah.

No proof is offered at this point, and the omission is instructive. The sūrah's arguments will come — signs in creation, the history of Israel, the challenge to produce a single sūrah like this one — but the opening sentence asserts before it demonstrates. That is the order in which the Book describes itself throughout: it states what it is, then gives the reader every opportunity to test the statement.

**Doubt That Is Denied Rather Than Forbidden**

The Arabic word rendered doubt, *rayb*, carries suspicion and unease as well as uncertainty. The verse does not command anybody not to doubt; it declares that the Book offers no grounds for it. The claim concerns the text rather than the reader's emotions, which is a stronger statement and a harder one to make.

That self-description recurs in the sūrah's vocabulary. The Qur'an calls itself *“the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom”* (10:1) and *“the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom”* again at the head of Luqmān (31:2), and it addresses the People of the Book with the words *“There certainly has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book”* (5:15). Elsewhere it distinguishes between two kinds of verse, precise and elusive, and asks the reader to accept both (3:7). The absence of doubt is being claimed for a Book that openly includes passages its readers will not fully master.

**Guidance Is the Book's Function, Not Its Contents**

The sentence does not say that the Book contains guidance; it says the Book is a guidance. The Qur'an tends to describe itself by what it does, and that habit gives its claims a practical edge. A guide is judged by whether anyone reaches the destination. The Book states its own purpose in the same terms elsewhere: *“This is an insight to humanity —a guide and a lesson to the God-fearing”* (3:138), and of the month of its revelation, *“Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity”* (2:185).

Read with the previous sūrah, the claim is continuous. The Fātiḥah asked for guidance along a straight path; al-Baqarah opens by naming itself the guide. The request at the end of the Fātiḥah is answered by an object the reader can hold, and the answer is not a feeling or an inspiration but a text that can be recited, memorised, disputed and obeyed.

**taqwā: Guarding, Not Cringing**

The people this Book guides are called *muttaqīn*, from a root that means to shield or protect oneself. The word does not name an emotion; it names a practice. A *muttaqī* is someone who keeps watch, who places a barrier between himself and what he fears. In the religious sense the barrier is obedience, and the fear is the loss of what matters most.

The Qur'an defines the term by what it is not before it lists what it is: *“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets”* (2:177), after which the verse adds giving, prayer, alms and keeping promises. The Book's other portrait of such people is similar: *“those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it. These are the ones ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah”* (39:18). Mindfulness, in this vocabulary, is attentiveness carried into action.

**Guidance on Only One Side of the Sentence**

The verse places two claims side by side with a single dash between them: the Book admits no doubt, and it guides the mindful. The pairing has been read as a philosophical problem — how can a guide be universal if its guidance reaches only some? — and the Book answers the question by describing reception rather than by softening the claim. Elsewhere the answer is put in a single sentence: *“Allah surely guides the believers to the Straight Path”* (22:54).

A light does not illuminate an eye that is shut, and the Qur'an's argument places the difference in the disposition of the reader, not in the strength of the light. What this verse does not do is divide humanity into the learned and the unlearned. The quality it requires is not intelligence but a willingness to be corrected, which the sūrah's third line will spell out as belief in what cannot be seen, prayer, and spending from what one has been given.

**Why the Book Is Described Before It Is Explained**

The sūrah names its intended readers before it presents its evidence. Verses 2:2–5 give a portrait of the mindful, then 2:6–7 present those who reject warning outright, then 2:8–20 turn to the people who live among the believers while working against them. The order matters, because the reader is being shown what the Book is looking for before he is told what the Book contains.

That order also matches the sūrah's scale. Al-Baqarah is the longest sūrah of the Qur'an, 286 verses, revealed in Madinah after the community had a city, a treasury and laws to administer. Its opening does not begin with legislation. It begins with a declaration about the text itself, followed by a description of the reader who will profit from it, and only then does it turn to the people who will not.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:3

> who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Faith Directed at What Cannot Be Checked**

*Ghayb* means the absent, what is out of sight. In the Qur'an it covers the realities no instrument reaches: God, the angels, the revealed Books, the messengers, the Last Day, and the decree that governs events. A well-known report of the Prophet's teaching, the ḥadīth of Jibrīl recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50, defines faith itself as belief in those six articles, and lists them as a single act of assent rather than six separate commitments.

The order in this verse is therefore not arbitrary. The first mark of the mindful is belief in what cannot be seen, because what can be seen does not require faith. The community described in this sūrah has not watched the hereafter or inspected God; it has been told, and it has accepted the report. The rest of the verse turns on that acceptance: what a person believes about the invisible decides what he does with the visible.

**Prayer as Something Kept Standing**

The verb here is not "they pray" but *yuqīmūna al-ṣalāh*, they keep the prayer standing. Its root means to rise, to set upright, to maintain. The form of the verb describes a practice held in place rather than an act completed, and the choice is precise for a ritual performed daily under conditions that encourage neglect.

The Qur'an's own instruction on the subject ties the practice to remembrance: *“So worship Me ˹alone˺, and establish prayer for My remembrance”* (20:14). Prayer is the one mark in this verse whose object is the same unseen God the believer has just affirmed, and it converts an invisible conviction into a routine that can be seen. Nothing in the verse suggests that belief and prayer are alternatives offered to different temperaments. The Book presents them as two stages of one movement, and the third stage will leave the interior of a person entirely.

**"From What We Have Provided": Wealth as a Trust**

The verse does not say that the believers give charity from their own property. It says they give from what *We* have provided, with God as the speaker and the provider, and that pronoun changes the nature of ownership. What a person holds is received, and what is received can be spent as the giver intended. The Qur'an makes the same point in the imperative mood: *“Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and donate from what He has entrusted you with”* (57:7).

The amount is left unspecified here, which is why the verse speaks about giving generally before the sūrah lays down the obligation of alms-tax in detail. The Qur'an treats this giving as a return rather than a loss: *“If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you would never be able to number them”* (16:18), and a gift received among countless gifts cannot be treated as untouched private property. The believer gives from what is not, strictly speaking, his.

**Why Belief, Prayer and Giving Appear in This Order**

The three marks move from what nobody can see to what only God sees to what everybody sees. Belief has no witness except God. Prayer has a witness when it is performed in company and no witness when it is performed alone. Giving has a witness whenever it happens, because something changes hands. The sequence is a description of a whole life rather than a checklist of duties, and it escalates from the most private to the most public.

The pairing of prayer and alms-tax runs through the Qur'an roughly thirty times, which makes it one of the Book's most insistent combinations. One purifies the body and the day, the other purifies wealth and the relation to those who need it. Reading them together, the sūrah is describing a community whose worship costs it both time and money, and it names generosity in the same breath as belief.

**The Community That Had Not Yet Been Named**

These verses in Madinah describe a community that the rest of the sūrah will address in the second person. The Book establishes what such people are like before it issues instructions to them, and the description is deliberately ordinary: assent to what is unseen, a maintained prayer, and spending. No miracles, no prestige, no claim on lineage; the identity of the believers is drawn entirely from practice.

That is why the same three traits recur throughout the Book as a shorthand. When the Qur'an wants to describe the believers it reaches for the same words: *“those who humble themselves in prayer”* (23:2), and the giving that follows in the same list. Al-Baqarah opens by defining the human being whose company it will seek for the remaining two hundred and eighty verses, and it does so before presenting either the rejecters or the hypocrites.

**Belief Without a Deadline**

The verse asks for belief in what cannot be verified, and the Book acknowledges what that costs. The Qur'an's answer to the difficulty is not to remove it but to make the request explicit and then reward it: *“This is the truth from your Lord. Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve”* (18:29). Faith in the unseen is a decision made without a receipt, and the sūrah's next verses will describe those who refuse that decision.

What the Book never does is pretend the unseen has been shown. The entire arrangement of the sūrah depends on the distinction: those who accept what they cannot inspect are called mindful, and the passage that follows turns to people who will not accept anything they cannot inspect. The three marks listed here all follow from the first one, and the first one is a choice made in the dark.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:4

> and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Revelation Received and Revelation Already Given**

The verse names both directions of belief in one clause. The believers accept what has come down to the Prophet ﷺ in their own time and what came down before it, and the two are treated as members of one family rather than as rivals. The Qur'an states the same position in the final verses of this sūrah: *“The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”* (2:285)

That sentence places the Books of God among the articles of faith, alongside angels and messengers. Believing in the Qur'an while denying the scriptures that preceded it is not a stricter form of belief in the Book's own terms; it is a failure to accept what the Book says about itself. The revelation is presented as the latest instalment of a series, and the community is defined by its acceptance of the series.

**Earlier Revelation Is Not a Rival Document**

The Qur'an treats earlier scriptures as its own inheritance and its own confirmation. It describes the single way God ordained for the prophets collectively: *“He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding:˺ ‘Uphold the faith, and make no divisions in it.’”* (42:13)

The verse also anticipates the objection that this privilege belongs to one community. The Qur'an praises believers among the People of the Book who accept the new revelation without abandoning the truth they already hold: *“Indeed, there are some among the People of the Book who truly believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you ˹believers˺ and what was revealed to them. They humble themselves before Allah—never trading Allah's revelations for a fleeting gain.”* (3:199). The faith described in this verse is not a new religion replacing an old one. It is the recognition of a message in an existing line.

**Certainty About the Hereafter**

The third element in the verse is not belief in the Hereafter but certainty of it. *Yūqinūn* comes from a root meaning to be settled, to have no wavering left. The Qur'an uses it for knowledge that has stopped being a hypothesis, and it places that certainty beside the two forms of revelation because the three belong to one structure: revelation given before, revelation given now, and the accounting that will settle what was done with both.

Certainty about that accounting changes how the present is valued. A person convinced that the ledger remains open after death will accept costs in this world that others will not, and the Book treats that conviction as a practical matter rather than a mood. The Qur'an's arguments for the Hereafter are arguments for the reasonableness of a life conducted with reference to it; the verse therefore ends not with a description of paradise but with the mental condition of the believer.

**Does the Verse Continue the Portrait or Start a New One?**

Commentators asked whether this clause describes the same people as the previous verse or introduces a second group. The first reading takes the conjunction as continuing: the mindful are those who believe in the unseen, pray, give, and accept both revelations, and await the Hereafter. The second reading takes this verse as describing believers from among the People of the Book who accepted the Prophet while remaining attached to what they had received.

Both readings have grounds. The first follows the grammar of a single unbroken description, and it is supported by the fact that the sūrah opens by describing one audience. The second explains why earlier revelation is mentioned at all, since it would have had little relevance to an audience of former polytheists, and it is supported by the praise given to believers among the People of the Book in 3:199. The stronger position holds the two together: the verse continues one portrait, and that portrait includes whatever believers from the earlier communities it succeeds in describing.

**"Revealed to You": An Address That Includes Everyone Else**

The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ in the second person singular. He is the one to whom the revelation has come, and the community's belief in it is belief in what was given to him. The Book uses the same construction throughout, and its effect is to keep the community's faith attached to a messenger rather than to a text that arrived unattached.

Muslims who recite these words take part in a sentence addressed to someone else. That is the ordinary situation of the sūrah: it was given to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah, and it is recited by everyone who comes after him. The fourth line of the Book thus establishes both the continuity of revelation and the particular channel by which the latest instalment arrived.

**Certainty and the Shape of Ordinary Life**

The verse ends with the Hereafter because conviction about it is what makes the earlier clauses portable. Belief in the unseen, prayer, giving and acceptance of revelation are all commitments that can be abandoned if death ends everything; certainty about a reckoning makes them reasonable when they are expensive. The Qur'an rests the whole moral order on that conviction.

It states the alternative without softening it: *“And say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord. Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve.’”* (18:29). The Book's believers are not described as people who have answered every question. They are described as people who have settled the question of what their lives are for, and who have arranged their prayer, their money and their expectations accordingly.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:5

> It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pronoun That Closes a Portrait**

*Ulāʾika*, rendered here as *it is they*, is the demonstrative Arabic uses to deliver a verdict. The sūrah has spent three verses listing four marks — belief in the unseen, established prayer, giving, and acceptance of both revelations along with the Hereafter — and then closes the list with a single sentence that assigns the outcome. The verdict is God's, and it is stated before any of the sūrah's opponents have been presented.

The same construction appears throughout the Book in both directions. It pronounces on the guided here, and it pronounces on the losers elsewhere: *“Do not let your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. For whoever does so, it is they who are the ˹true˺ losers.”* (63:9). The device is symmetrical. The Qur'an uses identical grammar to identify the two ends of the same road, which means the sentence is a decision rather than a compliment.

**Guidance Traced Back to Its Source**

The verse does not say the believers are guided; it says they are guided *by their Lord*. The phrase names the source of the guidance rather than the quality of the guided, and it makes the sentence a statement about God before it is a statement about people. The Qur'an uses the same construction whenever it explains who finds the road: *“He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path”* (2:142), and of the Book itself, *“Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity”* (2:185).

Attribution to God also rules out a reading in which guidance is self-generated. The people described in the previous verses have behaved in specific ways, but the sentence does not reward their behaviour with a promotion; it says they are guided *by their Lord*, which means the road they are walking was opened for them. The marks listed in 2:3–4 are the shape their guidance takes, not the price they paid for it.

**Success Is Cultivation, Not Escape**

The word rendered successful, *mufliḥūn*, comes from a root associated with farming. Its sense is thriving, ripening, producing; Arabic uses the same root for the farmer who breaks ground. The Qur'an applies it to those who have brought something to harvest, and it keeps the word close to the action that produced it: *“Successful indeed are the believers: / those who humble themselves in prayer”* (23:1–2), and *“Successful indeed are those who purify themselves”* (87:14).

That etymology matters for how the sentence is read. Success in this vocabulary is not escape from a disaster or a verdict delivered at the end; it is what a life yields when it is worked properly. The community that prays, gives and believes is described as a crop that comes in, and the future tense of the second clause places the harvest at the end of the process rather than at its beginning.

**Two Clauses, Two Times**

The sentence divides into a present standing and a future outcome. The first clause speaks in a nominal sentence: the demonstrative and the participle describe a condition that is true now. The second clause announces what those people will be. The structure is one of the Qur'an's most common arrangements, and it holds a practical balance: guidance is available in the present, and its result is delivered later.

Nothing in the verse offers a schedule or a guarantee of visible reward in this world. The Book makes the same distinction elsewhere and warns against reading prosperity as a verdict: comfort in this life often accompanies rejection, while the reward of the patient is held back. The two clauses of this verse correspond to the two worlds, and the sentence that names success does so in the future because the harvest has not yet been brought in.

**Why the Pronoun Is Repeated**

Arabic could have said they are guided and successful in a single clause. Instead the demonstrative is repeated with a separate pronoun: it is *they*, and again it is *they*. The construction restricts the statement to the group just described and excludes anyone else from the claim. It answers in advance the kind of claim that the sūrah will shortly put in the mouths of others.

That exclusivity is a burden and a protection at once. It means the marks in the preceding verses are not one path among many, and it also means the verdict is not open to revision by the crowd. The Book has already used the same emphatic construction for guidance in the Fātiḥah; here it uses it to attach a specific future to a specific way of living, and it leaves the reader to decide which clause he is standing under.

**A Verdict With No Inherited Qualification**

None of the four marks in the preceding verses can be inherited. A person cannot inherit belief in the unseen, a maintained prayer, generosity from his own means, or certainty about the Hereafter; each one is done by the person who does it. The verdict in this verse therefore ignores the criteria that usually determined standing in the society the sūrah was addressing, where tribe, descent and wealth decided most questions.

That is the point of the demonstrative. The Book identifies its successful people by what they do rather than by who they come from, and it does so before it turns to the people who claim a place in the community without accepting its obligations. The sentence that follows this one begins the sūrah's second portrait, and the contrast rests on the plain fact that the first group's identity was entirely a matter of practice.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:6

> As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sentence the Book Repeats**

The Qur'an states this proposition more than once, which is why it reads as a rule rather than as a report about particular people. Sūrah Yā Sīn has it almost word for word: *“It is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe.”* (36:10). A prophet's people answer in the same terms: *“It is all the same to us whether you warn ˹us˺ or not.”* (26:136), and elsewhere the warning is said to be useless for another reason — the ones addressed cannot respond at all, *“It is all the same whether you call them or remain silent.”* (7:193).

The repetition is deliberate. Each occurrence attaches the statement to a different situation — a prophet's frustration, a community's defiance, a futile appeal to idols — and each time the sentence closes a door that the address itself had opened. The Qur'an is teaching its messenger that the outcome of his work is not proportional to the effort he puts into it.

**Disbelief as Covering Something Over**

The Arabic verb *kafara* means to cover or conceal, and Arab farmers used it for burying seed in the ground. Those who *kafarū* are not people with unanswered questions; in the Qur'an's usage they are people who have covered over what they know. The verse's opening construction, *those who persist in disbelief*, describes a settled condition rather than a momentary doubt.

That settled quality is what makes the sentence in the second half possible. Warning addresses a person who is still in motion, and the verse describes people who have arrived at a position. The Book elsewhere draws a line between those who have not yet accepted and those who will not: an invitation stands open, and a decision has been made. The Qur'an treats the second category as a fact about the world that its messenger must learn to work with rather than as a problem to be solved by better argument.

**The Warner's Task Is Announcement**

The Qur'an repeatedly limits the messenger's responsibility to delivery. *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. / You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:21–22). The same boundary appears in the instruction to the Prophet in argument: *“your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺”* (3:20), and again at 42:48 and 64:12, where the messenger is told he is not a keeper over the people he addresses.

The verse in al-Baqarah is the negative version of the same principle. If the warning changes nothing for a particular group, the message has still been delivered and the messenger's commission is complete. The Qur'an never presents the refusal of an audience as a failure of the message, nor does it ask the messenger to accept responsibility for the spiritual condition of another person.

**Not-Yet-Believing and Never-Believing**

The sentence is narrower than it sounds, and the rest of the Book shows the difference. Al-Baqarah itself will state that there is no compulsion in religion, since the truth has become distinct from falsehood (2:256), and the Qur'an addresses an uncommitted audience with an open choice: *“Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve”* (18:29). Invitation, argument and warning all assume that the person addressed can still move.

The verse therefore does not describe everyone who has not yet believed. It describes people whose rejection has become a settled feature of their character, and the Book's word for that condition is the same one it uses for a seed buried under earth. What is covered becomes inactive, and the verse's purpose is to tell the messenger in advance that such a condition exists and that his grief cannot alter it.

**The Grief the Sentence Was Meant to Prevent**

Telling a messenger that his warning will do no good sounds like cruelty, and the Qur'an shows why it is a mercy. The Prophet ﷺ is addressed twice with an image of self-destruction: *“Perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their disbelief.”* (26:3), and *“Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial”* (18:6). A third passage removes the burden directly: *“So do not grieve yourself to death over them ˹O Prophet˺.”* (35:8).

The verse in al-Baqarah belongs to that pattern. It is given at the head of the longest sūrah, before the long history of rejection that the sūrah will narrate, so that the messenger knows from the outset that some doors will not open. The statement is not a verdict on the messenger's effectiveness but a limit on his responsibility, and it frees the work from the impossible demand of universal agreement.

**Who the Words Were First Said Of**

Commentators connected the passage with the leaders of rejection in the sūrah's setting: the Qurashī notables who had settled into hostility and the Jewish leaders of Madinah who had decided against the Prophet before hearing him. The Book does not list names here, and the absence of names is what makes the statement usable across generations. The condition is described; the people who fit it change.

That anonymity also protects the community from using the verse as a label for its opponents. The verse cannot be applied by a believer to anyone except in the terms it sets out — a rejection so complete that warning makes no difference — and no human being can inspect that condition. The sentence is addressed to the messenger about his work, not to the community about its neighbours.

**Two Kinds of Failure at the Head of the Sūrah**

The place of this verse in the sūrah's opening sequence clarifies what it is doing. Verses 2:2–5 describe people who accept guidance they cannot verify; 2:6–7 describe people who have covered over what they knew; 2:8–20 describe people who say one thing and hold another. Three portraits, three failures, and the middle one is the plainest.

The distinction between the second and third portraits is the reason the sūrah spends so much more time on the third. A rejection that is out in the open can be answered, argued with or avoided. A profession without conviction cannot be answered at all, because the person making it has already agreed with everything that could be said against him. The Book gives the settled rejecter two verses and the hypocrite thirteen, and the proportion measures the difficulty rather than the guilt.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:7

> Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Seal, and the Three Faculties It Closes**

The verse names three organs in a fixed order. The heart comes first because the Qur'an treats it as the organ of understanding rather than merely of feeling; hearing follows because it is the channel by which revelation arrives; sight comes last, and it receives the weakest treatment of the three, a covering rather than a seal. The Arabic verb for sealing, *khatama*, is the verb used for closing a container and stamping a document.

The Qur'an issues the same challenge elsewhere as a question of power: *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, ‘Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight, or seal your hearts—who else other than Allah could restore it?’”* (6:46). Both verses treat the faculties as possessions that can be withdrawn. Hearing, sight and understanding are not the private property of the person who has them in this Book; they are grants, and the verse describes a grant that has been taken back.

**Cause or Consequence? The Question the Verse Raises**

If God seals the hearts of those who disbelieve, the objection writes itself: what freedom is left to them? The commentators answered along two lines. One reading takes the seal as a cause, God's prior decree governing who believes. The other takes it as a consequence, the natural end of a choice already made, so that the closing of the heart is a sentence passed on a settled direction rather than a trap set in advance.

The second reading gathers more support from the sūrah's sequence, since the previous verse described people whose rejection is already complete, and it is supported by the way the Qur'an states the rule elsewhere: *“This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers”* (7:101), and after the rejection of earlier messengers, *“This is how We seal the hearts of the transgressors”* (10:74). The same sentence pattern appears at 16:108 and 18:57, where the sealing follows a refusal that is already narrated. The verse does not describe an arbitrary verdict. It describes what happens to the faculty of understanding when a person uses it against what he knows.

**The Heart in the Book's Vocabulary**

The Qur'an's heart is not the sentimental organ of modern speech. It is where a person knows, decides and believes, and it is capable of being changed in either direction. The revelation reaches it directly: *“he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah's Will”* (2:97). It can be hardened: *“Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder”* (2:74). It can be stained: *“In fact, their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit!”* (83:14).

A report recorded in Sunan al-Tirmidhī 3334 describes the process in physical language: a black mark appears on the heart when a servant sins, and if he abandons the sin and repents, the heart is polished, while returning to the sin increases the blackness until it covers the heart. The Prophet ﷺ in that report identified the covering with the verse *“their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit”* (83:14). Sinning, on this account, is not neutral in its effects on the organ that understands.

**Three Verbs for One Condition**

The Arabic does not use the same verb three times. A seal is placed on the heart and on the hearing, while over the sight a covering is stretched. The change of image is not stylistic variation; it describes two types of closure. A sealed container is closed to its own contents, while a covered eye is separated from what it is built to perceive. The faculties that receive warnings are shut, and the faculty that could notice a warning is veiled.

The verse then states the outcome: a tremendous punishment. The word is the same one the Book uses for rewards of the largest scale, and it places the sentence on the same footing as the promise given to the mindful in the previous verse. The sūrah's opening portraits are balanced deliberately, and the punishment is stated as a fact without an interval of argument.

**What the Verse Refuses to Say**

The passage does not say that these people never had the opportunity to believe, and it does not say that the seal was placed on a blank page. The previous verse described warning offered and refused; this one describes the state that follows the refusal, which is why the Book can hold a person responsible for a condition he did not choose at a single moment. Responsibility in the Qur'an attaches to the direction of a life rather than to the individual decision that began it.

Nor does the verse cancel the preaching that has already failed. The messenger is told in 2:6 that his warning will not change these people, and his task remains what it was. The Qur'an keeps the two claims side by side: the hearts are sealed, and the reminder continues to be delivered, because the outcome is God's and the delivery is the messenger's.

**Why the Passage Sits Where It Does**

The three portraits at the head of al-Baqarah follow a pattern: the mindful with their marks, the settled rejecters with their seal, and then a third group whose membership is hidden. Placing the closed heart between the believer's portrait and the hypocrite's is instructive, because the sūrah's next passage will describe people whose condition is the opposite of a sealed heart — a public confession attached to a private denial.

The verse therefore functions as the far end of a road. Its punishment is stated without description, and the sentence is short; the rejection it describes required no elaborations. What the Book withholds from a sealed heart is precisely what it gives to the mindful earlier: the faculties of hearing and sight are named in both passages, and in one they receive guidance while in the other they are closed.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:8

> And there are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Third Group Enters the Sūrah**

The opening of al-Baqarah now turns to a new category. The mindful were described in the second through fifth verses; those whose rejection is settled occupied the next two; here a group appears whose speech and conviction do not match. The sūrah's first twenty verses present these three portraits in order, and the third is the longest and most detailed, running from this verse through verse 20.

The historical setting explains why. In Madinah, after the migration, profession of Islam had become the price of belonging to a community that was also a political order. That situation produced a class of people whose interests lay with the community's enemies while their public position lay inside it. The Qur'an gives them the name by which the whole subsequent tradition knows them: the hypocrites.

**A Profession Quoted and Denied**

The verse does not paraphrase the hypocrite; it quotes him. The sentence *We believe in Allah and the Last Day* is placed inside quotation marks and then contradicted by the clause that follows it, which states that they are not believers. The Book uses this technique repeatedly for this group, letting them speak and answering their words, and quotation marks are the only way a text can stage an opponent.

Two features of the quoted creed are notable. It names God and the Last Day and omits the Messenger, the Book and the Hereafter's details. It is a formula general enough to survive inspection and empty enough to avoid commitment. What the Qur'an denies is not the vocabulary but the claim attached to it: people who say these words are being told that saying them has not made them true.

**Why Deception Is the Wrong Description of What They Do**

The next verse will describe their attempt to deceive God and the believers, and the sūrah's placement of the denial before the attempt is precise. A person who says the words of faith to gain a place among the believers is not deceiving God, since nothing is hidden from God; he is misrepresenting himself to a community that cannot read hearts. The Book's verdict here interrupts the project at its first step: the words are not accepted as evidence.

The Qur'an describes the same people with the limbs of a different scene, when they stand for prayer *“half-heartedly only to be seen by people—hardly remembering Allah at all”* (4:142). In both passages the criterion is identical: what is done before witnesses is measured against what is absent when the witnesses are gone. This verse states the verdict on the public side, and the following verses will describe the private one.

**The Hypocrite as a Recurring Type**

Sūrah 63 is named for the hypocrites and opens by describing their characteristic act, an oath of witness that the Book calls a lie (63:1). The category is treated throughout the Qur'an as a permanent feature of religious communities rather than as a scandal confined to the Prophet's lifetime. Wherever a group holds power, prestige or protection, people will attach themselves to it for those reasons, and where those incentives disappear, so will some of the attachments.

The Book does not answer this with a demand for proof of sincerity, which no human being could supply, and it does not dissolve the community into a group of the verified. It defines the offence, describes its costs, and leaves the judgement to the one who knows what is in the hearts. Verse 8 states a fact about God's knowledge; the community that receives it is not given the same instrument.

**ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and the Politics of Divided Loyalty**

The reports identify ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, a leading man of the Khazraj tribe of Madinah, as the most prominent figure of this kind. He entered Islam without conviction, negotiated on behalf of the city before the migration, and lost standing when the Prophet ﷺ arrived and the tribes gave him authority. The literature of the sūrah's setting shows a man whose position inside the community kept improving as his commitment to it stayed minimal.

His case shows what the verse describes without naming names. The problem for a community is not the presence of a disbeliever, who can be dealt with openly; it is the presence of a member whose loyalty cannot be audited and whose interest is served by every division he can create. The Qur'an's answer at the head of this sūrah is to describe the condition and its end, not to issue a list of suspects.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah's Opening Argument**

The sūrah is the longest in the Qur'an, 286 verses, and it spends most of its length on law, history and argument. It opens, though, with a sorting of humanity into three portraits and a definition of what each responds to: guidance accepted, guidance refused, guidance claimed without being held. Everything that follows in the sūrah is addressed to a community that contains all three, and the legislation that begins later will assume the third group's existence.

That is why the denial in this verse is stated as a clarification rather than a curse. The sentence does not expel anyone from the community, and it does not name a punishment. It corrects a description: the words have been said, and the words have not been made true. What the verse announces is an accountability that the community cannot enforce and that the speakers cannot escape.

**A Present Tense Without a Fixed Membership**

The verse says that there are some who say, not that there were some. Arabic carries the distinction in a verb that describes an ongoing situation rather than a completed event, and the choice keeps the sentence open. The reports preserve the names of specific men in Madinah whose conduct matched the description, and the Book itself declines to supply them. A reader who is given a description instead of a list must decide what to do with it.

That silence serves two purposes at once. It protects the community from turning the passage into an instrument against named neighbours, which no human being could apply reliably, and it prevents any reader from closing the file with the conclusion that the matter concerned only a generation already dead. The description is present tense because the type it names is present.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:9

> They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verb That Turns Back on Its Speaker**

Arabic has a form of the verb that expresses mutual action, and the Qur'an uses it here: *yukhādiʿūn*, they seek to deceive. The form implies two parties exchanging deception, which is exactly what is not happening. On one side stands God, who knows what is concealed; on the other stands a community that can be fooled but not indefinitely. The reciprocity implied by the verb is empty, and the verse completes the thought by supplying the only party that is actually deceived.

The Qur'an states the exchange more directly elsewhere: *“Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them.”* (4:142). The counter-action in that sentence is expressed with the same reciprocal verb form, so God's response is described in the vocabulary of the plotter's own activity. The Book does not say that God is fooled and then recovers. It says the strategy encounters a strategist.

**Two Addressees, One of Whom Cannot Be Reached**

Naming God and the believers as the objects of the deception is theologically blunt. Nothing about a human being is hidden from God, and the Qur'an never offers the hypocrite the comfort of a successful fraud in that direction. The deception of the community, by contrast, is entirely possible; it happens whenever standing is granted on the basis of speech, and every religious community has to live with that possibility.

The Book's response splits the two cases. Against the impossible deception, it reports God's counter-plan; against the possible one, it describes the cost to the deceiver. The verse's rhythm moves from the attempt to its result in a single sentence, and the sentence is constructed so that the second half answers the first. What the hypocrite hoped to do to others he does, in fact, to himself.

**Self-Deception as the Only Successful Fraud**

The verdict *they only deceive themselves* is a piece of psychology before it is a punishment. To sustain a lie about one's own belief, a person must first arrange his own mind around the story he is telling; the mask has to be believable to the person wearing it. The further the arrangement goes, the less access the liar has to what he originally knew about himself.

The Qur'an's final clause makes that condition explicit: *they fail to perceive it*. The sūrah closes three of its portraits of this group with a comment on their awareness rather than on their guilt, and the emphasis is deliberate. Fraud against God is impossible and fraud against a community is temporary, but a person can spend years successfully deceiving himself about the state of his own heart, and that is the only deception in the verse that works.

**The Book's Vocabulary for Human Scheming**

Divine counter-planning is a recurring theme in the Qur'an, and it is always described in the same register. *“Those ˹disbelievers˺ before them ˹secretly˺ planned, but Allah has the ultimate plan. He knows what every soul commits.”* (13:42). Another passage uses the imagery of reversal: *“And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware.”* (27:50). A third states the outcome of a plot against a messenger: *“And the disbelievers made a plan ˹against Jesus˺, but Allah also planned —and Allah is the best of planners.”* (3:54).

The pattern behind these verses is consistent. The Book does not deny that human beings have plans or that plots succeed for a time; it denies that a plot against God's purposes can end as its author intended. The language of measure and counter-measure places God's action inside history rather than outside it, and it leaves the schemer responsible for a scheme that his opponent has already accounted for.

**Perception Lost and the Limits of Advice**

The clause about perception raises a practical problem for the community. If the hypocrites cannot see what they are doing, then no warning addressed to them can land as a warning. The sūrah is nonetheless addressed to them, and its admonitions are meant to be heard by everyone, which means the verse is written for two audiences at once: those it describes, and those who might recognise the description in themselves.

The Qur'an uses the same phrase in several places, and it usually attaches it to people who believe their position is better than it is. Sūrah 7 states the principle in its general form: such people *“have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with”* (7:179) — the faculties built for seeing the situation are the ones that have been disabled. What the verse announces is not that the hypocrite is ignorant, but that the instrument he would need in order to notice his condition is the very thing his condition has compromised.

**Why the Sentence Ends Where It Ends**

The verse could have continued to the punishment, and it does not. It stops at the point where the reader can see what the people involved cannot, and the restraint is the point: the sentence is about blindness rather than about sentence. The sūrah is still in the middle of a portrait, and the following verse will supply the diagnosis of their condition, then the increment of it, then its price.

The order of the Book's teaching matters here. The account of blindness comes before the account of the disease, the disease before its increase, and the increase before the punishment. A reader who has followed those steps discovers that the punishment is neither random nor excessive; it is the end of a path whose earlier stages are described in detail. The last clause of this verse is the first clear sign that the travellers on that path do not know where it leads.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:10

> There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sickness Is Doubt, Not Infection**

The commentators who examined this verse in the earliest generations were unanimous about one thing: the disease is not physical. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, followed by al-Ṭabarī, read *maraḍ* here as doubt and hypocrisy — a defect in the religion of the person rather than in his body. The Qur'an uses the same word for the same condition elsewhere, and one of those passages supplies the definition directly: *“But as for those with sickness in their hearts, it has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness, and they die as disbelievers.”* (9:125).

The choice of vocabulary is a diagnosis. A person whose heart holds doubt about what he professes is ill in the place where belief is produced, and the rest of the verse treats that illness as active rather than static. Sickness in this imagery does not sit still. It grows, and the growth is what the second half of the sentence is about.

**Increase as Consequence, Not Infliction**

God is the subject of the increase: *lets their sickness increase*. The Qur'an states the same law in several places, and it consistently presents the increase as the outworking of a direction already chosen. Sūrah 9 says of the same people that revelation *“has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness”* (9:125). Sūrah 74 describes a sign given *“so that those ˹hypocrites˺ with sickness in their hearts and the disbelievers will argue”* (74:31), where the same disease produces the same argument.

The pattern is one of correspondence. The Book does not describe a disease injected into a healthy person as a test; it describes a condition that feeds on what the person does with it, so that every further choice makes the condition harder to reverse. The verse's grammar keeps God as the agent of the increase, which means neither the outcome nor the process escapes His government — and the sūrah leaves both facts standing together.

**A City Where Profession Was Required**

The setting of these verses explains why hypocrisy is treated as an illness of a community rather than an individual failing. In Madinah after the migration, the community had become a body with a treasury, an army and a legal order, and the price of membership was a public profession. People whose interests lay elsewhere had reason to make that profession and no reason to mean it.

The Book's response to this situation is not a screening procedure. It is a description so precise that the people involved could recognise themselves in it, if they chose to look. The illness it names is the corrosion of the inner life under the pressure of outward conformity, and the sūrah treats that corrosion as a public danger precisely because it is invisible to the public.

**Punishment for Lying, in the Distinctive Sense of the Verb**

The verse ends with a painful punishment *for their lies*. Two readings of the final word have been transmitted: *yakdhibūn*, they lie, and *yukadhdhibūn*, they deny. Al-Ṭabarī preferred the first, and the Qur'an supports him elsewhere: the opening of Sūrah 63 says of the hypocrites that when they testify to the Prophet's mission, *“Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars”* (63:1).

Lying, in this usage, is not a matter of incorrect facts. A person who says what he does not hold to be true is not making an error about the world; he is misrepresenting himself, and the Book names that act by its proper name. The punishment corresponds to the offence in the precise way the sūrah has been arranging from its opening: the liar is measured against the truth he covered.

**Illness Named So That It Can Be Treated**

The Qur'an does not describe spiritual illness only to condemn it. Other passages use medical vocabulary for revelation itself: *“O humanity! Indeed, there has come to you a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers”* (10:57), and *“We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers”* (17:82). The Book that diagnoses the disease also presents itself as its cure.

Read together, the diagnosis in al-Baqarah and the healing announced elsewhere belong to one argument. Sickness in the heart is treatable while the person still perceives it, which is why the sūrah's refrain about awareness — repeated at the close of three consecutive portraits — carries such weight. The verse states that a condition exists and grows; it does not state that the growth is beyond interruption.

**The Order in Which the Sūrah Tells the Story**

The sequence from verse 8 to verse 10 narrates a decline in three steps. A claim is made and denied; an attempt at deception is described and reversed; then the condition that produced both is named and its direction established. The Book begins with what the hypocrites say, moves to what they do, and only then states what they are.

That order is a rhetorical strategy as much as a diagnosis. The reader of the sūrah meets the people before the disease, and the portrait is recognisable from behaviour that anyone can observe rather than from a condition that only God can inspect. By the time the illness is named, the evidence has already been laid out, and the punishment announced in the last line reads as the natural end of what the reader has just been shown.

**A Description Written for the Community That Reads It**

The portrait of the hypocrites serves the community as much as it serves the people described. A body that cannot name a disease cannot decide how to treat it, whether with argument, patience or distance. The sūrah names the condition, traces its growth and states its price, and it does all of this at the head of a book of law.

The sequence is worth noting in a sūrah that runs to 286 verses. The longest chapter of the Qur'an teaches its readers to recognise a divided heart before it begins to legislate for the community that contains one. Everything that follows — the rules on marriage, debts, fasting, warfare and inheritance — will be administered by people whose inner condition the Book has just taught everyone else to identify.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:11

> When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Word for Damage and the Word Set Against It**

*Fasād* names the ruin of something that was sound: the spoiling of land, the breakdown of an arrangement, the corruption of a community. Its opposite in the Qur'an is *iṣlāḥ*, the act of setting something right, and the Book uses the pair as moral opposites throughout. *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people's hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return to the ˹Right Path˺.”* (30:41).

The same pair appears in a warning aimed specifically at the people under discussion: *“Now if you ˹hypocrites˺ turn away, perhaps you would then spread corruption throughout the land and sever your ˹ties of˺ kinship!”* (47:22). The Book also names the activity as a standing characteristic rather than an accident: *“they strive to spread corruption in the land. And Allah does not like corruptors.”* (5:64). The command in this verse is not a general appeal to good behaviour. It forbids specific damage that the Qur'an expects from this group.

**The One Who Rebukes Is Left Unnamed**

The verse says *when they are told* without saying by whom. Commentators offered several candidates: the Prophet ﷺ, the believers, or any person who suffers from the damage and speaks up against it. Al-Rāzī noted the openness and treated it as an extension of the verse's reach, since a rebuke can come from many mouths and still carry the same content.

The device also keeps the verse's focus on the reply. The Book is not reporting a particular conversation; it is documenting a reflex. Wherever the warning comes from, the answer is the same, and the sameness is the point. The verse reads like a law of group behaviour: a rebuke that names the damage, and a defence that renames it.

**"We Are Only Peace-Makers"**

The noun *muṣliḥūn* describes people who set things right, and *innamā*, rendered *we are only*, restricts the claim to that role alone. The speakers do not deny that something is in dispute. They claim to be the ones repairing it. Their answer concedes the need for repair while placing themselves on the side that supplies it, and the move is familiar in any community where factions form: the mediator's position is the most respectable place to stand.

What the verse exposes is the difference between a role and a result. The Book does not question their intention; it questions the outcome, and it does so in the next verse with a verdict rather than an argument. A person can sincerely believe he is holding a community together while the activity he calls mediation is the thing pulling it apart, and the sūrah gives that possibility a name.

**Corruption as a Public Condition**

In the Qur'an, *fasād* is often a matter of the land and of the community rather than of private conduct. The verse at 30:41 links it to what people's hands have earned and to the ecological damage the expression describes; 5:64 links it to hostility that continues *“until the Day of Judgment”*; 47:22 joins it to the severing of kinship ties. Contemporary readers have applied the term to the destruction of the environment, and the application follows the vocabulary rather than departing from it.

Applied to the hypocrites of Madinah, the same word covers the work of men who carried messages between the city and its enemies, discouraged the community at moments of danger, and profited from every division. None of that activity looks like corruption to the person performing it. It looks like prudence, and the difference between prudence and corruption is precisely what the verse's reply is unable to see.

**A Report About a Later People**

Al-Ṭabarī records a statement attributed to Salmān al-Fārsī that the people described in these verses had not yet appeared when the verses were revealed. The commentators accepted the report, and their acceptance shows how they understood the passage: as a description of a recurring type rather than a snapshot of a few individuals in Madinah.

The implication is uncomfortable and deliberate. A verse that can be fulfilled by later generations cannot be filed away as history, and the traits it names are not the property of one faction in one city. The Book's description of a community's inner corrosion is written so that any community that reproduces the conditions can find itself inside the description.

**What a Person Thinks He Is Doing**

The verse sets a person's account of his own conduct against the effect of that conduct, and it refuses to treat the account as evidence. That refusal is the epistemological claim at the centre of the sūrah's portrait of the hypocrites. The Book is not describing villains who know themselves to be villains; it is describing people whose self-image and whose impact have come apart.

The reply *we are only peace-makers* is stated as a quotation, which means the Qur'an preserves the voice of the defence and places the verdict elsewhere. In the next verse the verdict arrives in a single clause, and the reader who has followed the argument has already been shown what it rests on. The measure is not what a person claims to be doing but what is done.

**A Prohibition Still Addressed to Its Hearers**

The command in this verse is phrased as a prohibition with continuous force: stop doing the thing you are doing. The Book does not address the hypocrites as an alien party to be expelled, and it does not treat the damage they cause as beyond repair. They are told, which means they are still being spoken to, and the address is preserved inside a portrait written mainly for the believers.

That double audience explains the tone of the passage. A revelation that had finished with these people would not need to argue with them, and it would not need to report their replies at such length. The sūrah keeps their words on the page because the warning is still being issued, and because a community that reads the exchange learns to hear the same reply in its own mouth.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:12

> Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verdict Stated as a Definition**

The Arabic opens with an attention particle, rendered *indeed*, then a demonstrative pronoun, *it is they*, and then a definite predicate: *the corruptors*. In Arabic, a sentence built from a demonstrative and a definite predicate does not list a quality among others; it identifies a category. The verse is not saying that these people also cause damage. It is saying that the damage is their defining activity.

The same construction has already been used twice in the sūrah, once for the guided and once for those who fail to perceive. The Book's grammar is symmetrical in this way: it uses identical formulas for the two ends of the moral scale, and the reader who has noticed the pattern from the beginning of the sūrah is being asked to place each portrait accurately. Verse 12 takes the phrase the hypocrites applied to themselves and moves it to the other column.

**Why the Participle Matters**

The word *mufsidūn* is an active participle, naming the ones who produce the corruption rather than the ones affected by it or associated with it. This is stronger than saying corruption occurs in their vicinity, and it distributes responsibility for the damage in a particular way: those who do the work carry the name, whatever their stated purpose.

The Qur'an's other declarations on the subject use the same noun in the same sense. At 2:27 it describes people who break the covenant of Allah and *“spread corruption in the land”*; at 13:25 the same conduct is attributed to those who sever what God has joined. In each case the participle is attached to conduct that can be observed, and the verse in al-Baqarah attaches it to a group whose conduct has just been described in detail.

**The Refrain About Perceiving**

The last clause repeats a phrase from the ninth verse, where the same words were used of the same people after their attempt at deception. The repetition inside four verses is a structural signal. The sūrah is telling its readers something about the hypocrites that the hypocrites do not know about themselves, and it repeats the fact so that nobody mistakes it for an incidental comment.

The Book uses the vocabulary of perception for this group rather than the vocabulary of ignorance, and the distinction is worth keeping. The person described in this verse has not failed to gather information; he has lost the capacity to judge what he has. Sūrah 7 puts the same principle in a sentence the Book offers as a general rule about human beings, that the blindness which matters is not the blindness of eyes but of the hearts that understand.

**Corruption Carried Out in Good Conscience**

The most unsettling feature of the portrait is that the people it describes do not consider themselves corrupt. Earlier in the sūrah they deny the charge in the language of service, presenting themselves as the ones repairing the damage. The verse's verdict and their self-assessment cannot both stand, and the Book tells the reader which one to hold.

The Qur'an treats this gap as typical rather than exotic. Sūrah 18 sets the truth-seeker beside a man whose garden is destroyed while he believed his position secure, and 47:22 warns the very group in question that their political choices would end in the spread of corruption and the severing of kinship. The Book's moral instruction repeatedly warns that the measure of an act is not the actor's satisfaction with it.

**Neutrality That Produces Wreckage**

Read with the city's history in mind, the verse describes a recognizable political type. The hypocrites of Madinah presented themselves as the party of compromise between a community and its enemies, and the sūrah accepts neither the compromise nor the description. A position can be held in the middle and still produce damage at both ends, and it can be advertised as the only reasonable place to stand at the very moment when the damage is greatest.

The verse's last clause accounts for why such a person cannot be warned by pointing at the wreckage. The wreckage is interpreted as the cost of everybody else's intransigence. What cannot be seen from inside that position is the contribution of the person holding it, and the Book states that the failure belongs to perception rather than to the facts.

**A Sentence Without Qualifiers**

The verse does not say that they are among the corruptors, or that they have begun to corrupt, or that they corrupt when provoked. It states an identity, and it declines to soften the sentence with an explanation. The Book's verdicts on the two groups at the head of the sūrah share this quality: the guided are the guided, and the corruptors are the corruptors, and the distinction is drawn by God.

That absence of qualifiers is what makes the verse a test rather than a description of somebody else. A reader who finishes it and finds the whole sentence pointed outward has applied it to a class of people he is pleased not to belong to. The Book's next line turns the same measure onto the reader from another angle, asking what it means to believe at all when belief has become something other people do.

**A Verdict the Community Cannot Enforce**

Nothing in this verse authorises its readers to act. The sentence states a fact about God's judgement, and the sūrah supplies no procedure by which a community could identify the people it names. The Book elsewhere directs its followers to leave the inner question alone and to answer insults with better conduct, and it never issues a list of suspects for the community to police.

What the verse supplies is a standard rather than an instrument. A reader may use it to measure a claim he is tempted to make about himself, and he cannot use it to settle the condition of a neighbour who gave him no evidence beyond an irritating opinion. The verdict belongs to the one who knows what hearts contain, and the verse's final clause, that they fail to perceive it, is the reason the question cannot be settled from outside.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:13

> And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Faith Given a Public Shape**

The command in this verse names a standard rather than a content. The hypocrites are told to believe as the people believe, and the commentators took *al-nās*, the people, to mean the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, whose faith had a visible and shared form. The Qur'an does not treat belief as an inner state that each person is free to compose for himself; it treats it as a transmitted practice with a public shape.

That understanding fits the Book's habit of addressing faith in the plural. The prayer of the believers speaks in the first person plural, the community is addressed as one body, and the revelation is described as a guide for a people rather than for isolated individuals. The command in this verse is therefore not conformity for its own sake. It is an instruction to enter a practice that already exists, since the alternative on offer is not a private faith but no faith at all.

**The Insult and Its Return**

The reply uses one word: *sufahāʾ*, rendered here as fools. The Arabic noun describes the person whose judgement is unsound, whose understanding of consequences is light. The hypocrite uses it as a status weapon, implying that the believers' acceptance of a man of their own city was naive. The verse then takes the word and reassigns it: *it is they who are fools*.

The same term is used twice more in the sūrah, each time by the Qur'an for the people who sneered at the believers. At 2:142 the Book anticipates the objection to the change of prayer direction by saying that *the foolish among the people* will ask about it. At 2:130 the criterion is stated outright: *“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool!”* (2:130) In every case the word is applied to a refusal, not to an intellectual limit.

**Foolishness as a Moral Word**

In the Qur'an's usage, a fool is not stupidity's technical name. He is a person who has misvalued something: who trades an enduring good for a passing advantage, or smothers what he already knows to be true. That is why the Book can apply the word to the learned and the powerful as easily as to the simple, and why the people mocked in Mecca and Madinah were mostly without rank, whose faith had cost them a great deal.

The criterion behind the word is a practical one, as 2:130 implies: the fool is the one who rejects a way he has already heard about. Knowledge, in this Book, is measured by what a person does with what has reached him, and honesty about the limits of one's own position is part of it. The reply in this verse is that rare thing, a self-description by the person the Qur'an has already described, and the two accounts agree less than the speaker thinks.

**Mockery as a Form of Status**

The reply is aimed at an audience, not at the person giving the command. Calling a group foolish is a way of claiming the superior position in a conversation, and in a city where status had recently been redistributed, the claim carried material weight. The Companions had lost the standing they once held in the Quraysh's hierarchy, and attachment to them brought no rank.

The Qur'an answers the insult with an inversion rather than a defence. It does not argue that the believers were intelligent, and it does not list their merits; it assigns the word they used to the people who used it. The sūrah's method is consistent throughout its portrait of this group: their own vocabulary is taken from them and returned in the correct arrangement.

**The Three Endings and Their Precise Verbs**

Three consecutive portraits close with the same kind of comment: the deceivers *fail to perceive it* (2:9), the corruptors *fail to perceive it* (2:12), and the fools *do not know* (2:13). The Book uses its verbs of cognition carefully. Perception concerns noticing what is in front of a person; knowledge concerns the settled understanding of it. The first failure is a problem of attention, and the second is a problem of what attention has been used to build.

The three endings also track a decline. The claim made in 2:8 was about what the speakers believed; the deception in 2:9 was an attempt to manage the community; the charge in 2:13 is a public insult. As the conduct becomes more visible, the warnings move from a private deficiency to a public one, and the sentence that names it becomes correspondingly direct.

**When the Accusation Cannot Be Refrained**

The verse does not allow the readers of the sūrah to borrow its verdict. The word *fool* belongs to God here, and the Book's general rule about the terms refuses the community's own use of them: it never authorises its followers to dispatch their opponents' characters, and it repeatedly commands the believers to answer an insult with something better. What the verse records is a divine description of a state, not a licence for name-calling.

The distinction matters for how a person reads the sūrah. The portrait from 2:8 to 2:13 was assembled to be recognisable, and any reader may find in it something of himself. The Book's verdicts are stated so that the reader will submit to the description before he applies it, and the verse's closing clause, that they do not know, is the reason no outsider can settle the question from the outside.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:14

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Rooms, Two Confessions**

The verse puts one group of people in two settings and lets the difference between them speak. In the presence of the believers they recite the creed of the community; in the company of their own kind they withdraw it and describe the earlier performance as theatre. Nothing in the report suggests that the retraction was dragged out of them or that the first statement was sincere and the second a slip. The order is the other way round: the private confession explains the public one.

That arrangement is what separates this verse from a description of weakness. A person who fails under pressure tells one story and regrets it; the men described here keep two and choose between them by audience. The revelation records the exchange without commentary, because the two sentences placed beside each other are the commentary. What follows in the next verse supplies the verdict, and the verse itself supplies the evidence.

**Who the "Evil Associates" Are**

The Arabic word is *shayāṭīn*, the plural of *shayṭān*, and it does not always name a creature of smokeless fire. The Qur'an uses the same word for human beings who lead others into ruin: *“And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception.”* (6:112). The verse before the reader follows that usage, and the men to whom these hypocrites speak are their own allies and leaders.

Reading the word this way removes a difficulty. If the verse placed the hypocrites in conversation with unseen devils, the scene would describe something the community could never observe; if it places them with human confidants, the whole report becomes the kind of thing witnesses would bring back. The Qur'an is describing a conversation held in a room, and it names the men in that room by their function rather than their species.

**Them Mocking Whom, and What They Were Doing**

Their own words specify the object of the mockery. The phrase *we were only mocking* comes after a declaration of solidarity with the other side, so the thing mocked is the faith they had just professed to the believers. The Qur'an preserves the word in their own mouths and does not soften it into a misunderstanding.
