A later sūrah gives the same men the same activity and shows them unsettled by the risk: *“The hypocrites fear that a sûrah should be revealed about them, exposing what is in their hearts. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Keep mocking! Allah will definitely bring to light what you fear.’”* (9:64).

The Book then treats mockery of the believers as mockery directed higher. The same chapter records a taunt aimed at those who gave charity in small amounts and answers it as a financial matter between the mocker and God: *“Allah will throw their mockery back at them, and they will suffer a painful punishment.”* (9:79). Derision in this Book is never a private amusement. It is a position taken on a question that does not belong to the person taking it.

**Loyalty Measured by the Private Sentence**

The verse establishes a criterion, and the criterion is not what a person announces where he is heard. Loyalty is measured by what is said where no one is watching, because the private room is where a person invests nothing and risks nothing. Sūrah 63 describes men who used their oaths as cover: *“They have made their ˹false˺ oaths as a shield, hindering ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah.”* (63:2).

The Qur'an keeps this measure for the same people in other passages: it reports prayers performed *“only to be seen by people”* (4:142), and it describes those who conceal the very knowledge they have been given. What all these portraits share is a gap between the outer and the inner man, and the gap is never detected by argument. It is detected by watching where a person does not expect to be reported on.

**Nothing Hidden From the One Who Hears Both Rooms**

The verse works because the reader has been shown both conversations, which no human observer could have. The Qur'an is not reporting a rumour that reached the Prophet ﷺ; it is making public what was said in private, and the act of publication is itself the point being made to the men involved. What they took to be the safe half of their lives is now in the Book, recited in prayer, memorised by children.

The Book states the principle elsewhere in the plainest terms: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, it is known to Allah. For He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.’”* (3:29). The sentence removes the last hiding place available to a person who divides his life into an audible half and an inaudible one, and it does so without needing to accuse anyone of anything. The two rooms in this verse are finally one room.

**Faith Reduced to a Membership Card**

What the private sentence reveals is what the public one was for. These men were not seeking guidance or appealing to God; they were managing their position in a community whose protection had become worth having and whose commitments had become inconvenient. Faith, in their hands, was a status that could be worn and removed, and the mocking tone is the sound of a man holding a position he does not believe in.

The Book answers this without inventing an inspection. It does not authorise the community to interrogate confessions or to test loyalties by force; it publishes the conversation and leaves the judgement where it belongs. The verse's function is to end the assumption that a sufficiently careful performance can be sustained indefinitely — and the sentence that follows shows what happens to the performance when its author is the one being addressed.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:15

> Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mockery Returned to Its Owners**

The sentence takes the activity described in the previous verse and answers it in kind. The Arabic verb expresses a deliberate response rather than an accident of history: the mockery does not simply rebound on its own, it is sent back by the one who was not fooled. Sūrah 9 states the same promise in the same words for a different group of mockers: *“Allah will throw their mockery back at them, and they will suffer a painful punishment.”* (9:79).

The Book repeats the phrase because the situation repeats. Whenever a community receives a revelation, there are people who treat the whole business as a performance to be managed with a smirk, and the revelation consistently tells them that the smirk is being recorded by the one who will settle accounts. The answer is not a rebuke in kind by the believers. The believers are not told to answer derision with derision; the response is reserved for God.

**When God Is Named as the One Who Mocks**

Attributing mockery to God raises an obvious difficulty, and the commentators addressed it directly. One line of explanation treats the statement as the law of recompense: the mocking returns upon the mocker as a consequence of his own act, so that God is named as the one who brings it about rather than as someone who enjoys the activity. Another line treats what God does as a state rather than a mood — the disgrace into which the mocker settles, long drawn out, which is the same thing the verse says of them in the second half.

Neither reading turns God into a participant in the world's mockery. Both treat the divine response as the precise application of a correspondence that runs through the Book: as a person treats the truth, so the truth treats him. The verse's vocabulary is chosen to make the symmetry exact, and the symmetry is the sentence.

**The Law of Correspondence in the Book**

The Qur'an states this law repeatedly, and always in the language of the opponent's own behaviour. Of the hypocrites who plotted while pretending to pray: *“Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them.”* (4:142). Of those who planned against a prophet: *“And the disbelievers made a plan ˹against Jesus˺, but Allah also planned —and Allah is the best of planners.”* (3:54). Of a company that plotted in secret: *“And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware.”* (27:50).

Each sentence takes a verb that describes the plotters' activity and applies it to God with a difference. The human verb names a finite, contingent attempt; the divine counterpart names an outcome no human being can arrange or foresee. The mockery in this verse follows the same pattern. What returns to the mocker is not an insult. It is a state of affairs he cannot manage, arriving on a schedule he does not control.

**Wandering Blindly, and the Vocabulary of Drift**

The second half of the verse names the condition into which these people settle: left to wander in their excess. The Arabic verb *yaʿmahūn* comes from a root denoting blindness and confusion, and it describes a person who moves without being able to orient himself. The Qur'an uses the same vocabulary for the same phenomenon elsewhere. One passage states the rule in general terms: *“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance.”* (6:110).

The Book's narrative of refusal regularly ends not with a blow but with a stated inability to find the way. The point of the vocabulary is that the punishment begins inside the person's own perception. He is not stopped by a wall; he is released into a landscape where every path looks usable and none arrives, and nothing he does in that landscape will correct his sense of direction.

**Ṭughyān: Going Beyond the Limit**

The word rendered defiance, *ṭughyān*, describes the crossing of a boundary, and the Book attaches it to individuals and to regimes that overran the limits set for them. Pharaoh is named with it as a warning delivered by Moses: *“Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all limits˺.”* (20:24). The sūrah that will contain this verse's portrait is still in its opening pages, and the word chosen for the hypocrite is the word the Qur'an uses for tyrants.

The choice ties the small deception to a large category. What the men in the two rooms were doing looked like social management rather than tyranny, but the Book classifies it as trespass, because the boundary they crossed was the boundary of honesty about the revelation and their own position toward it. The verse then places them in a condition where the trespass itself becomes their horizon.

**Punishment That Adds Nothing to the Crime**

The verse describes a penalty that can be mistaken for a lack of one. The men are not struck; they are let alone, with their own directionlessness as their company. The Book has already stated a similar sentence over the people whose hearts were sealed, and it states the principle again in this verse: the answer to a chosen blindness is deepened blindness, and the increase of the condition is the punishment.

Read with the mockery that provoked it, the sentence is exact. The mocker measured the faith of others by nothing and treated it as an amusement. He is now measured by nothing in return, and left to wander in a space where no measurement can correct him. The verse gives no timetable, and it does not say how long the wandering lasts. It says only where the road is heading, and leaves the men described here to consider it.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:16

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Transaction Described in Commercial Terms**

The verse converts a spiritual collapse into a business deal, and it uses the vocabulary of the market deliberately. Arabic *ishtarā* means to buy, and the sentence says they acquired misguidance by parting with guidance, with the price named first in the reader's mind because it is the thing that was given away. The Qur'an returns to this metaphor repeatedly in this sūrah and outside it, always with the same accounting: *“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire!”* (2:175), and *“Those who trade belief for disbelief will never harm Allah in the least, and they will suffer a painful punishment.”* (3:177).

The metaphor has a fixed shape across those verses. One side of the exchange is always a reality that guides; the other side is a state that ruins. Nobody is described as accidentally ending up on the wrong side of the bargain, and the transaction is always the same transaction.

**Which Direction the Bargain Runs**

Some commentators read the verb as preferring rather than purchasing, since Arabic uses the root that way in a verse about a people who chose their own blindness: *“they preferred blindness to guidance”* (41:17). Read that way, the verse describes a selection rather than an exchange, and the commercial language that follows is a way of showing what the selection cost. The two readings arrive at the same place, and the mention of trade in the very next clause supports the second: whether the man bought ruin or chose it, the ledger records a loss.

What the difference in reading affects is the question of what a person holds to begin with. Guidance in the Qur'an is given before it is traded: the sūrah has already called itself a guide and described those who accept it, and the audience for this verse is made up of people who had access to what they abandoned. The bargain is described as a sale of something the seller possessed, not of something he never had.

**Profit and Loss as the Book's Accountancy**

The verse closes the deal with a verdict drawn from trade: the transaction brought no profit. The Book keeps a running account of this kind, and it never leaves the arithmetic ambiguous. Those who break the covenant after it has been affirmed *“are the ˹true˺ losers”* (2:27), and the same sūrah warns that anyone diverted from the remembrance of God by wealth or children *“it is they who are the ˹true˺ losers”* (63:9).

The word for profit here is the ordinary word for commercial gain, and its absence is stated as a fact about the outcome rather than as a moral comment. A merchant who sells an asset for nothing and calls it a strategy has not made a mistake about morality; he has made a mistake about arithmetic. The verse treats the spiritual case as the same kind of error, and it states the loss in the plainest available language.

**Guidance Held in Trust, Not Owned**

The metaphor also decides how guidance should be understood. If guidance were a possession, selling it would be a straightforward exercise of ownership; the verse's tone suggests something closer to betrayal, and the rest of the Book supports that tone. Guidance is granted, and what is granted can be refused, neglected or covered over, but the refusal does not make the grant into private property.

The sūrah's own description of the guided supports this. They are described as guided *by their Lord*, and the response of the human being is described as acceptance and practice. Nobody in these verses produces his own guidance and then trades it away. The men in this verse were members of a community that had received a message, and what they sold was their position inside it.

**A Verdict That Leaves Nothing to Negotiate**

The second half of the sentence is emphatic in the way the Book reserves for final statements: *it is they* who failed, and *it is they* who are not guided. The construction repeats the pattern used earlier for the guided and later for the corruptors, and it places this verse in a series. The sūrah is assigning identities, and it does so with the same grammatical instrument for every group it describes.

The verdict does not say they are being punished, and it does not say their state is permanent. It says the trade produced nothing and that its author did not arrive. The Book elsewhere describes people who returned from such a position, which means the sentence is a description of the condition rather than a lock on it. What the verse establishes is where the road they chose actually goes, and it uses the plainest available measure — the balance sheet — to say so.

**Why the Hypocrite Is Described as a Trader**

The image fits the men described in the preceding verses precisely. A trader wants the value of a good while keeping the capital that could be put at risk, and the hypocrite wants the standing that comes with faith while keeping himself free of its obligations. He performs the profession, keeps the protection and the social position it brings, and preserves his connections to the other side against the day fortunes turn.

The Qur'an calls that position a losing trade, and the loss it names is measured in the thing that was surrendered. What the buyer receives in exchange is the absence of the guidance he wanted to keep available as an option. The verse states that the option has been exercised and the asset is gone, and the last two words of the sentence record the result without a single word of encouragement or reproach.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:17

> Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Parable Stated as Their Own Description**

The sentence opens with the possessive: *their* example. The Book is not offering an illustration that happens to resemble these men; it is naming the shape of their situation. Parables in the Qur'an work this way throughout the sūrah, and the next verses carry two of them, so that the portrait of the hypocrites ends in images rather than in verdicts. The images are meant to be remembered, and the men described in them are meant to recognise themselves.

What makes a parable useful here is the limit of plain description. The preceding verses have told the reader what these people say in two different rooms and what they lost in the exchange. What they cannot be told directly is what their condition feels like from the inside, and the two likenesses in this passage supply that. The first describes what happens to light a man has just made.

**One Kindles the Fire, and Then It Is Not His**

The grammar shifts inside the sentence: a single person lights the flame, and then the light that is removed belongs to a plural. The kindling was one act, and the loss is shared, which fits a passage addressed to a group whose members behave identically. Each man in the story is the one who struck the match, and every one of them loses the same thing.

That structure also fixes the asymmetry the sūrah has been building. The human being in this parable has real power to act; he can bring a fire into being. What he cannot do is retain the light it produces, because the ownership of light in this Book belongs somewhere else. The Book's account of human capacity repeatedly draws the same line: action is granted, results are not, and the gap between the two is where its moral teaching lives.

**What the Fire Was Lit For**

Al-Ṭabarī records the reading that the light here is the declaration of faith and the protection it brings, since a person's public profession of Islam in the new community of Madinah granted him the standing to eat, marry, inherit and travel under the community's safeguard. That account fits the men described in the previous verses precisely. They had recited the profession, and they had collected everything that came with it.

On that reading the parable is exact about what was lost. The fire was not imaginary and the light was not fake; the man enjoyed both while they lasted, and the hypocrisy consisted in pretending the flame was his. Which is why the loss arrives at a point he cannot anticipate or postpone. The Book makes the same point about the value of that social light elsewhere, in the scene where the hypocrites discover that their illumination has failed: *“On that Day hypocrite men and women will beg the believers, ‘Wait for us so that we may have some of your light.’”* (57:13).

**Light as a Category the Book Returns To**

The Qur'an uses light for guidance, revelation, life and the presence of God, and it never treats illumination as a metaphor with no content. The most concentrated statement is the verse of light: *“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. His light is like a niche in which there is a lamp, the lamp is in a crystal, the crystal is like a shining star”* (24:35), which ends by saying that God guides whom He wills to His light and sets forth parables for humanity.

Against that passage the Book sets the darkness that follows its removal: *“Or ˹their deeds are˺ like the darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves upon waves, topped by ˹dark˺ clouds. Darkness upon darkness! If one stretches out their hand, they can hardly see it. And whoever Allah does not bless with light will have no light!”* (24:40). The image in this verse belongs to that family of passages, and it ends with the same finality. The last sentence of the parable gives no indication that the man has a second match.

**Complete Darkness, and the Loss of Bearings**

The verse ends with the phrase *unable to see*, and it has already said that the darkness is complete. The two clauses work together: nothing in the surroundings is lit, and the faculty that could have compensated for the lack of light has also gone dark. A person in that condition has not merely lost a convenience; he has lost the means of deciding which direction is forward.

That is the second time in this opening passage that the Book has described people as unable to locate the road. The sentence passed on the rejecters earlier left them wandering blindly in their excess, and the sentence here leaves these men standing in the dark. The vocabulary is the Book's ordinary way of describing a spiritual condition: not a stated punishment that arrives from outside, but a capacity quietly removed, with the person still moving.

**Kindling Without Ownership**

The parable states a relation between effort and outcome that runs through the whole sūrah. The man had initiative, and he used it; what he lacked was the authority to keep what his initiative produced. Later in the same chapter the Book will put a sharper edge on the same lesson when it tells the believers that the light they will carry on the day of accounting is theirs to ask for but not to manufacture: *“Our Lord! Perfect our light for us, and forgive us.”* (66:8).

Read that way, the fire is a warning to anyone who believes his standing rests on a light he himself kindled. The flame in the parable is real, and it is not enough, because the thing that matters in this Book is not whether a person can make light but whether he is among those to whom light is given and kept.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:18

> They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Faculties Named in One Beat**

The Arabic of this verse is a short, closed sequence of three adjectives with the same ending: *ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun*. Recited aloud, the repetition of the sound performs the condition it describes, and the commentators remarked on it. The Book is describing people who cannot take in a message, cannot answer one, and cannot see the road they are on, and it does so with three words that strike the ear like a locked door.

The triad is not unique to this sūrah. The Qur'an returns to it when it describes people dragged into judgement: *“And We will drag them on their faces on the Day of Judgment—deaf, dumb, and blind.”* (17:97). What in this verse is a condition of the mind becomes there a condition of the body, and the correspondence is deliberate. The Book's account of the afterlife keeps matching the shape of the life that preceded it.

**Deaf to What Was Actually Said**

Deafness in the Qur'an is not a physical handicap and the Book is careful about its object. People described this way have heard the recitation, understood the argument and watched the signs; what has closed is their responsiveness. Another verse gives both halves of the condition in one sentence: *“Those who deny Our signs are ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb—lost in darkness.”* (6:39). The translation adds the word wilfully, and the addition reflects a pattern in the Book, where this deafness is chosen rather than suffered.

The mechanism is described elsewhere: *“There are some of them who ˹pretend to˺ listen to your recitation ˹of the Quran˺, but We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears.”* (6:25). The verse in al-Baqarah states the resulting condition without the process. It does not say the hearing was blocked at some moment; it says these people are deaf, and the Book's earlier statement of the same fact explains how the state came about.

**Mute When the Truth Is at Stake**

Muteness is the strangest of the three, because the men described in this sūrah talk a great deal. They produce confessions in public, retractions in private, and accusations of foolishness against the believers. Their mouths are working; what has failed is their capacity to say something true about the matter that counts, and the contrast is the point.

The Book's portrait of honest speech elsewhere confirms what muteness here must mean. A believer asks God for forgiveness and mercy with the same organ the hypocrite uses to manage his position, and another verse records the speech of a servant who admits a wrong with no hedging: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves.”* (7:23). Speech, on this reading, is the faculty by which a person aligns himself with reality, and it can be lost while the voice continues to work perfectly.

**Blind While the Eyes Function**

The third adjective completes the set, and the Book is explicit that the blindness in question is not of the eye. A verse in the pilgrimage passage makes the distinction a general principle: *“Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind.”* (22:46). The heart in the Qur'an is the organ of understanding and decision; when it is described as blind, the person is still seeing the world and no longer seeing what it means.

The same portrait appears with the consequences spelled out: *“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with.”* (7:179). That verse ends by comparing its subjects to cattle and then placing them below that comparison. The sūrah here uses the shorter form, and by the time the reader reaches the final clause, the three deficits have been gathered into one fact about movement.

**A Verdict About Return, Not About Rescue**

The sentence closes with the result: they will not return. The verb describes going back to a place a person has left, and its object in the Book is nearly always guidance itself. The point being made is directional. These people are not described as unable to hear a fresh argument or as incapable of receiving a new sign; they are described as unable to come back to what they already had and abandoned.

That distinction matters for how the verse is read beside the sūrah's other verdicts. It does not say their condition cannot be changed by God; the Book elsewhere states plainly that *“the Most Compassionate will allow them plenty of time”* (19:75) and that forgiveness is available to those who turn. What it says is that the men being described are no longer travelling in that direction. The faculty that would have to do the returning is the one that has gone dark.

**The Portrait Completed by Subtraction**

The two parables in this passage work by taking things away. The fire is lit and the light removed; the faculties are named and each one is reported lost. Nothing in the sequence adds to the people described; everything subtracts from them, and the subtraction is what makes the portrait coherent. The men who carried two versions of their faith into two different rooms end up with no capacity to tell which version is true.

The Book leaves the sentence where it stands. No explanation follows, no appeal is made, and the next verse introduces a different scene with the same subjects caught in a storm. What the reader carries forward from this line is the arithmetic: a person can hear everything and end up deaf, say everything and end up mute, look directly at the road and end up blind.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:19

> Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Likeness Introduced by a Choice of Word**

The verse begins with the Arabic *aw*, or, which marks an alternative rather than a new topic. The Book's custom is to place two comparisons where one would do, and the two here describe the same people under different pressures. The first likeness showed a light withdrawn; this one shows a storm that will not stop, and the men caught under it are handling it by covering their ears.

The change of scene is a change of problem. In the first parable the question was what the man had and lost. In the second, the question is what a person does when the sky is loud, the ground is dark, and something dangerous is suddenly visible in flashes. Both images come from a landscape where rain is an event and lightning is a threat, and both take the weather seriously as a way of describing spiritual exposure.

**The Storm and Each of Its Elements**

The Arabic word rendered rainstorm, *ṣayyib*, names a cloud heavy with rain, and the verse then lists its contents: darkness, thunder, lightning. Rain that arrives in the desert is a gift, and this verse turns the gift into the setting of a crisis, because the men in it experience the sky only as noise and danger. The Book elsewhere describes the same sky in terms of its beauty and mercy: *“Have they not then looked at the sky above them: how We built it and adorned it ˹with stars˺, leaving it flawless?”* (50:6).

The elements are not decorative. Thunder and lightning appear together in the Qur'an as signs that produce fear in the observer: *“He is the One Who shows you lightning, inspiring ˹you with˺ hope and fear, and produces heavy clouds.”* (13:12), and the verse that follows reports that the thunder itself glorifies God's praises along with the angels (13:13). Two verses later in this sūrah, the same flash is described as nearly destroying the eyesight of the men who depend on it (2:20), and elsewhere as almost taking away eyes: *“The flash of the clouds' lightning nearly takes away eyesight.”* (24:43).

**Fingers in the Ears at Every Clap**

The gesture is described with an unusual amount of physical detail: the fingers are pressed into the ears, and they are pressed at each thunderclap rather than once for the duration of the storm. The Book is showing men reacting repeatedly, and the repetition is the point — a person who has decided how to handle a danger has to keep on handling it.

What the gesture states is the absence of any other response. The men do not flee, argue with the sky or help each other; they stop their ears and wait for the sound to pass. The Qur'an's portraits of the hypocrites elsewhere show the same pattern of minimal self-protection, and one verse says it plainly: *“The hypocrites, both men and women, are all alike: they encourage what is evil, forbid what is good, and withhold ˹what is in˺ their hands.”* (9:67). The detail of the fingers fits a people whose whole method is damage limitation.

**Fearing Death in a Storm**

The verse names the motive: fear of death. That phrase is what lifts the description out of the weather and into the sūrah's argument. What these men are protecting is their lives, and the storm is only the occasion on which that priority becomes visible. Given a threat to their safety, they shut out the thing they cannot control and keep their attention on what they can.

The Book treats fear of death as a diagnostic. It tells the Prophet that among these people he will find those who cling to life, and it records the same priority in their refusal to risk anything for the community they publicly belong to. The storm in the parable is a small laboratory: it applies pressure for a few minutes and shows what a man's loyalty is anchored to. Nothing about the sky is unusual, and nothing about the response would surprise anyone who had watched these men in a week of ordinary politics.

**Encompassed, Which Leaves No Route Out**

The verse closes on God: He encompasses the disbelievers. The Arabic participle describes a circle drawn completely around something, so that no gap remains on any side. The Book uses the same root for the divine throne: *“His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him.”* (2:255), and it uses it when it tells the Prophet that the community's enemies cannot outmanoeuvre the one who holds the whole field in view.

That closing clause is what the men in the story do not know. They are concentrating on the two ways the weather can hurt them, hearing and sight, and the sentence states that neither of those is the real situation. The Book's answer to their panic is not reassurance about the storm; it is the information that they were never outside the circle to begin with, and that the one who drew it is measuring the same thunder and the same darkness against them.

**What the Second Parable Adds**

The first likeness took a man's light away, and the second leaves its subjects in the dark with the lights still flashing. In the first, the crisis is that something has been removed; here the crisis is that something keeps arriving and cannot be absorbed. Taken together, the two parables describe the same spiritual position from two sides, and the sūrah's portrait of hypocrisy closes with an image of people whose environment is beyond their control and who have no plan except to cover their ears.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:20

> It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Sight Nearly Snatched by the Thing That Lights the Road**

The verse keeps its subjects under the same sky as the previous one and changes the problem. What threatens them now is the flash itself, bright enough to be felt as an assault on the eyes. The Arabic phrasing describes a near-event: the lightning almost takes the sight it is being used to see by, so that the very illumination these men depend on is also the danger they cannot escape.

That double-edged quality is the point of the image. Guidance in this Book lights the road, and it also exposes what is on it, which means the same revelation that shows a man where to walk also shows him what he would rather not have seen. The men described here want the benefit of the light without the discomfort of what it reveals, and the flash that helps them is nearly the thing that blinds them.

**Walking Only While the Flash Lasts**

The second clause reports a pattern of movement tied entirely to conditions: whenever the light is on, they walk. They are not described as running from the storm, sheltering, or turning back; they advance while the way is visible and only for as long as visibility lasts. The Book uses the same picture for people whose commitment follows their convenience rather than preceding it.

The Qur'an's portrait of this group elsewhere records the same timing. It reports that when they stand for prayer they perform it *“half-heartedly only to be seen by people—hardly remembering Allah at all”* (4:142). The obedience is real and it is intermittent, and its boundaries are set by what the situation rewards. In the parable the intermittency is written into the weather itself: the men do not choose the rhythm they live by, and they follow it exactly.

**Standing Still When the Light Goes**

The third movement is a halt. When the darkness covers them, they stand; the Arabic verb describes a person planted in place, making no progress in either direction. The failure is not rebellion but paralysis, and the verse gives it the same amount of attention as the walking, because in this Book a man who never moves is as lost as a man who moves on the wrong road.

The imagery here connects back to the earlier verdict that the people under discussion will not return to the right path. Standing still is the physical equivalent of that sentence: a person who has left the road, cannot see it, and will not go looking. Nothing in the verse suggests that these men are waiting for guidance. They have arranged their lives so that faith is a resource drawn upon when it is visible and dispensed with when it is not.

**The Unfulfilled "If God Had Willed"**

The sentence that follows ends the storm with a statement about what did not happen: if God had willed, their hearing and sight would have gone. The Book uses this construction repeatedly, and its function is to place what a person keeps in the same category as what he has already lost, both being grants held at the discretion of the one who gave them.

A verse in Sūrah al-Anʿām states the same conditional as a question put to the deniers: *“Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight, or seal your hearts—who else other than Allah could restore it?”* (6:46). The reminder in both places is about ownership rather than punishment. The faculties named in this parable, hearing and sight, are the same ones that were reported lost in the previous verse, so that the conditional in this verse touches something the reader has just watched happen to somebody else.

**The Closing Name: Capable of Everything**

The verse ends with *qadīr*, rendered here as Most Capable. The word is built on the root of measuring and determining, and it names a power that operates by design rather than by impulse. Spoken at the end of a passage about light granted and withdrawn, the name explains the pattern rather than softening it.

The Book puts the same name where it wants the reader to consider the scale of what can be granted or withheld: *“Blessed is the One in Whose Hands rests all authority. And He is Most Capable of everything”* (67:1), and again at the end of a passage about the creation of the human being out of clay and the breathing of a spirit into him (32:9-30). In this verse the name covers both halves of what the storm has already shown: the power that sustains the sight of a man walking by a flash, and the power that could end it between two steps.

**Two Parables That Leave the Same Impression**

The first likeness ended with a man in complete darkness, and the second ends with men who cannot keep their footing when the light goes. Neither closes with a punishment described in detail; both close with the position of the people concerned, which is why each is remembered as a picture rather than an argument. The Book has been unusually patient with its portrait of these men, giving them two parables in addition to the report of what they say in private, and the images make the same point twice so that it cannot be missed.

What the images have in common is a dependence on light that the men themselves cannot secure. Their walking, their standing and their blindness are all decided by a flash that arrives when it will. The rest of the sūrah moves away from these men to address everyone in the city, and the address begins with a call that puts their situation in a single sentence.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:21

> O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Call That Addresses Everyone Present**

For the first time in this sūrah the Book speaks to the whole of humanity rather than describing a group. The Arabic address, *yā ayyuhā al-nās*, gathers everyone in hearing distance: the believers whose marks were listed at the beginning, the rejecters whose hearts were sealed, the men of the two rooms, and any reader who has recognised a fragment of himself in those portraits. After twenty verses of sorting, the text opens out and speaks to all of them.

The placement is a deliberate change of register. What precedes it is diagnosis, and what follows it is argument, and the pivot between the two is an invitation. Nobody is asked to explain his previous position first; the call arrives before any response and is addressed to the whole crowd at once. The sūrah's method here is characteristic: it identifies what is wrong with people and then speaks to them as though the identification were not the end of the matter.

**Worship Argued From Creation, Not From Threat**

The reason given for worship is the act of creation, and the Book tends to lead with this reason before any other. The Qur'an states it as a general conclusion elsewhere: *“That is Allah—your Lord! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. ˹He is˺ the Creator of all things, so worship Him ˹alone˺. And He is Maintainer of everything.”* (6:102). The command follows from a fact about origins rather than from a warning about consequences.

That ordering shapes what the verse is asking for. A demand backed by punishment produces compliance where the power is felt and silence where it is not; a demand argued from creation addresses the person's own existence, which he cannot deny having received. The Book's calls to worship return to this reasoning again and again, and they return to it in moments when the audience is least receptive, as if the argument were the point rather than the prelude.

**"Those Before You" as Part of the Evidence**

The clause about previous generations does more work than it appears to. Everyone addressed knows that he did not make himself and that the world was already furnished with occupants when he arrived, and the ancestors he can name were in the same position. The argument therefore leans on testimony the audience already accepts, and it does not require them to trust a new claim about history.

The point is pressed further elsewhere in the Book, where the audience's own admission is used against them: *“And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will definitely say, ‘Allah!’ Say, ‘Praise be to Allah!’ In fact, most of them do not know.”* (31:25). The people of the sūrah were not atheists arguing that the world had no maker. They already named God as the creator of the sky, and the verse here holds them to what their own answer implies about loyalty.

**Whose Hope Is It, Anyway**

The aim of the command is *taqwā*, and the Arabic construction *laʿallakum* attaches a hopeful outcome to God's side of the sentence. Commentators discussed the difficulty in that phrasing, since hope and anxiety are conditions of creatures, and one solution they offered was to read the hope as a promise: for God, *perhaps* means *certainly*, since nothing can obstruct what He has decided. Another was to attach the hope to the human beings who are the subject of the statement rather than to God.

Either way the sentence describes a relationship in which worship leads to a state of guarded awareness, and the Book treats that state as desirable in itself rather than as a means to some other reward. The sūrah opened by describing the Book as a guide for the mindful (2:2). The command in this verse names the same quality as the goal of worship, which ties the sūrah's first description of its readers to its first universal instruction.

**Reverence as the Fruit of Worship**

The word *taqwā* comes from a root meaning to shield and protect, and the Book treats it as a practical competence rather than a mood. The person who has it keeps watch over what he does, because he is aware of being seen; the Qur'an's portrait of such people elsewhere shows the vigilance expressed in ordinary choices: *“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets”* (2:177), after which the verse lists giving, prayer and keeping promises.

Reverence, then, is what worship produces when it is practised rather than performed. The command in this verse asks for worship and names the awareness that follows from it, which means the sentence is not a transaction in which an offering is exchanged for a benefit. It is a description of how a person changes when he directs his life toward the one who made him.

**An Open Door at the Head of the Sūrah**

The address stands directly after the Book's most severe statements about people who cannot hear, speak or see their way. Coming there, the call to humanity reads as an announcement that the diagnosis was not a sentence. The men described in the preceding parables are still in the audience, and the summons in this verse is addressed to them among everyone else, which is why the next verse continues to reason with the same audience rather than expelling it.

The Qur'an states the policy elsewhere in an instruction that governs how the message is carried: *“Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner.”* (16:125). This verse is that invitation in its shortest form. It names God as the Lord of the people being addressed, credits Him with their creation and their ancestors', and asks for one act in return.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:22

> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Earth Prepared as a Place to Live**

The verse describes the ground under its audience as something made ready rather than stumbled upon. The Arabic word rendered settlement compares the earth to a spread-out bed, and the word for the sky compares it to a structure raised overhead. Both terms are domestic: the planet is furnished for a resident, and the roof is built over him, which is a way of describing creation as hospitality rather than as spectacle.

The same picture is drawn with almost the same words later in the sūrah's own book: *“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form.”* (40:64). Elsewhere the earth is described as spread out and fitted with mountains and pathways so that its inhabitants can find their way across it: *“And We have placed firm mountains upon the earth so it does not shake with them, and made in it broad pathways so they may find their way.”* (21:31). The Book consistently presents the world's habitability as a deliberate arrangement, and it names the arranger in the first word of the sentence.

**From Sky to Fruit, in One Clause**

The verse then runs the chain of provision in a single breath: water from above, fruit from the ground, food on the table. Nothing in the chain can be produced by the people who benefit from it, and the Qur'an draws out the dependence with the same imagery elsewhere — *“He is the One Who sends down rain from the sky, from which you drink and by which plants grow for your cattle to graze. With it He produces for you ˹various˺ crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and every type of fruit”* (16:10–11). Another passage ties the gift to gratitude directly: *“It is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you.”* (14:32).

Read with the previous verse, the argument is continuous. The first sentence asked for worship on the ground of creation; this one supplies the daily evidence of the same care. The point is not that God once made the world, but that food keeps arriving in it by a chain that no human being controls, and the verse presents the ordinary meal as the standing proof of the claim.

**"Do Not Set Up Equals, While You Know"**

The prohibition comes at the end and turns the whole description into a charge. The Arabic word rendered equals, *andād*, names things placed on the same level, and the Book uses it for the idols and for anything else given the loyalty that belongs to God. The final phrase, *while you know*, is what gives the sentence its edge: it addresses people who already accept the premise of the argument.

A report in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4477, narrated from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, records that the Prophet ﷺ was asked which sin is greatest before God and answered with this very act, describing it as setting up a rival to God though He alone created you. The chapter of the collection in which that report appears carries this verse of al-Baqarah as its heading, which is why the prohibition is treated in the tradition as the sūrah's answer to the practice of associating partners with God. The phrase *while you know* excludes the excuse of ignorance, not the possibility of repentance.

**What the Equals Were, and What the Argument Said About Them**

The men being addressed in Madinah and Mecca were not claiming that their idols had built the sky. The Book states their position plainly in the previous verse's terms: they already attributed creation to God. What the idols received was the loyalty, the petition and the ritual that the argument of this verse assigns to the provider of the rain. The Book's rejoinder to that arrangement is to invite its audience to follow their own admissions to their conclusion.

The sūrah makes the same move with the images of thunder, rain and provision that the parables have just used, and it presses the point about the worthlessness of the partners in plainer language later in the chapter, where the idols are said to be unable to create even a fly (22:73) and are described as fuel for the fire that awaits those who rely on them (21:98). The logic of this verse is that everything the partners are credited with is being supplied by somebody else.

**Why the Argument Is Addressed to Worshipers**

The sentence presupposes an audience that is already religious. It does not argue that worship is unnecessary or that human beings are self-sufficient; it takes worship as a given and asks who should receive it. The Book tends to argue this way, because the alternative it confronts is not unbelief in a maker but the distribution of loyalty among claimants that the maker never authorised.

The sūrah's method here is the method of the whole opening section: it presents the world's order as evidence, names the one who arranged it, and then states the one thing being asked of the people who live in it. What follows the prohibition is a challenge that tests the audience's confidence in their own position, and it addresses them on the basis of the very knowledge this verse has just reminded them that they have.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:23

> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Challenge That Waits for Doubt**

The verse does not respond to an argument; it responds to a suspicion, and it offers a procedure for settling one. The condition is doubt about what has been sent down, and the remedy proposed is a competition. Anyone who thinks the text is the work of a human being is invited to demonstrate it in the one way such a claim can be demonstrated: by producing something comparable and letting the comparison speak.

Nothing in the sentence forbids doubt or punishes it. The Book's method here is to meet the objection on the objector's own ground, and the later part of the sūrah does the same thing when it tells the Prophet to announce that whoever wishes may believe and whoever wishes may disbelieve. The challenge is not the voice of an author closing the discussion. It is the voice of one carrying a case that is prepared to be tested.

**"Our Servant," and What the Title Confers**

The revelation is described as what has come down to *Our servant*, and the epithet is the highest title the Book gives the Prophet ﷺ. The same word marks the gift at the head of another sūrah: *“Blessed is the One Who sent down the Standard to His servant, so that he may be a warner to the whole world.”* (25:1). In this Book the servant, not the lord, is the one who carries revelation, and the irony of the challenge rests on that relationship. Men who were willing to accept a messenger from among themselves were being asked to attack the message rather than the messenger.

The title also frames the terms of the contest. If the reciter of the Qur'an is a servant who received what he carries, then the question of authorship is a question about the source. The Book does not claim literary credit for the Prophet; it claims that what he recites came from its giver, and the challenge is addressed to anyone who says otherwise.

**One Sūrah, the Smallest Unit of the Demand**

The challenge asks for a sūrah, not for a book, a law code or a civilisation. The word names the shortest recognised unit of the revealed text, so the demand has been reduced to its smallest workable size, and the Qur'an grades the same test elsewhere at several levels: *“Or do they claim, ‘He made it up!’? Tell them ˹O Prophet˺, ‘Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can— other than Allah—if what you say is true!’”* (10:38). Other passages raise the bar to ten sūrahs (11:13), and one raises it to the whole of the Qur'an with every possible ally enlisted: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘If ˹all˺ humans and jinn were to come together to produce the equivalent of this Quran, they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other.’”* (17:88).

The scale of the request matters, because it is easy to misread it as an impossible demand dressed up as fair play. One short passage of comparable quality is the whole thing being asked for, and the Book repeats the offer across at least four passages, including a taunt that reduces the task further: *“Or do they say, ‘He made this ˹Quran˺ up!’? In fact, they have no faith. / Let them then produce something like it, if what they say is true!”* (52:33–34).

**Helpers and Witnesses Named Inside the Challenge**

The next instruction is to call upon helpers and allies, and the invitation is remarkable for how little it withholds. The Arab poets, rhetoricians and soothsayers of the time were being offered the entire field; the sentence does not restrict the assistance to one tribe or one art. Any power short of God is admissible. The point is not that the challenge is unwinnable because the rules are tilted; it is that the rules have been written to exclude every excuse.

The Book elsewhere describes the human material it is made of, which is the same material the audience used every day: letters, words, speech. Sūrah Yūnus states the relationship in similar terms, and the sūrah's own opening letters make the claim that the revelation is built from the alphabet its hearers owned. The challenge stands on that basis. If the raw material is common, then what is being compared is arrangement.

**Inimitability, a Doctrine Built on This Demand**

Later Muslim scholarship named this claim with a term the Qur'an itself does not use, *iʿjāz*, and treated the text's power to silence challengers as the central miracle of Islam. The miracle, on this account, is not an event that happened once to an audience; it is a property of the revelation that any generation can test. The Book's self-descriptions supply the terms: the Qur'an calls itself a light and a clear Book (5:15), and it presents clarity as one of its own features rather than something the reader must supply.

What the doctrine rests on is the comparison this verse invites, and the comparison has been taken up repeatedly over fourteen centuries. The sūrah's next sentence assumes the outcome of that test before it happens, and it draws a conclusion about which the audience is asked to think carefully. The argument of the passage is cumulative: the Book offers itself for examination and then states what it believes the examination will show.

**"If What You Say Is True"**

The verse ends by handing the standard of proof back to its audience. The claim being made by the doubters was that the Qur'an is human work; the sentence says, in effect, that the claim should be supported the way any claim about human work is supported, by demonstration. The Book's own case is on the table, and the burden it places on the other side is the ordinary burden that anyone making an assertion accepts.

That is the shape the passage gives to the whole dispute. It offers an invitation, defines the smallest possible test, removes every restriction on assistance, and leaves the final clause with the people who were objecting. What follows in the next verse is the conclusion the Book draws from its own challenge, and it continues to address the same audience on the same terms.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:24

> But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Condition Answered Before It Is Attempted**

The sentence opens where the challenge left off: if you have not managed it. Then it adds a clause that turns a possibility into a certainty, stating that the attempt will never succeed. Arabic marks the two halves differently — a plain conditional for the first, an emphatically negated future for the second — and the effect is a door closing while the invitation to knock remains printed on it.

The structure is the same one the sūrah used a few verses earlier when it described the hope attached to God's own purpose. Just as *perhaps* in a divine sentence amounts to a promise, here a conditional that sounds open ends in a flat denial. The Book is not being coy about its expectations. It has assessed the field and published the result before any contestant steps forward.

**Two Words for Fuel, Both Chosen With Care**

The fire is described by what feeds it: people and stones. The Qur'an uses the same pair in an exhortation to the believers: *“Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, overseen by formidable and severe angels.”* (66:6). The classical commentators read the stones two ways, and the readings are not exclusive. One takes them as the black, sulfurous stones that burn hotter than wood, describing the fire's intensity. The other takes them as the idols themselves, the stone images that had been objects of worship, so that the worshipper and the thing he worshipped meet the same end.

The second reading fits the logic of the previous verse, where the audience was reminded that God made the sky a canopy and the earth a bed before being told not to set up equals to Him. The Book makes the point explicitly in another sūrah: *“Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell. You are ˹all˺ bound to enter it.”* (21:98). Nothing that was relied upon instead of God survives the fire, and the fuel list includes both the idol and the one who trusted it.

**The Command Turns From Argument to Warning**

Having finished the demonstration, the verse issues an instruction: fear the Fire. The Arabic verb comes from the same root as *taqwā*, the objective named in the call to worship two verses earlier. Reverence was presented there as the fruit of worship and the mark of the mindful; here the same vocabulary is turned toward a specific danger, as though the shield were being carried into a burning field.

That double usage shows how the Book handles its central virtue. Reverence in the Qur'an is not a general piety with no object; it is the protective awareness of someone who knows what is at stake and acts accordingly. The same sūrah that calls the Book a guide for the mindful now tells its audience what awareness is for, and it names the danger in the plainest available terms rather than leaving it to be inferred.

**Prepared, Which Means It Is Waiting**

The fire is described as prepared for the disbelievers, and the word indicates something made ready in advance rather than something improvised at the moment of judgement. The Book uses the same construction for the reward of the righteous: the sūrah's next sentence promises Gardens prepared for those who believe and do good, and elsewhere paradise is described as prepared in the same terms. The two destinies are presented as arrangements already in place, waiting for their occupants.

That presentation is uncomfortable and deliberate. A reader is not offered a period in which the outcome is undecided and being negotiated; he is told that the destination exists on the shelf, so to speak, and that the only open question is which one he is travelling toward. The Book uses this kind of language to remove the assumption that the reckoning can be deferred by inattention, and it does so in the middle of a lecture on evidence.

**The Wager Inside the Challenge**

Read as a whole, the passage from the previous verse to this one is an argument built like a stake. A claim is made about the revelation; a test is offered; the failure of the test is predicted in advance; and then the consequence of the failure is named. What the audience is asked to consider is not merely whether the Qur'an is beautiful, but what follows if they are wrong about it.

The Book takes this approach repeatedly, and it always places the cost on the side of the person being addressed rather than on the side of the claim. There is no attempt to prove the text's divinity with an argument that admits no counter-consideration. The proposal on the table is a comparison that anyone is free to attempt, and the sentence that closes the challenge states what the Book believes is at stake in refusing it.

**An Audience Still Being Addressed**

The most important detail in the verse is its grammar. The imperative addresses the doubters directly, which means the warning is being issued to the very people whose failure to match the revelation has just been predicted. If the passage were only a verdict, the imperative would be pointless; coming as it does, the verse tells its hearers that the prediction about the contest is not a statement about them.

That is the same pattern the sūrah has followed from its opening pages. It described people whose hearts were sealed, and then called upon all humanity to worship their Maker. It reported that some would never believe, and then invited everyone to consider the evidence. The warning in this verse belongs to the same arrangement: the outcome has been announced, and the door is still open while it is being announced.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:25

> Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Good News, and the Shape of the Sentence**

The verse opens with an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ to announce glad tidings, and the Arabic verb carries the sense of news that changes a person's face. It arrives immediately after a warning about a fire prepared for the disbelievers, and the pairing is standard throughout the Book: two destinies, stated in consecutive sentences, with the hearer addressed in both.

What distinguishes the announcement here is the description attached to the people who receive it. They are named by belief and by righteous action in a single clause, so that the promise is not attached to an inner state alone. The sūrah has already described the mindful in similar terms, and the Book maintains that pairing consistently: the destination is promised to people whose faith has produced something.

**Rivers Running Under Gardens**

The Garden is described by its water, which is a description chosen for an audience that lived on the edge of a desert. The Arabic says the rivers run beneath the gardens, and the commentators took the phrase to mean that the water flows lower than the vegetation, which is the arrangement of any well-tended orchard and the opposite of what a traveller in Arabia expected from water in the ground.

The Book's paradisal water arrives elsewhere in greater variety: *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that in it are rivers of fresh water, rivers of milk that never changes in taste, rivers of wine delicious to drink, and rivers of pure honey. There they will ˹also˺ have all kinds of fruit, and forgiveness from their Lord.”* (47:15). Another verse summarises the permanence of the garden's resources in the same breath as its shade: *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that under it rivers flow; eternal is its fruit as well as its shade.”* (13:35). Water, fruit and shade are the three goods a desert dweller values most, and the Book promises all three in durable form.

**"This Is What We Were Given Before"**

The inhabitants of the Garden receive fruit and remark that they have been given this before, and the verse explains the remark: what they are served resembles what they knew. The commentators debated what the resemblance amounts to. Some held that the fruits are identical in kind with those of this world, so that the recognition is literal. Others read the sentence as surprise rather than memory, since nothing in the next life resembles this one except the names. The most commonly adopted reading is that the forms are similar while the taste is not, which fits the phrase the verse uses for likeness.

There is a practical generosity in the arrangement. A reward that could not be pictured at all would mean nothing to the people being addressed, so the Book describes a garden in the vocabulary of the gardens they knew, and then quietly raises what is inside it beyond comparison. The sūrah later uses the same root for verses whose full meaning eludes the reader, which suggests that likeness with a difference is one of the Book's ordinary ways of describing what human language can only approach.

**Spouses Made Pure**

The Garden is then said to contain spouses who are purified, and the commentators explained the purification in terms of this world's discomforts rather than in terms of status. They listed freedom from injury and illness, from the bodily functions and conditions that make people reluctant to be near one another, and from whatever would disturb the peace of the household. The major commentaries do not read the phrase as referring to virginity — a point worth stating because the translation's *pure* can suggest otherwise to an English reader.

What the clause contributes to the verse is companionship without friction. The Book's descriptions of the Garden regularly include relationships as well as goods, and it treats the household as part of the reward rather than as an accessory to it. A community that had endured exile, division and the loss of family ties in the migration is told that the home it lost is not the last word on the subject.

**A Stay Without an End**

The sentence closes with permanence, and the Book repeats that note so often that it becomes a refrain of the descriptions of both destinies. The Arabic word for abiding carries the sense of remaining, and the Book sometimes strengthens it with an explicit phrase for eternity, and sometimes qualifies it with a clause about God's will, which the commentators took as an acknowledgement of divine sovereignty rather than as a threat to the promise.

The promise of an unending stay is the part of the description that carries the most weight in the Book's moral argument. A reward that ends would eventually turn into a loss, and the sūrah's account of the hypocrites earlier used exactly that kind of arithmetic: a trade that produced no profit. The verse here uses the opposite language. What is given to the people described in it is given without a term limit, and the promise is attached to belief and good action rather than to tribe, lineage or wealth.

**The Two Destinies Stated Side by Side**

The verse was revealed in the same breath as the warning before it, and the pairing is one of the sūrah's structural habits. A fire is described as prepared; a garden is described as promised; the same audience is addressed in both sentences. What the Book is doing with this arrangement is not balancing terror with comfort but stating the two outcomes that follow from two ways of responding to the same revelation.

The order matters as well. The warning comes first because the argument of the passage has just reached its conclusion, and the good news then arrives to describe what the invitation leads to. Throughout the sūrah this pattern recurs: an argument, a warning about what refusal costs, and an announcement of what acceptance produces. In this verse the announcement is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ as an instruction to deliver it, which makes the glad tidings a duty rather than an optional comfort.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:26

> Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?” Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Parable That Needed Defending**

The verse answers an objection rather than making an argument, which means the objection came first. The reports connect it with the two parables about the fire and the storm earlier in this sūrah, and with other passages where the Book compares its opponents to a fly or a spider: *“those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah can never create ˹so much as˺ a fly”* (22:73), and the shelter of a spider (29:41). Critics found these comparisons undignified and said so, and the reply opens by naming the criticism.

The Arabic word rendered shy away carries the sense of being restrained by shame, and the sentence denies that God can be restrained in this way. What the Book refuses is the premise of the complaint — that some subjects are too small to be used for serious instruction. The reply does not apologise for the comparison, and it does not offer a grander one.

**A Gnat, or Something Smaller Still**

The creature named is the gnat or mosquito, and the phrase that follows it has two readings. It can mean something above it in size, which extends the range upward, or something beyond it in insignificance, which extends it downward. One scholar noted that the second reading makes the point sharper: if God can take the smallest creature in sight and build a lesson on it, then no part of creation is excluded from that use.

The Book's argument for this position is stated elsewhere in its own terms, when it calls attention to the creation of that sky and that earth as signs for people who reflect, and when it tells the reader that everything in the heavens and the earth serves a purpose given by its maker. Nothing in a world so constructed is too trivial to be evidence, and the objection to the gnat is finally an objection to the idea that God's teaching can reach that low.

**One Parable, Two Responses**

The verse then divides its audience by reaction. The believers know the parable is the truth from their Lord; the disbelievers ask what God meant by it. The believers are not described as understanding every detail of the comparison—they are described as accepting that it comes from the right source—while the critics are not described as failing to grasp a point but as turning a question into an accusation.

The Qur'an gives the same question to the same people in another passage, where the argument is about the number of angels guarding the fire: *“so that those ˹hypocrites˺ with sickness in their hearts and the disbelievers will argue, ‘What does Allah mean by such a number?’”* (74:31). Asking what a text means is ordinarily the beginning of study. In both verses it is described as the behaviour of people who have already decided against the text and are looking for a way to put the burden on the other side.

**Guidance and Misguidance From the Same Source**

The sentence that follows is one of the sūrah's most demanding statements: by this, God leaves many to stray and guides many. The same revelation that instructs one reader confirms another in his objection, and the Book states the outcome without apology. It states the same law when it describes the fate of the revelation itself: *“We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss.”* (17:82).

The key to the sentence is the clause that precedes it. The ones who stray are not strayed by the size of the creature in the comparison; they go astray by the same route they were already taking, and the parable supplies the occasion rather than the cause. The Book's description of the sealed heart earlier in the sūrah works on the same principle: what happens to a faculty that has been deliberately misused is a consequence rather than an ambush.

**None but the Rebellious, and the Meaning of the Word**

The verse ends with a restriction: none are left to stray except the rebellious, and the Arabic word for them, *fāsiqūn*, names people who have broken out of a boundary. It is the same word the sūrah has already used of the corruptors, and it recurs for the hypocrites elsewhere: *“They neglected Allah, so He neglected them. Surely the hypocrites are the rebellious.”* (9:67). The vocabulary is consistent: the rebellion comes first, and the misguidance follows.

That ordering is the verse's answer to a free-will objection it anticipates. If a parable can mislead, and God sends it, then the responsibility appears to move away from the reader; the last clause moves it back. What the Book never does is describe someone being confirmed in error because he had asked a question.

**Why Small Creatures Make Good Tests**

The objection that provoked this verse is itself the illustration of its claim. A reader's reaction to a gnat in a book he has already decided is divine reveals what he thinks about the author, and the Book uses small things for exactly that reason. The sūrah has just put three portraits and two parables in front of the same audience, and this verse steps back and explains what the reactions to them mean.

The answer it gives is not that the parables are unimportant. It is that the scale of the comparison has nothing to do with the scale of what is being taught, and that the people who cannot get past the creature have revealed something about their own attention. What follows this verse is a portrait of the people who are said to be left to stray, and the description begins with what they break.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:27

> those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Portrait Attached to the Previous Sentence**

This verse supplies the description that the previous one promised. The rebellious were named there as the people left to stray; here the Book says what they do, and it lists three activities in ascending reach: a covenant broken, a set of ties cut, and damage done across a whole land. The order runs from a private agreement, through relationships between people, to the condition of the community they live in.

That sequence is the sūrah's ordinary way of connecting a person to a place. The Book rarely treats wrongdoing as an isolated transaction between an individual and God; it follows the damage outward until it reaches the ground other people stand on. The three clauses are therefore one charge with three faces, and the sentence ends by naming who pays for it.

**A Covenant Broken After It Was Affirmed**

The Arabic verb describes the pulling down of something that has been bound. What is being violated is a covenant that had been confirmed, which rules out the defence of ignorance and rules out the excuse of an agreement never properly made. The Book uses the same imagery of a bond in the passage that records the original acknowledgement of God's lordship: *“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify regarding themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ ‘Am I not your Lord?’ They replied, ‘Yes, You are! We testify.’”* (7:172).

Commentators applied the phrase to three different covenants, and each has grounds. One reading takes it as the general obligation to acknowledge God and worship Him, witnessed in the primordial testimony of every human being. A second takes it as the solemn oaths the Arabs swore before the Prophet's coming that they would follow a warner if one came. A third takes it as the specific covenant made with the People of the Book. The three are not rivals so much as three settings of the same failure, and the verse's language covers all of them.

**Breaking What God Ordered to Be Joined**

The second clause is the one that turns the verse toward social life. The Book does not specify here what the ties are, and the commentators filled in the answer from elsewhere. Family relationships are the most frequent candidate, and the Qur'an commands them in the earliest address to humanity: *“O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women. And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties.”* (4:1). The duty of relatives toward one another is stated elsewhere as a matter of divine ordinance, and the Book warns the very audience under discussion here that turning away would mean severing kinship ties (47:22).

A wider reading takes the clause to cover any bond God has commanded be kept, whether of blood, of neighbourhood, of treaty or of faith. The generality is probably intended, and the strength of the charge comes from that. What is being severed is not one particular connection but the network of obligations that holds a community together, and the Book treats their maintenance as something God has ordered rather than merely recommended.

**Corruption in the Land as the Third Clause**

The third activity repeats a charge the sūrah has already brought against the hypocrites earlier in the same chapter, where they claim to be peacemakers while the Book calls them corruptors. What makes the repetition significant is the wider claim it carries in the Qur'an: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people's hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return to the ˹Right Path˺.”* (30:41).

The Book's conception of corruption is not confined to moral or political breakdown. It describes damage to the land itself as the fruit of human conduct, and it treats the damage as a form of instruction, sent so that people might turn back. In this verse the corruption is the visible result of the two broken commitments that precede it: a community whose covenants are dissolved and whose ties are cut will produce exactly this kind of wreckage, and the wreckage is described as an activity performed rather than a misfortune suffered.

**The Losers, in the Book's Ledger**

The verdict is brief: it is they who are the losers. The Book uses the same word at the closing of the parable of the man who traded guidance for misguidance, where the trade is said to have produced no profit, and in the promise attached to those who hold to the covenant rather than break it. The word describes a person who has given away something valuable and received nothing in return, and the sūrah has been teaching its readers to keep accounts in exactly those terms.

The Book's usage elsewhere supplies the other side of the ledger, so that the verdict is not a slogan: *“Surely humanity is in ˹grave˺ loss, / except those who have faith, do good, and urge each other to the truth, and urge each other to perseverance.”* (103:2–3). Loss, on this understanding, is the default condition of a life, and what rescues a person from it is a set of practices that are the opposite of what this verse describes. The people in this verse do not merely err; they dismantle the arrangements by which others are held together, and the sentence states the result without further comment.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:28

> How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question Put to People Who Already Knew the Answer**

The verse opens with the Arabic interrogative of astonishment rather than of information, and its force depends on its audience. These were not people arguing that the world had no maker; the sūrah has already shown them naming God as the creator of the sky when asked. What the question exposes is the distance between an admission they were happy to make and the loyalty that admission requires, and the Book expresses the gap as disbelief.
