The same device appears throughout the Qur'an's arguments with its first audience, and it always works the same way. The sentence does not begin by proving God's existence. It takes the existence as the common ground and asks how a person can hold it while living against it, which is a question about consistency rather than about evidence.

**Lifeless, and Then Alive**

The first stage describes a condition before life, and the Arabic word used is the ordinary word for being dead. Commentators explained it in three ways: existence as material in the earth or in one's ancestors, existence as a thing unremembered, and non-existence before this life altogether. Their explanations agree on the essential point, which is that the human being was not the author of his own beginning and did not bring himself into the world.

The Qur'an states the condition of that stage elsewhere with an image: *“Is there not a period of time when each human is nothing yet worth mentioning?”* (76:1). The comparison in this verse is between a state with no capacity at all and a state of full vitality, and the Book presents the transition as a single act performed by somebody else. What the audience is being asked is not a metaphysical question but the simplest question available: who did that?

**The Two Deaths and the Two Lives**

The verse then runs forward: He will cause you to die, then bring you to life again, and then to Him you will return. The full sequence appears in other passages with the same accounting. Sūrah al-Mu'min records the confession of those who have seen the outcome: *“Our Lord! You made us lifeless twice, and gave us life twice. Now we confess our sins. So is there any way out?”* (40:11). Another verse names the same three events in order without the final return: *“And He is the One Who gave you life, then will cause you to die, and then will bring you back to life.”* (22:66).

The pattern of life, death and life again is one of the Book's most frequently stated teachings, and it is presented as an ordinary exercise of the same power that produced the first life. Sūrah al-Rūm states the principle in nature before it states it about human beings: *“He brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. And He gives life to the earth after its death. And so will you be brought forth ˹from the grave˺.”* (30:19). Resurrection, on this argument, is not a novelty requiring a separate proof. It is the same act performed a second time.

**Why the Argument Runs Through Death**

The sequence is chosen so that death cannot be used as an escape clause. A person can tell himself that the world came into being by processes he does not need to think about, and that the question of what happens after death is beyond verification. The verse makes the two questions one question by placing the giver of life at both ends of the sequence, so that the power which began the story is the power which ends it.

The Book returns to this reasoning when it wants to answer denial of the Hereafter, and it does so with the same vocabulary of giving life and causing death: *“And He is the One Who gives life and causes death.”* (53:44). What the Book does not do is describe the mechanics of the process or offer a timetable. It states that the events are acts of the same agent, and it moves directly to their consequence.

**"To Him You Will Be Returned"**

The final clause names the destination rather than the event. Return, in this Book, carries the sense of arriving back at the source from which one came, and it is used for the whole of humanity without exception. The same sūrah states the theme repeatedly, and one of its most direct statements addresses the reader's own journey: no creature is outside the arrangement.

That clause is where the verse's argument lands, and it explains why the astonishing question at its opening is an argument about responsibility rather than about metaphysics. A person who accepts that his life was given, that it will be taken, and that he will be brought back is not in a position to treat his conduct as a private matter. The verse brings those facts together in a single sentence, and it does not add a threat to them.

**A Question Addressed to the Sūrah's Whole Audience**

The verse follows a passage about covenant-breakers and precedes a description of the earth and the heavens. It belongs to the stretch of the sūrah in which the Book is arguing with everyone rather than describing the three groups from its opening pages, and its question is put to the same audience that was called to worship its Maker two verses earlier. Nothing in it restricts the address to the hypocrites or to the rejecters.

That breadth is consistent with the way the sūrah builds its case. It names what people have received, asks them to account for their response, and then, in the next verse, points at the world around them as further evidence of the same generosity. The argument accumulates, and the astonished question is one step in a case that is being assembled rather than an isolated rebuke.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:29

> He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Everything on the Earth, Made for Its Occupants**

The verse begins with a claim about purpose, and it is stated without qualification: what is on the earth exists for the people being addressed. The Book repeats this statement in a number of places and with the same directness, including passages that extend it beyond the planet: *“Have you not seen that Allah has subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has lavished His favours upon you, both seen and unseen?”* (31:20), and *“He ˹also˺ subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all by His grace. Surely in this are signs for people who reflect.”* (45:13).

Read beside the previous verse, the argument builds in a particular direction. That verse established that the human being did not make himself; this one establishes that the world he was placed in was furnished for him before he arrived. The Book treats the arrangement as evidence of intention, and it uses the evidence the way a host uses a prepared table — as a reason for the guest to consider who prepared it.

**Turning Toward the Heaven and Forming Seven**

The second sentence describes the making of the heavens, and the Arabic verb rendered *turned towards* is the same one the Book uses for God's establishment on the throne in several passages (7:54, 10:3, 32:4, 57:4). Its sense in those contexts is a rising or a settling, and the commentators discussed at length what such language can properly mean when applied to God, generally concluding that the manner of the act is not accessible to human description.

What the verse states without ambiguity is the result: seven heavens. The number appears elsewhere with descriptions attached. One passage says they are layered: *“˹He is the One˺ Who created seven heavens, one above the other. You will never see any imperfection in the creation of the Most Compassionate.”* (67:3). Another states the same fact with a question: *“Do you not see how Allah created seven heavens, one above the other”* (71:15), and a third mentions the creation of the earth's like in number (65:12). Sūrah Fuṣṣilat describes the fashioning in two days, with each heaven given its mandate (41:12).

**A Sequence the Commentators Discussed**

The order in the verse has attracted attention, because the earth's contents are mentioned before the forming of the heavens, while other passages describe the heavens being made first. Commentators reconciled the two by reading the sequence here as a description of what was prepared for human beings rather than as a chronological report of creation, since the point being made is about provision rather than about the schedule of events.

The readings differ on detail and agree on emphasis. What the verse is doing is arranging the world's furniture in front of its inhabitants and naming the one who arranged it, and the mention of the seven heavens serves to extend the scale beyond the ground underfoot. The sūrah will return to the same created order in a later passage where the audience is invited to consider the alternation of night and day as evidence, and the argument is the same one.

**"He Has Knowledge of All Things"**

The verse closes with knowledge, and the placement is deliberate. The claim just made about the earth being made for human beings is the kind of statement that raises a question about scale: human beings are small, their lives are brief, and the assertion that the universe was arranged around them invites scepticism. The closing clause answers by naming the one whose knowledge covers the whole arrangement without exception.

The Book returns to this attribute in the verse of the throne (2:255), where it explains that God knows what is ahead of His creatures and what is behind them, and that no one grasps any part of His knowledge except by His will. The same pair of attributes closes other passages about the created order, including the declaration that God is the Knower of the seen and the unseen, the Almighty, the All-Wise (64:18).

**Provision as a Ground for Loyalty**

This verse supplies the premise that the earlier command to worship was resting on. The Book does not ask for worship on the basis of a claim nobody can check; it points at what its audience already possesses — the ground, the water, the fruit, the roof of the sky — and then asks who arranged it. The sūrah used the same sequence two verses before, and it will keep returning to provision as its standing evidence.

What the verse never does is describe the arrangement as a payment. Nothing here states that the world was made for human beings because they deserved it, and the Book elsewhere presents the same gift as a test as much as a favour. The clause about knowledge over all things is the one that keeps both aspects in view, since the same knowledge that accounts for the gift also measures what its recipients do with it.

**What "For You" Implies About the Human Being**

The claim that the earth's contents were made for human beings carries an obligation inside it, and the sūrah draws that obligation out later in the same chapter. Everything named as subject to human use — the ground, the water, the produce, the animals — is described elsewhere as given for a purpose, and the Book states the purpose repeatedly: that people might give thanks, reflect, and act rightly.

The Qur'an never presents the arrangement as a licence to take without consequence. The same passage that grants human beings succession on the earth adds that they will be tested by what they have been given (6:165), and another verse describes the earth's corruption as the fruit of human conduct rather than as an accident of nature (30:41). The verse here supplies the gift; the Book's treatment of the gift as a trust follows directly from it, and this sūrah is the chapter in which most of that treatment is worked out.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:30

> ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Appointment Announced Before It Is Made**

The verse opens a scene that the sūrah presents as a remembered conversation, and the first thing said in it is a declaration of intent. God informs the angels of a decision to place an authority on the earth. The Arabic noun rendered here as successive authority is *khalīfah*, and it carries the sense of a successor or a deputy: something or someone that comes after and stands in place of what preceded it.

The word has held a fixed place in Muslim political vocabulary ever since, through the title given to the leaders who came after the Prophet ﷺ. In this verse the term is being used about the human being as such, and the sūrah will treat the appointment as the beginning of a history rather than as the founding of an office.

**Successor to Whom, According to the Commentators**

Two readings dominate. On one, the *khalīfah* is Adam, and the word describes his standing as God's representative on the earth, charged with carrying out what he has been commanded. On the other, the word is singular in form but describes a succession: human beings who come one after another, each generation replacing the last and taking responsibility for the world it inherits.

Both readings have support in the Book's usage. Where the term appears elsewhere in the same grammatical form, it tends to describe a whole people rather than an individual: *“He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you.”* (6:165), and *“Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act.”* (10:14). A third passage pairs the appointment with deliverance from distress: *“And ˹Who˺ makes you successors in the earth?”* (27:62). The two readings are not in conflict; Adam is the first of the line the verse describes, and the office is shared by all who follow him.

**The Question the Angels Asked, and Why They Asked It**

The angels do not simply accept the announcement. They ask whether the one being placed will spread corruption and shed blood, and the Book records the question without censuring it. Commentators offered two explanations of the motive. One treats the question as wonder at the divine wisdom — the angels know that bloodshed will occur and do not see how it serves the purpose — while affirming that God's decision is right. The other connects the question with experience: if the earth had previous inhabitants who ruined it, the angels would be speaking from what they had watched happen.

The reports that fill in that background are mixed in quality. One widely repeated account holds that the jinn lived on the earth before human beings, that they corrupted it, and that Iblīs was among those who fought them. Another describes Iblīs as belonging to a tribe of angels called *al-ḥinn*. The sūrah al-Kahf identifies Iblīs plainly as one of the jinn, which tells against the account that makes him an angel, and al-Rāzī preferred the simpler position that God addressed all the angels without reference to a prior population. What the Book itself supplies is the fact of the question and the fact of the answer.

**Glory and Holiness Named as the Angels' Own Work**

The angels support their question with a description of their own activity: they glorify God's praises and proclaim His holiness. They are not represented as claiming a status they do not have, and their words are not a demand for the position on their own behalf. What they offer is a comparison between a creature that will ruin the earth and creatures that do not, and the Book leaves the comparison standing without accepting it as a valid argument.

The Book's own descriptions of the angels elsewhere match their self-description. The Qur'an states that the heaven and the earth and everything in them glorify God, and that no creature is exempt from that glorification even if human beings cannot comprehend it (17:44). The verse here presents the angels as precisely that kind of creature, engaged in unceasing praise, which makes their question about the value of the new creation a natural one.

**The Answer That Declines to Explain**

The reply is a single sentence: I know what you do not know. It does not deny the corruption, and it does not offer a defence of the human record. It states that the account being kept contains information the angels do not have access to, and it leaves the matter there. The Book's most characteristic answer to a question it does not choose to answer fully is exactly this refusal, and it places the refusal in the mouth of God rather than in a commentator's note.

What follows in the sūrah supplies part of the missing information. The verses immediately after this one show a capacity in Adam that the angels do not share, and the scene closes with a demonstration that vindicates the appointment. The sentence at the end of this verse is therefore not a dismissal. It is a promise that the reasons exist, and the next verses begin producing them.

**The Weight the Word Khalīfah Carries**

The noun chosen for the appointment is one of the most consequential in Muslim thought. It names a creature placed on the earth to carry out a commission that is not his own, and the Book attaches it to the whole human species rather than to a single individual. The point of using it here, before the disqualifying question is even answered, is that the appointment is a responsibility rather than a crown.

Later passages use the word and its plural in the language of testing: the Book tells a whole community that they have been made successors in the land precisely so that it may be seen how they act (10:14), and an earlier verse says the same of those who followed a destroyed people (7:69). The term therefore carries judgment inside it from the start. To be placed on the earth as a deputy is to be observed in that role, and the sūrah's account of the first human being sets the terms for every successor who follows him.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:31

> He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true? ”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Teaching as the First Act in the Scene**

The proof that follows the angels' question is not a display of power. It is a lesson, and the lesson is given to the creature whose appointment was being questioned. The verse does not say that Adam was made stronger, holier or more obedient than the angels; it says he was taught, and it places that fact before the demonstration that follows.

The Book treats knowledge as a gift from God rather than an achievement of the knower, and it does so consistently. The Qur'an describes writing and instruction as among the earliest favours shown to humanity: *“Who taught by the pen— / taught humanity what they knew not.”* (96:4–5). Another sūrah opens by tying revelation itself to the same verb: *“The Most Compassionate / taught the Quran”* (55:1–2). In this verse the subject of the verb is God and the student is Adam, and the pattern of giving followed by receiving is the same one that governs the whole Book's account of knowledge.

**What Was Taught, and How the Commentators Read "Names"**

The Arabic is precise: the names, all of them. Commentators differed on the scope of the phrase. Some took it as the vocabulary human beings use among themselves for ordinary things — a man, a sea, a mountain, a pot. Others read it as the names of everything that exists. A third view restricted it to the names of the angels, and a fourth took it as the names of Adam's descendants, a reading al-Ṭabarī preferred because the pronoun attached to the presentation is the masculine plural, which in the Book's usage ordinarily refers to beings with reason.

Al-Rāzī drew a wider conclusion from the same evidence: if Adam was taught the names of all things, then he was taught the languages in which things are named, and the diversity of tongues among his descendants is a later development rather than an original condition. Whatever the scope of the teaching, the verse gives the first human being a competence the angels do not possess, and it presents that competence as the reason the question in the previous verse received the answer it did.

**The Presentation of the Named Things**

The verse says the things themselves were placed before the angels, and then the challenge was issued: give the names. Commentators noted an ambiguity in the Arabic — what was presented could be the names or the objects named — and the practical sense of the scene is unaffected, because the angels are being asked to demonstrate knowledge of the created world they have lived alongside.

The Book does not describe how the presentation looked. That silence matters for how the passage is read. The scene's meaning lies in the exchange — a question asked, a test set, an answer withheld — rather than in the visual arrangement, and the sūrah's next two verses complete the exchange. What is on display is not a spectacle but a difference in knowledge.

**"If What You Say Is True"**

The closing clause refers back to the words the angels had spoken in the previous verse. Their question about corruption and bloodshed amounted to a claim about the relative worth of the new creation, and the challenge here asks them to support it. The wording is the same style of challenge the sūrah has already used against the doubters of the revelation, who were invited to produce a sūrah like it if their position was sound.

The Book's argumentative habits are consistent in this regard. When a claim is made against God's arrangement, the Book asks for the evidence, and it does so in the language of ordinary dispute rather than of reproach. The angels are not accused of anything, and no punishment is mentioned. They are asked to substantiate the implication of their own question, and the verse ends before they answer.

**Knowledge as the Qualification for the Appointment**

The placement of this verse explains what the appointment of a *khalīfah* on the earth is to consist of. It is not a promotion over the angels or a licence to act without account; it is a responsibility carried by a creature able to recognise, name and therefore think about what he has been given. The Book elsewhere ties the human being's standing to faculties of this kind, and it holds those faculties accountable when they are neglected.

Sūrah al-Isrāʾ records the same scene and adds the command that the angels prostrate to Adam, which the sūrah will report in a few verses' time. The teaching in this verse is placed before the prostration, so that the honour given to Adam rests on the knowledge he was granted. That order is the sūrah's answer to the question about corruption: the creature being appointed is one who can understand what he is doing, and who can therefore be held to it.

**A Report About the Clay He Was Made From**

The tradition preserves a report from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī that the Prophet ﷺ described the making of Adam in related terms: God created him from a handful taken from the whole of the earth, so that human beings resemble the earth — some red, some white, some black, mixed, smooth and rough, good and bad (Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4693, graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī; the same report appears in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2955 with a ḥasan chain). The report connects the diversity of human temperaments and appearances to the material of the first creation, and the verse's claim that Adam was taught the names of all things fits a creature made from a mixture.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:32

> They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Reply That Begins With Praise**

The angels answer the challenge without making an attempt at it. Their first words are an act of glorification, and the Arabic formula declares God free of any deficiency that could be imagined of Him. Beginning a reply to a divine command with praise is the pattern the Book gives to creatures throughout: the answer to a question from God is not an argument but a turning toward Him.

That opening also settles the tone of the whole sentence. The angels are not confessing a defect in themselves in a tone of complaint; they are naming the source of everything they know before they admit that their knowledge is limited. What they say in the second clause only makes sense because of the first.

**The Admission of Limit, Stated Without Excuses**

The middle of the sentence concedes the point of the test: they have no knowledge except what they have been taught. The phrasing is exact. It does not say they have little knowledge, or that the question was unfair, or that the objects were outside the scope of their expertise. It states that everything they possess came by way of instruction, which makes their entire competence a gift rather than a property.

The Book gives human beings the same assessment about their own capacities in passages that read like footnotes to this one: *“Its nature is known only to my Lord, and you ˹O humanity˺ have been given but little knowledge.”* (17:85). And it instructs the Prophet ﷺ to ask for more of it rather than to rely on what he already has: *“and pray, ‘My Lord! Increase me in knowledge.’”* (20:114). The angels in this verse are models of the attitude those commands describe.

**Two Names Chosen to Answer the Question**

The reply ends with two of the divine names: the All-Knowing and the All-Wise. They answer the two halves of the situation precisely. Knowledge answers the test that has just been set, since what the angels could not name is known to God before and after the naming. Wisdom answers the question they asked in the previous verses, since the objection about corruption and bloodshed was an objection about the fitness of the arrangement.

The Book pairs these two names repeatedly, and the pairing is always doing work of this kind. The sūrah declares that God knows what is ahead of His creatures and what lies behind them, and that none grasps any part of His knowledge except as He wills (2:255). Another passage closes a description of the whole creation with the same pair: *“˹He is the˺ Knower of the seen and unseen—the Almighty, All-Wise.”* (64:18). Knowledge accounts for the facts, wisdom accounts for what is done with them.

**The Difference Between Conceding and Resigning**

What the angels do is not the abandonment of a question. They had asked something real, and their reply accepts the answer they were given earlier in the scene: there is knowledge the creature does not have. Their response preserves the question in a form that permits an answer, which is a different thing from withdrawing it or repeating it more loudly.

The Book treats this as the proper posture for any inquiry about God. The verse that classifies the Book's verses separates those that are precise from those that are elusive, notes that the deviant pursue the elusive ones looking for trouble, and then describes the stance of those who are well grounded in knowledge: *“We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord.”* (3:7). The angels' sentence in this verse is the same stance applied to the appointment of the human being.

**The Test Served Its Purpose**

Nothing in the scene suggests that the angels were humiliated by the test. The Book does not describe a defeat; it records a concession and a name. The being whose appointment was questioned had been taught something the questioners had not, and the exchange ends with the questioners acknowledging the limit of their own knowledge rather than disputing the demonstration.

That outcome is what makes the passage a lesson about the difference between two kinds of ignorance. A person who does not know a thing and admits it stands inside a relationship where he can be taught. A person who does not know a thing and demands that the arrangement be justified to him stands outside it. The sūrah has already used the second posture for the critics of its parables and will use it again for the objectors to the very revelation in its hands.

**A Sentence the Book Gives to Creatures**

The words of this verse are reported as the speech of angels, and they are the words the Book teaches human beings to use in a range of situations. Praise in the face of something not understood, an admission that everything one knows was received, and the naming of God's knowledge and wisdom as the ground of confidence: that is the whole content of the reply, and it is available to any reader who finds himself in the position the angels were in.

The sūrah does not leave the scene at this point. The next verse returns to Adam and completes the demonstration, and in doing so it shows what the admission of the angels looks like from the outside when the missing knowledge is supplied. What they conceded is then displayed, and the display is described in one sentence that belongs to God rather than to the creature.

**The Model This Reply Sets for Inquiry**

The sentence has become the template for how Muslim scholarship describes the limits of reason in matters that revelation alone settles. The angels do not pretend to a knowledge they lack, do not speculate about the purpose behind the appointment, and do not treat their own excellence as evidence of a right to decide. They praise, they concede, and they name the two attributes that make the unanswered question livable: full knowledge and full wisdom.

That posture is what the sūrah's later verse on the Book's ambiguous passages asks of its readers, and it is what the Book praises when it describes people who accept what has come down to them without splitting into factions over what they cannot verify. For a tradition that has spent centuries debating the relationship between reason and revelation, this reply supplies the terms of the settlement: whatever is known was taught, and the teacher of it is both knowing and wise.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:33

> Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Demonstration Replaces the Argument**

The last step of the scene is an instruction, and it is given to the one whose standing had been questioned. Adam is told to supply what the angels could not, and the record states in a subordinate clause that he did it. His answer is not reported; only the fact of it, which keeps the attention on what the demonstration establishes rather than on how it sounded.

The structure of the passage is worth following from beginning to end. A decision is announced; a question is raised; a test is set; the questioners concede; the one who was questioned is asked to perform; he performs; and then the point of the test is stated aloud. The sūrah builds the case and only then names the conclusion, so that the reader has watched the evidence accumulate before he is told what it proved.

**What the Confrontation Establishes**

The instruction is addressed to Adam in the presence of the angels, and it makes the knowledge he carries public. Up to this point, the fact that he had been taught the names was information the reader held and the angels did not. What happens in this verse is that the private gift becomes a visible competence: the angels watch him do what they could not do.

That is the whole vindication of the appointment, and it is a vindication by demonstration rather than by decree. Nothing in the scene orders the angels to accept Adam on authority. They are shown what he can do, and the earlier question about the value of placing a creature like him on the earth is answered by the display. The Book repeatedly prefers this method, presenting evidence and letting the reader draw the conclusion it has already drawn in its own voice.

**God's Own Recollection of the Earlier Exchange**

The sentence that follows the demonstration is addressed to the assembly, and it refers back to the earlier discussion: did I not tell you? The verb is the one the sūrah used for the divine declaration about knowledge at the end of the appointment scene, and the question form is the interrogative of confirmation rather than of information. God is not adding a new claim; the claim was already made before the test, and the test has now confirmed it.

The Book's account of human knowledge consistently places its origin in God's, and it does so in passages whose vocabulary matches this verse. Elsewhere the Book states that God knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth and what human beings hide in their breasts (35:38), and it repeats the same claim in the closing verse of a sūrah about speech and intention: *“Surely Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and earth. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.”* (49:18). What is being announced in this verse about the unseen is not a new attribute of God. It is the attribute the whole scene has been demonstrating.

**"What You Reveal and What You Conceal"**

The final clause narrows the scope from the cosmos to the people in the room. God knows what is said openly and what is held back, and the two halves are named separately because they have different audiences in the world of creatures. The Book states the same principle directly to human beings in a passage that leaves no room for managing appearances: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, it is known to Allah. For He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.’”* (3:29).

Commentators took the concealment in this scene to have a referent. Al-Ṭabarī records readings that attach it to the pride in Iblīs that had not yet surfaced in words, or to a belief the angels are said to have harboured, that God would never create anything nobler than them. The passage itself does not name what was hidden, and the omission is deliberate: a sentence that identifies hidden things in general does not need to identify one of them to make its point.

**The Stakes the Scene Sets for the Rest of the Sūrah**

The question of who was qualified to be placed on the earth has now been settled in front of its questioners. What the sūrah does next is turn the same scene toward the one member of the assembly whose reaction was not praise or acceptance. The verses that follow report a refusal in the presence of the same command, and the contrast with the angels' conduct is sharpened by their admission in the previous verse.

For the reader, the lesson of the passage is not limited to the original audience. The Book tells human beings that their dignity rests on a capacity to know what they are given, and it warns them of an ambition that refuses to acknowledge an order larger than its own. The sūrah's next step shows how the second of those two possibilities behaved when it appeared, and the whole human story in the Qur'an begins from that contrast between knowledge that accepts and pride that does not.

**Two Names, One Meaning, One Warning**

The scene closes with God naming what He knows rather than with a rebuke or a verdict, and the point of the naming rests on what the reader has watched. A capacity was granted to one creature which the others lacked; a question about fitness was raised; the answer was supplied by the creature in the presence of those who questioned it; and the conclusion was stated without argument. Nothing in the passage suggests that God was obligated to show His reasons — the earlier answer, that He knows what the angels do not, was already sufficient.

What happens in this verse is that the reasons appear. That is the mercy in the structure of the sūrah's telling. The human being is not told to accept his standing without knowing what it rests on, and the reader who has followed the scene from the appointment to the display is left with a definition of the human vocation. It consists in being taught, in learning what was taught, and in being answerable to the one who knows what is shown and what is hidden.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:34

> And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Command, One Refusal**

The scene that began with the appointment of a deputy on the earth reaches its first crisis here. A command is issued to the angels, and the Book states the response in two movements: they all prostrated, and one did not. The exception is placed at the end of the sentence, so that the reader sees the unanimity broken only after he has seen it established.

The Book reports the same scene in several other sūrahs, and each telling supplies a detail the others leave out. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf gives Iblīs's reason (7:12), al-Ḥijr states the command's setting (15:29–31), and al-Kahf supplies his origin (18:50). Taken together, the accounts describe a single act of refusal narrated from several angles, which is how the Qur'an teaches the same history repeatedly rather than once.

**Refusal and Arrogance, in That Order**

Two verbs carry the sentence: he refused, and he acted arrogantly. The order runs from action to motive, so that the reader learns what he did before he learns why. The Book treats the pair as connected everywhere it tells this story, and the connection is stated as a rule of human character in a report the Prophet ﷺ gave: no one who has an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 91). When a companion asked about liking fine clothes and shoes, the answer distinguished appearance from the vice itself and defined arrogance as rejecting the truth and looking down on people.

That definition fits this verse exactly. Iblīs rejected a command whose rightness did not depend on his opinion of it, and he did so on the basis of a comparison between himself and another creature. The Book gives the comparison in his own words: *“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* (7:12).

**Who Iblīs Was**

The reports differ on his kind. One widely repeated account places him among a group called *al-ḥinn*, made from smokeless fire, and describes him as a custodian of Paradise; another attaches him to the angels. The Qur'an states his status without ambiguity in the sūrah of the Cave: *“but not Iblîs, who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord.”* (18:50). The Book's own identification settles the question the popular narrations left open, and al-Rāzī noted the same point, concluding that material describing him as an angel cannot be relied upon.

What all accounts agree on is his position at the moment of the command. He was present, he heard it, and he was capable of obeying. The verse's charge is built on that presence, which is why the Book does not describe a foreign power entering the scene. The refusal came from inside.

**Prostration to Adam, Worship of God**

The command raises a question the commentators addressed at length, since prostration in the Qur'an ordinarily belongs to God. Their answer is that the act here is a greeting and an acknowledgement of honour, not worship, and that the one being worshipped is God in both cases: Adam is the qiblah of the moment, so to speak, and the obedience is rendered to the command. The same reading covers the prostration of Joseph's family in the later sūrah, which the book records without censure.

That distinction is what makes Iblīs's answer intelligible as a theological error rather than a defence of monotheism. His words in al-Aʿrāf are about *merit* — fire against clay — not about the exclusivity of worship, and the verse here names the result of the whole exchange: he became one of the unfaithful.

**"Becoming Unfaithful": the Word's First Appearance**

The Arabic term rendered unfaithful is *kāfirūn*, and the verse places it at the end of the sentence as a verdict rather than a description of his initial state. The Book uses the word throughout for covering over what one knows, and Iblīs's refusal fits the usage precisely: he did not lack awareness of God or of the command. He had both, and he set them aside.

The Qur'an reports the scene without adding a punishment here because the sūrah is not finished with him. What the reader takes from this verse is the shape of the failure — a creature in possession of knowledge, ordered to acknowledge a peer, refusing on grounds of rank — and the sequel in the coming verses shows where that refusal led, first for Adam and then for all who inherit his position.

**The Threshold of the Human Story**

This verse closes the scene of the appointment and opens the story of the fall. The sūrah put a question in the angels' mouths, answered it by demonstration, and now records the one reaction that was neither praise nor acceptance. Everything after it in this sūrah's telling of human history depends on that reaction, because the enemy of the human being is introduced before the human being's first mistake is narrated.

The Book describes the same adversary as a declared enemy from the start: *“Would you then take him and his descendants as patrons instead of Me, although they are your enemy?”* (18:50). The warning is given before the temptation, which is the pattern the sūrah follows throughout: the danger is named first, and the failure is recorded second, so that no reader can claim the opposition was a secret.

**The Enemy Introduced Before the Temptation**

The order of the sūrah's narrative is part of its teaching. The refusal of Iblīs is reported before Adam is placed in the Garden, so the reader meets the adversary before he meets the test. Nothing that follows in the story can be blamed on a surprise, and the Book states the enmity outright in the same passage where it names his origin: Iblīs and his descendants are described as enemies of the human being who must not be taken as patrons (18:50).

That arrangement shapes how the whole account of the fall should be read. The human being was warned, the opponent was identified, and the terms of residence were set before the deception occurred. What the sūrah records is therefore not the ambush of an innocent but the failure of a warned creature, and the mercy that follows in the next verses is measured against that knowledge.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:35

> We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Permission With One Exception**

The command given to Adam is framed as an invitation. He is told to live in the Garden with his wife and to eat from it freely, and the Arabic verb for that freedom is the strongest available for unrestricted enjoyment. The one limit is attached afterwards, in a short clause, and the sentence therefore opens with generosity and closes with a boundary.

That structure is how the Book introduces the moral life of humanity. The Garden is not presented as a place of scarcity regulated by anxious rules; it is a place of abundance with a single prohibition, and the prohibition is stated in the plainest terms. The very shape of the sentence — a wide permission followed by a narrow limit — tells the reader something about the relationship being established.

**The Garden as the Book Describes It**

This same Garden is described elsewhere in terms of what is absent from it: *“Indeed, you will neither go hungry nor naked there, / nor will you ˹ever˺ suffer from thirst or ˹the heat of˺ the sun.”* (20:118–119). Another telling of the same scene uses nearly the identical wording for the command that is quoted here: *“O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat from wherever you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”* (7:19).

The Book's descriptions of the place are about sufficiency rather than luxury. Food, clothing, water and shade are the four goods named, and they are the four a desert community would count as the whole of security. Adam is placed in a condition where the basic problem of living has been solved, which is precisely what makes the one prohibition the only thing left to test him.

**"Do Not Approach," Not Merely "Do Not Eat"**

The wording of the prohibition is preventive. Adam and his wife are not told to abstain from the fruit; they are told not to come near the tree, and the same technique appears throughout the Qur'an when the Book wants to close off a road rather than punish a step. Islamic law later made the same move a principle, the blocking of means to a prohibited end.

The effect on the reader is to make the boundary generous rather than restrictive. A limit that forbids only the final act leaves the actor free to approach, look, and deliberate; a limit that forbids proximity removes the entire space in which the act becomes imaginable. The Book records the command at the outer edge so that the test is placed at a distance from the crime, and the failure described in the next verse then reads as a deliberate journey toward it rather than a slip.

**The Tree the Book Never Names**

The Qur'an does not say what kind of tree it was, and the commentators filled the silence with guesses drawn from a wide range of sources: grain, grapevine, fig, and others. Al-Ṭabarī registered a number of these reports, and the material varies enough in quality that modern scholarship treats much of it as folklore rather than as transmitted teaching.

The Book's silence on the point is consistent with how it handles the story's other details. It does not name the tree, does not describe the form Iblīs took, and does not give the conversation that led to the fall much stagecraft. What interests the Qur'an is the structure of the event — a command, a whisper, a choice, a consequence — and the details left out are the ones that would satisfy curiosity without changing the lesson. Readers who supply them are adding to a story the Book deliberately left spare.

**"Or You Will Be Wrongdoers"**

The consequence attached to the prohibition names a category the sūrah has already used several times: those who wrong. The Arabic term describes the person who places something where it does not belong, and the Book applies it to a wide range of acts, from the rejection of revelation to the refusal of a command to the corrupting of a community.

What is notable about its use here is that the wrongdoer would be the one wronged. Adam is not told that he will injure God or damage the Garden; he is told that he will place himself outside the condition he was given. The sūrah will state the principle in a later verse: God does not wrong human beings in the least; they wrong themselves. The prohibition in the Garden is the first instance of that pattern in the Book's account of the human story.

**Freedom and Its Boundaries in the Same Breath**

The verse gives the human being a home, a companion, and an unlimited table, and it sets one boundary across them. Nothing in the sentence suggests that the freedom was reluctant or the limit arbitrary; the two are stated at the same moment, which is how the Book treats them everywhere. Obligation in the Qur'an is not a tax levied on liberty but the shape liberty takes, and the scene in the Garden establishes that relationship before the human being does anything at all.

Read beside the appointment of a deputy in the previous scene, the verse describes what that office looks like in practice. The deputy receives what he is given, acts within the limits set for him, and answers for the difference. The test that follows is small in appearance — one tree out of a whole Garden — and the sūrah treats it as the first exercise of the responsibility that was announced in heaven.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:36

> But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Fall Traced to a Single Act of Deception**

The sentence begins with the cause. Satan caused them to slip, and the Arabic verb describes a foot losing its hold rather than a wall being pushed down. The Book had just recorded a command with a limit; here it records the movement across that limit, and it attributes the movement to an outside agent without removing the two who moved.

The Qur'an tells this part of the story in more detail in two other places. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf supplies the whisperer's words and his oath: *“Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.”* (7:20), followed by *“And he swore to them, ‘I am truly your sincere advisor.’”* (7:21). Sūrah Ṭā Hā adds the promise of a kingdom: he offered them *“the Tree of Everlastingness and a kingdom that never decays”* (20:120). The sūrah of al-Baqarah compresses the whole episode into the verb.

**The Method of the Liar: Oaths and Promises**

The Book records what the tempter actually said, and the content is instructive. He did not tell them that obedience was wrong or that God was absent; he told them that the prohibition concealed something worth having, and he swore an oath about his own sincerity. Every element of the pitch is a distortion of something true — angels do exist, immortality is real — and the whole is delivered under the guarantee of a false oath.

That combination is what the Book means by deception, and it warns human beings about it from the beginning of their history. The sūrah's later portrait of the hypocrites keeps the same mechanics in view, where men use oaths as a shield and elegant words to cover their intentions. What changes across the Book is the scale of the audience, not the method of the argument.

**"Descend, Enemies to One Another"**

The command to descend is addressed in the plural, and the commentators took the addressees to include Adam, his wife, and the one who had deceived them, with all their descendants implied. The plural matters because it announces a condition rather than an eviction: from this point, the relationship between human beings and the deceiver is one of declared enmity, and the Qur'an keeps that word for Iblīs consistently.

The same command appears in three places with nearly identical wording, and it is paired in each with the promise of guidance to come. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf records it after the exposure of their nakedness: *“Descend as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”* (7:24), and Sūrah Ṭā Hā pairs the descent with a promise that whoever follows God's guidance will not go astray or fall into misery (20:123). The Book's account of the expulsion is therefore also an account of a commission.

**What the Fall Is Not**

This verse is not the story of a human nature corrupted in its essence by an inherited fault. The Qur'an does not carry the doctrine of original sin, and the verses that follow show Adam receiving words from his Lord and being forgiven, with the offence ending there for him. What propagates from this scene is the conditions of earthly life and the enmity of the deceiver, not guilt for an act somebody else committed.

The Book makes the same point about responsibility throughout: nothing is carried by one person for another, and every soul answers for what it has done. The fall is therefore a beginning in the geographical sense — the descent to a place where testing occurs — and a warning in the moral sense, since the method that worked in the Garden is still in circulation.

**"A Residence and Provision for an Appointed Stay"**

The terms of the descent are stated in two nouns. The earth will be a place of settlement, and the arrangement includes provision, which echoes the earlier statement that the earth was furnished for human beings before their arrival. The Book does not describe the earth as a prison; it describes it as a dwelling with supplies, and it adds a term limit.

The Arabic phrase rendered *appointed stay* names a fixed period, whether that period is a person's life or the whole span of human history on the earth. The Book uses the same vocabulary when it describes everything in the world as measured, and the sūrah's earlier passage on the appointment of a deputy said the same about the earth's provision. The human being is placed in a working environment with a deadline attached, and the deadline is stated to him from the start.

**Earth as the Place Where the Commission Runs**

The scene in heaven is finished, and the scene on earth begins. Everything the sūrah has described up to this point — the appointment of a representative, the demonstration of knowledge, the single prohibition, the fall — now takes place in the world that the reader actually inhabits, and the Book's account of that world will keep returning to the enmity announced here.

The verses that follow complete the sequence with forgiveness and guidance, so that the descent is not the last word of the passage. What the reader carries from this verse is the arrangement: a dwelling, a provision, a term, and an enemy — and a Book that will describe how to live inside all four. The dwelling, the provision, and the term are named together in the sentence, and the sūrah's later verses return to each of them as the account of the human life unfolds.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:37

> Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Words Were Given, Not Invented**

The Arabic verb in this sentence describes receiving something, and its subject is Adam. He did not compose a defence or negotiate a settlement; he was given words, and the Book presents the gift as the first step in his recovery. The initiative in this verse belongs to God from beginning to end: the words are supplied, and the acceptance of the repentance is stated as the consequence.

That order matters for what the verse teaches. A guilty person's most urgent need is not a strategy but a vocabulary, and the Qur'an presents repentance as something a human being learns rather than something he improvises. The same pattern recurs throughout the Book, where the servants of God speak in sentences supplied by revelation, and the sūrah's own text is the largest instance of it.

**What the Words Actually Were**

Commentators identified the received words in several ways. The most direct identification is the plea recorded in al-Aʿrāf: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”* (7:23). Another report holds that God taught Adam and Eve the rites of pilgrimage, describing the pilgrimage itself as the words. A third transmits a longer prayer of confession and appeal, beginning with the declaration of God's unity and ending with a request for forgiveness.

Al-Rāzī listed the options and left the question open, which is the posture he takes on several details of this story. What the readings share is the content of the sentence: an admission placed on the speaker, an appeal addressed to God, and no attempt at a justification. Whether the exact wording is the plea of 7:23 or a longer formula, the verse in al-Baqarah tells the reader that a confession was given and that it was accepted.

**The Verb That Runs in Two Directions**

Arabic uses one root for the human act of turning back and the divine act of turning toward, and the two are distinguished only by the preposition attached to the verb. The noun *tawbah* therefore means a return, and the Book's usage presents repentance as a movement in two directions at once: the servant comes back to God, and God turns toward the servant.

The name that closes this verse belongs to the same root in its intensive form, and the Book applies it to God repeatedly, including in the promise of acceptance to anyone who turns. The vocabulary is worth noticing because it removes the idea of repentance as a transaction with a reluctant party. The Book's God is described as the one who responds to the turning, and the verse states the acceptance in the same sentence as the confession.

**The Two Names at the End**

The verse ends with a pair of names, and the pairing answers two needs the situation creates. The Accepter of Repentance addresses the question of whether the confession will be received; the Most Merciful addresses the question of what happens to the wrong that was committed. Both names are attached to an event that occurred in the very first generation of human history, before any law had been revealed and any community existed.

The sūrah will use these names again, and the Book uses them in contexts where human failure has been severe. The same mercy is offered to people who have gone far past the boundary: *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”* (39:53). The first instance of forgiveness in the Book establishes the pattern that the rest of the Book will follow.

**Repentance Established as a Standing Law**

Nothing in this verse suggests that Adam's case was an exception, and the Book never treats it that way. The sentence is narrated as the beginning of a permanent arrangement between human beings and their Maker, and the sūrah's own later passages apply the same remedy to the community addressed by the revelation. A mistake, an admission, and a return: this is the cycle the Book presents as normal rather than extraordinary.

The contrast with the previous scene is deliberate, though the Book leaves the reader to observe it. Iblīs refused a command he knew, defended himself with an argument about merit, and is never described as asking for pardon. Adam crossed a line, was given words, and used them. Two failures are narrated in sequence, and the difference between them lies entirely in what the offender did after the offence.

**A Fall That Ends in a Pardon Rather Than a Sentence**

The verse closes a unit within the sūrah. The appointment, the demonstration, the prohibition, the deception, the descent, and now the pardon: the sequence is coherent because it ends with the remedy in place before the human story on earth begins. Adam goes down to the earth forgiven, and the terms of his residence have already been set.

That is the reading the Book supports throughout, where the mercy of God is described as preceding and surrounding human weakness without excusing it. The verse does not tell us that Adam escaped consequences or that the offence was trivial. It tells us that the relationship was restored, and it names the two attributes by which the restoration was possible.

**Pardon Given Before the Earth Was Reached**

The forgiveness recorded in this verse takes place while the couple are still in the Garden, before the descent commanded in the following verse. Adam goes down with the offence already settled, and the sūrah's account gives the reader the full sequence in order: command, failure, confession, pardon, and only then the change of residence.

That sequence is the reason the Book does not carry a doctrine of inherited guilt. What descends to the earth is a forgiven man and a commission, not a debt owed by his children. Comparatively, the Book gives human beings the same remedy that Adam used, and it addresses later communities with the invitation to turn back on the same terms. The verse also supplies the vocabulary for it, since the two names at its end describe the acts of accepting a return and showing mercy, and both were demonstrated before the first law was given.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:38

> We said, “Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Same Command, With Something Attached**

The command to descend is repeated here, and the repetition carries an addition. The first time the verse concluded with a dwelling, provision and a term; this time it concludes with a promise about guidance that has not yet arrived. The sūrah is showing the reader what the descent means: not only a change of address but the beginning of an arrangement in which revelation will keep arriving.

The addressees are named in the plural again, and the commentators took the group to include Adam, his wife, and their descendants, or at least to stand for humanity as a whole. That reading is supported by what follows, since the promise about guidance is not spoken to two individuals in a garden; it is addressed to everyone who will live on the earth.

**Guidance Announced Before It Is Given**

The sentence promises a future arrival: when guidance comes to you from Me. Nothing is said about what form it will take, when it will come or through whom, and the reader of the sūrah knows what the original hearers could not, since the Book in his hands is the thing being promised. The Qur'an treats its own descent as the fulfilment of this sentence, and it describes itself in the terms used here: the sūrah's second verse calls the Book a guide for the mindful (2:2), and another passage states the same purpose in one line: *“O humanity! Indeed, there has come to you a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers.”* (10:57).

That sequence is how the Book presents the history of revelation. Guidance is promised first and delivered later, and each delivery is announced as the fulfilment of an earlier undertaking. The promise in this verse is general enough to cover every messenger who came after Adam, which is precisely the reading the Book's own history requires.

**"Whoever Follows It"**

The condition attached to the promise is not hearing, believing or admiring; it is following. The Arabic verb describes walking behind someone along a road, and it is the same verb the sūrah uses at its opening when it says the Book is a guide for the mindful who follow what has come to them. Following in the Qur'an is a physical metaphor for a deliberate life, and the Book consistently ranks it above the possession of information.

The verse therefore places the entire promise on a single act that any person can perform, and it leaves nothing in the sentence that depends on lineage, intelligence or status. Adam's descendants are addressed as individuals who will each have to decide whether to walk. The Book's later addresses keep the same condition in the same words, and the sūrah will use them again when it turns to the community of Madinah.

**No Fear and No Grief**

The promise attached to following is stated in a formula that recurs throughout the Qur'an. Fear looks forward to what may come; grief looks back at what has been lost. The Book removes both for the person who follows the guidance, and it does so in the same order every time, as in the verse that pairs the promise with the service of God: *“There will certainly be no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve.”* (10:62).

The pairing is deliberately comprehensive. A human being's distress is usually either anxiety about the future or regret about the past, and the promise in this verse addresses both without suggesting that the follower's circumstances will be easy. What is removed is not hardship but the two emotions that make hardship unbearable, and the Book offers this as the reward of following rather than as a consequence of comfort.

**A Report About What Adam Was Taught on Earth**

Several reports describe instruction given to Adam after he came down. One account transmitted from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī says that God revealed to him that four things contain everything for him and his children: what belongs to God, which is worship without association; what belongs to the human being, which is the reward of his deeds; what lies between them, which is supplication and the answer to it; and what lies between him and other people, which is treating them as he wishes to be treated.

The reports are not of the highest grade and the sūrah does not depend on them, but they show how the earliest readers understood this verse. The promise of guidance was heard as the beginning of a whole teaching, and the four-part summary describes the same structure the sūrah itself follows: obligations toward God, obligations toward oneself, prayer, and conduct toward others.

**The Future Left Open in the Text**

The verse ends without naming the guidance, describing the messengers, or stating when the promise will be fulfilled. What it gives the reader is a condition and a result: guidance will arrive, and the person who follows it will be safe. The sūrah moves directly from this sentence to the fate of those who do the opposite, and the two destinies are placed side by side before the Book turns to the community it will address for the next eighty verses.

That transition is worth noticing for what it says about the Book's method. Before any law is given, before the history of Israel is recounted, and before the first command of the detailed teaching arrives, the reader is told what the two roads lead to. The Qur'an does not begin with legislation; it begins with a description of where each of the two possible responses ends.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:39

> But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verdict Standing Where a Warning Was Expected**

The sentence states an outcome rather than issuing an instruction, and it completes the pair begun in the previous verse. A promise was made to those who follow; here the opposite case is stated, in a form that identifies the people involved and their destination. Nothing in between is left undecided, and the sūrah then moves on to its lengthy address to a particular community.

This way of putting matters together is a pattern in the Book. Even where the surrounding passage is narrative, the Qur'an places the two results side by side, so that the reader is never left with a promise whose alternative is unstated. The verse is short, and its brevity is part of the effect: the destination is named, the duration is named, and no description is offered.

**Two Verbs, and the Difference Between Them**

The people in this verse are described with two words. The first describes covering over what one knows, and the Book's usage is consistently about concealment rather than mere absence of information. The second describes calling something a lie, and it applies to the signs themselves: revelation, evidence, the marks of God's work in the world.

The pair recurs together in the Qur'an, and it appears in the same order in a later sūrah where the same judgment is passed: *“As for those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the residents of the Hellfire.”* (5:10). The Book tends to list the two together because they describe two stages of one movement: first the covering over of what was recognised, then the public designation of it as false. The verse in al-Baqarah states the end of that movement.

**What "Our Signs" Includes**

The Arabic word for signs covers everything that points to its maker: the verses of the revelation, the phenomena of nature, and the events of a person's own life. The Book states the range in a single sentence: *“We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this ˹Quran˺ is the truth.”* (41:53). Denial in the Qur'an is therefore not limited to rejecting a book; it can be directed at the world, at the self, or at both.

That breadth explains why the sūrah's earlier portraits of rejection were not confined to people who argued about revelation. A man who calls the evidence around him a product of chance has denied a sign in the same sense this verse uses, and the Book treats the two denials as one act of the same will.

**Residents, and the Word the Book Uses**

The term rendered residents describes people who belong to a place, in the way a householder belongs to his house. The Book uses it for both destinations, so it speaks of the companions of the Garden and the companions of the Fire, and the choice of the word implies permanence rather than a period of detention in an unfamiliar setting.

That permanence is confirmed in the closing clause, which states the duration. The Book repeats the phrase often enough that it becomes one of the recognisable marks of the descriptions of the Fire, and the sūrah will use it again later in its own text. The effect of repeating it is to prevent the reader from reading the sentence as a threat whose scale is unclear. The Book tells him exactly what it means.

**Forever, in the Book's Vocabulary**

The Arabic word for abiding carries the sense of remaining where one is, and the Book sometimes strengthens it with explicit language of endlessness and sometimes qualifies it with a statement of God's will. The Qur'an applies the same vocabulary to the reward of the righteous in the sūrah describing the Paradise promised to them: *“eternal is its fruit as well as its shade”* (13:35).

The Book uses the term consistently for both destinies, and it does not soften either. What varies in the passages is not the duration but the condition of the people concerned, and the commentary tradition spent considerable effort distinguishing those who enter the Fire permanently from those Muslims who enter it temporarily for purification. What the verse states is the case of those who die in the position it describes.

**Why This Sentence Precedes a Long Address**

The verse closes the account of Adam and the fall, and immediately after it the sūrah turns to the Children of Israel and speaks to them for the better part of a hundred verses. The transition is abrupt, and the placement is instructive: the address that follows is delivered to a community that already knows the difference between the two destinations outlined here.

The Book's order is to state consequences before it issues commands, which is the opposite of how a legal code is usually arranged. The reader encounters the two ends of the road first, and everything the sūrah goes on to request is then heard in the light of what has just been said about where the two responses lead. The command to fulfil a covenant comes after the reader has seen what is promised to those who keep one and what belongs to those who call the evidence lies.

**A Verdict That Closes a Unit**

This sentence ends the passage on Adam, and the sūrah moves at once to a lengthy address to a particular people. The placement is deliberate: the reader has been shown the two destinations, stated in consecutive verses, before a single command of the detailed teaching has been issued. When the address to the Children of Israel begins, everything it asks for arrives in the light of what the reader already knows about the two roads.

The Book's habit of ordering its material this way is visible throughout the sūrah. It states outcomes, then grounds them in history, then issues instructions, and it does not leave the reader to guess what follows from either response. The two verses about the guided and the deniers are the frame on which the rest of the chapter is hung.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:40

> O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine, and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Community Addressed by Name**

After thirty-nine verses the sūrah turns to a named people and speaks to them directly. Israel is another name for Jacob, and the Book addresses his descendants as a family with a recorded history rather than as a religious category. The community living in and around Madinah at the time of the revelation was being spoken to about its own ancestry, and the sūrah will continue in this mode, with a few interruptions, for most of its middle section.

That choice of audience explains the character of what follows. What the sūrah asks of this community is not conversion to an unfamiliar religion but fidelity to an existing relationship. The God speaking in these verses is the one who delivered their ancestors from Egypt, and the Book presents itself as a continuation of a story the audience already knows.

**"Remember My Favours"**

The favours being invoked are named a few verses later in the same recitation: deliverance from the persecution of Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, and the provisions given in the desert. The Book also summarises the same history in terms of what this people received in religious goods: *“Indeed, We gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood; granted them good, lawful provisions; and favoured them above the others.”* (45:16). Scripture, wisdom and prophecy are named there alongside the bread and the safety.

The word for favour in this verse the Book uses to cover both kinds. Its sense is generous, and its range includes the rescue of a slave people, the sending of messengers, and the establishment of a community with a law. The command to remember is therefore a command to read history as a record of gifts rather than as a claim of ancestry, and the sūrah will shortly fill the record in for anyone who has forgotten it.

**The Covenant, and How the Book Describes It**

Two covenants are described in detail elsewhere. One is made with the Children of Israel collectively, and it lists the terms: *“If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend to Allah a good loan, I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow.”* (5:12). The other covenant is made with the prophets as a body, binding each of them to believe in and support a messenger who comes after them confirming what they have (3:81).

The Book treats both as the same kind of arrangement, and the sūrah here addresses a community that inherited the first. What the verse asks is that the terms of that arrangement be honoured, and the sentence is explicit that the arrangement was mutual: they fulfil their side, and God fulfils His.

**"And I Will Fulfil Mine"**

The divine side of the promise is stated in the same sentence as the human obligation, and the Book never leaves the reader to guess at God's fidelity. The verse's grammar makes the two halves conditional on each other, but the Book elsewhere states God's trustworthiness as a settled attribute rather than a possibility: the covenant with the prophets is answered with an affirmation, they accept it, and God declares the witnesses.

Read against the human record the sūrah will go on to recount, the structure is an act of extraordinary generosity. The community being addressed has a history in which the covenant was repeatedly broken, the calf was worshipped, and the book was partly concealed. The promise in this verse is not withdrawn for that reason. It is reissued, with the terms restated, to the audience at hand.

**"And Stand in Awe of Me Alone"**

The command returns to the vocabulary the sūrah has used since its second verse: the quality rendered here as awe is the same one that describes the people for whom the Book is a guide. The word comes from a root that means to guard or shield oneself, and the Book treats it as the discipline of a person who arranges his conduct around what he knows is coming.

The addition of the word *alone* in this verse carries the weight. A community with a long history of foreign rule had every reason to fear the powers around it, and the sūrah's address to Israel includes instructions that will require courage and public conduct. The command to stand in awe of God alone is therefore not an emotional prompt but a political orientation, and it sets the terms for everything the subsequent verses require.

**Continuity Rather than Replacement**

The verse addresses a covenant rather than announcing a fresh one, and it invokes a memory rather than a discovery. That framing governs the next several pages of the sūrah, in which the revelation does not ask this community to repudiate its own scriptures but to accept what those scriptures pointed toward. The Book's claim about itself in this section is continuity, and the terms of the address in this verse prepare the reader for that claim.

What the sentence establishes is a relationship with a past, and the sūrah will make the same argument to the same community repeatedly. The favours named are their favours; the covenant is theirs; the God being addressed is the one their ancestors knew; and the request being made is that the record be honoured.

**Whose History the Sūrah Is Telling**

The address claims the audience's own ancestry and reads the record of that ancestry as a series of gifts. The Book states the terms of the covenant with this community in a later passage as an ordinary agreement with items on both sides: prayer, almsgiving, belief in the messengers and support for them, answered by forgiveness and gardens (5:12). The same chapter records the covenant with the prophets as a body, binding them to accept a messenger who confirms what they have (3:81).

Neither passage is presented as an innovation. The sūrah's argument to this audience assumes that the arrangement already exists and that the audience knows it exists, and that is why the command in this verse is to remember rather than to learn. What the Book adds is the claim that its own messenger belongs inside that existing history, which is the point the following verses develop.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:41

> Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Confirmation, Stated as the Book's Own Claim**

The verse asks its audience to accept a revelation on the ground that it confirms what they already possess. The claim is made for the Qur'an in several places, and in one of them the mechanism is named: the same angel who brought earlier messages brought this one, *“confirming what came before it”* (2:97). Another passage describes the revelation as a criterion and a light: *“There certainly has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book”* (5:15).

On the Book's own account, confirmation means two things, and the commentators kept both in view. The revelation agrees with the genuine content of the earlier scriptures, and it fulfils the announcements those scriptures carry about what was to come. Under the second reading the verse becomes a demand rather than a compliment, since a community that reads its own books would be reading a prediction of the very thing it is being invited to accept.

**"Do Not Be the First to Deny"**

The instruction is directed at people who were in a position to lead. The Book's phrasing implies that denial would spread from them to others, and the commentators read the warning as addressing those whose standing made their refusal consequential: scholars, teachers, and the men whose opinion the community followed. A farmer's rejection of a claim affects his own harvest; a teacher's affects everyone he teaches.

The Book's broader treatment of this community makes the same point about responsibility. Elsewhere it says that they were given the Scripture and knowledge, and that their failure would therefore be measured against what they knew (7:169). What the verse adds is a warning about sequence. Whoever is positioned first in a matter carries more of its weight, and the Book tells these readers that their place in the order is part of what they will answer for.

**"Or Trade Them for a Fleeting Gain"**

The second prohibition uses the market language the sūrah has already used for a spiritual loss, where the men who preferred their position to guidance were described as traders whose commerce failed them.
