The Book states the same charge against this community many times, and one verse names the price exactly: the covenant was taken from those who received the Scripture that they would make it known and not hide it, *“yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain. What a miserable profit!”* (3:187).

The profit in such cases is small in reality and large in appearance, which is why the phrase describes it as paltry. What could be bought with the truth about a coming prophet? Standing in a community, an appointment, an income, the approval of men whose opinion carried weight. The verse states the exchange without describing the currency, because the reader who knows the value of the thing sold does not need the price itemised.

**The Word for the Gain, and Its Implication**

The Arabic adjective rendered fleeting describes something slight in quantity and brief in duration. It is used in the Book for the whole of this world's goods when they are compared with what comes after, and it is applied to wealth, comfort and status without exception. The word's double sense — trivial and temporary — makes it a particularly precise instrument for this verse, since the things being purchased with the signs of God share both properties.

The Book's treatment of this language is not asceticism for its own sake. It does not tell its readers that standing, income and respect are worthless; it tells them that these goods have a shelf life and that truth does not. The trade being prohibited is a comparison, and the verse assumes the reader is capable of making it.

**"And Be Mindful of Me"**

The instruction returns to the word that opened the sūrah's description of the people who profit from the Book, and it closes the verse on a note of individual discipline. The other verbs in the sentence concern belief and honesty; this one names the condition that makes both possible over time. A person who guards himself is aware that the buyer in the transaction is not the community around him but the one who sees the exchange.

That closing clause also catches up with the previous verse, where the same command was given its full form: stand in awe of Me alone. The repetition is deliberate. What the sūrah is asking of this audience is that the regard they extend to their own position in society be measured against a loyalty that does not depend on that society, and the vocabulary carries the requirement straight through from one verse to the next.

**What Confirmation Requires of a Reader**

The logic of the verse is cumulative. If the revelation confirms the scriptures, then a person who values those scriptures has a reason to consider it; if he is placed where others will follow his lead, the cost of refusing grows; if the refusal is bought with advantages that will not last, the trade is a bad one; and if God is watching, the transaction is not private. The sentence assembles those four considerations and asks for one act.

The Book states the same case to the same audience again later, in different words. This verse is the compressed version, and it is placed near the beginning of the longest address in the Qur'an to this community, so that the argument is on the record before the history is recounted, the errors are listed, and the invitation is repeated.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:42

> Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Charge Is Adulteration, Not Denial**

The Arabic verb in the first clause carries the sense of clothing one thing with another, so that what is visible is no longer what is underneath. Its use here describes the blending of true and false in a single body of teaching, and the offence it names is a more careful crime than simple denial. Nobody is accused of renouncing the scripture; the accusation is that the scripture is being presented in a form that no longer says what it means.

The Book makes the same charge elsewhere with the same verb, and the translators render it either as mixing or confusing depending on the nuance being carried across. What remains constant is the concept: a message whose true content has been covered by an addition, so that the reader cannot separate the two and does not know that a separation is needed.

**Concealment Named as a Separate Act**

The second clause states a related offence in different language: hiding the truth deliberately. The Book treats the concealment of revelation as a breach of a specific undertaking, and it says so in a passage addressed to those who received scripture earlier: *“˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain.”* (3:187).

That covenant is the context for this verse, and it explains why the two clauses belong together. Concealment is the negative act — a part of the truth is removed from view — while mixing is the positive one, in which something else is put in its place. A teacher who does either has changed what his students receive, and the Book holds him responsible for the change regardless of how sincerely he may believe in it.

**"Knowingly": The Word That Removes the Excuse**

The final word of the sentence fixes the mental state of the offender. The Book draws the line between error and guilt at the point of knowledge, and it does so consistently: a person who misstates something he does not know is not the subject of this verse, while a person who knows what the text says and presents it otherwise is.

That distinction has consequences for how the passage should be read by any reader. The Book does not forbid teaching, interpreting or disagreeing; it forbids the deliberate alteration of a message one has been trusted with. The qualifier also protects honest scholarship from the accusation, since the offence requires knowledge of the truth being displaced, and no court of human beings can determine that condition. The verse is addressed to conscience.

**What the Community Was Concealing**

The reports connect the charge with the description of the coming prophet that this community's scholars were said to find in their own books, and with the clarity of the signs that identified him. Without adjudicating the details, the sūrah's context makes the general charge plain enough: the revelation in Madinah had come to a community that possessed earlier scripture, and the argument of these verses is that the new message matches what the old one contained.

The Book states the same claim about itself everywhere it addresses this community, and it always phrases the claim as confirmation rather than supersession. What the verse adds is that the possession of scripture is not a neutral fact. A community that holds a text holds a message, and a message belongs to the people it was sent to, not to the scholars who administer it.

**The Liability of Those Who Know**

The Book's harshest passages are reserved for the knowledgeable who mislead, and this verse is one of them. It is placed in the middle of a series of instructions that will include prayer, almsgiving, humility and patience, and it belongs to a category of offence that has no equivalent in ordinary criminal law. Nothing physically changes hands when a text is misrepresented; what changes is what other people will believe, and the Book treats that as the substance of the harm.

The sūrah will return to this theme with a question that sharpens it further, asking its audience how they can instruct others in righteousness while neglecting it themselves. The two verses work as a pair. One addresses the content of what is taught, the other the conduct of the teacher, and together they describe a community whose relationship to its own scripture has come apart.

**The Clothing Metaphor and What It Implies**

The metaphor buried in the verse's first verb is worth stating plainly. Clothing exists to cover, and a person who puts truth inside falsehood has decided that the truth needs covering. The Book's image suggests a deliberateness about the act that the rest of the sentence confirms, and it also suggests what the offender knows: nobody dresses something he values in something contemptible by accident.

That is why the two clauses are joined by a single command rather than presented as alternatives. Mixing and concealing are two ways of managing a truth that has become inconvenient, and the Book's remedy is stated in the same sentence form as everything else in this passage — a prohibition addressed to people whose position allowed them to confuse others. What the verse asks of them is the opposite of what it describes: let the truth stand where it can be seen.

**The Cost of a Managed Text**

A community that manages its scripture pays in a currency it does not immediately notice. Teaching that has been adjusted to fit a position produces students who cannot test the position, and the loss becomes visible only when a claim arrives that the adjusted text cannot evaluate. The sūrah's own audience is being addressed at exactly that moment, and the Book's argument to them assumes they still have access to what was written.

That is why the verse presents the offence as a breach of trust rather than a doctrinal error. The Book claims the ability to be checked, describing itself as a clear Book and inviting its hearers to compare it with what they already possess. Mixing and concealing make the comparison impossible, and the loss falls on the people who are prevented from making it rather than on the text.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:43

> Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Commands in One Sentence**

The verse gives its audience three instructions in a single line, and it arranges them from the individual to the communal. Prayer is first, the alms-tax second, and the act of bowing in company third. The first concerns a person's standing before God, the second concerns his obligations to the society around him, and the third concerns his visible membership in a body of worshippers.

The Book pairs prayer and almsgiving so regularly that the combination functions as a single idea in its vocabulary. The two together cover the two directions in which religion is expressed — toward God and toward people — and the sūrah's own description of the mindful at its opening named them in the same pair, with the giving described as coming from what God has provided. The command here is given to a community whose covenant included these terms, and the reader of this verse is being asked to recognise that the requirements are continuous with the ones his own tradition set.

**"Establish" Rather Than Merely "Perform"**

The Arabic verb for prayer in this verse is the one that means to set something upright and keep it standing. The Book uses it consistently for this command, and the choice distinguishes a practice that is maintained from an act that is completed once. A person who establishes a practice has arranged his day and his obligations around it; a person who performs an act has satisfied a requirement and moved on.

That distinction is important in a passage addressed to a community with a long ritual history. The Book does not tell them to begin worshipping; it tells them to make worship structural. The instruction is therefore about the shape of a life rather than the addition of a duty, and the Book's choice of verb carries the difference into every other passage where the same command appears.

**Almsgiving as a Term of the Covenant**

The second command names the obligatory payment of a portion of wealth, and the Book folds it into the same covenant whose terms it describes to this community elsewhere: *“If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend to Allah a good loan, I will certainly forgive your sins.”* (5:12). The verse at hand is a compressed version of that list, and the two items it selects are the ones the Book treats as the foundation of a religious community's public life.

The Book's usage of the term is not confined to one religious community. It states that earlier prophets commanded their people to pray and to give, and it presents the practice as part of the worship of God from the beginning. The sūrah is therefore not introducing a novelty and not imposing an Islamic institution on an unrelated tradition. It is telling this audience that the elements of its own covenant are still standing.

**"Bow With Those Who Bow"**

The third command is surprising for its specificity. Prayer and almsgiving are named as duties; the third is the act of bowing, and it is qualified by the people one bows with. The Book could have said "worship" and left the details to the reader; instead it names a physical posture and attaches it to a congregation.

The instruction carries two meanings at once. It requires participation in communal worship rather than a private observance, and it requires that the participant take his place beside others rather than preside over them. The physical fact of a row of worshippers lowering and rising together is one of the Book's recurring pictures of a community, and the command here makes that picture a requirement rather than an option.

**A Command Given to Israel and Kept by the Muslims**

The three acts named in this verse reappear in the Book's instructions to the new community, and the sūrah uses the same verbs. That continuity is the point of the verse in its context. The Book is addressing a people whose tradition already contained prayer, charity and prostration, and it names those practices rather than replacing them, so that the new revelation appears as the continuation of what the community already does.

The differences that later Islamic law introduced — the times, the forms, the amounts — do not change the underlying continuity the verse is asserting. What the sūrah assumes is a shared religious grammar, one in which a person stands before God, gives from what he has, and joins a congregation. The Book asks this community to keep the grammar it already knows rather than abandon it in favour of something else.

**Worship as a Public Fact**

The verse's three commands, taken together, describe a religious life that can be seen. Prayer has a timetable that others can observe, almsgiving moves property, and bowing is performed in the presence of other people. Nothing in the sentence is hidden, and the sūrah's audience is being asked for a form of piety that shows itself in conduct rather than in claims.

That theme runs through the entire address to this community, which will go on to fault scholars for teaching what they do not practise and to insist that the book in their hands be acted upon. The command in this verse sets the standard first, before any accusation is made: worship established, wealth shared, and a body of worshippers joined.

**The Congregation as a Public Standard**

The command to bow with those who bow makes worship a visible fact of community life, and the Book elsewhere uses the posture to describe the people it approves. A later passage lists the marks of the believers and includes among them the acts of bowing and prostrating themselves, together with encouraging good and forbidding evil (9:112). Posture appears on both lists, which means the Book treats the physical form of worship as part of what identifies a community rather than as a private detail.

A person who takes his place in such a row has accepted a discipline he cannot customise. The timing is set by others, the recitation is led, and his own condition is exposed to whoever stands beside him. The verse asks this audience for that kind of participation, and it does so before it raises any of the objections that will occupy the rest of the passage.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:44

> Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand?

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question Addressed to Teachers**

The verse is built as a question, and the question is aimed at people whose role was to instruct others. The Arabic verb describes ordering and commending something to another person, and the sentence is not about private devotion but about the public work of telling others how to live. The Book is asking how a person can recommend a good and then not perform it.

That situation is not unique to one generation. Any community that has a text, a school and an expectation that the learned will guide the unlearned will contain people whose instructions outrun their conduct. The sūrah places the question in the middle of its address to a community with a long tradition of scholarship, and it does so without softening the terms.

**Righteousness as a Word Wider Than Ritual**

The word being preached is rendered as righteousness, and the Book gives the term its fullest definition elsewhere in the same sūrah: *“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets”* (2:177), after which the verse lists giving to relatives, orphans, travellers and beggars, establishing prayer, paying alms, keeping promises, and patience in hardship.

The definition is worth keeping in mind when reading this verse, because it means the standard being preached and neglected is not a small one. Righteousness in the Book covers belief, generosity, worship, honesty and endurance together. A person who urges that whole on others while practising part of it has not merely failed at a detail; he has separated a single word into a message for his listeners and an exemption for himself.

**The Charge Is Not Ignorance**

The verse adds a clause that closes the obvious excuse: they read the Scripture. Whatever the source of their conduct, it is not a lack of information. The Book is explicit about this pattern elsewhere, describing a community that was well versed in its teachings and still departed from them, and asking whether a covenant had not been taken from them in the Scripture (7:169).

The sūrah's accusation is therefore about knowledge that has failed to become conduct. That is a different matter from a person who does not know what is required, and the Book holds the two cases far apart. Its harshest language is reserved for those whose position came from knowing, since their influence multiplied whatever example they set.

**"Do You Not Understand?"**

The closing question appeals to the faculty the Book elsewhere treats as the seat of accountability. It is not asking whether the audience has mastered a text; it is asking whether they see the contradiction in what they are doing. The Book uses this kind of question repeatedly, and its function is always to place the listener inside the judgement rather than outside it.

The implication is that the absurdity is available to reason and does not require revelation to detect. Anyone can notice that a rule he presses on others also applies to him, and the Book treats the failure to notice as a failure of the understanding rather than of the memory. The question is therefore not rhetorical abuse; it assumes the audience is able to answer it correctly and is not doing so.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**

Nothing in the sentence forbids instruction. The Book commands that knowledge be conveyed and warns against concealing it, and the preceding verses of this sūrah fault this same community for hiding what they were given. The verse rebukes a gap between teaching and conduct, not the act of teaching, and it leaves the duty to instruct in place.

That distinction matters for anyone who reads the verse as a reason to fall silent. The Book's position is that the message should continue to be delivered and that the messenger should be the first to comply with it. The question in this verse is addressed to a teacher mid-lecture; it does not stop the lecture, it corrects the situation of the person giving it.

**A Measure That Turns Back on the Reader**

The verse is written in the second person plural, and it is addressed to a specific community in a specific place. Nothing about it restricts the scope of the correction, and the sūrah's later treatment of the new community shows why: the Book warns the believers against the same pattern, and it does so in a passage that rebukes those who say what they do not do. The correction is a permanent feature of the Book's teaching about knowledge.

A reader who finishes the sentence and applies it only to the people being addressed has not read it. The Book's habit is to record a fault of one community and then hold every subsequent community to the same standard, and this verse is placed near the beginning of the longest such record in the Qur'an. The question remains open to everyone who has ever urged a good on someone else, and the Book's next sentence supplies the remedy rather than leaving the reader to find one.

**The Order of the Sūrah's Correction**

The correction is not delivered as an accusation followed by a threat. The sūrah gives the community three commands in the previous verse, then asks a question about the gap between teaching and conduct, and then immediately supplies the remedy in the next: seeking help through patience and prayer. The instruction, the diagnosis and the treatment arrive in that order.

That arrangement is worth noting for anyone reading the passage as a polemic. The Book does not use the community's failure as a reason to set them aside. It continues to speak to them as people whose speech about righteousness was right, and it treats the problem as one of practice. The question in this verse and the counsel that follows are addressed to the same audience in the same breath, and the sūrah will go on addressing them for another fifty verses.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:45

> And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Instruments Offered After a Rebuke**

The verse arrives immediately after a question that exposed a failure, and it does not continue the accusation. It offers a method. The audience has been told that its conduct and its teaching disagree, and the Book's response to that diagnosis is to name two practices that carry a person through the difficulty of correcting himself.

The sūrah has already paired these two activities in its description of the believers: faith in the unseen, prayer, and giving from what they were provided. Here the pairing appears as counsel rather than description, and the difference in function is worth noticing. The Book does not only tell its readers what a believer looks like; it tells them what to do when they are not yet that.

**Patience as Both Endurance and Persistence**

The Arabic word rendered patience carries two senses that English splits apart. It means bearing hardship without collapsing, and it means staying on a course without drifting, and the Book uses it in both ways. The same word stands behind the closing injunction of the sūrah that describes human beings as being in loss unless they believe, act rightly, urge one another to truth, and urge one another to perseverance (103:3).

That double meaning explains why the Book treats patience as a resource rather than a virtue to be admired. A person correcting his own conduct needs the first sense, since change involves loss and discomfort; a person holding to a position against pressure needs the second. The verse offers the word as an instrument, and it assumes both needs are present in the audience being addressed.

**Prayer as the Second Resource**

The second instrument is the act of worship, and the Book names it here without describing its content. The assumption is that the audience knows what it means to stand before God, since the same sūrah's instruction to this community has already told them to establish the practice. What the verse adds is the purpose of turning an ordinary duty into assistance.

The Book describes prayer as remembrance elsewhere and ties the practice to the presence of the one being addressed: *“So worship Me ˹alone˺, and establish prayer for My remembrance.”* (20:14). It also states the same counsel to the new community in almost the same words, adding a promise to the command: *“O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient.”* (2:153). What the Book offers in this verse is therefore not a technique for feeling better but an orientation for the day.

**"It Is a Burden"**

The Arabic word rendered as burden is a noun denoting something weighty, and the Book does not pretend that the practice is light. Fasting, giving, waking for prayer and tolerating criticism all cost a person something, and the verse acknowledges that cost in a single clause rather than promising that the difficulty will disappear.

The Book's honesty about this is characteristic. It describes the night prayer as an effort, the fight for justice as painful, and the giving of wealth as a sacrifice, and it does not sell its requirements as easy. What the sentence does is name the exception that makes the burden bearable, and the exception is not a technique or a mood but a disposition.

**The Exception: The Humble**

The last word of the verse identifies the people who can carry the practice lightly, and the Arabic term comes from a root describing lowering oneself and settling calmly. The Book uses it for the bearing of a person who accepts his position before God without resentment, and it connects the quality directly to the acceptance of guidance.

The link with the sūrah's previous narrative is worth noticing. Iblīs refused a command because he considered himself the superior party, and his refusal is the Book's standing example of a creature whose sense of rank closed him to an instruction. The humble in this verse are the exact opposite kind of person, and their reward is that the same practices others find intolerable become the means by which they are helped.

**Why Help Is Asked For Rather Than Assumed**

The verse's instruction is that assistance be sought, not that it be expected as a matter of course. The Book consistently recommends petition and practice together, and the counsel here is addressed to people who have a problem they cannot solve by intending to do better. What they are told is to hold on and to worship, and the next sentence describes the people for whom those two acts are not a burden.

That next sentence identifies a state of mind rather than a level of performance, and it is the hinge on which the whole instruction turns. The Book's counsel about patience and prayer is not offered to the strong; it is offered to everyone, and it works for those who have already settled the question of what they are and where they are going.

**Help Sought for the Work That Was Just Required**

The two instruments in this verse are given for a specific difficulty. The previous verses required prayer, almsgiving and public worship, and then faulted the community for teaching what it did not practise. Patience and prayer are offered as support for doing exactly those things, which makes the sentence a practical answer to a diagnosis rather than a general remark about hardship.

The Book warns the believers in another sūrah against the same gap between speech and action, asking why they say what they do not do and describing the inconsistency as despicable in the sight of God (61:2 to 61:3). The counsel in this verse is what the Book offers both audiences in place of the gap. Nobody is told that the standard will be lowered or that his conduct is acceptable because his intentions are sound; he is told where to find strength for the work.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:46

> those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Humble Identified by What They Expect**

The previous verse named a group who find prayer and patience manageable, and this verse says who they are. The defining mark the Book chooses is not a practice but a conviction about the future. What distinguishes these people is that they are settled about a meeting and a return, and everything else in the sentence follows from that.

The Book's method here is to attach a behaviour to a belief rather than the other way round. The verse does not say that people who fast and give will come to believe in the Hereafter; it says that people who are certain of meeting their Lord find the practices light. The order tells the reader where the sūrah thinks the difficulty of religious practice actually lies.

**Certainty, and the Word the Book Uses for It**

The Arabic verb rendered as being certain also carries the sense of supposing and of expecting, and the Book uses it across that range depending on context. In this verse the meaning is conviction, and the qualifying construction gives it the strength of a settled conclusion rather than a hopeful guess. Commentators were alert to the ambivalence of the verb, and they read the context as determining which sense applies.

The Book uses the same root elsewhere for the suppositions of people who are wrong, which shows that the word itself does not guarantee the quality of what is thought. What makes the usage in this verse significant is its object. The thing these people are certain about is not a forecast or an opinion but an appointment, and the Book presents that certainty as the axis on which a whole life turns.

**"Meeting Their Lord": the Book's Term for the Hereafter**

The phrase recurs throughout the Qur'an as one of the standard names for the world to come, and the Book uses it in promises and in warnings alike. It tells the Prophet to announce that whoever hopes for this meeting should act rightly and worship God alone (18:110), and it states that the appointed time for it is certain to arrive (29:5). Against those statements it sets the loss of those who deny it: *“Lost indeed will be those who denied the meeting with Allah, and were not ˹rightly˺ guided!”* (10:45), and a sūrah that describes such people as carrying their burdens on their backs (6:31).

The phrasing is worth noting because of what it says about death. The Book does not describe the end of life as an ending; it describes it as an arrival before someone, which is why the vocabulary of meeting appears so often where a modern reader would expect the vocabulary of death. What is being denied by the deniers in those verses is a confrontation, not an extinction.

**"And to Him They Will Return"**

The second half of the verse states the direction of the journey, and the Book uses the image of return for the whole of human existence: *“O humanity! Indeed, you are labouring restlessly towards your Lord, and will ˹eventually˺ meet the consequences.”* (84:6). The term implies that the creature has come from where it is going, so that the end of life is neither a novelty nor an exile but a movement back toward its source.

That image governs how the Book evaluates everything else. Wealth, standing and difficulty are all temporary because the traveller is temporary, and the sūrah's earlier argument about provision and the earth being arranged as a dwelling for a limited stay rests on the same conception. The people described in this verse live with the destination in front of them, and the verse presents that arrangement as the reason they can carry what others cannot.

**Why This Conviction Makes Discipline Bearable**

The connection between this verse and the previous one is causal. Prayer requires a person to interrupt his day and present himself before a God he cannot see; patience requires him to absorb losses without retaliation. Both are only rational if the story continues past death and if the account is settled by someone with authority over the whole of it.

Strip the certainty away and the arithmetic changes. A person who believes that this life is all there is has good reason to treat prayer as an interruption and forgiveness as a surrender. The Book does not argue that such a person lacks motivation; it states plainly that the practices it recommends are a burden except for those who know how the story ends, and it leaves the reader to work out which description fits him.

**The Portrait Completed in Two Clauses**

The verse describes one group of people with two statements, and together they rule out the two most common ways of getting the future wrong. A person who expects a meeting but does not expect a reckoning has only exchanged one form of comfort for another. A person who expects judgement in general but not a return to a particular Lord has not understood who is doing the judging. The verse states both facts and attaches them to the same people.

What the sūrah has done with these two verses is to answer the question its earlier rebuke raised. The previous passage accused a community of teaching what it did not practise, and the Book's response was to name two practices and the state of mind that makes them possible. The portrait in this verse is the standard the reader is invited to measure himself against, and the sūrah moves from it to the further favours owed to the community it has been addressing.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:47

> O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Summons, Almost Word for Word**

The verse repeats the opening of the address given seven verses earlier, and the repetition is intentional. In the Qur'an, a command to remember that is issued twice marks the theme as central to the passage, and the intervening verses have in the meantime supplied content for the memory: the covenant, the confirmation of scripture, the prohibition on mixing truth with falsehood, the three commands, the rebuke about teaching, and the portrait of the humble.

So the reader reaches this verse with a filled-in picture of what remembering means. It is not nostalgia and it is not a compliment to ancestors. The Book's use of the verb here carries the sense of bringing something to mind in a way that changes present conduct, and the second issuance of the command makes the requirement unmistakable.

**"Above the Others," and What It Consisted Of**

The Book explains the favour in concrete terms rather than leaving it as an honorific. One verse lists the components: *“Indeed, We gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood; granted them good, lawful provisions; and favoured them above the others.”* (45:16). Another summarises the same history from Moses' mouth: *“Remember Allah's favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign, and gave you what He had never given anyone in the world.”* (5:20).

Elsewhere the Book states the choice in one line: *“And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others.”* (44:32). The favour was therefore historical and specific. A people held in slavery received deliverance, a law, a land, and a continuous line of messengers, and the Book treats that record as the fact the community's identity rests on.

**Favour as a Trust Rather Than a Privilege**

The Book nowhere treats the election as an unconditional possession. It states the conditions attached to the favour in the same passage that commands the community to remember it, and it makes fidelity to the covenant the means by which the favour continues. The most striking statement of this appears in the description of the messenger awaited in their own scriptures: the one described in the Torah and the Gospel, who commands what is right and relieves burdens (7:157).

That description turns the favour into an examination. A community that has been given prophets and books is a community that has been given the means to recognise the next messenger when he arrives, and the Book's address to this audience assumes exactly that situation. What was granted as a gift functions in the argument of the sūrah as a responsibility that is now coming due.

**The Shift the Book Announces Elsewhere**

The Qur'an does not present the favour as a permanent entitlement that no later community can share. In a passage addressed to the believers, it declares: *“You are the best community ever raised for humanity—you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah.”* (3:110), and the same verse goes on to say that some among the People of the Book are faithful while most are rebellious. The favour in this verse is therefore a historical fact, not a claim that survives every generation unchanged.

The sūrah's audience was in a position to test this against its own situation. The community addressed in Madinah had the scripture, the learning and the standing that came with an old tradition, and the Book tells it that these assets are held on terms. The reminder of honour received is followed by the obligation to make one's conduct consistent with it.

**Why the Reminder Comes Before the Reckoning**

The verses that follow this one recount the favours one by one: the deliverance from Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, the appointment with Moses, and the forgiveness after the calf. They also record the failures in the same sequence, so that the section is a history with two columns. The Book begins with the good column, and it does so twice.

That order is not merely polite. The Book's purpose in the passage is to renew an invitation, and a recitation of failures that opened the section would have foreclosed the argument before it started. The reminder of favour is the ground on which the later questions rest, and the command to remember appears at the head of the passage because memory is what makes the rest of the address intelligible.

**Memory as Accountability**

The verb at the centre of this verse is used in the Book for a mental act with consequences. To remember a favour, in the Qur'an's usage, is to be aware of it in a way that shapes what one does next, and the Book's frequent pairing of memory with gratitude and with conduct follows from that. A person who forgets what he has received will read his own position as something he produced.

The community being addressed is therefore not asked to feel a particular way about its history. It is asked to keep in view the fact that its scripture, its teachers and its standing came from someone, and that the same someone is now speaking to it again. The verse names the favours and the honour in a single sentence, and it leaves the consequences of remembering to the verses that follow.

**How This Verse Sits in the Address**

The summons brackets a block of argument. The first occurrence opened the address with a command to remember the favours and honour the covenant; the verses between it and this one supplied the terms of that covenant, the instruction to believe what confirms the existing scripture, the prohibition on mixing and concealing, three commands, a rebuke about conduct, and a portrait of the people who find the requirements light. This second occurrence closes that block and turns it toward the historical record.

The repetition also prepares the reader for what follows. From the next verse onward the sūrah recites the favours in detail and then reports the failures that accompanied them, and the command to remember is what authorises the whole recitation. The audience is being asked to accept its own history as evidence, and the Book issues the summons twice so that nobody reaches the list of failures without having first been told what the list is for.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:48

> Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Warning Framed as Self-Protection**

The verse opens with the same verb that stands behind the Book's central term for God-consciousness: guard yourselves. Its force here is literal rather than emotional. The audience is told to put something between itself and a named event, and the rest of the sentence explains what the event will be like by listing four things that will not work.

The sentence is not a description of the Day for its own sake. The sūrah has been addressing a community with a long tradition and a strong sense of its own standing, and the list of what fails on that Day is a list of precisely the resources such a standing might suggest. Nothing else in the verse explains its contents, and the audience of the revelation is expected to recognise its own arrangements in it.

**No Soul Aids Another**

The first clause removes the possibility of assistance from any human being at all. It does not say that some will be unable to help; it states a general condition of the Day, and the Book repeats it in its description of other scenes: the same sūrah will state it again later in almost identical words, and the sūrah that describes the Day as an hour-long recollection notes that people will appear as strangers to one another (10:45).

The Book's point is not that human beings become indifferent in the afterlife. It is that the ties and exchanges on which human society runs have no purchasing power there. A tribe can defend its member before a ruler; a family can share a fine among its sons; a patron can speak for a client. The verse states that the whole apparatus will be absent, and it states this to a community whose identity rested on lineage.

**Intercession and the Conditions the Book Attaches**

The second clause denies that intercession will be accepted, and the Book elsewhere places intercession under the authority of God: *“Say, ‘All intercession belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. To Him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.’”* (39:44). The sūrah's own verse of the throne states the doctrine in the form of a question: *“Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission?”* (2:255).

The two passages show that the Book does not abolish intercession as such; it removes it from the category of things a person can arrange. Intercession exists in the Qur'an on terms that are not disclosed to the parties involved, and none of the Book's statements about it can be converted into a personal guarantee. What this verse denies is the use of a sponsor in the way a client is used in a courtroom.

**Ransom Rejected and the Currency That Fails**

The third clause names a specific transaction: the payment offered for release. The Arabic word describes a substitute given in place of the thing owed, and the Book uses it when it describes the wealth that will not be accepted in exchange for relief. The world's currencies, in the Book's account of the Day, do not exist; wealth is left behind with everything else, and the price of a person's conduct is not money.

The Book's treatment of this theme in the sūrah echoes its earlier discussions of trade and profit, where the men who preferred their position to guidance were described as merchants whose business failed. The connection is direct: the same measure of value the Book applies to worldly bargains is applied here, and the result is the same in both cases.

**The Four Denials and Their Order**

The sentence lists its four clauses in an order that moves from the general to the specific and back again. It begins with the failure of all human assistance, narrows to the two mechanisms by which such assistance was actually procured in the society being addressed — intercession and ransom — and closes by stating once more that no help will be forthcoming.

The repetition at the end is not stylistic padding. The Book's audiences had practical confidence in three things: their kin, their intercessors and their wealth, and the sentence removes them in reverse order of confidence. The last clause summarises the result: none of the three will function, and no fourth avenue is suggested.

**What the Verse Assumes About Its Audience**

The prohibitions in this verse would be unnecessary in a community that placed no value on the things being denied. The Book is speaking to people whose social world ran on patronage, ancestry and negotiated compensation, and the warning is framed in their own currency. The same technique appears throughout the Book's descriptions of the Day: the scenes are built from the institutions the audience actually used, so that the removal of those institutions is felt rather than merely reported.

The command that opens the sentence is therefore addressed to people who have something to lose, and the point of the warning is to move them before the loss occurs. The verse does not describe the Day in order to satisfy curiosity about it. It names the day, removes the four supports, and asks its hearers to arrange their lives while the arrangement is still possible.

**Preparing for Obedience That Costs Something**

The warning immediately precedes a passage of commands addressed to this community, and it removes the assumptions that would make obedience optional. A person who believes that a relative can settle his case, that a patron can speak for him, or that a payment can be arranged has reason to postpone attention to his own conduct. The verse states that on the day that matters, none of those arrangements will exist.

What the Book does with the warning is practical rather than speculative. It does not describe the Day in order to satisfy curiosity; it describes it in order to make the audience act while action is possible. The three supports the sentence removes are the three the community actually relied upon, and their removal is stated in the plainest language available. Everything the sūrah asks of the audience afterwards is asked of people who have been told that they will stand alone.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:49

> ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Favour Named in Full**

The command to remember the favours, issued twice in the preceding verses, now begins to be answered with specifics. The first item on the list is a rescue, and the Book describes it by describing what was being escaped. The sentence gives the oppressor, the method of oppression, and the two categories of victim, so that the reader understands the scale of what the community was brought out of.

That order matters for the passage. Before the Book asks anything of this community, it recites what the community received, and it recites it in the vocabulary of an ordinary historical record rather than of a sermon. The deliverance is presented as an event the audience is expected to know, and the memory is being invoked as evidence of the relationship that the following commands will ask them to honour.

**The Killings and the Policy Behind Them**

The oppression is described with two clauses that belong to a single policy: the male children were killed and the women were kept alive. The Book states the same arrangement in the sūrah of Stories: *“Indeed, Pharaoh ˹arrogantly˺ elevated himself in the land and divided its people into ˹subservient˺ groups, one of which he persecuted, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women. He was truly one of the corruptors.”* (28:4). The purpose of such a measure is control, and it explains why the community could not grow out of its position.

The Qur'an does not supply a reason for the killing beyond that, and the commentator al-Rāzī noted the implications. Since Pharaoh threatened the same policy again when Moses had grown up, the murders are better understood as a standing instrument of domination than as the result of an astrologer's prediction about a child who would overthrow him. The Book's own account supports the broader reading by tying the persecution to the policy of dividing a subject people.

**"Keeping Your Women"**

The second half of the phrase is easy to pass over and is part of the same description of tyranny. To keep the women alive was to keep them without protection, and the arrangement ensured both that the community could not increase and that its members could be used at the will of the ruling house. The Book includes the phrase in each of the two passages where it describes these events, which means it is not incidental to its account of the suffering.

The Qur'an's concern with this kind of detail is consistent. When it describes the affliction of a people, it names the specific harms done to those who had no power to prevent them, and it treats the fate of the vulnerable as the measure of a regime. The verse's hearers are being shown their own history as the Book remembers it, and the memory emphasises the position they once occupied.

**"A Severe Test From Your Lord"**

The closing clause names the whole experience a trial, and the word carries the sense of testing that reveals something. The Book uses it for both hardship and prosperity, and it applies the term to what a person goes through rather than to what a person deserves. In this case the trial is the suffering itself, and the Book presents it as having come from the Lord of the community that endured it.

The phrasing therefore holds two facts together: the oppressor is responsible for the cruelty, and the event takes place within the government of God. The Book nowhere treats tyranny as an accident or an absence of providence, and the verse assigns the trial to God without diminishing the guilt of the ones inflicting it. That combination recurs throughout the Qur'an's accounts of the prophets, where the persecution of a messenger and his people is described as a test and the persecutors are held to account for every act.

**What the Memory Was For**

The verse is the first item in a list of favours that the sūrah recites to prepare its audience for a request, and the sequence is instructive. Deliverance from a murderous regime comes first, and the Book states the deliverance before it narrates the escape itself. The reader learns that a people was saved from its oppressor before he learns how the saving happened.

The sūrah then continues to the sea and to the appointment with Moses, so that the passage amounts to a recitation of the community's foundations. What the Book is doing is claiming the audience's own history and reading it as a series of gifts. When the request to accept the confirming messenger arrives, it arrives to people who have just been reminded that everything they are as a community began with an act of rescue.

**What the Book Does With Oppression**

The Book records the persecution of a people in specific terms, and it does so in a passage that has nothing to gain from embellishment. The pharaoh's policy, the killing of male children and the retention of the women, is named in two separate sūrahs with the same vocabulary, and another verse explains the policy as part of a systematic division of a subject population (28:4). The Qur'an does not present tyranny as an unfortunate accident of politics; it presents it as a crime with a method.

The detail about the vulnerable is part of the Book's manner throughout. When it describes the suffering of a community, it names the harm done to those who could not defend themselves, and it treats those specifics as the measure of the regime. The audience being addressed is told what their ancestors endured, and the memory is placed at the head of the favours because deliverance from it is the foundation of everything that follows.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:50

> And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rescue Described as an Event They Watched**

The second item on the list is the crossing, and the Book reports three things in one sentence: the sea was divided, the community was saved, and the pursuing regime was destroyed. The closing phrase, that this happened before their eyes, turns the event into testimony. The audience being addressed is not being reminded of a story it heard; it is being reminded of something its ancestors saw.

That detail is part of the sūrah's argument throughout this passage. The Book recounts the favours of a community as matters of public, observable history, and it attaches the identity of the audience to those events. An appeal to a memory that everyone in the audience shares is an appeal that cannot be answered by denial, and the passage builds its case on that ground before it makes any demand.

**How the Book Tells the Event Elsewhere**

Another sūrah records the mechanism with a single command and a single result: *“So We inspired Moses: ‘Strike the sea with your staff,’ and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain.”* (26:63). The Book uses the image of mountains for the walls of water, which conveys both the scale of what was divided and the impossibility of the crossing without it.

Elsewhere the Book connects the crossing to the pursuit, so that the deliverance and the destruction are two aspects of one event. What is constant across the tellings is the absence of any account of engineering or effort. The people are commanded to move, the water opens, they cross, and the enemy behind them does not. The Book's narration of the event is spare, and its emphasis falls on who did it rather than on how it was done.

**"Before Your Very Eyes"**

The phrase is worth its own consideration, because the Book uses the visibility of an event to establish a standard of responsibility. A community whose ancestors watched an intervention does not need to be convinced that God acts in history; the question posed to it is what it does with the knowledge. The same logic governs the sūrah's treatment of the signs in creation, which are described as visible to anyone who looks.

The wording also disposes of a possible objection. The crossing could have been narrated as a rescue reported to a later generation, which would make the audience's acceptance a matter of trust in a tradition. By attaching the event to their own sight, the Book addresses the descendants as people who have seen it, and it treats the interval of generations as no barrier to the claim being theirs.

**The Drowning of the Regime**

The third clause names the destruction of the people of Pharaoh, and the Book does not soften the account. The same water that carried the rescued carried the pursuers down, and the Book's version of the event gives no indication that this was anything other than a judgment executed by the power that made the crossing possible. The Book elsewhere calls Pharaoh and his hosts corruptors and oppressors, and the phrasing here makes clear that the death of the regime was part of the deliverance rather than an incidental by-product.

That pairing is one of the Book's frequent patterns. The Qur'an describes the relief of the oppressed and the fall of the oppressor in the same passage, and it does not present the second fact as something to be overlooked. Within the sūrah's list of favours, the destruction of the enemy is the last item in the sentence that describes the rescue, and it appears as its completion.

**The Same Water Serving Two Ends**

Nature in the Qur'an belongs to its maker and follows commands that are not its own, and the sea in this verse is a particularly clear instance: it becomes a road for one party and a grave for another in the course of a single night. The Book uses water the same way in the story of Noah, where the flood is both rescue and judgment, and it tells the reader that the created world is not indifferent to the moral order established by its Lord.

The Book makes the point explicit when it describes the sea's opening as an act carried out for a people who had no part in bringing it about. Nothing in the account credits the community with the miracle; the command is given to Moses, and the result is credited to God. What the community is given is the crossing and the memory of watching it.

**From Rescue to Obligation**

The passage continues from this verse into the appointment with Moses and the incident of the calf, so that the Book alternates between gift and failure for the rest of the section. What the reader is meant to carry from the crossing is not only gratitude but the recognition that the community's very existence on the far shore was granted. There would have been no people to receive a law if the sea had not opened.

That is the standing assumption of the address that ends the section, and it explains why the Book keeps returning to this particular event. A people that understands where it came from is in a position to hear what is being asked of it now, and the sūrah's recitation of the rescue is doing the work of preparation.

**The Sea as a Witness Left Standing**

The crossing is treated in the Qur'an as a sign that outlives the generation that watched it. The Book refers to the event in several sūrahs, always with the same elements: the command to strike the water, the splitting, and the destruction of the pursuers. What the sūrah here adds is the standing of the event as a favour owed to the descendants of those who crossed.

That treatment has a consequence for how the audience should read its own position. A community whose origin is a rescue cannot explain itself in terms of its own achievements, and the Book keeps the event in front of its hearers precisely because it settles the question of who is responsible for their existence. The mercy that opened the sea is the same mercy being appealed to in the address that continues through the rest of the section.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:51

> And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully.

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Appointment and an Absence**

The verse places two events in a single sentence: a meeting arranged between God and Moses, and the conduct of the community while their leader was away. The two are joined by the word rendered *then*, which makes the second event follow the first in time and stand against it in character. The reader gets no explanation of the interval; the Book allows the contrast to do the work.

The structure is characteristic of this section, where the favours and the failures of the community are arranged next to each other. Deliverance from Pharaoh and the crossing of the sea have just been recited; the appointment on the mountain is a further honour granted to the people through their prophet; and the sentence ends with what the people did with the time it gave them.

**The Forty Nights**

The Book states the duration of the appointment in one number and explains the detail elsewhere: *“We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten— completing his Lord's term of forty nights.”* (7:142). The passage also records what Moses did before he left, placing his brother in charge of the people with an instruction to act rightly and not to follow the corruptors.

The thirty plus ten tells the reader that the period was extended, and the sūrah of al-Baqarah compresses the whole into the final total. What matters for the argument here is that the period was set by God and known to Moses. The community was not abandoned in the dark about their affairs; they had a leader who had been summoned, a deputy who had been appointed, and a stated duration to wait.

**What They Made While He Was Away**

The Qur'an describes the object in detail in another sūrah, and the description aims at its absurdity: *“In the absence of Moses, his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound. Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path? Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers.”* (7:148). The Book's account names the material, which was the wealth they had been given, and the sound, which was the full extent of its powers.

The verses in al-Baqarah do not repeat these details, and the omission is part of the sūrah's manner in this section: it states the act and lets the reader who knows the fuller account supply the picture. What the shortened version preserves is the sequence — appointment, absence, worship of a thing made by hand — and the judgment it deserves.

**"Acting Wrongfully"**

The closing phrase uses the same word the sūrah has applied to Adam's transgression and to Iblīs's refusal in different forms. The Book's vocabulary for wrong in this chapter is consistent: it describes the person who places a thing where it does not belong, and it applies the term to the one who damages himself as readily as to the one who damages others.

Here the wrong is unmistakable. A people who had been rescued from a regime that claimed divine status had turned, within weeks of their rescue, to an object they had manufactured. The Book does not present this as a lapse in information. The command against association with God had been given, the signs had been public, and the man who had led them out of Egypt was still on the mountain that had been split open before their eyes.

**The Test Hidden in a Leader's Absence**

The episode establishes a pattern the sūrah uses for the rest of its address to this community. A leader is removed for a while, and the community's conduct in the interval reveals what their commitment rested on. The Book elsewhere reports Moses' own words on returning and Aaron's answer about being unable to control the people, and it treats the failure as a test of the community rather than of its prophet.

That reading is consistent with the sūrah's earlier account of Adam, where the test was also a relatively small prohibition under conditions of abundance. The Qur'an tests by removing supports rather than by applying pressure directly, and the absence of Moses was the removal of a support. What the calf-worship shows is that the faith of the crowd had been anchored to a man rather than to the Lord who sent him.

**What the Book Makes of the Episode**

The sūrah returns to this failure later in the chapter when it recounts the community's own words about it, and it uses the incident as one item in a long list of violations. The Book's purpose in repeating it is not to humiliate an ancient people but to make the record complete, because the request being made to their descendants in Madinah rests on the whole of it.

Placed where it is, the verse also prepares the reader for what follows. The sūrah has just described the rescue at the sea, and it now reports the first major failure in the community's history as a free people. The verses that follow will state the pardon extended to them, which means the passage is moving in its familiar rhythm: gift, failure, mercy, and a fresh invitation.

**Jewellery From Egypt and the Speed of the Decline**

The Book notes where the material for the idol came from: gold ornaments, which in the fuller account were the jewellery the community had carried out of Egypt (7:148). What was given as the spoil of their rescue was melted down to make the thing that replaced their rescuer. The detail is not incidental; it is the Book's way of showing how quickly a gift can be turned against its giver.

The interval matters as well. The appointment lasted forty nights, which is a short period even by ordinary human measure. Within it, a people who had watched the sea open took up worship of an object they had made and could hear making a lowing sound. The sūrah does not explain the psychology of the change, and it does not need to. The sequence is stated, and the reader is left with the contrast between what they had seen and what they did.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:52

> Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pardon Stated After Idolatry**

The verse follows a report of worship offered to a manufactured idol, and it begins with a concessive phrase that acknowledges the severity of what it is passing over. The Book does not minimise the offence; it names it and then states that forgiveness was granted anyway. The effect is a sentence in which the mercy is measured against the transgression rather than against a general human frailty.

That combination recurs throughout the Qur'an's account of this community, and it recurs with the same verb. Time after time the narrative runs from a specific breach to a specific pardon, and the Book repeats the pattern enough that the reader cannot mistake it for exceptional treatment. The pardon here is not described as a reward for anything the community did between the two events, because the record gives no such interval.

**The Concessive Word and What It Conveys**

The phrase translated as *even then* sets the sin and the forgiveness side by side and lets the reader supply the surprise. Used in this position, it makes the second half of the sentence an act of restraint rather than a legal outcome, and the Book's language elsewhere confirms that reading: it describes God as slow to punish, forbearing, and willing to accept repentance from a people whose record would justify otherwise.

The sūrah's earlier account of Adam uses the same pattern, where a transgression is narrated and a pardon is stated in the next verse. What differs between the two scenes is the scale of the offence: one prohibition was crossed in a garden by two individuals, and in this case an entire community turned to an idol after watching the sea divide. The Book's willingness to state both pardons in the same tone is itself a teaching about the scope of divine mercy.

**The Verb Behind the Forgiveness**

The Arabic verb used here carries the sense of effacing or wiping away a trace, and the Book uses it for the removal of sins rather than for the cancellation of their natural consequences. That distinction matters for how the passage should be read, because the community in this story went on to face other consequences of its conduct. What is removed by the pardon is the standing charge, not the memory of the event.

The sūrah will keep mentioning the calf in later verses, which shows that the Book does not treat a pardon as erasure from history. The community carries the record, and the reader is told about it in revelation. What the pardon restores is the relationship that the offence had broken, and the Book presents that restoration as the point of the whole arrangement.

**The Purpose Named: Gratitude**

The sentence ends with a stated intention, and the purpose named is not obedience or fear but thankfulness. The Book links gratitude to increase in a well-known verse: *“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord proclaimed, ‘If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.’”* (14:7). Gratitude in the Qur'an is therefore not merely a sentiment but a response that changes what follows.

Gratitude is also the appropriate answer to a pardon, and the Book treats it as such in this verse. A community that has been spared a punishment it had earned has nothing to offer in return that would match the gift. What the verse asks for instead is recognition — a people that knows what it was given and acts accordingly.

**Grace Without Approval of the Act**

Nothing in this verse suggests that the worship of the calf was acceptable or that the community's conduct was ultimately harmless. The Book's judgment on the act stands in the previous sentence and in the later passages that refer back to it, and the pardon concerns the persons rather than the deed. The sentence therefore holds two facts in balance: an act deserving punishment, and a people not punished for it.

That balance is the Book's regular way of describing divine forgiveness, and the sūrah will state the same arrangement in the prayer of its final verse, where believers ask for pardon, forgiveness and mercy. The whole of al-Baqarah ends with a request for exactly what this verse reports as already granted in the story of Israel, which ties the community of the revelation to the community of the exodus.

**Rescue, Failure and Pardon as a Pattern**

This verse is the third movement of a sequence that the sūrah has repeated several times. A gift is given, the recipients fail, and mercy follows. The sequence is not presented as a cycle without end, and the Book does not suggest that the pardon removes the need for change. Several of the verses that follow will raise further failures from the same community's history, and the tone of the address will not weaken.

What the reader is meant to take from the pattern is the persistence of the offer. The sūrah is addressing a later generation of the same people and asking them to accept a messenger who confirms what they already have. Before it makes that request, it establishes, in its own record of their history, that the door has been repeatedly reopened. The sentence ends with gratitude because gratitude is what the situation calls for.

**Why the Record Is Preserved**

The Book keeps the failures of a favoured people in its text, and this verse is one of the places where it does so without softening the facts. A community's history is recorded complete: the rescue, the crossing, the appointment, the idol, and the pardon. Nothing is edited out on either side, and the reader is invited to draw conclusions from the whole of it.

That preservation serves the argument of the address to the community's descendants. If the record had been limited to the favours, the later reproaches would have rested on nothing the audience had been told. If it had been limited to the failures, the pardon in this verse would have had no counterpart. What the sūrah presents is a full account, and it presents it as the ground on which the request to accept a messenger is being made.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:53

> And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺ that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Things Given Together, a Book and a Criterion**

The sentence names two objects in one gift: the Scripture and the standard of judgment. The Arabic for the second is *furqān*, from a root meaning to separate or distinguish, and it describes that by which truth and falsehood are told apart. The Book uses the same word as a name for the Qur'an itself, which is why this verse is read as a statement about the function of revelation generally and not only about what Moses received.

The pairing tells the reader what a revealed book is for. It is not presented as an archive of information about God but as an instrument for making distinctions; the same verse states the purpose as guidance for the people who received it. The Book's self-descriptions use the same vocabulary, and the sūrah's second verse had already described its own contents as a guidance for a particular kind of reader.

**What the Book Says About This Gift Elsewhere**

Other passages fill out the content of the gift. One states that Moses and his brother received a light and a reminder (21:48). Another records the granting of the Scripture with its purpose attached: *“And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guide for the Children of Israel”* (17:2). A third describes the same revelation as completing the favour on those who do good, detailing everything, and serving as a guide and a mercy (6:154).

The most detailed statement of the Scripture's role appears in the sūrah of the Table, in the context of the judgments its judges are to make: *“Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light, by which the prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah, made judgments for Jews. So too did the rabbis and scholars judge according to Allah's Book, with which they were entrusted and of which they were made keepers. So do not fear the people; fear Me! Nor trade my revelations for a fleeting gain.”* (5:44). That verse names guidance and light, it names the office of those who hold the book, and it repeats the warning against selling revelation that the sūrah has already given its audience twice.

**Furqān: an Attribute or a Document**

Commentators discussed whether the standard named in this verse is a second book or a description of the first one. The sūrah of the Prophets mentions the gift as something granted to Moses and Aaron together, and the term there is joined to light and remembrance, which suggests a quality rather than a separate volume. Elsewhere the Qur'an itself is called the standard, and the Book also describes wisdom as given alongside scripture.

The readings converge on the same function. Whether the standard is a distinct document or the discriminating power of the revelation in the hands of a prophet, the effect is that what is given enables a person to tell one thing from another. The Book's practice supports this: the verses that follow in this sūrah will continue to separate the conduct that deserves blame from the conduct that deserves praise, and the reader is being invited to perform the same operation on himself.

**"That Perhaps You Would Be Guided"**

The stated purpose of the gift is guidance, and the construction attaches a hopeful outcome to it. The same purpose is attached to the revelation throughout the Book, and the sūrah's opening sentence describes the Book as guidance for the mindful. What the verse adds here is the historical claim that the guidance given to Israel came with the same intention and in the same form.

That continuity is the point of the whole passage. The Book has been reciting the favours granted to this community, and it now names the greatest of them: the arrival of a text with the means to judge by it. Anyone holding a book of this kind is in a position to recognise what comes next, and the argument of the address rests on that position being taken seriously.

**The Closing Item on the List of Favours**

The verse completes the recitation of gifts that began with the deliverance from Pharaoh. Rescue, crossing, appointment, pardon, and then the Scripture: the sequence ends with the instrument rather than with the escape, which places the community's guidance above its safety in the order of importance. The Book's way of ranking the two is consistent, and it treats a people's possession of a criterion as the greater of the two endowments.

The passage then continues into the account of later failures, and the reader who has followed the list understands what those failures cost. They were not committed in the dark. A community provided with a text that distinguishes right from wrong, and with a history of pardon after failure, had every means to act differently. The sūrah has now supplied all the material its later reproaches will assume.

**Scripture Named Last in the List of Gifts**

The recitation of favours ends with the arrival of the book rather than with the escape from slavery, and the order is deliberate. In the Book's scale of value, a community's possession of a criterion outranks its delivery from danger, because the first governs what the community does with the second. A rescued people without a text has been given a life; a rescued people with a text has been given a life and a way to live it.

That is the ground the sūrah builds for the requests that follow. The audience addressed in Madinah holds a scripture of this kind, and the Book's argument is that a text of that sort comes with the obligation to test what claims to confirm it. The list of gifts closes here, and everything the passage does after this point rests on the community having exactly what it has been told it received.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:54

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Diagnosis Before a Demand**

Moses opens with an accusation and closes with a treatment, and the order is deliberate. Before he tells the people what to do, he tells them what has happened to them: the worship of the calf was a wrong done to the wrongdoers themselves. The Arabic phrasing places the damage on the people who committed it rather than on God, and the sūrah has been saying the same thing about Israel's failures in every verse of this passage.

That diagnosis sets up everything that follows. A community that believes it has merely offended a rule can negotiate; a community that understands it has injured itself has a reason to accept a costly remedy. Moses names the wound first, then prescribes the cure, and the verse ends with the announcement that the cure was accepted.

**Repentance Directed to "Your Creator"**

The command to turn is addressed to a word that appears only here in this narrative: your Maker, the one who brought you into being. The Book's choice of that name in a passage about a manufactured idol is pointed. The people had turned to something they had made with their own hands; they are told to turn back to the one who made them, and the contrast is contained in a single noun.

Repentance in this verse is therefore not regret alone. The Arabic term describes a return, and a return requires a place to return to. The sūrah's earlier account of Adam used the same vocabulary and the same sequence — a failure, a turning, and an acceptance — which ties the first human being and the people of Moses to one pattern of recovery. The Book applies one remedy to both.

**The Command to Execute Their Own**

The instruction that follows is the hardest line in the passage. The people are told to kill one another, and the commentators explained the phrase in the way that fits the Book's other uses of the same construction: the guilty are to be executed by their own community, at the hands of their own relatives, without a foreign power being brought in to do the work. The reports add that those killed in this way are counted among the martyrs, and that the men who carried out the sentence had their repentance accepted as well.

Such a reading makes the punishment collective in effect as well as in instruction. Every household was implicated in the act of restoring the community, and the Book presents the severity as the measure of the offence rather than as an arbitrary cruelty. The alternative reading, which sees the command as an inner killing of the ego, is a later spiritual interpretation, and it does not remove the plain sense of the sentence.

**Where the Verse Says the Good Lies**

The sentence gives a reason: that is better for you in the sight of your Creator. The Book does not present the command as an arbitrary test or a demonstration of authority. It states a comparison and asks the people to accept the divine assessment of which option is better, even though the option named involves the loss of life.

That is the structure of the Book's moral instruction everywhere. God's commands in the Qur'an are consistently presented as the better of the available courses, and the human being's difficulty lies in his own assessment rather than in the command's reasonableness. Here the community is asked to accept that a painful, publicly administered punishment is better than the condition they had entered, and the verse reports their acceptance as a fact.

**An Acceptance Stated With Two Names**

The forgiveness is announced in the past tense by the verse itself: He accepted your repentance.
