That is why the verdict here attaches to the surrounded condition rather than to an individual offence, and why the next verse names the opposite condition for those whose conduct went the other way.

**Faith and Deeds Held Together**

The following verse pairs belief with good conduct and promises the Garden as a permanent home. Read together, the two sentences state the Book's standard in the form this sūrah applies throughout: conviction expressed in action, or action without conviction that eventually closes in on the person doing it.

The pairing is not a claim that works save anyone independently of faith, and it is not a claim that a profession of faith settles a person's fate independently of his conduct. The Book uses the same structure in its repeated descriptions of those who believe and act rightly, and the community's scholars drew from the two verses the position that a person's final standing is determined by both together.

**The Early Controversies**

Later schools read this verse and its partner in diverging directions. The Khawārij treated the commission of a major sin as grounds for declaring a Muslim outside the faith, taking the "engrossed" clause as applying to anyone who fell into grave sin without repenting. The Murjiʾa moved the other way and detached faith from action, holding that a profession of belief settled a person's fate whatever his conduct. The Muʿtazila held that the two together decided reward and punishment and that neither could substitute for the other.

The Book's own answer lies in its repeated treatment of sin and repentance: it commands turning back to God and states that He forgives those who do so. The mainstream position of the scholars therefore read the permanence described here as applying to a person who dies in the condition named, since a life whose sins have closed in around it is by definition a life without the repentance that opens a way out.

**Permanence Stated in Both Directions**

The sūrah assigns the same eternity to the residence of the believers in the next verse that it assigns here to this group. The symmetry is part of the passage's argument: a claim that the punishment of a community would be brief is answered by a statement of permanence the Book applies to those who have enclosed themselves in wrongdoing.

The verse names no community, and its conditions are phrased so that any reader can apply them to himself. That is deliberate, since the sūrah's readers include the believers, and every warning addressed to the People of the Book in this passage will be turned on the Muslims in one form or another before the sūrah is finished.

**A Standard Rather Than a Verdict on Others**

The sentence states a criterion, and the criterion is not the identity of the person being described. A reader who uses the verse to settle the fate of a community has converted a test into a label, and the Book's own usage resists that move. The two destinies are described in general terms, and the entries are moral rather than genealogical.

What the passage then does is return to the covenant the community had ratified and broken, and it measures their conduct against their own undertaking. The verse's function in that sequence is to make the outcome explicit before the evidence is set out, so that the reader knows what is at stake when the covenant's terms and the breach of them are presented in the verses that follow.

**Where the Verse Places Responsibility**

The sentence describes a condition rather than a category of person, and it places responsibility for reaching that condition on conduct. The Book's order is consistent throughout: a person acts, the action accumulates, and the accumulation eventually surrounds him. Nothing in the verse suggests the conclusion arrives without the conduct that produced it, which is why the Qur'an's commands to repent are addressed to people in every state short of death. The verse is therefore not a sentence passed on a group but a warning about a trajectory, and the sūrah states the opposite trajectory in the next line so that the two directions can be compared. A community that reads the passage as an account of somebody else's fate has missed the function the Book assigns to it in this place.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:82

> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Half of a Pair**

The previous verse stated the condition for the Fire and the permanence of that residence. This one states the condition for the Garden and gives the same duration. The two sentences stand directly beside each other so that the reader receives both halves of the Book's standard at once, and neither is left to inference.

The arrangement matters for the passage that follows. The sūrah is about to describe a covenant this community ratified and then broke. A reader needs to know what was offered before the breach can be measured, and this verse supplies the terms: belief, good conduct, and a lasting home for those who hold both.

**Faith and Action Named Together**

The Book pairs belief with righteous conduct in dozens of places, and the pairing is its most frequent description of the people it praises. The phrase occurs so regularly that a reader new to the text soon notices the Book rarely states one without the other, and the reason is that each term is incomplete in the Book's vocabulary without its partner.

The works in question are not confined to ritual. The Qur'an includes prayer, charity, and the freeing of a slave among the deeds of a life completed by faith, and it applies the same formula to men and women alike. The verse therefore describes a way of living rather than a checklist, and it treats conduct as the visible surface of conviction.

**Residents of Paradise**

The word rendered as residents describes permanent dwelling rather than a visit. The Book uses it for the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire in the same passages, and it does so in order to place both outcomes on the same timescale. Whatever a person is called in the Book's final accounting, the description holds without an end date attached.

Later verses of this sūrah describe the reward in sensory terms: gardens beneath which rivers flow, shade and fruit that do not fail, and an abode whose greatest element is the pleasure of God. This verse mentions only residence and duration. Readers have always taken the two descriptions together, since the brief statement here establishes the condition and the later passages fill in what the condition contains.

**The Answer to a Claim About Duration**

The two verses together dismantle the community's claim in three steps. The claim was that the Fire would touch them only for a limited period. The first verse removed the limit for people whose sins surround them. The second assigned permanence to people who believe and act rightly, and left the other category with no such promise at all.

The Book does not offer a ledger of days or a schedule of punishments. It offers a test of character applied to two kinds of life, and it lets the reader work out for himself which of the two descriptions fits him. That is how the passage can correct a specific claim made by a specific community while remaining useful to every reader of the Book, whatever scripture he was raised on.

**What the Verse Does Not Say About Numbers**

The sentence avoids any treatment of proportion between deeds and sins, and it does not present the matter as a balance a person can compute. The next passage sets out the covenant's demands in detail and leaves the accounting to God, and later parts of the Book describe the weighing of deeds on a day when no soul will be wronged in the least.

The omission is deliberate. The Book does not encourage its readers to estimate their own standing, and it gives the two outcomes in their general form so that a person examines the direction of his life rather than the arithmetic of it. The community's claim about numbered days was an attempt to do the opposite, and this answer removes the material such a calculation would need.

**A Promise Framing the Covenant That Follows**

The verse closes a section that began with the hardening of hearts and moved through concealment, speculation, forgery, and a claim about the Fire. Each of those sentences described a departure from a trust. This one describes the people who kept the trust, and it does so immediately before the covenant narrative resumes.

Readers of the sūrah have long noticed that the passage's most demanding commands — the covenant verses about parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and how people speak to one another (2:83) — arrive right after this promise. The arrangement makes the reward the frame for what comes next, and it puts the community's breach of its own undertaking in the sharpest available light.

**Why the Verse Belongs to Everyone Addressed**

The sentence names no group, and it uses the same two conditions the sūrah applies to the Muslims in its opening definition of the successful. Its function in this passage is to close the argument about inherited guarantees that ran from the claim about numbered days through the description of the forgeries.

What remains for the sūrah is the record. The next verses turn from what people assume about their standing to what they actually agreed to do, and they set out the covenant's terms clause by clause. The promise in this verse is the standard against which that record will be read.

**The Verse in the Chapter's Architecture**

This promise and the warning before it form a hinge in the sūrah. The passage so far has described a community that received a covenant, broke it, and then defended itself with claims about limited punishment and closed hearts. The two destinies are now stated in plain form, and the covenant narrative resumes immediately afterwards with the terms written out in full. The placement means the reader meets the covenant a second time knowing what is at stake, so the breach recorded in the following verses lands against a background of consequences rather than in a vacuum. The Book often arranges its material in this order, promising before commanding and rewarding before warning, and the arrangement teaches its hearers to read the account of an earlier community as instruction rather than as history.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:83

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Covenant Recalled to Another Community**

The sūrah returns to the history of the children of Israel, and it tells the story in the second person, addressing the descendants of the people who made the agreement. The command to remember introduces a scene rather than a rule, and the scene is a binding undertaking made before God with a list of obligations attached.

This is not a new episode in the narrative. The sūrah has already referred to the covenant in the passage about the mountain being raised and the oath taken at Sinai, and the verses that follow will return to the same agreement twice more. The repetition is deliberate. The Book builds the case against a people out of their own recorded words rather than out of an outsider's accusation.

**Worship Directed to God Alone**

The list opens where the Book's ethical teaching always opens, with the exclusive worship of God, and the remaining commands follow as its consequences. The Qur'an does not treat the social obligations as a separate moral code that can stand without the first one. Later in the sūrah the same order appears when the Book instructs people to worship God and join no partner with Him, and immediately joins to that command kindness to parents and relatives and the feeding of the poor.

Commentators note that this opening clause is the foundation of everything the verse asks afterwards. A person who has no one above him but God has no human being whose approval he must purchase, and the kindness commanded later in the sentence rests on the independence that the first clause establishes.

**Kindness to Parents, Relatives, Orphans, and the Needy**

The Arabic verb used for the treatment of parents describes good conduct more than it describes obedience, and it covers the way a person speaks, listens, and provides. The Book develops the theme at length elsewhere, forbidding even a word of irritation to ageing parents and pairing their care with God's own right (17:23).

The list then widens from the family outward: relatives, orphans, and the poor. The choice of the orphan is not accidental in a passage addressed to a community with a long history of prophets, since the Book repeatedly reminds it that many of its own great figures were raised without fathers. The needy appear last in the list and without qualification, which the commentators noted as a sign that no distinction of tribe or religion should be applied to this obligation.

**Kind Speech as an Obligation**

The middle item in the list is the one most often overlooked: speak kindly to people. The command is addressed to the community in general rather than to its leaders, and the Arabic wording asks for a manner rather than a message. The Book states the same requirement as a test of the trust it places in its own followers, and it forbids harshness in the invitation to faith itself.

Ibn Kathīr and others noted that this clause makes courteous conduct toward everyone a covenant obligation rather than a courtesy. The community being addressed had a long record of quarrelling with its own prophets; the command to speak gently to people stands in the sentence as a correction of that habit, and it applies with equal force to the community now receiving the revelation.

**Prayer and Alms as the Spine of the Covenant**

The list closes with the two practices the Book treats as the standing marks of a life turned toward God: the prayer and the giving of alms. Both are commanded here as covenant terms rather than as personal devotions, and both appear in the Book's descriptions of every community that received a scripture.

The pairing is consistent across the Book, where the two are named together in accounts of the prophets and their peoples, and the Qur'an treats the neglect of them as evidence of a broken relation with God rather than a failure of private piety. The verse therefore ends its list with the duties that the community can neither delegate nor conceal.

**Turned Away, Except a Few**

The sentence then states the outcome, and it does so in the second person: they turned away and were indifferent. The word describing their state suggests a shrug rather than an attack, and the Book's choice of it is exact. The community did not renounce the covenant; it let the terms lapse and treated the lapse as unremarkable.

The exception in the sentence is important. The verse preserves the fact that a few of them kept their word, and the sūrah repeats this qualification at intervals throughout the passage. The Book's judgments in this section are aimed at the majority who defaulted, and the passage records from the first that faithfulness was possible and was practised.

**Why the List Is Read Before the Breach**

The sūrah presents the terms before it presents the failure, and the order is the argument. Someone hearing only of the breach would have to take the accusation on trust; hearing the covenant first allows the failure to be measured against terms the community itself accepted. That is why the verses that follow repeat the same sequence with a second set of terms and a second failure, and why the chapter's later treatment of the same community keeps returning to what they had agreed.

**The Exception as a Standing Invitation**

The closing phrase of the verse preserves the fact that a few of the community kept faith, and the sūrah repeats that qualification whenever it returns to this people. The exception does not soften the account; it keeps the account honest, and it also keeps an opening for anyone listening who had not defaulted with the majority. The Book's practice in these passages is to leave a door visible even while it records a failure, and the invitation to believe what confirms the earlier scripture runs through the whole section. What the verse offers is therefore a choice rather than a verdict. A community that turns away except for a few has shown what the majority are likely to do; it has not determined what any individual member of that community will do, and the sūrah continues to address them directly for many verses afterwards.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:84

> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Clause of the Same Agreement**

The sūrah returns to the covenant with a different set of terms. The previous verse listed what the community was to do; this one lists what it was forbidden to do to itself. Both are introduced with the command to remember, and both end with evidence that the agreement had been accepted.

The Book's method in this passage is to build the case in layers. It first established the positive obligations, then the prohibition on internal violence, and it will then report the violation in detail. Each step narrows the gap between what the community claimed about itself and what the record shows. The two lists cover different ground: what the community owed to God and to its weakest members, then what it owed to one another simply by belonging to the same people. The second list requires no shared belief to be understood, which is how the Book can hold a community to it on the strength of its own agreement.

**Bloodshed Within a Community**

The prohibition is not about war with an outside enemy. The verse speaks of shedding one another's blood, and the wording identifies the victims and the perpetrators as members of the same people. What is being forbidden is civil conflict, and the covenant places the life of a member of the community under the protection of the agreement rather than of the tribe.

The Book treats this category of killing as a distinct offence. Elsewhere it states that whoever kills a believer deliberately has a punishment awaiting him from God, and it treats the killing of a person without lawful cause as a crime against the whole of humanity (5:32). The list in this verse shows what a community's own commitments look like when written out in full. Elsewhere the Book treats the killing of a single person as an offence against the whole of humanity, and the wording is sterner still when the victim belongs to the same covenant. The chapter of the women records the community's own pledge on this point, so the prohibition in this verse was not a new demand invented for the occasion.

**Expulsion Treated as a Form of Killing**

The second prohibition extends the first: not to expel one another from their homes. The Book pairs the two offences consistently, here and in the verse that reports the violation, and the pairing shows how it weighs dispossession. A person driven from his land with his family loses what a killed man loses, with the difference that he lives to watch it.

The pairing appears again in the sūrah's account of the punishment of a people who drove others from their homes, and the Book applies its language about oppression to the act of dispossession itself. In this covenant the two clauses stand side by side as a single undertaking, and the community's failure is recorded against both. The association of the two offences outlived the occasion. The Book treats the protection of life and the security of residence as parts of a single guarantee, which is why the following sentence can describe a people shedding blood and driving out families in one breath and treat both as the same breach.

**They Gave Their Pledge and Bore Witness**

The verse closes by recording that the community consented to the terms and confirmed them. The two verbs are legal in flavour: a pledge freely given, and testimony offered by the ones who had agreed. The record is therefore not an outsider's account but the community's own acknowledgment.

The Book returns to this point repeatedly in the passage because it removes the defence of ignorance. A community that gave its own word and then acted against it is not being accused of a mistake; it is being held to an undertaking whose terms it fully understood. The same standard is applied to the listeners of the revelation when the sūrah turns to the Muslims later in the chapter. Legally the two verbs do different work: the first says the community accepted the terms, and the second says it can be called to account for them. The charges in these verses are always of that kind, resting on what a community acknowledged rather than on what an outside party alleges about it.

**The Parallel With the Book's Other Covenants**

The Qur'an records covenants with other communities in similar terms, and the comparison is instructive. The chapter of the table describes an agreement taken from the children of Israel with promises of God's support attached, and the chapter of the women summarizes the same history in a single verse about their pledge and their subsequent breaking of it.

The Book's use of these accounts is not archival. When it reports an earlier community's covenant and its failure, the report is directed at the community reading it, and the sequence of commands and prohibitions in this passage is followed by warnings addressed directly to the believers. The sūrah's later verses will tell the Muslims to keep their own agreements and not to make their oaths a means of deceiving one another.

**Why the Two Clauses Are Stated Before the Breach**

The order of the verses is the sūrah's argument. If the breach had come first, the reader would judge the community on the strength of an accusation. Coming after the terms, the breach is measured against the community's own undertaking, and the reader is placed in a position to see how a people can hold a written covenant and violate it in practice.

That position is what the next verse exploits. It addresses the same community in the present tense, describing the conduct that contradicts what they have just been reminded they promised, and it asks them how they reconcile the two. The sūrah builds the question carefully so that its force does not depend on an orator's skill. Something similar happens later when the sūrah turns to the Muslim community, where the commands come before the warnings and the warnings before the reminder of what is at stake. The pattern is a method of teaching, and in this passage it also serves an argument: the community is shown what it promised before it is shown what it did.

**A Covenant That Concerns the Community Itself**

The terms in this verse are unusual among the Book's commands in that they protect the community against itself. No foreign threat is mentioned and no external enemy is named. The undertaking is to refrain from violence inside the household of the covenant, and the Book treats the violation of that internal limit as the clearest evidence of what a people's religion has become in practice.

**An Undertaking Containing Its Own Enforcement**

Covenants in the Book are usually described as obligations owed to God, and this one adds a feature that makes it unusual. Its terms protect the community from itself, and their enforcement depends on the members of that community. No outside power is named in the verse to punish a man who kills his own cousin, and no foreign enemy can be blamed for the expulsion of a family from its home. The offences are described as things done to one another, which means the damage and the responsibility stay inside the household of the agreement. That is why the following verse addresses the community in the present tense and simply describes what they are doing, naming the acts by which the covenant was broken rather than accusing them of breaking it in the abstract.

**Why the Terms Sound Like a Legal Document**

The vocabulary of the verse is transactional. A covenant is taken, a pledge is given, and witnesses are named, so the community's commitment is recorded in the same forms that governed agreements between tribes. The Book adopts those forms deliberately, because it is describing an undertaking that was publicly known and publicly accepted rather than a private understanding. What the phrasing rules out is the possibility that a later generation could treat the covenant as a matter of interpretation. Its terms were stated, its acceptance was witnessed, and the community that accepted it did so in the plainest available language. The Book's case against the community therefore does not rest on an argument about intention. It rest on what was agreed and what was done, in that order.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:85

> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Breach Set Out in Detail**

The verse turns from what the community promised to what the record shows, and it uses the present tense. Each clause corresponds to a term of the covenant that the previous verse recorded, so that the reader can match the violation to the undertaking. The Book is not making a general charge of hypocrisy; it is naming the exact clauses that were broken.

This is one of the longest sentences in the sūrah, and its length is part of its effect. It accumulates the offences without pausing to condemn each one, and it finishes with the question that reduces the whole account to a single issue.

**Killing, Expelling, and Aiding One Another**

The first two offences repeat the prohibitions of the previous verse, and the third explains how they became possible: the community aided one another in sin and aggression. The Book's analysis of the collapse is social rather than theological. People did not break their covenant in isolation; they organized around their factions and found partners for whatever their side wanted to do.

That clause names the mechanism by which a moral community dissolves. When loyalty is transferred from the undertaking to the group, the undertaking loses its hold, and the Book states elsewhere that cooperating in righteousness is commanded while cooperating in sin and hostility is forbidden (5:2). The verse shows what happens to a community that reads only the first half of that rule.

**Ransoming the Captives, Rejecting the Cause**

The most specific charge in the verse concerns the captives. The community that had expelled some of its own people would then pay to redeem those same people when they were taken prisoner elsewhere, and the Book presents the contradiction in a single breath. The ransom is not credited to them as generosity; it is entered as evidence that they knew the terms of their own scripture perfectly well.

Commentators connected this clause to the alliances of Madinah's tribes in the period before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, when factional fighting between the Aws and the Khazraj drew in the Jewish tribes allied to each side. The tribes would fight one another, then ransom their captives according to a rule they all acknowledged, and the Book treats the ransoming as proof that the prohibition on killing and expulsion was never unknown to them.

**Believing Part of a Book and Rejecting the Rest**

The verse then asks the question that governs everything before it: do you believe in some of the scripture and reject the rest? The formulation identifies the real offence, which is not ignorance of the text but a selective relationship with it. A community that ransoms according to one clause while shedding blood against another has not lost its scripture; it has taken it in parts.

The Book returns to this charge at several points in the sūrah, and it treats the partial acceptance of revelation as a serious category of unbelief rather than a lesser form of belief. The criterion it applies is not the quantity of commands observed but the authority recognized, and the verse exposes a community that was prepared to obey where obedience was already in its interest.

**Disgrace in This Life and the Harshest Punishment**

The consequence is stated in two parts, and the first is temporal. Disgrace in this worldly life is the predictable result of a community whose internal wars are common knowledge, and the Book describes it as part of the punishment rather than as a coincidence. The second part is reserved for the Day of Judgment, where the Book calls the punishment harshest, a term it uses sparingly.

The pairing of the two is a feature of this sūrah's treatment of the community's history. The Book does not present the worldly consequence as the whole penalty, nor the final judgement as an abstract threat disconnected from conduct now. Both are named in the same sentence, and the ordinary reader is meant to see continuity between them.

**The Closing Attribute**

The sentence ends with a statement about God's knowledge rather than about His decree, and the sūrah has now appended this attribute to several of the charges in this passage. It removes the last possible refuge, which is the assumption that a violation committed inside a community remains a private matter.

What makes the ending effective is its placement. The verse has just described deeds that its perpetrators would have regarded as legitimate acts of tribal loyalty, and the final clause informs them that no such category exists in the accounting the Book is describing. The following verse draws the conclusion in one line about what such a community has traded away.

**A Charge Directed at a Method, Not a Lineage**

The verse names no individual and passes no sentence on a people as a whole. It describes a set of practices that a community had adopted while holding a scripture that forbade them, and it asks the members of that community how they reconcile the two. The question is addressed to conduct, which means any reader who recognizes the pattern in himself has been addressed as well, whatever scripture he carries.

**A Question That Exposes the Criterion**

The question in this verse deserves isolating from the rest of the sentence. It does not ask whether the community accepts the scripture, since that was never in dispute. It asks whether they accept some of it and reject the rest. The distinction drawn here governs everything that follows in the sūrah's treatment of this people, and it governs the sūrah's treatment of the believers too, since the same question returns in addresses to the Muslims about the parts of the revelation they find convenient and the parts they set aside. What the verse establishes is that selective acceptance is not a middle position between belief and unbelief. A person who obeys only what suits him has made his own preference the authority over the text, and the Book's term for that arrangement is not partial belief but disbelief in part.

**What the Ransom Clause Reveals**

The detail about the captives has always been the sharpest part of the charge. The community paid to redeem members of its own tribes whom its own factions had helped to enslave, and the payment showed that it knew the value of the lives it had been expelling. A rule the community kept when it suited them stood beside a rule it broke when breaking served the faction, and the Book places both facts in a single sentence. That contrast is what makes the verse a study in selective obedience rather than a list of crimes. The ransoming was not an act of mercy offered by outsiders; it was the community's own law applied to the community's own people, and it demonstrates that the rest of that law was never unknown to them.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:86

> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verdict in Two Lines**

The previous verse reported the community's conduct in detail; this one states in a single sentence what the conduct amounts to. There is no new accusation and no further evidence. The sūrah simply names the transaction, and the naming is the judgment.

That is how the Book often closes a case. The evidence has been laid out clause by clause, and the summary line identifies the nature of the act rather than repeating its details. A reader who has followed the passage from the covenant's terms through the ransoming of captives already knows the facts, and this verse tells him what to call them.

**The Direction of the Trade**

The image is of an exchange, and the wording is precise about what was given and what was taken. The community handed over the Hereafter and accepted this present life in return. The Book uses this commercial language for religious failure throughout, and it always preserves the direction of the trade, so the reader can see that a durable asset has been surrendered for a perishable one.

The buying and selling metaphor recurs in describing those who purchase error at the price of guidance, and the sūrah's own opening used a similar figure when it described people who sold guidance for misguidance and made no profit. The vocabulary is consistent enough that readers of the Book recognize the transaction as soon as it is named, and the trade in this verse is the same one in a different currency.

**What Makes This Trade Possible**

A trade requires a valuation, and the community in this passage had assigned its values before it acted. A shared tribal loyalty was worth more than a covenant; a moment's advantage over a rival outweighed a prohibition its own scripture stated plainly. The verse does not say these people denied the Hereafter; it says they priced it and found it worth less than something closer at hand.

The Book's treatment of this error is not to add another command but to reorder the reader's estimation of what lasts. Its repeated contrast between the passing nature of this world and the permanence of the next is aimed at exactly that faculty, and the sūrah's earlier verses used the same argument when they asked people not to expect the Fire to be brief and then described two permanent residences.

**Punishment Not Reduced**

The sentence's first consequence is that the punishment will not be lightened. The Book uses this formula for those whose position has been settled, and it places it here immediately after the community's claim that its punishment would be limited to a number of days. The answer to that claim is not a different number but the removal of the arithmetic altogether.

The formula also appears in the sūrah's description of the fate of those who persist in hostility, and it recurs in other passages where the Book describes people for whom intercession and compensation will not be accepted. The Book's point in each case is the same: the resources by which a person might ordinarily avert a penalty have been exhausted by the nature of the offence.

**Nor Will They Be Helped**

The second consequence is that no help will arrive. The Book uses this phrase for the removal of every possible source of assistance: allies, intercessors, and substitutes. In the sūrah's account of the Day of Judgment no soul will pay anything on another's behalf, and no plea will be entertained for those whose account has been closed.

That second clause is where the community described here is cut off from the loyalty on which it relied. The tribal system that made their conduct reasonable provided protection, mutual aid, and the expectation that one's people would stand by one, and the verse states that this system does not extend to the court that will hear this case.

**The Warning Reaches the Believers**

The verse is addressed to a community that had been given a scripture and had acted on part of it. The warning is therefore available to any community in the same position, and the sūrah will shortly address its own followers in these terms. Later chapters speak of people trading faith for worldly advantage in exactly the commercial vocabulary used here, and they include the Prophet's companions among the people addressed.

That is the pattern of the whole passage. The Book reports an earlier community's failure in order to establish the principle, and then applies the principle to the people now holding the revelation. A reader who studies the sūrah to learn what happened to other people will find the same standard turned on him before the chapter ends.

**The Verdict Left Unqualified**

The sentence attaches no community to the description and no duration to the penalty. What it fixes is the nature of the choice and the finality of its outcome. The verses that follow return to the history of this people with a different subject, the messengers sent to it, and the account of a community that refused what it recognized continues to build the case the chapter is making.

**Who Pays the Price for a Community's Choices**

A trade is normally made by the people who benefit from it, and this verse states that the community sold its own souls. The leaders who arranged the factions and the ransoms are not named separately from the people who fought in their wars. The Book spreads the responsibility across everyone who accepted the arrangement, which is why the passage has taken such care to describe the community's conduct as a collective act. That refusal to separate the architects from the followers is one reason the sūrah's account reaches across generations. A community's inherited assumptions are held by each of its members individually, and the sentence here treats the wrong choice as the property of whoever makes it, regardless of whose idea it originally was or which ancestor first struck the bargain.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:87

> Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Chain of Revelation**

The verse changes register. After the account of broken covenants and traded inheritances, the sūrah reminds its hearers of the provision that made all of that possible: God did not leave the community without guidance. He gave Moses the Book, and He sent messengers after him in succession, so that the history being described is a history of continuous divine attention rather than of abandonment.

The word rendered successive is literal in the Arabic traditions of reading: the prophets came one after another, replacing one another as the carriers of a single message. The Qur'an states the same idea when it describes the messengers as following in one another's footsteps, and the sūrah's audience is asked to see its own refusal against that background of repeated provision. The word translated as successive carries the sense of each messenger following in the footsteps of the one before, a picture the Book uses elsewhere for the unity of the message. Its presence here reminds the hearer that the refusal was made against a pattern rather than during an interval of silence.

**Moses and the Book**

The verse names Moses first because the community's own foundation rests on him. The Book given to him is described elsewhere in the sūrah as guidance and light for the people, and the Qur'an insists repeatedly that the revelation to Muhammad ﷺ confirms it rather than replaces or contradicts it.

That emphasis runs through the whole passage. The charge against this community is not that it lacked a messenger or a scripture. It is that it stood in the middle of an unbroken line of revelation, was reminded of it constantly, and still treated each new messenger as an inconvenience to be removed. The insistence on continuity explains why Moses is named first. He stands for the moment the community received a written law, and every later messenger was measured against that gift. The complaint in this passage is that the people who honoured the earlier revelation treated its continuation as an intrusion.

**Jesus, the Clear Proofs, and the Holy Spirit**

The verse then names Jesus, son of Mary, and attaches two things to him: clear proofs and the support of the holy spirit. The proofs in the Book's own account include healing, raising the dead, and the signs the people witnessed, and the holy spirit is explained by the commentators in several ways, the most widely reported being the angel Gabriel.

The Qur'an uses the phrase elsewhere in an account of the annunciation, where the spirit is sent to Mary in the form of a man, and it describes support given to Jesus by the spirit in several passages. The point the verse makes with the phrase is support given directly by God to a messenger, and readers have noted that the same expression is used of the Prophet's own support during the migration.

**Arrogance as the Root of the Charge**

The question in the verse identifies the motive before it identifies the offence. Every time a messenger brought something the community did not like, it grew arrogant, and the arrogance produced two results in sequence: rejecting some messengers and killing others. The Book's diagnosis is that the problem was never the evidence; it was the requirement to accept a message that cut against the community's preferences.

That analysis is why the passage has been building through covenants and breached undertakings. A refusal driven by appetite rather than by argument cannot be answered with more evidence, and the sūrah will say as much when it tells its readers that signs do not persuade people who have already decided. The verb for arrogance here is the same one the Book used earlier of a figure who refused a command out of pride, and it is a deliberately consistent vocabulary.

**Rejecting Some and Killing Others**

The two verbs are joined, and they form a descending scale. The community's refusal began with rejection — declining to accept a messenger, disputing his claim, waiting for him to fail. It progressed to violence, and the Book states elsewhere that this people killed a series of prophets whose only fault was to bring commands that were unwelcome.

The charge is repeated later in the sūrah when the community is asked why it killed the prophets in earlier times if it truly believes in what was sent down to it (2:91). The repetition is not redundancy. The Book is establishing that this conduct was a pattern rather than an incident, and the word *every time* in this verse makes that explicit. The pair of charges returns when the sūrah reports the answer this community gives to the Prophet ﷺ, which includes the same two offences against the messengers who came before. The Book presents the whole history as one continuous attitude rather than as a series of unrelated incidents.

**The Question That Closes the Verse**

The sentence ends with a question, and it is put as though the reader could answer it. Why does a messenger's arrival with unwelcome news produce violence rather than reflection? The question is not answered in the verse, because the Book's answer is spread across the whole passage: because a community had attached its identity to a set of claims that revelation kept challenging.

The Arabic construction of the question, addressed directly to the Israelites, carries the same force the sūrah has used with the same community elsewhere. It presumes that the hearer knows what drove the conduct and simply does not want to say it aloud, and the sūrah leaves the presumption standing. The question is put to people who could have answered it from their own history, and the silence it produces is the argument. The Book uses this form sparingly, only where the answer is already known, and here it appears twice within two verses, which marks how thoroughly the record is expected to speak for itself.

**A Warning Encoded for Later Readers**

The verse names a specific community, and the pattern it describes is not specific to them. Any community that receives revelation, builds an institution around it, and then finds a later messenger inconvenient faces the same choice between adjusting and refusing. That is why the sūrah's later addresses to the Muslims use the same verbs, and why the passage as a whole can be read as a warning about what a religious community becomes when its standing matters more to it than the message it holds. The sūrah does not leave the application implicit. Later in the same passage it addresses the Muslims in the second person about their own obligations, and the chapter's closing exhortations return to gratitude and steadfastness. What this community's history teaches is meant to be used by the community now receiving the revelation.

**Why a Message and Its Messenger Are Not the Same**

The verse identifies the error that makes a community's refusal possible: it separates the message from the messenger and treats the arrival of a prophet as an event to be managed. The proofs had been given, the confirming scripture was in their hands, and yet each new messenger was weighed by what he asked people to give up. The Book uses the same terms for the reaction to Muhammad ﷺ, and it describes this community's ancestors reacting in exactly that way to Jesus and to the prophets before him. What the sūrah wants its hearers to notice is that this pattern needs no new motive each time. One preference, held consistently, produces the same result whenever a messenger arrives, and the question in the verse is designed to make that repetition visible.

**An Unbroken Line of Provision**

The verse's opening clause is easy to pass over, and it carries the passage's argument. Revelation did not arrive once and then stop; messenger followed messenger, each confirming the one before, and no generation of this community was left without guidance. Against that record, the charge in the question at the end of the verse lands differently. A refusal by people who had never heard a prophet would be a failure of opportunity; a refusal by people standing in the middle of a continuous line of provision is a failure of response. The sūrah states the provision before it states the offence precisely so that its hearers weigh the two together, and the same order governs the sūrah's later addresses to the Muslims about the revelation they have received.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:88

> They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Excuse Offered in Their Own Words**

The sūrah quotes the community's explanation for its refusal, and the explanation is a claim about their own condition rather than an argument about the message. The messengers arrived, the evidence was presented, and the answer returned was that the hearts receiving it were closed. The Book reports the sentence without comment and then supplies the comment in the next clause.

Quoting an opponent's own words is a technique the sūrah has used several times in this passage. It lets the reader hear the position from inside, and it makes the correction that follows land on the speaker rather than on a description of the speaker. The Book's method is not to characterize the claim but to expose it.

**What the Word Behind the Translation Means**

The Arabic word in the quotation is one the commentators discussed at length, and it is usually explained as meaning covered, wrapped, or closed. Some readers connected it to the description of a heart that has been sealed, and others noted that the word shares a root with the idea of uncircumcision, which is how several older translations rendered it. Under every reading, the claim is that the community's hearts cannot receive what is being offered.

The same excuse appears elsewhere in the Book in the account of a people who told Moses that their hearts were wrapped, at a point where they had already broken their covenant and killed their prophets (4:155). The wording is repeated in both places, which suggests the sentence had become a standing formula in the community's vocabulary for declining a messenger.

**The Book's Answer**

The answer occupies the rest of the verse, and it rejects the claim at its root. God has condemned them for their disbelief. What the community presents as an inability is described as a consequence, and the Book reverses the order in which the two events happened. The hearts did not close first and produce the disbelief; the disbelief produced the closing.

That reversal is a recurring theme in the Book. It states elsewhere that God turns the hearts of those who do not believe, and that He leaves a person in the deviation he has chosen. The Qur'an's account of hardening is consistent: it follows the exercise of a person's own will, and it is described as a judgment that follows on conduct rather than as an arbitrary act that precedes it.

**A Small Amount of Faith**

The verse closes with a statement about the quantity of faith the community possessed. The translation renders it as very little. Commentators read the clause in two related ways, one taking it as a description of the actual belief held by some members of the community, and the other as an ironic statement about a faith that refuses to accept what its own scripture announced.

The reading that fits the surrounding verses is the second. A community that says its hearts cannot receive is not describing a small faith but a faith that has been made conditional on terms, and the sūrah continues to state that such belief does not satisfy the requirements of the covenant. The phrase is therefore not a measurement but a verdict on the quality of what the community retained.

**Why the Excuse Fails on Its Own Terms**

If the hearts really were closed by nature, the closing would not be a fault, and the Book would not hold the community responsible. The sūrah's entire passage on this people, however, treats them as responsible, and the previous verses described people who understood the scripture, distorted it knowingly, and killed men sent to them. The excuse contradicts the record the Book has just laid out.

That is why the reply in this verse takes the form of a judgment. The community is offering a description of itself as a defence, and the Book accepts the description and turns it into the charge. Their hearts are closed, and the verse states who closed them and why.

**The Believers and the Same Warning**

The sūrah applies this vocabulary to its own audience later, when it warns the believers not to become like those who forgot God and were made to forget themselves. Verse after verse in this Book describes the sequence of choice, consequence, and hardening, and the warning to the Muslims is always that the sequence is universal.

Read as a warning, the sentence has a practical edge. A person who habitually declines what he does not want to hear is not merely losing arguments; he is training the faculty that would have recognized the next truth that came to him. That is the mechanism the verse describes in three words, and the Book presents it as the most dangerous process a religious person can undergo.

**A Question About Hearts, Not Lineage**

The verse is often quoted as a description of one community, and the Book's use of the same language about its own followers rules out that reading. What is being described is a condition that anyone can enter, and the description is offered to the reader as a possibility rather than as a fact about someone else.

**How a Community Explains Itself to Itself**

The formula quoted in this verse has a function beyond refusing a messenger. It converts a history of choices into a statement about nature, and communities repeat that conversion. A group that has repeatedly declined what it did not want to hear will eventually describe its own condition as permanent, and the description begins to sound like humility rather than stubbornness. The reply in this verse refuses the conversion. What has been called a closed heart is named as a consequence, and the consequence is attributed to the conduct that produced it. That reversal makes the sentence useful far beyond its original occasion, since anyone can test it: a condition presented as incapacity is being described by someone who has not yet seriously attempted to act against it.

**When a Condition Becomes a Destiny**

The claim in this verse describes a permanent state, and permanence is the part the Book rejects. A heart that has hardened can be softened, which is why the Qur'an's warnings about hardened hearts are always accompanied by commands to remember God and to seek forgiveness. The community's formula removed that possibility at a single stroke by converting a consequence into a nature. What the Book answers with is not only a correction of the claim but a statement about responsibility: the condition was produced by choices, and choices are the kind of thing their maker can revisit. The verse is therefore a rebuke to despair as much as to stubbornness, since it refuses to let a person settle permanently into the position his own conduct has placed him in.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:89

> Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Book They Recognized**

The verse adds a circumstance that makes the refusal harder to explain. The community had not been ignorant of what was coming. Its members had asked for help against their enemies through the arrival of a prophet, and when the Book came confirming the scripture already in their hands, they recognized it and turned away.

The Book states the recognition as a fact rather than a possibility, and it will do so again later in the sūrah when it compares their knowledge of the revelation to a man's knowledge of his own children. The refusal being described is therefore not a failure of identification. It is a decision made after identification. That the community's expectation had circulated among its neighbours is preserved in the sūrah's account of the tribes of Madinah, who had heard the report of a coming prophet and were told what it signified. The verse's opening clause rests on knowledge that was public in the region before it became an accusation.

**The Prayer That Preceded the Revelation**

The first clause refers to a practice the community had maintained before the Prophet ﷺ came: they would ask God for victory and relief against the polytheists of Arabia, and they did so appealing to the messenger they expected. Commentators explained that the tribes of Madinah had long lived alongside Jewish communities and had received from them the report that a prophet was to appear in the region.

The Qur'an records the same expectation elsewhere when it describes a community that had announced the coming of a prophet and then declined to accept the one who came. The verse's first clause is therefore not a decoration. It establishes that the community's own position, before the event, was that the arrival of this messenger would settle the dispute in their favour.

**The Criterion of Recognition**

The middle clause states that the Book confirmed the scripture already in their hands, and that they recognized it. The Book's argument here does not rest on the Prophet's lineage or on political considerations; it rests on a criterion the community itself accepted, which is that a scripture which confirms the earlier revelation and agrees with it must be from God.

The verse therefore treats the community's own standard as the ground of its indictment. If their scripture was the measure, the new revelation matched it, and the sūrah's opening passages made the same claim when they described the revelation as confirming what had been sent before it and as a guidance for people who were conscious of God (2:2, 2:4, 2:41).

**The Rejection and Its Motive**

The verse does not spell out why the community rejected the Book. Its members had reasons they kept to themselves, and the next verse names one of them: envy that the grace of God had been given to another people. What this verse establishes is the fact of the rejection, and it leaves the motive to be reported by the sentence that follows.

That order is characteristic of the sūrah's argument. It establishes the recognition first, then the rejection, then the motive, and the reader assembles the case. The result is an account in which the community's conduct is condemning on its own terms before any judgment is pronounced. That the motive is withheld here is part of the construction. The Book withholds the reason for one verse and then reports it as envy, which obliges the hearer to weigh the rejection on its own terms before learning what drove it. The effect is that no explanation can rescue the decision.

**The Curse at the End of the Sentence**

The verse closes with a statement that God's condemnation rests on the disbelievers, and the placement of that clause at the end of an account of recognized but refused truth gives it a specific weight. The Book uses the language of removal from mercy in passages where people have been given knowledge and then acted against it.

The sūrah will use the same vocabulary in the verses that follow, where the community's rejection is described again and the curse is restated. Repetition of this kind serves the passage's purpose: the reader is not allowed to pass over the community's position as a minor episode in the history of the region. In the Book's usage the removal of divine favour describes the condition of a people rather than a sentence announced by a judge, and it follows conduct instead of producing it. Here it closes an account in which the community recognised a book, and the placement ties the verdict to the recognition.

**What the Verse Establishes About Knowledge**

The most important implication of the sentence is that knowing the truth and accepting it are separate events. A person or a community can recognize a revelation as genuine and still refuse it, and the Book treats such refusal as a heavier matter than the unbelief of people who never encountered the message at all.

That distinction runs through the sūrah's account of this people from its opening verses onward. The community had been given more than its neighbours, had been told what to expect, and had asked for the event itself. The Book's portrait of its refusal is designed to make the reader uncomfortable about the possibility of inherited knowledge without submission. The sūrah draws the same distinction later when it describes the learned among this people who accepted the revelation and those who turned away with the same material in their hands. What divides them in the Book's account is willingness rather than information, and this verse states the division in its simplest form.

**Recognition Before Rejection**

The order of events in this verse is what gives it its force. The community asked for the messenger, the Book arrived confirming what they already held, they recognised it, and only then did they reject it. Each stage removes a possible excuse, and the Book states them in the order in which they occurred rather than assembling a case after the fact. That structure is why the sūrah can appeal to the community's own scriptures throughout this section without seeming to argue from an outside authority. The evidence being used against them is theirs, and the recognition the verse describes was their own act before it became their problem. The sequence also explains why the sūrah keeps addressing this community as one that possesses knowledge. The passage treats them as people who understood what they were declining, and the rest of the section argues from their learning rather than from their ignorance, which is a harder case to answer.

**What the Verse Leaves for Its Own Hearers**

The sentence is addressed to a community that had asked for relief, received guidance, and then protected its position instead of accepting the answer. The sūrah keeps the account in the Book for later audiences, and what it carries is not a fact about one people but a warning about the moment when a hoped-for truth actually arrives. The Book describes the same hazard for its own followers when it warns them against measuring revelation by what it costs them, and the sūrah's later addresses to the believers return to the possibility that they might do what this community did. The verses are remembered because the sequence they describe is repeatable in any generation.

**A Book That Was Expected**

Communities that wait for something often prepare for its arrival in ways that make acceptance harder. The expectation in this verse had been voiced for generations, and the report of a coming prophet had become part of the community's standing among its neighbours. When the Book arrived, acceptance meant revising the position that expectation had built. The sūrah's account of the refusal names recognition as the step before rejection, which means the community's difficulty was not identifying the messenger but adjusting to what his arrival required. That is why the verse belongs in a chapter addressed to people who have already accepted the revelation, and why the warning it carries is aimed at the same hazard in a different community: the truth that arrives is rarely the one that was expected.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:90

> Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Price and the Commodity**

The verse returns to commercial language, and this time it names both items in the transaction. What was sold is the soul; what was received is described as a miserable price. The Book has already said that this community traded the Hereafter for this present life, and the present sentence tells the reader what the trade cost them personally rather than collectively.

The word for the price is a term of contempt, and its placement at the start of the sentence gives the verse its tone. Before naming the offence, the Book states the verdict, so that the reader hears the accusation of a bad bargain before hearing what was sold.

**Denying What Was Recognized**

The first half of the charge is the denial of God's revelation, and the previous verse had already established that this community recognized the revelation it denied. The Book does not handle this as a lesser form of unbelief. It treats knowledge that is refused as the substance of the charge, and the sūrah's opening description of people who broke their covenant after it had been confirmed rests on the same principle.

That framing explains the weight of the sentence. A person who never encountered a message has an excuse the Book acknowledges; a community that had been waiting for the message and then rejected it when it arrived has none. The verse states the denial and leaves the reader to supply the awareness that makes it serious.

**The Motive Named as Envy**

The second half of the charge identifies what drove the rejection: resentment that God granted His grace to whom He wills of His servants. The Book does not say the community doubted the credentials of the messenger or found the content of the revelation inadequate. It says the community objected to the choice.

That diagnosis recurs throughout the Book's account of opposition to the messengers, and it names the precise sin involved, which is not theological error but a claim on God's freedom to give. The sūrah will restate it in the years ahead of its revelation as the community's central grievance, and later chapters describe the same resentment in other people who could not accept that revelation had passed to a nation they considered beneath them.

**Grace Given to Whom He Wills**

The clause about God's grace is stated as a fact about God's sovereignty rather than as a rebuke. The Book uses the formula "to whom He wills" whenever it wants to remove the assumption that divine gifts follow a fixed order of merit, and it applies the formula to prophecy, to mercy, and to the ability to receive guidance.

The community's objection presupposed that the covenant created a permanent entitlement to revelation. The verse answers with a statement about who decides, and the answer is not a negotiation. That is why the sentence moves directly to consequences without an intervening argument; the dispute had reached the point where argument ends and the verdict begins.

**Wrath Upon Wrath**

The expression for the punishment is unusual, and the commentators read it as the accumulation of successive periods of divine anger. One reading takes it as wrath earned by this rejection piled on wrath earned by earlier offences, and another takes it as wrath in this world followed by wrath in the next. Under both readings, the phrase describes a sentence that compounds rather than a single penalty.

The Book uses anger language sparingly, and when it does, it marks the point at which a community's record has passed a threshold. The sūrah's narrative has now traced that record from the covenant at Sinai to the rejection of the Prophet ﷺ, and the phrase at the end of this sentence functions as the summary of the whole sequence.

**A Humiliating Punishment**

The final clause specifies the character of the punishment as humiliation. The Book distinguishes between suffering and humiliation in its accounts of the Hereafter, and it reserves the second for people whose offence involved pride or the pursuit of status. A community that rejected the truth in order to protect its standing is matched with a penalty that removes standing altogether.

The word choice also matches the community's own conduct in the passage. These were people preoccupied with their rank among the tribes of Madinah and their standing as the possessors of a scripture, and the verse that ends their account in this section describes them enduring the loss of the very thing they had defended.

**A Warning the Believers Receive as Well**

The passage is written so that its warnings apply to the readers who come after. The Qur'an tells the believers in other chapters that some of them will be tested by their own preference for worldly gain over the commands of God, and it warns against envy, which it names as a sickness of the heart. The situation described in this verse is not confined to the community that first provoked it.

That is the function of the sūrah's long treatment of this people. By the time the chapter turns to the Muslims, the record of a community that knew its scripture and refused it has been established in detail, and the exhortations that follow are addressed to people who have been shown exactly what such a refusal looks like from the inside.

**The Terms of the Charge in One Sentence**

The sentence packs together the sale, the commodity, the motive, and two stages of punishment, and each element has been established by the verses before it. What this verse adds is the connection between the motive and the outcome. A community that objected to God's freedom to grant His grace to whomever He chose received the opposite of what it sought, and the Book describes the result as humiliation because the aim had been standing. The closing attribute of the previous passage and the curse that precedes this one make the same point from different directions: nothing in the account escapes notice, and no position defended against revelation is preserved by the defence. Later generations have read the verse as a summary of what happens when a people measures revelation by what it does for them.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:91

> When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Invitation and the Reply**

The verse presents a scene that must have repeated itself often in Madinah: a believer invites a member of the Jewish community to accept what God has revealed, and the answer comes back that the community believes only in what was sent down to it. The Book records the exchange in two clauses and then proceeds to examine the position.

The reply has the shape of a principled statement. It sounds like fidelity to a tradition, and it was probably defended as exactly that. What the next clause does is test whether the loyalty it expresses is a loyalty to revelation or to a community's possession of it. What makes the exchange worth recording is its ordinariness. The invitation is the one the sūrah extends throughout this section, and the reply is the one it keeps meeting, so the verse serves as a specimen of the larger argument rather than as a report of a single incident.

**Belief Confined to What Was Sent to Us**

The phrase the community uses divides revelation by its recipients rather than by its source. The Book does not accept that division, and it states its own criterion repeatedly: all of the revealed scriptures come from one God, confirm one another, and address one another's peoples. The Qur'an describes itself as confirming what came before it and as a criterion over it, and it describes the earlier scriptures as guidance and light that were given to be followed.

The sūrah's opening had already presented the revelation as confirming the scripture that existed before it and as guidance for people aware of God, and the community's formula in this verse rejects the very continuity the Book is asserting. The sentence being quoted is therefore not a cautious position but a claim to own revelation exclusively.

**Denying What Came Afterwards**

The Book then states that the community denies what came after its own scripture, and it does so in a manner that treats the denial as the real position behind the formula. A person who believes only in what was sent down to him is not necessarily denying anything else; a person who denies what came after has made a decision about a specific text.

The distinction is not a technicality. The verse's charge is that the community reorganized its beliefs around the date of a revelation rather than around its content, and the following verses of the sūrah press the point when they ask why the same community killed prophets who preceded its own scripture. The Book dates the refusal to the arrival of the later revelation rather than to anything in the earlier one. Its charge is that a fixed point in history became the boundary of belief, so whatever came after it was dismissed for the fact of its arrival rather than for anything in its content.

**The Truth That Confirms Their Own Scriptures**

The clause in the middle of the sentence removes the last plausible ground for the refusal. What the community rejects is the truth, and the truth is described as confirming its own scriptures. The Book's argument is self-referential in the strongest sense: the community's own text, by its own standard, is evidence for the revelation it is refusing.

This is the same method the sūrah used in the previous verses, where it established that the community recognized the Book before it rejected it. The passage builds a consistent case: recognition first, confirmation second, refusal third, and the motive named last. The reader is left with a decision to make rather than a fact to weigh. The claim being made is that the two revelations agree, which means the refusal cannot be explained by a doctrinal clash. Later the same community is asked how it can reject a book that matches what it already has, and the question presupposes that no such clash exists.

**The Question About the Prophets**

The verse ends with a question the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to put to them. If the community truly believed in what was sent down to it, how does it explain the killing of the prophets who came before? The question is aimed at the notion that loyalty to a scripture produces loyalty to revelation in general, since the community's own history shows that it did not.

The Arabic form of the question is a challenge to the claim of belief, not an invitation to debate. The Book's method here is to hold the community to the record it cannot deny and to let the record contradict the position it has just declared. The question does not require the audience to accept any new premise; it works entirely from the community's acknowledged history.

**Why the Question Cannot Be Answered**

The community's answer in the previous clause was that it believes what was sent down to it. The question supplies a counter-example drawn from that same tradition: messengers sent by the same God to the same people were rejected and killed. If the formula meant what it said, the killings would be inexplicable.

The Book does not resolve the difficulty for the reader, because the point is the impossibility of resolution. A position that survives only by ignoring its own history is exposed by one question, and the sūrah lets the question stand without an answer. The next verse continues the historical record by recalling the calf, and the pattern of claim-and-contradiction repeats with a different offence. An answer would require the community to distinguish between messengers, and that is exactly what the Book's account of prophecy refuses. The Qur'an presents the messengers as one series carrying one message, so a community that accepts some and rejects others has broken the series rather than discriminated within it.

**The Standard the Passage Leaves Behind**

Read as a whole, the verse sets out a criterion for belief: what God has revealed is accepted because of its source, not because of the community it reached first. The claim to own a revelation exclusively is what the Book rejects in its own readers as well as in the community it is addressing here.

That criterion is what makes this passage still useful to a Muslim reader. The sūrah's account of a community that treated its scripture as an inherited possession is followed later by exhortations to the Muslims about their own treatment of the Qur'an, and the same test is applied to anyone who has received a book and made a privilege of it. Applied broadly, the standard is a criticism of every community that converts revelation into an inheritance. The verse therefore belongs beside the sūrah's warnings to the Muslims, since a people who receive a book and treat it as their property reproduce the position this community is being asked to defend.

**A Heritage Held as a Claim**

There is a difference between inheriting a scripture and belonging to it, and this verse turns on that difference. The community's answer identifies its revelation by the people it reached rather than by the God who sent it, and once that identification is made, later revelation arrives as a rival instead of a confirmation. The Book's response is to test the claim against the community's own history, and the test produces the question about the prophets. A position that treats divine guidance as property has no way to explain why its own ancestors treated guidance as an intrusion, and the sūrah leaves the question standing. The next verse continues the record with the calf, and the passage builds a case in which the community's own memory supplies every piece of evidence.

**Why the Prophets Question Still Lands**

The question at the end of this verse has an unusual force for a short sentence, and its strength lies in what it does not require. No new evidence has to be accepted, no authority from outside the community has to be admitted, and no interpretation of a disputed text has to be settled. The community's answer was that it believed what had been sent down to it, and the question simply asks how that statement fits the record of the messengers sent down to the same people with the same God behind them. The Book's method here is to let an accepted premise do the work. The historical fact of the killings is not in dispute, and the contradiction between it and the claim of exclusive fidelity does not need an outsider to point it out.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:92

> Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Single Verse Containing a Whole History**

The sentence compresses an entire episode into one line. The prophet arrives with proofs, the people wait while he is away, the calf is taken up as an object of worship, and the verdict is stated. The Book is not narrating for information here; it is citing an event that the community itself remembers and that its own scripture records.

The brevity is deliberate. The sūrah's argument does not need the details, because the people being addressed already know them. The verse's function is to place a remembered failure in front of the community one verse after its claim to believe only in what was sent down to it, and to let the contradiction speak. The compression also keeps attention on the verdict. A longer account would invite debate about how the calf was made and who led the people to it, and the sūrah supplies those details elsewhere where they serve a purpose. In this place the bare sequence is the argument.

**Clear Proofs Given to Moses**

The phrase describing what Moses brought is repeated throughout the Book for the signs given to messengers, and it covers both the miracles and the arguments. The sūrah has already described the community's experience of those proofs in earlier verses: the sea divided, the mountain raised, the water brought from rock, and the provision sent down in the desert.

The verse therefore opens with the strongest possible statement of what the community had received. The offence it goes on to describe is not committed in a vacuum or from a position of ignorance; it happens to a people who had just watched a sea open in front of them, and the Book states the advantage before it states the failure. The signs listed in the earlier verses are the community's own traditions, which the Book treats as established history rather than as claims under dispute. That is why the sūrah can use them as evidence, and why the failure recorded here is presented without any suggestion that the people had been given too little.

**The Calf in His Absence**
