Read in that sequence, the verse carries a practical edge. The community's loss is presented not as a subject for speculation about its fate but as a warning to the people now receiving revelation, and the conditions it names are the ones the sūrah will keep repeating as the chapter continues.

**What the Community Could Have Had**

The reward the verse mentions is left undescribed, and the omission is deliberate. The Book's habit in such sentences is to make the comparison the point rather than to inventory the alternative, and the reader is left to weigh what was purchased against what was available. The sūrah describes the Garden at length elsewhere in the chapter, and the details it supplies there fill in what this sentence leaves open.

What the verse provides is the structure of the decision: a community chose one course when another was on offer, and the difference between them was not a matter of degree. The next verses turn to the believers with instructions about prayer and charity, and the placement makes the passage's purpose plain. The account of what was lost stands beside the commands that describe how it can still be obtained.

**A Note on the Book's Method**

The verse does not explain why the community chose as it did, and it adds no threat to the regret it expresses. The Book repeatedly presents its warnings in this register, leaving the reader to infer the consequence from the comparison on offer.

The effect is a passage that argues by showing rather than by accusing, and the reader who has followed the account is expected to reach the conclusion without being told. The next verses continue in a different key, turning from the record of a community that lost its way to instructions for the community that has accepted the message. The chapter's warnings are consistently framed this way, leaving the hearer to work out the cost of a course of action from the comparison the verse presents. The method expects an attentive reader, and the sūrah's later commands assume the same attention.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Command About Words**

The sūrah changes addressee and turns to the believers with a rule about how they speak to the Prophet ﷺ. The instruction is specific to a single expression, and the change of subject is abrupt after the long account of the earlier community. The chapter's concern, however, is continuous: it has been describing how communities treat revelation and the men who bring it, and it now regulates the speech of the community that has accepted the revelation.

The placement of the command also gives it a practical purpose. The Muslims had been using a phrase that carried a mocking sense in the usage of the region, and the verse replaces it with an expression that conveys the same request without the insult.

**The Two Expressions**

The term that is prohibited was part of an idiom meaning to lend an ear, and the commentators explain that it had acquired a demeaning or mocking tone among the people of Makkah and Madinah. The Arabic construction allowed it to be turned into a joke at the expense of the person addressed, and the Book instructed the believers to stop using it.

The replacement carries the sense of attending to someone, of looking after him and giving him one's attention. The request made to the Prophet ﷺ in both cases was the same; what changed was the manner of addressing him, and the sūrah chose the expression that respected the one being asked. The change also shows that the request itself was not objectionable. The believers were not forbidden to seek the Prophet's attention; they were given the words in which to do it, and the substitute supplied by the verse carries the same meaning with the courtesy the earlier phrase lacked.

**Why Wording Mattered**

Al-Ṭabarī grouped this instruction with the Prophet's guidance about naming things and people with the most dignified available words, and he rejected the suggestion that the prohibited phrase had been borrowed from another language and misused unknowingly. His reasoning was that the command is addressed to the believers, who would not have adopted an expression they did not understand.

A parallel passage in the chapter of the women lists the same phrase among the verbal games of a party that distorted words from their places and said things calculated to injure the faith (4:46). The Book treats speech as conduct, and it regulates the vocabulary of its community accordingly. The Book elsewhere treats speech as conduct that is recorded and answered for, and it lists the guarding of the tongue among the marks of the faithful. A correction aimed at a form of address is consistent with the Book's habit of regulating the smallest expressions of a community's attitude.

**Respect for the Messenger**

The instruction belongs to a wider teaching about how the Prophet ﷺ was to be addressed. The Book commands the believers not to treat the calling of the Messenger as they treat their calling of one another, and it warns that doing so can nullify a person's deeds. The phrase that was prohibited fell into the category the Book is guarding against, since it allowed familiarity to shade into mockery.

The Prophet's companions, whose relation to him was the least formal in the community, are the ones the Book addresses here, and the instruction therefore sets the standard for every later generation. The sūrah's rule is that closeness to the Messenger does not relax the reverence owed to his office.

**"And Listen"**

The command to listen follows the instruction about wording, and the commentators noted that the verb carries the sense of obeying as well as hearing. The Book often pairs hearing with obedience when it describes the response of the faithful, and its rebukes to the earlier community were aimed at people who heard and did not obey.

The placement gives the sentence its balance. A corrected form of address without attention to what the Prophet says would be an empty courtesy. What the verse asks for is both the respect of the tongue and the acceptance of the message, and the Book's later verses describe the believers as those who say they hear and then act. The command completes the instruction, since a corrected greeting without attention to what is said would be an empty courtesy. The Book's later descriptions of the believers include hearing that leads to obedience, and it places the blame for the earlier community's failures on people who heard and did not act.

**The Warning at the End**

The sentence closes by stating that the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment, and the mention of the disbelievers at this point serves a purpose. The conduct being corrected among the believers was the conduct of people who had rejected the revelation, and the Book's method is to distinguish the community's discipline from the position of those outside it.

The warning is not addressed to the believers as a threat but as a statement of the contrast. What the sūrah has been describing for several verses is the response of people who declined what they recognised, and the instruction about speech stands in the middle of that account as a picture of how a believing community behaves instead.

**Adab as Part of the Argument**

The verse may look like a small matter of etiquette set inside a doctrinal passage, and the Book's treatment shows that it is not. A community's language is one of the ways it carries its reverence for revelation, and the sūrah's attention to a single phrase indicates how much is being guarded. The rest of the chapter continues with commands and warnings to the same community, and this instruction stands as the first of them. The instruction is placed at the start of a series of commands and warnings addressed to the believers, and the sūrah's decision to open that series with words rather than with worship is deliberate. A community's language is one of the ways it carries its reverence for revelation, and a rule about a single phrase marks how much is being guarded.

**Speech as a Form of Obedience**

The Book treats words as acts, and this verse applies that principle to a community whose members were in daily contact with the Prophet ﷺ. Their familiarity was a privilege, and the instruction ensures that it does not become a licence. The sūrah's concern runs further than one expression, since a community's habits of speech shape what it thinks it may do with sacred things. Later commands to the believers about lowering the voice in the Prophet's presence and about not treating his call as an ordinary call belong to the same teaching, and the discipline they require is one of the ways a community keeps its reverence alive. What the verse establishes is that the manner of a request can be as important as the request, and that the standard applies first to those closest to the message.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Attitude Described**

The verse states that the two groups outside the faith did not want the believers to receive anything good from God, and it names them both: the disbelievers from among the People of the Book and the polytheists. The sentence describes a disposition rather than an act, and the disposition is the one the passage has been documenting in the form of conduct.

The sūrah has already named the motive behind the rejection of the revelation as envy that God's grace had been given to another people (2:90). This verse returns to the same subject from the perspective of the believers, and it describes what their position looks like from those who declined the message. What the verse reports is a state of mind, and the passage has been building a portrait of that state through the conduct it describes. The verse states the wish behind the conduct so that the reader sees the conduct as the expression of something settled.

**The Blessing in View**

Commentators understood the blessing mentioned here as the revelation itself and the wisdom that came with it, since the verses immediately before and after concern the sending down of clear revelations and the guidance they carry. The gift the two groups resented was therefore not a material advantage but the prophethood granted to Muhammad ﷺ.

That reading ties the sentence to the verse about the angels, where the objection to Gabriel was traced to a preference about who should carry the revelation to whom. The Book identifies the resentment as resistance to God's choice of a recipient, and it presents that resistance as the common ground between two groups that were otherwise opposed to each other. The reading ties the sentence to the verse about the angels, where an objection about who carried the revelation was traced to a preference about who should receive it. The Book identifies the resentment as resistance to God's choice of a recipient.

**Allah Selects Whom He Wills**

The middle clause restates a principle the sūrah has used already, and its repetition in this passage is deliberate. Divine favour is not distributed according to a community's merits or a people's lineage; it is granted by God to whomever He chooses, and the statement is made without an explanation that would satisfy the objecting parties.

The Book uses the same formula when it describes the granting of prophecy, of mercy, and of the ability to receive guidance, and it applies the formula to believers and communities alike. The sūrah's opponents are not answered with an argument about who deserved the gift; they are answered with a statement about who decides. The same wording appears wherever the Book speaks of prophecy, of mercy, and of the capacity to accept guidance, and it is addressed to communities as well as to individuals. The sūrah's opponents are not answered with an argument about who deserved the gift.

**Lord of Infinite Bounty**

The closing attribute describes the abundance of God's provision, and it is attached to the statement about selection in order to show that the grace given to one people does not diminish what is available to another. The Book's understanding of divine bounty is not a fixed quantity distributed among claimants, and the resentment described in this verse rests on a premise the attribute denies.

The sūrah uses this name for God in other places where it describes gifts given without measure, and it attaches the same attribute to the guidance sent down to the believers. The sentence therefore ends with a claim about God's generosity that makes the envy described in its first clause both groundless and revealing. The attribute is attached to the statement about selection in order to show that the grace given to one people does not diminish what is available to another. The Book's understanding of divine bounty is not a fixed quantity distributed among claimants.

**Envy as a Spiritual Condition**

The verse treats envy as a matter of the heart before it becomes a matter of conduct, and the Book elsewhere warns its own community against the same sickness. The Prophet ﷺ described the envy that is permitted and the envy that is not, defining the acceptable form as a wish to have what another has been given in order to do good with it, which is the opposite of wishing the blessing away.

The distinction is important for the reader, because the verse's first clause could be mistaken for a general judgment on two communities. What it describes is a particular wish, and the Book's treatment of envy as a disease of the heart applies to believers as well. The command to the Muslims later in this sūrah not to envy what others have been given belongs to the same teaching.

**The Believers' Position**

The sentence is addressed to the believers as an explanation of hostility they had encountered, and it assures them that the opposition was not evidence of a defect in what they had received. The Book often pairs its instructions with accounts of opposition, and the pairing serves to steady a community that is being resisted.

What the verse supplies is a perspective rather than a policy. The response to the attitude it describes is set out in the following verses, in the commands to prayer and almsgiving and in the reminder that whatever good the believers send ahead will be found with God. The closing attributes of the two verses stand side by side: the Lord of bounty on one side, and the All-Seeing who records what is done on the other.

**Why Envy Is Diagnosed in the Heart**

The verse locates the problem in a wish, and the Book's treatment of envy elsewhere shows why that diagnosis matters. A person who resents another's gift has already decided that the gift was misdirected, and from that position arguments become instruments rather than inquiries. The sūrah has already recorded the community's objection about the angel who carried the revelation, and its observation about the angel covered a complaint about the people who received it. Naming the wish exposes what the argument was for. The Book does not leave the diagnosis with the opponents, since it warns the believers against the same condition and describes the acceptable form of envy as the wish to have what another has in order to use it well. What the passage establishes is that a community's reaction to another's blessing is a test of its own relation with God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:106

> If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Objection Being Answered**

The verse responds to a question that the community had raised about the revelation: if the Book is from God, why does one instruction give way to another? The sūrah does not avoid the question. It states the principle behind the practice and attaches to it a claim about God's capability, so that the reader understands the change as an exercise of authority rather than a correction of an error.

The Book's method here is to describe what is happening in its own terms before its opponents can frame it. The revelation announces that rulings may be replaced, and it supplies the guarantee that accompanies the replacement, so that the practice is a declared part of the message rather than a problem discovered in it.

**What the Word Behind Abrogation Means**

The Arabic root behind the term carries the sense of removing or copying out, and the classical explanations compare its action to the sun erasing a shadow, the wind smoothing over dust, or old age effacing the strength of youth. The word is used sparingly in the Book, and the four places where it appears are instructive: this verse, the inscription of the tablets given to Moses, the passage where God eliminates what Satan casts into a prophet's recitation, and the record of human deeds that speaks on the Day of Judgment.

Those uses share a single idea, which is the removal of one thing by another that takes its place. Applied to rulings, the term describes a legal instruction being superseded by a later one, with the original text remaining in the Book as recitation while the practice it commanded gives way.

**The Scope of the Concept**

The scholars of the community developed the concept carefully, and their discussions set limits on it. Abrogation in the classical understanding concerns commands and prohibitions, which is to say legal rulings, and it does not apply to statements about God, the Hereafter, history, or the moral law. A verse such as the one declaring that God has power over all things is not a ruling, and it cannot be abrogated.

The mainstream position also excludes the universal commands, such as the prohibition of murder and theft and the obligation of kindness to parents, from the operation of abrogation, because they were never subject to change. What the concept covers is the area of practice where the Book legislates for a community at a particular stage of its development, and the sūrah's later verses about fasting and prayer illustrate the change in the same chapter.

**Better or Similar**

The verse states that a replacement is either better than what it replaces or comparable to it, and the commentators discussed what superiority could mean where a divine instruction is concerned. One line of explanation takes it as relief in matters of this world and greater reward in the next, and the examples usually given are the easing of the night prayer and the establishment of the Ramadan fast.

Al-Ṭabarī noted that the comparison applies to the ruling rather than to the wording, since the wording of the Book does not admit degrees. He drew a parallel with a verse in this sūrah where an implied phrase has to be understood for the sentence to make sense, showing that the Book's argument sometimes requires the reader to supply a word. Under his reading the verse says that no ruling is replaced without a ruling better or comparable in its place.

**The Range of Opinion Among the Scholars**

The community's scholars differed widely about how many instances of abrogation the Book actually contains. Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi counted five, al-Suyūṭī listed twenty-one, and Ibn al-Jawzī named a number in the hundreds, while a minority position, associated with Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, argued that the apparently conflicting rulings can be reconciled without abrogation at all.

The disagreements indicate how carefully the concept was handled. The mainstream scholars also distinguished abrogation from specification, where one verse narrows the application of another without cancelling it, and from the disappearance of the circumstances that gave a ruling its occasion. The practical question was whether two texts could be reconciled, and only when they could not did the term apply.

**Causing a Verse to Be Forgotten**

The verse also mentions the removal of a verse from memory, and the commentators explained the phrase in two ways. One reading takes it as God causing a text to be forgotten, and a report preserved by Ibn Kathīr describes two men who had learned a sūrah from the Prophet ﷺ and later could not manage a letter of it, and were told that it was one of those that had been abrogated and forgotten. The other reading takes the verb to mean abandoning or forsaking, as the Book uses the same root when it says of the hypocrites that they neglected God and He neglected them (9:67).

Under either reading the sentence asserts something stronger than the replacement of a command. It asserts that the revelation is under God's care in its transmission as well as in its content, and that nothing remains binding except what He establishes.

**The Closing Question**

The verse ends by asking whether the reader knows that God is capable of everything, and the question is the answer to the objection. If the authority that sent the revelation governs the affairs of creation, then the revision of an instruction is not a difficulty to be explained away; it is a demonstration of the same authority.

The next verse continues with a related question about the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and about the absence of any protector besides God, and the two sentences belong to a single argument. What the sūrah establishes in this passage is that the revelation comes from a source that is free to legislate for its creatures as it wills, and that the community's confidence should rest on that source rather than on the stability of any particular ruling.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:107

> Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah?

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question of Sovereignty**

The verse continues the argument of the previous sentence by asking about ownership. The heavens and the earth belong to God, and the consequence the verse draws is that no one else can act as a protector or a helper for human beings. The question form assumes that the answer is known and asks the hearer to follow it to its conclusion.

The sūrah has been answering objections about the revelation, and this sentence supplies the foundation for the answers. A community that questioned why a ruling had changed was questioning the authority of the one who legislates, and the verse restates the scope of that authority in its widest terms. The passage has been handling objections about the revelation, and this sentence lays the ground for the replies. A community that questioned why a ruling had changed was questioning the authority of the one who legislates.

**The Meaning of Kingdom Here**

The Arabic term describes both the territory under a ruler and the rule itself, and the Book uses it for God's authority over creation in passages that describe His provision, His judgement, and His sending of the messengers. The phrase in this verse covers the two realms the reader can observe, and the sūrah's later passages extend the same claim to the unseen.

The statement is not a general affirmation of belief in God's power; it is the premise of the argument the verse is making. If the whole of creation belongs to God, then the choices He makes about the revelation, including the replacement of an instruction, are decisions about His own property, and no third party has standing to object.

**No Guardian and No Helper**

The second half of the sentence names two roles that people look for: someone to take charge of their affairs and someone to assist them when they cannot manage alone. The Book uses the pair elsewhere in describing the helplessness of those who rely on anything other than God, and the verse states that both roles belong to Him alone.

In the context of this passage the statement answers a specific hope. The community had been looking for intermediaries whose standing would secure its position, whether through lineage, through a scripture, or through a favoured angel. The verse removes every candidate at once, and it does so without elaborating on the status of any of them. In the context of this passage the statement answers a specific hope, since the community had been looking for intermediaries whose standing would secure its position, whether through lineage, through a scripture, or through a favoured angel. The verse removes every candidate at once.

**The Shifting Addressee**

Commentators noted that the verse begins by addressing the Prophet ﷺ and then widens to address people generally, since the question about knowledge in the opening clause is followed by a statement that applies to everyone. Similar shifts occur elsewhere in the Book, and the sūrah uses them when it moves from a particular dispute to a universal principle.

The shift matters for how the verse is read. What begins as a reply to an objection about the revelation becomes a statement of the human condition, and the reader who follows it is included in the second half of the sentence. The Book often handles its arguments this way, moving from the occasion to the principle so that the passage retains its force beyond the dispute that produced it.

**What the Sentence Rules Out**

The verse excludes the possibility that any creature can guarantee a person's security or supply what God has withheld. The Book's later passages describe the day when every connection of kinship, alliance, and patronage will be of no use to those who relied on them, and the vocabulary used there matches the two roles named here.

For the community that had been told its standing was assured, the sentence is a direct answer. No protector outside God can secure it, and no helper can change the terms on which the Hereafter is entered. The sūrah has already stated that the community would never wish for death and has attributed the reluctance to its own record; this verse supplies the reason no other course is available.

**The Two Questions and Their Sequence**

The previous verse ended with a question about God's capability, and this one opens with a question about His ownership. Capability without authority would not settle the objection, and authority without the ability to exercise it would leave the community where it was. The sūrah places the two claims together so that the reader holds both.

That pairing is a feature of the Book's teaching about God's names and attributes, which are usually presented in pairs in the passages that argue with objectors. What the sūrah establishes in these two sentences is a complete answer to the question raised about the revelation, and the verses that follow turn to the believers with a caution about the way they should ask. An argument from power alone would not satisfy the objectors, and a claim of ownership without the means to act on it would leave them where they began. Both claims are given in a single breath so that neither is considered apart from the other.

**A Foundation for What Follows**

The next verse warns the believers against questioning their Messenger in the manner that Moses had been questioned, and the statement about sovereignty here prepares that warning. A community that understands who owns the heavens and the earth and who alone can guard or help has a standard by which to judge its own requests, and the sūrah lays the foundation before it delivers the caution. The next verse warns the believers against questioning their Messenger in the manner that Moses had been questioned, and the statement about sovereignty prepares that warning. A community that understands who owns the heavens and the earth has a standard by which to judge its own requests.

**Ownership and the Freedom to Legislate**

The claim that the heavens and the earth belong to God carries a consequence the sūrah draws out in the argument about the revelation. If the whole of creation is His property, then the terms on which He addresses His creatures are His to set and to revise, and no community has standing to require that a ruling remain as it was. The Book's teachers used this reasoning when they explained the place of abrogation in the divine legislation, and they placed it beside the statement that God is capable of everything. What the two sentences together establish is that the revelation comes from a source with both the right and the ability to order human affairs as it wills. The verse's second half then removes the hope that some other party might take charge or lend assistance, and it leaves the reader with the sovereignty stated in the first half as the only ground of confidence.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:108

> Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Caution Addressed to the Believers**

The verse turns to the Muslims with a warning, and it compares their situation to one that had already occurred in the history of an earlier community. The question is put in the form of a doubt about their intention, and the comparison supplies the answer before the command is even given.

The sūrah has been addressing the People of the Book for several verses, and the change of addressee here indicates that the lesson of the passage applies to the community now holding the revelation. The Book's practice of warning its own readers through the accounts of earlier communities is at work in this sentence. The sūrah has been addressing the People of the Book for several verses, and the change of addressee indicates that the lesson of the passage applies to the community now holding the revelation. Warning its own readers through the accounts of earlier communities is one of the Book's standard methods.

**How Moses Was Questioned**

The Book describes the requests made of Moses in several places. The people asked to see God directly, demanded a god like the gods of a neighbouring people (7:138), and called for signs that would settle the matter on their terms. The chapter of the women summarizes the demand to see God and the punishment that followed it, and it notes that the calf was taken up after clear signs had been given (4:153).

The point of the comparison is not that all questions are forbidden but that a community had turned the messenger into a supplier of proofs on demand. What had been given was treated as insufficient, and the requests were made in a spirit of testing rather than of learning.

**The Requests of the Quraysh**

Commentators connected the verse to demands made of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, including requests that he produce a book that could be seen, turn a hill into gold, or provide a tree for their rituals. The reports illustrate what the verse warns against, since the requests were not aimed at understanding but at putting the messenger in a position where he either produced a spectacle or was dismissed.

The Book elsewhere records the demands of those who asked for a different revelation or for changes in the one they had, and it answers each request with a statement about the messenger's role. He delivers what he has been given; he does not manufacture signs at the request of his audience.

**Questions That Are Not Condemned**

The Book's practice shows that inquiries of a different kind were welcomed. Many verses of the Qur'an came down in response to questions the companions asked about orphans, inheritance, charity, and the moon, and the sūrah's own discussions of intoxicants and charity are among them. What distinguished these from the requests being warned against was the purpose: the companions asked in order to act, and their questions produced legislation.

The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to avoid the multiplying of questions that had ruined earlier peoples, and he instructed them to do what they could of what they were commanded and to abstain from what they were forbidden. The instruction is not a prohibition on seeking knowledge; it is a caution against turning the messenger's mission into a debate and against asking about matters that create obligation without benefit.

**The Exchange Named**

The sentence states that whoever trades belief for disbelief has strayed from the level path, and the wording returns to the commercial image the sūrah has used throughout this passage. The community that demands proofs on its own terms is described as giving up one thing to obtain another, and the exchange rate is stated to be ruinous.

The word for the path describes a road that is straight and even, and the Book uses it elsewhere for the middle course that avoids both excess and neglect. Straying from it, in this sentence, is not a matter of a single misstep; it is the consequence of a disposition that treats revelation as something to be negotiated. The term for the path pictures a route that runs level and unbroken, and the Book applies it elsewhere to the balanced course between excess and neglect. Straying from it, in this sentence, is the consequence of a disposition rather than of a single misstep.

**What the Warning Preserves**

The caution protects two things at once. It guards the messenger's authority, since a prophet who answers to his audience's demands is no longer delivering anything, and it guards the community's own faith, since the habit of testing is what the verse identifies as the road to losing it.

The next verse returns to the People of the Book and describes their wish to turn the believers back, and the sequence shows what the sūrah is doing. It warns the Muslims against adopting the manner of those who had opposed the messengers, and then it describes the opposition they should expect. The two verses belong to a single instruction about how a community that holds revelation should behave. The caution protects two things at once: the messenger's authority, since a prophet who answers to his audience's demands is no longer delivering anything, and the community's own faith, since the habit of testing is what the verse identifies as the road to losing it.

**A Discipline Rather Than a Prohibition**

Read carefully, the verse does not forbid asking the Prophet ﷺ anything. It forbids the manner of asking that treats the messenger as an object of experiment, and the Book's own record of the companions' questions shows the alternative. What the sentence asks for is the trust that receives what has been given and seeks understanding within it, rather than the demand for evidence that would render trust unnecessary. The Book's own record of the companions' questions shows the alternative to the manner being warned against. The disposition the verse commends receives what has been given and studies it, instead of demanding proof that would make trust unnecessary.

**The Difference Between Inquiry and Testing**

The Book does not forbid questions, and its own pages contain many of them. The companions asked about orphans, inheritance, charity, and the moon, and legislation came down in response, which shows that an inquiry made in order to act is welcome. What the verse warns against is a different use of the same act: a request designed to put the messenger in a position where he must produce a spectacle or be dismissed. The distinction lies in what the questioner intends to do with the answer, and the Book's account of the earlier community's requests makes that clear, since the demands made of Moses were not followed by obedience when they were met. The sentence therefore protects the community from a habit that consumes the trust on which faith depends, and the next verse describes the opposition the believers should expect from outside.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:109

> Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wish Described**

The verse reports a desire rather than an act, and the sūrah has been handling this subject for several verses. The previous sentence warned the believers against demanding signs; this one tells them what to expect from those who had declined the message. The two are connected, since a community being warned about its own conduct is also being prepared for the pressure it will face from outside.

The Book describes the wish as envy, and the diagnosis matches what the sūrah said earlier about resentment that grace had been given to another people. The objection to the revelation is presented here in its emotional form, and the sentence states that the envy persisted after the truth had been made clear.

**The Occasion Reported**

Commentators connected the verse with a specific episode, in which Muslims who had formerly belonged to the Jewish community were taunted by their former coreligionists after a setback in battle, and some of them were drawn back to their earlier religion. The reports explain the tone of the instruction that follows, which is directed at a community under pressure rather than at one being rebuked.

Al-Rāzī and others noted that the verse applies more broadly than the occasion, since the wish it describes is not confined to one group or one moment. The Book's addresses often have a specific setting and a general function, and this sentence is written in a way that allows both. They account for the tone of what follows, since the command is given to a community under pressure rather than to one that needs rebuking. The Book's addresses frequently carry a particular setting and a lasting purpose, and this sentence is worded so that both are present.

**Envy After Clarity**

The phrase about the truth having become clear appears in the sūrah's account of the community's recognition of the messenger, and it recurs here to underline the nature of the offence. What the verse describes is not the envy of people who doubted the revelation, but of people who knew what they were resisting.

The Book treats knowledge that intensifies opposition as a particular danger, and it describes the same condition in other passages about communities that had been given scriptures. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of envy in a well-known report, limiting the acceptable form to the wish to have what another has been given in order to use it well, and the Book's warnings against the other kind are addressed to its own followers as much as to their opponents.

**The Command to Pardon**

The instruction that follows is among the most striking in the passage: pardon and bear with them until God delivers His decision. The communities had been described in the harshest terms, and the response commanded is forbearance rather than retaliation, with the matter left to God.

The sūrah uses the same instruction elsewhere when it addresses the Prophet's conduct toward those who opposed him, and the Book's treatment of hostility against the believers generally reserves the response to God. What the command does not do is require the believers to accept the behaviour; it requires them to endure it without making themselves the judges of it. The same command is given elsewhere in the Book, where the Prophet's conduct toward his opponents is guided by it, and the handling of hostility toward the believers is generally left to God. The command does not require the believers to accept the behaviour; it requires them to endure it without making themselves the judges of it.

**The Discussion About Abrogation**

The scholars discussed whether the command to pardon was later abrogated by the verses that permitted fighting, and they cited the passage about the tax paid by the People of the Book and the verse that grants permission to those who are being fought. The reports differ on which verse first authorized fighting and on whether this instruction was affected at all.

Al-Rāzī argued that the command concerns a virtuous disposition rather than a legal ruling, and that a virtue is not the kind of thing that abrogation affects. He pointed out that the Book commands patience and forbearance even in the conduct of war, and that the later verses about fighting do not contradict an instruction to endure provocation while the decision belongs to God.

**Until Allah Delivers His Decision**

The clause that closes the instruction places the timing of relief in God's hands, and the Book uses this formulation for matters that the believers cannot resolve by their own efforts. The sūrah's earlier verses have described communities that took their affairs into their own hands and violated their own covenants; this one tells the believers to do the opposite.

The ending also preserves the possibility that the decision will take a form no one expects. What the verse asks for is patience while the matter is open, and its closing attribute states that the One who will decide is capable of everything, which the sūrah has just said in the previous sentence. The clause places the timing of relief in God's hands, and the Book uses this formulation for matters the believers cannot resolve by their own efforts. It also leaves open the form the decision may take, which no one can predict.

**What the Passage Teaches About Opposition**

The verse supplies the believers with a model for living alongside people who resent them. The Book records the wish, identifies its cause, and instructs the community to endure it, leaving the outcome to God. That combination of clear diagnosis and restrained response runs through the sūrah's treatment of the People of the Book, and it is consistent with the invitation to debate with wisdom and kind advice that the Book gives elsewhere. What the verse supplies is a perspective rather than a policy, and the response to the attitude it describes is set out in the verses that follow. The commands to prayer and almsgiving give the believers work they can do while the matter remains in God's hands.

**Forbearance Until the Decision Arrives**

The instruction to pardon is paired with a time limit that no human being controls, and the pairing gives the command its character. The believers are not told that the hostility will end or that its authors will change; they are told to endure it while the matter is open. That arrangement places the community's conduct outside the outcome of the dispute, since patience is required whether or not relief comes. The Book's later verses about fighting do not contradict the instruction, as al-Rāzī argued, because the command concerns a disposition rather than a rule of war, and the Book requires the same virtues of those who defend themselves. What the verse therefore teaches is that a community's forbearance is not a concession to its opponents but an expression of its confidence that the decision belongs to God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:110

> Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Commands in the Middle of an Argument**

The sūrah interrupts its account of the People of the Book with an instruction to the believers, and the instruction consists of the two practices that the Book treats as the standing markers of a life turned toward God. The interruption is deliberate. The passage has described communities that broke covenants and discarded their scriptures, and the sūrah now tells its own community what to hold on to.

The pairing of the prayer and the alms appears throughout the Book in descriptions of the prophets and their peoples, and the sūrah itself listed them among the terms of the covenant given to the children of Israel (2:83). The commands here therefore echo the obligations whose neglect the passage has been documenting. The chapter has been recounting how earlier communities broke their covenants and set their scriptures aside, and its own community is now told what to keep. The commands echo the obligations whose neglect the passage has been documenting.

**Sending Good Ahead**

The verse describes good deeds as something a person sends forward, and the image treats a person's actions as provisions dispatched to a destination he has not yet reached. The Book uses the same figure in the chapter of the wrapped one, where the believers are told to send ahead whatever good they can and are promised that they will find it better and greater (73:20).

The metaphor answers the attachment to life described a few verses earlier, where a community wished for a thousand years instead of preparing for what follows. What the Book offers in place of that wish is a transaction whose return is guaranteed and whose terms are available to anyone, and the sentence states that what is sent ahead will be found.

**Found With Allah**

The promise is that the good will be found with God, and the commentators understood this to mean that the reward is stored and delivered on the Day of Judgment rather than in the present. The Book describes that day as the moment when every person finds what he has done present before him, and the sūrah's repeated promise in this passage uses the same vocabulary.

The phrase also identifies the security of the deposit. What a person sends ahead is not exposed to the hazards that attend property in this world, since the One who receives it does not lose what is entrusted to Him, and the sūrah's closing attribute states that nothing given in this way escapes His notice.

**The Prophet's Practice in Recitation**

A companion reported that when the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse he would follow it by affirming that God sees all things, and the report illustrates a practice of pausing during recitation to respond to the content of a verse with supplication or praise. The same practice is described for verses of glorification and verses of prostration, and it reflects a way of reading that treats the revelation as a conversation rather than a text to be completed.

The report also supplies a model for the reader of the passage. The verse's final clause is a statement about God's awareness, and the companion's account shows the earliest community answering such statements directly rather than passing over them. It also leaves an example of how the passage should be received. Since the verse ends with a statement about God's awareness, the report shows the first community responding to such statements aloud instead of passing over them.

**Instructions Between Arguments**

The sūrah's placement of a devotional command inside a long dispute has a pedagogical purpose. The passage has been analysing the conduct of communities that possessed revelation and failed it, and the risk for the new community is that analysis will substitute for practice. The sūrah answers by issuing two commands that are entirely within its own readers' control.

The commands are also the counterweight to the envy described in the previous verse. The believers cannot change what others wish for them, and the verse gives them work they can do while the matter is in God's hands. The two sentences that follow, one about the claims of the two communities and one about the submission that the Book accepts, continue the passage's argument about what actually counts before God.

**Fasting, Prayer, and the Chapter's Pattern**

The sūrah will return to these two obligations at intervals as the chapter continues, and it lists them among the marks of the believers in its description of the community's character. The obligations are given here without further qualification and without an explanation of their forms, since the community was already practising them.

What the reader receives from the verse is a pair of anchors set in the middle of a difficult passage. The arguments about covenants, magic, and exclusive claims occupy the surrounding verses, and the command to pray and give alms stands among them as the Book's answer to what a community should be doing while those arguments continue. The sūrah returns to these two obligations at intervals as the chapter continues, and it lists them among the marks of the believers in its description of the community's character. The obligations are given without further qualification, since the community was already practising them.

**The Closing Attribute**

The sentence ends by stating that God sees what the believers do, and the sūrah has used the same ending a few verses earlier in its description of the community that clung to life. The repetition places the two endings side by side: the same seeing that exposed the earlier community's attachment witnesses the deeds of the believers. The attribute is a comfort and a warning at the same time, and the Book leaves both implications with the reader. The sentence ends by stating that God sees what the believers do, and the sūrah has used the same ending a few verses earlier in its description of the community that clung to life. The same seeing that exposed the earlier community's attachment witnesses the deeds of the believers.

**Prayer and Alms as the Believers' Answer**

The two obligations named in the verse are the ones the sūrah listed among the terms of the covenant given to the children of Israel, and the passage has been describing what became of that covenant. The instruction therefore has a historical edge: the community now receiving the revelation is told to do what the earlier community was told and abandoned. The commands are also a practical answer to the envy and hostility described in the surrounding verses, since they give the believers a discipline that no opponent can interrupt and a form of wealth that no rival can take from them. What the sentence promises is that whatever good is sent ahead will be found with God, and the promise is stated in the language of deposit rather than of expenditure. The verse leaves the reader with two acts and one assurance, and the sūrah's later passages build on both.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:111

> The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Claim Stated Plainly**

The verse reports what two communities asserted about the Garden, and it places the assertions side by side so that their symmetry is visible. Each group reserved Paradise for itself, and the effect of the arrangement is that two mutually exclusive claims are presented in a single sentence, with no arbiter named by either side.

The sūrah has been dealing with the same instinct in its account of the People of the Book throughout the chapter, and it has recorded a similar claim from the community in connection with the Fire. The passage now names the belief outright and gives the Book's answer in a single instruction. The sūrah has been dealing with the same instinct throughout the chapter, and it has recorded a similar claim from the community in connection with the Fire. The belief is now stated in full, and the answer is given in one command.

**Desires Rather Than Proofs**

The sentence calls the claims desires, and the term in Arabic covers hopes and longings that a person entertains without evidence. The Book elsewhere uses the same word for the aspirations of people who expect a favourable outcome because of who they are, and the sūrah's use of it here reduces the two doctrines to the wish that produced them.

That reduction is the verse's argument. A claim about the Hereafter can be a conclusion drawn from revelation, or it can be the projection of a community's wish about itself, and the Book distinguishes the two by asking which one the claimant can support. The term chosen for the sentence indicates how the Book classifies the claims in question.

**The Parallel Passages**

The Book returns to this position at several points. In the same sūrah it reports the two communities each asserting that the other has nothing to stand on (2:113), and it records a claim that guidance means following only one's own religion (2:135). In the chapter of the table it reports Jews and Christians describing themselves as the beloved children of God, and in the chapter of the congregation it reports a claim to be God's chosen people apart from everyone else (62:6).

The pattern the Book identifies is consistent: a community converts a scripture into a title, and the title then generates claims about the Hereafter that the scripture itself does not make. The sūrah's answer in each case is the same, and it is not an argument about who is right but a demand for evidence.

**The Demand for Proof**

The instruction to the Prophet ﷺ is to ask for a demonstration, and the Arabic word describes an argument that establishes its conclusion rather than a mere assertion. The Book uses the term in other passages when it challenges those who make claims about God without grounds, and its appearance here places the community's doctrine in that category.

The demand is fair on its face, since both communities possessed scriptures and could be asked to produce what their texts actually said about the Garden. The verse does not deny that they had books; it asks them to produce the passage that supported the claim, and the silence that follows the request is the argument. On its face the request is reasonable, since both groups held scriptures and could be asked what those scriptures said about the Garden. The verse does not deny that they had books; it asks them for the passage that supported the claim.

**What the Next Verse Supplies**

The sūrah does not leave the position empty. The following sentence states the criterion the Book applies: whoever submits himself to God and does good will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will come upon them nor will they grieve. Read together, the two verses set aside communal categories and replace them with two conditions that any person can meet.

The sūrah's other descriptions of the people who enter the Garden follow the same pattern, naming belief and righteous conduct rather than affiliation. The Book's answer to an exclusive claim is therefore not a counter-claim on behalf of another community; it is a statement of the terms on which the Garden is entered. The following sentence states the criterion the Book applies: whoever submits himself to God and does good will have his reward with his Lord. Read together, the two verses set aside communal categories and replace them with two conditions any person can meet.

**Why the Verse Is Kept in the Chapter**

The passage belongs to the sūrah's long treatment of the People of the Book, and it also serves the community receiving the revelation. A Muslim reader who treats his own affiliation as a guarantee has reproduced the position the verse criticizes, and the Book's warnings to the believers in the chapter use the same vocabulary of hope without grounds.

The sentence therefore stands as a test rather than as a verdict on others. What it asks of any community is whether the confidence it holds about its standing before God rests on something God has said or on the comfort of belonging, and the Book's answer to the second kind of confidence is a request for proof that it never supplies.

**An Invitation Rather Than a Rebuke**

The command to the Prophet ﷺ is phrased as an invitation to present evidence rather than as a rebuke, and the Book often uses this tone in its disputes with the People of the Book. The community is invited to bring what it has, and the sūrah's confidence in the outcome is evident in the brevity of the sentence. The next verse supplies the position the Book holds, and the passage moves on to the mutual accusations the two communities made against one another. The command to the Prophet ﷺ invites the two communities to present evidence rather than rebuking them outright, and the Book often adopts this tone in its disputes with the People of the Book.

**The Test of a Claim About the Hereafter**

A claim about the afterlife cannot be checked in the way a claim about the weather can, and the Book's answer is to ask where the claim came from rather than to dispute its content. What the sentence demands is a demonstration, and the term chosen describes an argument that establishes its conclusion rather than an assertion repeated with confidence. The Book uses the same word in other passages where it challenges people who speak about God without grounds, and its appearance here places the two communities' claims in that category. The verse does not deny that they had revelation; it asks them to point to what their revelation says, and the silence that follows the request is part of the argument. The next sentence supplies the criterion the Book itself applies, and the passage moves from a contest between two communities to a standard open to everyone.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:112

> But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Corrective to the Previous Claim**

The verse opens with a negation that cancels the exclusive claim of the previous sentence, and it replaces it with a criterion that is open to anyone. The Book's habit in such places is to answer a restricted position with a universal condition rather than with a competing restriction, and the sentence follows that pattern.

The sūrah used a similar opening earlier when it answered the community's claim about the duration of punishment, and in both cases the correction is stated in the form of a principle. What the Book refuses is the idea that the Garden is distributed by affiliation, and what it puts in its place is a description of the people who enter it. The sūrah used a similar opening earlier when it answered the community's claim about the duration of punishment, and in both cases the correction is stated in the form of a principle. What the Book refuses is the idea that the Garden is distributed by affiliation.

**Submitting the Face**

The Arabic expression rendered as submitting oneself is literally a surrender of the face, and the commentators noted both the idiom and the image. The face is the most honoured part of a person, and the prostration in prayer places it on the ground, so the expression conveys a submission that involves the whole person rather than an opinion held in the mind.

The Book uses the same figure in other passages where it describes the surrender of a believer to God, and it pairs the act with good conduct in each of them. What the phrase excludes is a submission that remains internal while the conduct goes its own way, and the second condition in the sentence confirms the reading.

**Doing Good**

The companion phrase describes conduct that is good in itself and well performed, and the Book uses it for the quality of a person's actions as well as their content. The two conditions in the verse therefore cover the inward and the outward aspects of religion: the heart's surrender to God and the life that expresses it.

The sūrah's descriptions of the believers elsewhere use the same pair, and its account of those who enter the Garden names belief and righteous deeds together. The verse in this place is a summary of the Book's standard, and the sūrah establishes it in the middle of a dispute about which community owns the Hereafter. The companion phrase describes conduct that is good in itself and well performed, and the Book uses it for the quality of a person's actions as well as their content. The two conditions in the verse therefore cover the inward and the outward aspects of religion.

**The Two Conditions and Their Explanation**

Commentators discussed what the phrase requires and how its two parts relate. Al-Ṭabarī took the submission to mean the surrender of a person's body and actions to God, and Ibn Kathīr added that the conditions for acceptance are sincerity and conformity to the law, which together exclude both the hypocrite who lacks sincerity and the ascetic who follows no revealed guidance.

Al-Rāzī carried the analysis further and argued that the physical conformity required by the phrase limits it to those who follow a revealed code. Others read the sentence in the wider sense the verse's own wording supports, since the Book states that whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does good will have his reward, and the passage does not name a community.

**No Fear and No Grief**

The sentence closes with the two assurances the Book attaches to those who meet its conditions. The first concerns what lies ahead and the second concerns what has passed, and the pair covers the anxieties that occupy a person who is uncertain about his standing.

The phrase appears several times in the Book, including in the sūrah's description of the believers who follow the earlier prophets, and the repetition gives the community a fixed formula for what the reward includes. What the verse offers is not a description of the Garden's contents but a statement about the condition of the people who enter it, and the two negations are the Book's way of describing a settled state. The first assurance concerns what lies ahead and the second what has passed, and the pair covers the anxieties that occupy a person who is uncertain about his standing. The phrase appears several times in the Book, giving the community a fixed formula for what the reward includes.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah**

The sentence stands between the exclusive claims of the two communities and their mutual accusations in the following verse, and it functions as the Book's own position in the dispute. The sūrah does not join either party; it states the terms on which the Garden is entered, and it leaves the claimants to their evidence.

The same criterion appears later in the chapter when the Book describes the believers as those who submit and do good, and it appears in the sūrah's account of Abraham as a person who surrendered himself to God. The verse therefore belongs to a theme the chapter develops rather than to a single dispute, and its position in the passage gives the sūrah's answer to a question the communities had been arguing about.

**A Statement About Reward With the Lord**

The middle of the sentence locates the reward with God, and the phrase matches the promise to the believers earlier in the passage that whatever good they send ahead they will find with Him. The Book's terminology for the Hereafter consistently places the reward in God's keeping rather than among the things a community administers, and the sentence applies that terminology to the criterion it has just stated. The middle of the sentence locates the reward with God, and the phrase matches the promise to the believers earlier in the passage that whatever good they send ahead they will find with Him. The reward is placed in God's keeping rather than among the things a community administers.

**A Criterion Open to Everyone**

The sentence replaces a dispute about ownership of the Hereafter with a description of the people who enter it, and the description names no community. That is the point of the corrective opening: the Book's answer to an exclusive claim is not a counter-claim on behalf of another group but a standard that any person can meet or fail. The two conditions it names cover the heart's surrender and the life that expresses it, and the sūrah's descriptions of the believers elsewhere use the same pair. The verse therefore stands as a test for whoever reads it, including the community that received the revelation last. What the passage establishes is that the question worth asking is not which group has a claim on the Garden but whether a person has met the terms on which it is entered.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:113

> The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mutual Accusation**

The verse reports each community denying that the other stands on anything, and it sets the two statements beside each other so that the symmetry is plain. Each side makes the same charge against the other, and the sentence's arrangement shows that the accusation cannot be true of both.

The Book has just answered the claim that only one community would enter the Garden, and this sentence supplies the other half of the picture. The communities were not merely confident about their own standing; they had concluded that the other's was void, and they had been teaching the conclusion to their followers. The Book has just answered the claim that only one community would enter the Garden, and this sentence supplies the other half of the picture. The communities were not merely confident about their own standing; they had concluded that the other's was void.

**The Occasion Reported**

Commentators connect the verse with a dispute between a group of Jews and the Christian delegation from Najrān that came to Madinah, though others read it as a description that applies to the two communities generally and does not require them to have been present before each other. The reports agree that the exchange the verse records had an actual setting.

The occasion matters because it explains the tone of the ending. The verse does not settle the disagreement; it assigns the judgment to the Day of Resurrection, and the Book takes the same position in other passages where communities argue about religious truth. The occasion explains the tone of the ending, since the verse does not settle the disagreement but assigns the judgment to the Day of Resurrection. The Book takes the same position in other passages where communities argue about religious truth.

**"Although Both Recite the Scriptures"**

The middle clause supplies the Book's objection to the mutual charge. Both communities recited the scriptures, and the Book holds that each scripture affirms the truth that the other community was denying. The Torah speaks to the prophethood of Jesus, and the Gospel affirms Moses and the Book given to him, so the argument each side used to deny the other could be read in support of the other.

The Book's method here is to use the opponents' own texts as evidence against their use of them. The sūrah has already told the community that its scripture contained the marks of the messenger it declined, and this verse extends the same reasoning to the mutual denials of the two groups.

**Those Without Knowledge**

The sentence adds that those who had no knowledge said the same thing about people of faith, and the clause widens the diagnosis. The habit of denying that others stand on anything is not a peculiarity of communities with scriptures; it belongs to whoever assumes that his own position is the only possible one.

The Book mentions the polytheists in this connection, and the commentators noted that the clause also extends to nations before the two communities. What the verse identifies is a human tendency that revelation is meant to correct, and the addition of the pagans prevents the reader from treating the previous clause as a verdict on two particular groups. The clause widens the diagnosis, since the habit of denying that others stand on anything is not a peculiarity of communities with scriptures. The addition of the pagans prevents the reader from treating the previous clause as a verdict on two particular groups.

**Judgment Left to the Day of Resurrection**

The verse closes by stating that God will judge between the communities on the Day of Judgment concerning what they differed about, and the Book takes the same position in several places where religious disagreement is described. The Qur'an states in other chapters that the truth about such matters will be disclosed when the parties return to their Lord, and it repeats the formula in the chapter of the table and elsewhere.

That positioning serves two purposes. It removes the believers from the position of final judge between communities, and it affirms that the disagreements are not beyond resolution simply because the parties cannot resolve them. The Book's answer to a dispute it does not settle in this world is a statement about the next.

**Al-Kāshānī's Observation**

A commentator cited in the tradition observed that the two communities were veiled from the truth by opposite attachments: one by its fixation on the outward form and the other by its absorption in the inward meaning, and he added that similar problems appear among Muslim schools of thought. The observation does not settle the doctrinal questions the verse describes, and it identifies a pattern the Book's readers can recognize in their own disputes.

The sūrah's placement of the verse at this point in the chapter supports that reading. The communities being described had scriptures and recited them, and what divided them was not a lack of text but the way each selected from it. The Book's own community is warned against the same practice throughout the passage, and the warnings become explicit in the verses that follow.

**What the Verse Teaches About Disagreement**

Read with the surrounding verses, the sentence establishes the Book's manner of handling religious disputes among communities it addresses. It states the claims, identifies the contradiction, notes the scriptures that both parties recite, and leaves the verdict to God. The believers are instructed to pardon and bear with those who oppose them, and the argument is carried on by presenting what has been revealed rather than by pronouncing on the fate of others. Read with the surrounding verses, the sentence establishes the Book's manner of handling religious disputes among the communities it addresses. It states the claims, identifies the contradiction, notes the scriptures both parties recite, and leaves the verdict to God.

**Leaving the Verdict to the Day of Judgment**

The Book states in several places that God will inform people of their differences when they return to Him, and the repetition of the formula indicates how consistently the Qur'an declines to settle religious disputes within this world. That refusal is not a concession that the questions are unanswerable; it is a statement about who is competent to decide them. The believers are told what has been revealed to them and are instructed to present it with wisdom and kind advice, and the fate of those who decline is left where the verse leaves it. The same passage commands the believers to pardon and bear with those who oppose them, and the two instructions work together: the community states its case, conducts itself well, and leaves the judgment to the day when every dispute will be settled by the One who knows what people differed about and why.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:114

> Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them there is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question of Comparison**

The verse opens with a rhetorical question of the kind the sūrah uses when it wants to fix the limits of wrongdoing: who does more wrong than the person described here? The Book measures offences against one another, and it places the obstruction of worship at the extreme end of the scale, above the slanders and distortions that the preceding verses have been describing.

The charge has two halves. The first concerns hindering the mention of God's name in the places set aside for it, and the second concerns active effort to bring those places down. The Book treats the two together as a single offence against the right of human beings to worship, and it attaches the verdict to the conduct rather than to the community carrying it out.

**Which Places of Worship Are Meant**

The Arabic word rendered as places of worship is the plural of the term from which the act of prostration is derived, and the commentators applied it to different buildings. Some pointed to the Temple in Jerusalem and the Kaʿbah in Makkah, since the Book names both as mosques, and they connected the verse with differing accounts of the Temple's destruction. Others connected it with the incident at Ḥudaybiyah, where the Makkans prevented the Prophet ﷺ and his companions from reaching the Kaʿbah for worship in that year.

Al-Ṭabarī reasoned that the reference must be to the Temple, since the idolaters of Makkah never attempted to destroy the Kaʿbah and in fact maintained it. Other commentators read the sentence more widely, applying it to anyone who obstructs access to any house of worship. All the readings agree on the conduct the verse condemns, and the difference concerns which event supplied the occasion.

**Striving for Their Ruin**

The word for ruin in the original carries the sense of making something desolate, and the commentators extended its meaning beyond physical demolition. Filling the Kaʿbah with idols was described by Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī and others as a form of destruction, since the building no longer served the worship of the One God even while its walls stood.

That reading gives the verse a wide application. A place of worship can be ruined by what is put inside it, by whom it is closed to, and by the purposes it is made to serve, and the Book's language of desolation covers all of these. Some commentators connected the verse with a small mosque that Abū Bakr had in Makkah and which was destroyed by the idolaters, and the reports show how concrete the charge was in the earliest community.

**Entering With Fear**

The sentence then states that such people have no right to enter these places except with fear, and the commentators took the clause either as a description of their eventual condition or as an instruction about the standing they should have. The Book often allows an outcome to appear as a statement of what is fitting, and the effect here is that those who closed the doors of worship ended by standing outside them in fear themselves.

Some reports applied the clause to the indemnity paid by the People of the Book in later centuries, and others treated it as a general description of the humiliation that accompanies conduct of this kind. Ibn Kathīr preferred the broader reading and noted that the Prophet ﷺ used to ask God not to afflict him or his community with disgrace in this world, which shows that the outcome described here is a punishment rather than a policy.

**Disgrace in This World**

The verse assigns two consequences, one in this life and one in the next, and the first is described as disgrace. The Book distinguishes between hardship and humiliation, and it reserves the second term for people whose conduct involved suppressing the worship of God or the standing of His messengers. The ruin they sought for others returns to them in the form of dishonour.

Later history gave the sentence an unusual visibility, since communities that destroyed or closed places of worship repeatedly found their own standing diminished in the same regions. The Book presents the outcome as part of the pattern it describes rather than as a coincidence, and the pairing of the two punishments in a single sentence keeps the reader from treating the worldly consequence as the whole of the matter.

**A Tremendous Punishment**

The second consequence is reserved for the Hereafter, and the Book describes it with the same word it uses for the gravest offences. The sūrah has been listing charges against a community that received a scripture, and the sentence here stands apart from that sequence because its subject is conduct that any person or group can commit against any house of worship.

The verse therefore functions as a general statement placed inside a particular argument. It fixes a boundary that applies wherever and whenever it is crossed, and it explains why the Book treats the freedom to worship as something more than a matter of convenience.

**A Reported Interior Reading**

Some readers in the tradition of Islamic spirituality applied the verse inwardly and described the heart as a house of remembrance whose desolation is caused by unchecked desires. The reading is a homily rather than an interpretation of the occasion, and it does not displace the plain reference to buildings. Its value lies in the reminder that the same conduct the verse condemns can be carried out at the level of a person's own relation with God, when the place set aside for Him inside a life is filled with other occupants.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:115

> To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is AllEncompassing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sentence About Direction**

The verse states a fact about the ownership of the horizons and then draws a conclusion about prayer: wherever a person turns, he is facing God. The Book's argument moves from a claim about sovereignty to a practical assurance, and the sūrah will return to the subject of the direction of prayer in the verses that follow.

The sentence stands in the middle of a passage about the Kaʿbah, the Temple, and the obstruction of worship, and it prepares the reader for the change of direction that the sūrah announces later. Its function is to establish that the horizons themselves belong to God, so that no direction has any claim to exclusivity on its own account. The sentence also anticipates the dispute the sūrah is about to describe, when the change of direction became a subject of argument among the communities of Madinah. By assigning the horizons to God, the verse removes the ground on which any direction could claim a privilege of its own, and it prepares the reader for the instruction that follows without pre-empting it.

**The Question of the Direction of Prayer**

Commentators connected the verse to two matters. The first is the practical one, since the community's prayer was at first oriented toward Jerusalem and later toward the Kaʿbah, and some readers took the sentence as permission to pray in any direction at all. Reports indicate that the permission was understood to be abrogated by the verse that established the new direction, and other commentators applied it to voluntary prayer offered while travelling on a mount.

The second matter is doctrinal, and it concerns what it means that God is present wherever a person turns. The commentators were careful to exclude any suggestion that God occupies a place, since a body can be in only one location at a time, and the phrase was explained in several ways: as an affirmation that the worshipper meets God's acceptance, that God is the one addressed in every direction, or that no direction is devoid of His knowledge and care.

**The Reported Occasions**

The commentaries preserve several settings for the sentence. One describes Muslims who could not determine the direction of prayer during the night and later discovered that they had faced the wrong way.
