The Book describes the site where Abraham settled his family as an uncultivated valley, and the prayer in this verse asks for what the place could not supply on its own. The request for fruits is therefore a request for a condition rather than for luxury, since a sanctuary cannot function if its people must leave it to eat. The Book records the answer in the city's later history, where the pilgrimage brought provisions and markets from every region, and the community's own memory of Makkah before Islam included its role as a place of trade and gathering. What the verse establishes is that the sanctuary's material support was asked for and granted rather than assumed. The reader is shown a founder who prayed for the conditions of worship before he prayed for anything else, and the city's later prosperity is presented as the answer to that request.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:127

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Father and Son at Work**

The verse places two men at the same task: Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundation of the House. The Book elsewhere describes the site as assigned to Abraham, and this sentence presents the construction as a shared labour, with the prayer that accompanies it attributed to both.

The sūrah's account of Abraham has been building toward this scene, and the participation of Ishmael is important for the argument the passage is developing about the claims made in Abraham's name. The Book presents the sanctuary as the work of a father and a son whose descendants would later divide over the legacy, and it records their shared prayer before the divisions existed. The shared labour also answers a claim the sūrah is handling, since the Book presents the sanctuary as the work of the line that both communities honoured. The scene is recorded before the disputes that divided their descendants, and the reader receives it as the historical ground beneath the later arguments.

**The Raising of the Foundations**

The Arabic describes the two men raising or lifting the foundations, and the Book's other references to the House suggest that they were restoring what had been established earlier rather than beginning from nothing. Some passages state that the first house established for humanity was the one at Bakkah, a name connected with the site, and the commentators collected accounts of an earlier origin for the building.

The traditions they reported include stories of Adam and of a structure that was raised to the earth and later disappeared in the flood, so that Abraham's work was to bring out the foundations again. Al-Ṭabarī recorded these accounts while judging that they were not reliable as history, and other commentators accepted them, and the difference between the two positions shows how the community handled material of uncertain transmission.

**The Prayer Offered During the Work**

The prayer recorded in this verse is the first in a series that continues through the following two verses, and it consists of a single request: accept this from us. The two men had been given a task and had performed it, and what they asked for was not reward but acceptance.

That posture is characteristic of the Book's account of worship, where the work is done and the outcome is then entrusted to God. The same attitude appears in the Book's descriptions of those who spend, fight, or give, where the deed is performed and the hope is that it will be received, since nothing a person does obliges God. The prayer also establishes the pattern the following verses continue, since the petitions that come after it concern submission, descendants, rites, and a messenger. The request for acceptance is therefore the first item in a sequence that reaches from the building of the House to the community's life.

**"You Are the All-Hearing, All-Knowing"**

The two names at the end of the prayer give the reason for the confidence expressed in it. God hears the request and knows the intention behind it, so that nothing in the work escapes His notice and no nuance of the worshipper's purpose is lost.

The Book attaches these names to prayers and to statements about worship throughout, and they appear again in the sūrah's treatment of the community's own practices. For a reader performing a task with mixed motives, the names in the prayer carry the assurance that what God weighs is not only the visible work but the intention with which it was done. The two names also bear on the work itself, since what the two men were building was for God's worship and the acceptance they sought concerned the intention as much as the structure. The Book's attachment of these names to acts of worship occurs throughout the sūrah.

**The Claim This Scene Answers**

The sūrah has been addressing communities that treated Abraham as their own and traced their standing to him, and it is now describing what he actually did. He built the House with Ishmael, prayed for the city, and asked for a community and a messenger from among his descendants, and the Book uses those facts to test the claims made about him.

The direction of the argument is important. The passage does not set out to answer the communities' claims point by point; it narrates the founding of the sanctuary and records the prayers, and the reader is left to see which claims the narrative supports. By the time the sūrah turns to the direction of prayer, the ground has been laid.

**The Place of the Verse in the Sūrah**

The scene at the House stands near the middle of the sūrah, and the sūrah returns to the theme in later passages about the pilgrimage and the sacred months. Its function in this place is to ground the community's rites in the practice of a man whom the Book praises and whom the earlier scriptures themselves honour.

The next verses continue the same prayer, moving from the request for acceptance to petitions for submission, for descendants, for the rites, and for the raising of a messenger from among the people. Read together they present the sanctuary's founding as an act of worship accompanied by a hope for what would come after, and the sūrah will later state that the hope was fulfilled.

**Building and Praying at the Same Time**

The sentence places the construction and the supplication together, and the combination is one of the passage's most instructive features. The two men had been given a task, and they performed it while asking God to accept what they were doing. The Book's accounts of worship usually present the act and the hope in that order, since nothing a person does obliges God to receive it. The prayer is also the first in a series that runs through the following verses, so that the reader hears the founders of the sanctuary asking for the maintenance of what they had built: submission for themselves, a community from their descendants, the rites, forgiveness, and a messenger to teach. What the verse therefore presents is not a monument but a project entrusted to God at every stage, and the prayers of the two men supply the model for the community that would later face the same House.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:128

> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prayer for Submission**

The first request is that the two men be made submitters to God, and the Arabic term is the one from which the name of the religion later revealed through Muhammad ﷺ derives. The Book uses the same word for Abraham elsewhere and states that he was neither Jew nor Christian but one who submitted, which is why the commentators described this verse as one of the passages that show the universal meaning of the term.

The prayer is for an ongoing condition rather than for a single act. Abraham had already submitted when he was commanded, as the next verses state, and the request here is that the state be maintained, which is how the Book presents the life of the faithful as a continuing orientation rather than a completed event.

**A Nation From Their Descendants**

The second request widens the scope from two individuals to a community, and the Book uses the same word for a people that it will later apply to the community of Muhammad ﷺ. The petition asks that the descendants of the two founders become a nation of submitters, and the sūrah will later state that the community was given a role among humanity.

The commentators noted that the prayer concerns descendants rather than all people, and they explained the limitation by reference to the principle that a person's kin have the first claim on his concern. The request is not exclusivity, since the promise to make Abraham a pattern for humanity had already been given; it is the natural petition of a father for the line that would continue his work.

**"Show Us Our Rituals"**

The third request concerns the rites of worship, and the Arabic term is the one used for the practices of the pilgrimage, including the stations, the sacrifice, and the movements performed at the House. Commentators also read the phrase more broadly as a request for the acts of worship in general, and the Book uses the term elsewhere for the rites appointed to every community.

The prayer presupposes that the manner of worship is something God teaches rather than something people devise, and the Book's accounts of the prophets repeatedly present the rites as given. The sūrah's later passages describe the pilgrimage in detail, and the request here presents the community's practices as an answer to Abraham's petition. The request also treats the forms of worship as something God gives rather than something people settle for themselves. That principle appears elsewhere in the Book when it states that every community was given its rites, and the prayer in this verse places the community's practices in the same category.

**"Turn to Us in Grace"**

The fourth request asks God to turn toward the two men, and the Arabic verb describes a reciprocal movement, since the same root is used for a person's turning to God in repentance. The commentators explained the term as describing God's acceptance of a servant who turns toward Him, so that the vocabulary contains both the human act and the divine response.

The request follows the petition for the rites, and the sequence suggests that even the performance of worship requires God's acceptance rather than merely His instruction. The Book's teaching about worship elsewhere makes the same point, and the Prayer shows it in its opening chapter, where the worshipper asks to be guided along the path of those who have received favour. The petition also acknowledges what the two men knew about their own work: that performing what is commanded does not oblige God to accept it. The request for grace at the end of their petitions is therefore not a formality but the heart of the matter.

**The Names at the End**

The prayer closes with two names describing God as the one who accepts repentance and the source of mercy, and both names correspond to the request that preceded them. The names supply the ground of confidence for a person who has asked for acceptance and knows that his own work cannot require it.

The Book pairs these names in other passages about repentance and about the community's failures, and it uses them to close accounts of severe offences. Their appearance at the end of this prayer indicates that the request for the rites and for descendants is offered in the same spirit as the request for forgiveness, and the reader is shown the founders of the sanctuary asking for what every worshipper after them would need.

**The Sequence of the Prayers**

The verses that follow continue the petition with a request for a messenger from among the descendants, and the sequence is worth noticing: submission, community, rites, acceptance, and then a teacher. The sūrah presents the community's founding as a series of requests for the conditions of worship, and it will later describe how each request was answered. The order of the petitions also reflects the order of the matters themselves: the two founders ask first for their own state, then for the community, then for the practice of worship, and only then for the teacher who would instruct it. The structure is a model of how the Book presents the relation between commitment and instruction.

**A Prayer That Shaped a Community**

The petitions in this verse were answered in the history the sūrah goes on to describe, and the community's own rites and identity were traced by its scholars to the requests Abraham and Ishmael made at the House. The book that follows records the messenger raised from among the descendants, the rites taught to the community, and the direction of prayer established at the sanctuary, and each of those corresponds to an item in the prayer. What the sūrah is doing with the material is therefore more than telling a story about the past. It is presenting the community's worship as the fulfilment of a request made by the man both earlier communities venerated, so that the practices the Muslims observed were not an innovation but an answer. The reader who follows the sequence from the building of the House to the coming of the messenger is being shown a single continuous purpose, and the prayer in this verse is where its content is set out.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:129

> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, AllWise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Petition**

The prayer that began with the two founders at the House ends with a request for a messenger from among their descendants. The petition is the last in the series that runs through the previous verses, and it concerns the means by which everything the earlier requests asked for would be delivered.

The request is for a messenger raised from within the community rather than sent from outside it, and the Book notes the same feature when it describes the Prophet ﷺ as a messenger raised among a people who had not previously received a scripture. The prayer therefore asks for what the sūrah will later state was granted. The request also closes the series of petitions with a concern for what would come after the two builders. Their prayers had asked for their own submission, for a community from their line, and for the rites, and the final request supplies the means by which all of those would be maintained.

**The Functions Described**

The petition names three tasks: reciting the revelations, teaching the Book and wisdom, and purifying the people. The three appear in the same order later in the sūrah, where the community is reminded of the favour that a messenger was raised among them to perform exactly these services.

The sequence is instructive. Recitation comes first, which places the delivery of the divine speech before instruction about it, and the teaching of the Book follows the recitation rather than preceding it. The final task concerns the people themselves, since the effect of the message on its hearers is described as a purification, and the Book uses the term for the removal of what corrupts belief and conduct. The three tasks also provide the pattern by which the sūrah later describes the favour granted to the community, since it states that a messenger was raised among them to do exactly these things. The prayer therefore states in advance what the Book presents as its answer.

**The Book and Wisdom**

Commentators identified the Book with the Qur'an, and they understood the term that follows it either as the practice of the Prophet ﷺ or more broadly as understanding of the religion. The Book pairs the two in other passages as well, applying the same combination to Jesus, to the children of Israel, and to the family of Abraham.

The pairing indicates that the community received both a recited text and the knowledge of how it is to be applied, and the Book treats the two as inseparable in the life of a community. The prayer for a messenger therefore included the means by which the revelation would be understood and practised, not only the words themselves.

**Fulfilment of the Prayer**

The sūrah states later that God has sent a messenger from among the community who recites the revelations to them, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom, using the same language as this petition. The answer to Abraham's prayer is therefore registered in the same chapter, and the argument the sūrah is building for the reader depends on that correspondence.

The Book's presentation is that the messenger came in response to the prayer of the man both communities honoured, and that his coming did not represent a departure from the tradition of the House but its continuation. The reader who has followed the sequence from the purification of the House to this petition is given the conclusion before the argument is stated.

**"From Among Them"**

The petition asks for a messenger from among the community itself, and the Book treats the raising of a messenger from among a people as part of the favour shown to them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was raised among an unlettered people, and the Book describes that as one of the gifts granted to the descendants of Ishmael.

The detail also answers a claim that the sūrah has been addressing, which is that divine guidance should have remained confined to one line or one community. The prayer itself requests the opposite: it asks that the descendants be given a messenger of their own, and the answer to that petition is what the passage has been establishing.

**The Names at the End**

The prayer closes with two names describing God as the Almighty and the All-Wise, and the choices correspond to the content of the petition. The raising of a messenger requires power, and the choice of the messenger and the manner of the teaching belong to wisdom, so the two attributes frame the request with a statement of confidence in the One being asked.

The Book attaches these names to the discussion of prophethood elsewhere, and their presence here indicates the grounds on which the request was made. Abraham and Ishmael asked for a gift that only God could grant, and the names they used were those by which the granting is understood. The two names also match the content of the request, since the raising of a messenger depends on power and the choice of the messenger and his teaching belong to wisdom. The Book commonly closes a petition with the attributes that answer it.

**Closing the Cycle of Prayer**

With this verse the prayers that began at the House are complete: submission, community, rites, acceptance, and a teacher. The sūrah leaves the narrative of building and moves to a statement about the faith of Abraham and to the bequests he and Jacob left to their children, and the transition indicates the purpose of the whole cycle.

The passage has been assembling the case for the religion of Abraham as the Book understands it, and the requests attributed to him and to his son supply the chain from the founding of the House to the coming of the messenger. The verses that follow state the content of the faith in a single line and then present the words by which the two prophets passed it to their descendants.

**A Messenger From Their Own Number**

The petition asks for a messenger raised from among the descendants rather than sent from outside them, and the Book treats that detail as part of the favour granted. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was raised among a people who had not previously received a scripture, and the sūrah describes that as one of the gifts given to the line of Ishmael. The request in this verse also answers a claim the sūrah has been examining, since the communities that possessed earlier scriptures might have expected guidance to remain with them. Abraham's prayer requests the opposite arrangement, and the passage presents the messenger's coming as the fulfilment of the petition rather than as a departure from the tradition of the House. What the reader receives is a narrative in which the coming of the final prophet is traced to the request of the man whom both earlier communities claimed, so that the argument rests on their own ancestor's words.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:130

> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question of Comparison**

The verse opens with a rhetorical question that measures the refusal of Abraham's faith against the judgment of the person doing the refusing. The Arabic term rendered as fool describes a person whose understanding has been lost or whose judgment is impaired, and the sentence treats the rejection of Abraham's religion as evidence of exactly that condition.

The question form is one the sūrah has used repeatedly in this passage, and it has the effect of removing the dispute from the plane of neutral disagreement. A person who turns away from the faith of Abraham is not being told that he has made a different choice; he is being told what his choice reveals about him.

**The Faith of Abraham**

The religion referred to here is the submission described in the previous verses, and the sūrah will name it in the coming passage as the upright faith of a man who was not a polytheist. The Book uses the same term for the tradition traced back to Abraham when it tells the Prophet ﷺ and his community to follow it.

The phrase therefore has a specific content in the sūrah's argument. It is not a general reverence for the patriarch but a defined position: the worship of one God, the purity of the sanctuary established at His command, and the submission that the Book states Abraham practised before the later scriptures existed. The phrase also serves the sūrah's argument about the direction of prayer, since the community's rites are presented as the practice of Abraham's religion rather than as an innovation. The coming verses connect the Kaʿbah, the pilgrimage, and the community's own observances to that tradition.

**Who Would Turn Away**

Commentators identified those who reject this faith with the communities that traced their lineage to Abraham while declining the religion the sūrah describes. The Book had already begun that argument by describing people who claimed him as their own, and the question here states the criterion by which the claim is measured.

The sentence also addresses the reader of the Book in any generation. What is being rejected in the verse is a way of worship whose elements the Book sets out, and the refusal of an ancestor's religion in favour of inherited assumptions is treated as a failure of understanding rather than as an alternative tradition. The question also shifts the discussion from tradition to judgment. A person who prefers an inherited position to the religion described in the passage is not being accused of belonging to the wrong community but of failing to weigh what he has been shown.

**Chosen in This Life**

The middle of the sentence states that God chose Abraham in this world, and the Book uses the same language of chosenness for Mary, for Moses, for Adam, and for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and other prophets. The term indicates a selection for a purpose which the Book then explains through the life of the person selected.

For Abraham, the selection is documented in the sūrah's narrative: the test and the fulfilment, the promise of leadership, the founding and purification of the House, and the prayers for a community and a messenger. What the Book presents as his distinction is the conduct that followed the choice rather than a status that operated apart from it. The Book's use of chosenness for several figures also shows that the term describes a purpose rather than a privilege. Each of the chosen figures is described in the Book by what he was given to do, and Abraham's case is set out in the narrative of this passage.

**Among the Righteous in the Hereafter**

The closing clause states his standing in the next world, and the Book uses the same phrase to describe Abraham in another chapter where it also mentions the blessings granted to him in this world. The phrase combines the two horizons, so that what the community claimed for him is presented as the Book's own confirmation.

The Book's descriptions of the righteous elsewhere in this sūrah include the believers who submit and do good, which means the title is attached to a way of living rather than to a lineage. The reader is therefore shown that Abraham's position in the Hereafter is stated in the same terms the Book uses for anyone who follows his path.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence functions as the conclusion of the passage about Abraham and as the premise for the argument that follows. If his faith is the standard, then the community that follows it is following the religion of the man both earlier communities venerate, and the verse states that to turn from it is to fail in judgment rather than to preserve a tradition.

The next verses present the content of that faith in the words of the prophet himself, when he answered the command to submit, and then record the advice he and Jacob gave to their children. The sūrah is assembling its case from the words of the figures whose authority both communities acknowledge, and the question in this verse is the hinge that turns the narrative into an argument.

**What the Question Is Really Asking**

The rhetorical question does more than criticise those who decline the faith of Abraham; it asks the reader to consider what would have to be true for the refusal to be reasonable. If the religion described in the passage has the content the sūrah has set out, then turning from it would require a reason that outweighs the evidence assembled in the surrounding verses. The Book's method here is to let the reader perform that calculation. The passage has presented Abraham's testing, his fulfilment, the founding of the House, his prayers, and the bequest he left his children, and the question follows immediately. A reader who has accepted that material is being asked whether any consideration could justify setting it aside, and the wording of the sentence supplies the Book's own answer in advance. The verse therefore states the conclusion of the narrative in the form of a question and prepares the reader for the confession of Jacob's household that follows.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:131

> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command and the Answer**

The verse records a single exchange, and it belongs to the series of scenes in which Abraham's obedience is presented. The command is given in one word and answered in one sentence, and the brevity of the exchange is part of its effect.

The Book elsewhere describes Abraham as one who fulfilled what was commanded of him, and it lists his trials among the proofs of that description. The scene in this verse supplies the pattern of his life in its smallest form: a command and an immediate acceptance, without argument and without delay. The scene also illustrates the meaning of the term the sūrah has been using throughout the passage, since submission is presented here as a response to a command rather than as a general disposition. The Book's vocabulary for the religion is therefore given a concrete instance in the words of the man it praises.

**The Command to Submit**

The Arabic of the command uses the same root as the term for submission and the name of the religion, and the commentators noted that the word carries the sense of surrendering one's affairs entirely. The command therefore concerns the whole orientation of a life rather than a particular act.

The Book presents submission as the substance of the religion of every prophet, and the sūrah has used the term in the prayers at the House, in the request for a community of submitters, and in the scene that follows this one where the advice given to the children is to die in that state. The verse here supplies the pattern of the response on which all of those depend.

**"I Submit to the Lord of All Worlds"**

Abraham's reply names the one to whom he submits, and the phrase describes God as the Lord of everything that exists. The addition of the universal title is significant in a scene where the demand laid on him was absolute, since the answer identifies the authority being accepted as the authority over all creation.

The Book's use of the title elsewhere connects it with the provision and governance of every created thing, and the sūrah's opening chapter opens with it. Abraham's reply therefore states both his own act and the ground of it, and the reader is shown a submission that rests on the recognition of who God is. The reply also distinguishes submission to God from submission to any other authority, since the title names the Lord of everything and leaves no room for a rival claim. The words are brief, and the whole content of the religion the sūrah is defending is contained in them.

**Submission Before the Revelation of the Qur'an**

The commentators noted that the term used here describes a condition that existed long before the mission of Muhammad ﷺ, and that the Book applies it to the prophets of earlier generations and to their followers. The religion the sūrah is defending is therefore presented as the original one rather than as a novelty that came with the final revelation.

That reading governs the way the passage answers the claims of the communities that possessed scriptures. The Book does not argue that Abraham was a Muslim in the later, technical sense of belonging to the community of Muhammad ﷺ; it argues that the position he held, which the Book calls submission to God, is the one the revelation restores.

**The Speed of the Response**

The verse places the command and the answer side by side, and the Book does not record any hesitation between them. The same pattern appears in the account of his obedience regarding his son, where the Book states that he acted on what he had seen and that his son consented, and in the account of his migration and his confrontation with his people.

The sūrah's use of this scene is therefore exemplary rather than biographical. The Book is showing the reader what an answer to the command of God looks like, and it presents it in the words of the man whose faith the passage has been defending against the claims of later communities.

**What the Verse Contributes to the Argument**

The sentence supplies the definition of the faith the previous verse called on the reader to accept and warned against rejecting. The content of Abraham's religion was submission to the Lord of all worlds, and the remainder of the passage presents the same religion being passed to his children as a bequest.

The verses that follow record that Abraham left the advice with his descendants and that Jacob did the same, and they place the words in the mouth of the dying patriarch as well. The sūrah's argument rests on the continuity of this single position from Abraham through his line, and the exchange in this verse is its clearest statement. The sentence also provides the definition that the following verses apply to the descendants, since the bequest recorded next is an instruction to remain in the state Abraham took up. The narrative chain that runs from his answer to Jacob's deathbed is built on that single position.

**Submission as a Response to a Command**

The Book presents the religion it teaches as a response rather than as a system, and this scene shows what that means. God commands, and the servant answers; the answer is the religion, and the command is its occasion. The sūrah has been describing communities that received commands and did not answer, and it now places the opposite case in the mouth of the man both of them honoured. The brevity of the exchange also protects it from becoming a discussion. There is no negotiation, no request for delay, and no proposal of alternatives, and the Book records the words without commentary, leaving them to speak. The verses that follow carry the same content into the next generation, since the advice given to the children is to die in the state their father entered. What the reader receives from the scene is the shape of the obedience that the Book calls submission, stated in two short sentences that the community has recited ever since.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:132

> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Bequest Rather Than a Command**

The verse describes what Abraham and Jacob gave their children, and the Arabic word for advice carries the sense of a charge left by someone who expects to be gone. What the two prophets passed on was not a piece of information but an instruction about how to live and how to die.

The sūrah has presented Abraham's faith as a submission and his obedience as an example, and it now shows him handling the same legacy to the next generation. The verse therefore supplies the link between the founder of the line and the descendants whose claims the passage has been addressing. The Book's use of the term for a charge also indicates the expectation that the speaker would not be present to see it carried out. What Abraham and Jacob left was a standard for their children to keep when the parents were gone, and the same concern runs through the sūrah's account of the community that received the later revelation.

**Jacob Included in the Advice**

The mention of Jacob in the same sentence is important for the argument, since the People of the Book traced their descent through him, and the sūrah is showing that he carried the same religion as Abraham. The Book treats the patriarchs as bearers of one position rather than as founders of separate traditions.

Jacob appears elsewhere in the Book as the father of Joseph and as one of the prophets named in the list that the sūrah gives later, and the story told in the chapter of Joseph presents him as a man of patience and trust. The verse here identifies him with the same submission his grandfather had practised, and the following verse records his final words on the subject.

**"Allah Has Chosen for You This Faith"**

The phrase states that the religion came to the children as a selection made by God rather than as an inheritance they had earned. The sūrah has used the language of choosing for Abraham himself, and the advice here applies the same idea to the descendants in a form that makes the gift a responsibility.

The Book's treatment of chosenness in the passage is consistent: what is chosen is chosen for a purpose, and the receiving community is answerable for what it does with it. The advice therefore opens with a statement about God's action and closes with an instruction about the recipients' conduct. The clause also answers any assumption that the religion was inherited automatically. The Book presents it as a gift chosen by God and entrusted to the children, which is the same understanding of provision the sūrah has been setting out in its treatment of the community's favours.

**"Do Not Die Except in Submission"**

The final clause instructs the children about the state in which they should leave the world, and the wording presupposes that death can arrive at any moment while the condition of a person's life is what determines what he dies in. The instruction is therefore about perseverance rather than about a deathbed formula, and the commentators read it as a command to remain in submission until the end.

The Book makes the same point elsewhere when it tells the believers to be mindful of God as He deserves and to die only in that state. The verse in this place presents the instruction as the content of a prophet's bequest to his children, and the community that reads the sūrah is addressed by it as the descendants of the people it describes.

**The Advice to Children**

The Book's accounts of the prophets regularly include their concern for their families and descendants, and the sūrah has already recorded Abraham's prayer for a nation from his line and his request for a messenger among them. The advice in this verse continues the same theme in the form of a direct instruction rather than a petition.

The commentators noted the general principle that a person's household has the first claim on his religious concern, and the Book elsewhere instructs the believers to protect themselves and their families from the Fire. What the verse records is the practice of two prophets carrying that duty out at the level of their own children, and the wording leaves the reader with the model. The passage also shows the prophets doing what the Book commands the believers to do with their households. What the verse records is not a formal testament but the ordinary concern of a parent for the religion of his children, and the model applies to every reader who holds the same trust.

**A Testimony to Universal Submission**

The passage is one of the places the community's scholars cite for the universal meaning of submission in the Book, since the term is used of Abraham, of his son, of Jacob, and of their descendants before the final revelation. The religion being described in the sūrah is presented as the original one, and the bequest in this verse belongs to the chain of transmission by which it was carried.

The verse also supplies the answer to the claims that the sūrah has been examining. The communities that traced themselves to Abraham and Jacob had received the same advice, according to the Book, and the passage that follows records the words in which Jacob's children answered their dying father, so that the reader hears the confession of the descendants in their own voice.

**The Last Instruction of a Prophet**

The sentence records what a prophet chose to leave his children, and the Book returns to the same theme at the death of Jacob in the following verse. Two generations are shown closing their lives with the same concern, and the repetition is what gives the passage its force: the religion was transmitted as a charge from parent to child before it became a subject of dispute among communities. The content of the charge is short. God has chosen the religion for them, and they are to die in submission. The instruction assumes that death can come at any time and that the state in which a person leaves the world is what matters, and it therefore concerns perseverance rather than a final moment. The Book presents the bequest as the settled conviction of the prophets about what their families needed, and the community that reads the passage is addressed as the household that inherited the same charge from the same line.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:133

> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers— Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question Put to the Audience**

The verse opens by addressing the reader directly and asking whether he was present at a particular deathbed. The question is rhetorical, and its function is to introduce a scene that the audience had never witnessed but whose record the Book is now supplying.

The sūrah has been handling claims about the patriarchs, and it introduces the final testimony of Jacob in order to let the reader hear what the ancestor and his children actually said. The Book's method here is to answer a claim about ancestry with a report of the ancestor's own words, and the instruction comes from the one who knows the past. The address also involves the reader in the scene, since the question asks him to consider what he knows about the past and where his knowledge comes from. The Book's answer is a report, and the audience is invited to receive it as the record of what the patriarchs actually said.

**Jacob at the End of His Life**

The Book presents Jacob as a prophet whose later years were marked by the loss of his son and by patience, and the chapter devoted to Joseph's story describes his trust in God throughout. The scene in this verse concerns his last concern before death, and it is not his property or his standing but the worship of his children.

The choice of subject gives the reader a measure of what the patriarchs valued. What a man asks about at the end of his life indicates what he has been living for, and the question recorded here is about the object of worship rather than about any worldly arrangement, which matches the bequest recorded in the previous verse.

**"Who Will You Worship After My Passing?"**

The question is direct and addressed to the children as a group. It presupposes that the answer matters and that the answer will be given by them rather than assumed from their family background, and the Book presents the exchange in order to make that point for its own audience.

The sūrah's argument throughout this passage concerns the claims a community makes about its forebears, and the question in the verse demonstrates that the forebears themselves treated the matter as one of personal commitment. What was entrusted to the children was not a status to be inherited but a worship to be maintained, and the question asks them whether they will maintain it. The question also identifies what the dying man considered essential. In a scene that could have concerned property, blessings, or family arrangements, the Book records a question about worship, and the answer follows the same theme, which shows what the patriarchs treated as the family's real inheritance.

**The Answer of the Children**

The reply identifies the God of their forefathers and names the three patriarchs: Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac. The list is instructive, since Ishmael is the uncle of Jacob rather than his father, and the Book elsewhere uses the term for forefathers broadly, covering ancestors in the line as well as the immediate parent.

The children's answer also affirms the oneness of God and attaches their own submission to it. The sentence therefore repeats the content of the religion in the words of the descendants, so that the reader hears the confession from the same generation the sūrah has been discussing. The reply also serves the sūrah's argument by showing that the descendants of Jacob knew what the religion of their forefathers was. The Book presents the answer as an item of family memory, so that the claims later made about the patriarchs by their descendants are measured against the confession recorded here.

**The Point of the Verse in the Argument**

The passage has been answering claims that the religion of Abraham belonged to one community, and it now supplies the testimony of the patriarch's own household. If the descendants of Jacob bore witness to the worship of one God and to their own submission, then the communities that later disputed over them were arguing about a legacy whose content the Book has now stated.

The verse also serves the community receiving the revelation, since the confession it records is the same one the sūrah asks of its readers. The Book presents the patriarchs as belonging to the religion of submission, and the reader who accepts the account is placed in the line of those who gave the same answer.

**The Names of God in the Verse**

The Arabic of the children's reply uses the general word for a deity rather than the proper name of God, and the commentators noted the distinction, since the phrase is the God of your forefathers, one God, rather than a repetition of the divine name. The wording allows the reader to see the confession as a statement about the object of worship, which is what Jacob's question had asked about.

The verse ends the cycle of Abraham material in the sūrah and prepares for the passage that follows, where the community is invited to identify itself with the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not a polytheist. The narrative of the patriarchs concludes with their descendants confessing the worship of the One God, and the sūrah's next argument concerns the community that claims them.

**The Religion the Patriarchs Left**

The scene at Jacob's death completes the chain the sūrah has been constructing from Abraham's first answer to the command to submit. Four generations are represented in the passage, and each of them is shown holding the same position: Abraham answered the command, Isaac is named among the forefathers, Jacob passed the charge to his sons, and the sons answered with a confession of the One God. The Book's purpose in tracing the sequence is to establish that the religion it defends is the religion of the patriarchs, so that the claims made about them by later communities can be tested against what they themselves said. The community reading the sūrah is asked whether it was present at the deathbed, and the answer is that the record now supplies what the audience could not have witnessed. What the reader is given is the family's own testimony, and the passage that follows turns from the testimony to the question of who is entitled to claim it.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:134

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Statement That Ends an Argument**

The verse closes a section in which the sūrah has been addressing claims made about the patriarchs, and it does so with a single principle. The community in question has passed from the world, and the reckoning concerns each party's own deeds. What the sentence removes is the practice of arguing about one's standing by appealing to the conduct of ancestors.

The Book states the point in the form of a division: theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you earned. The two halves of the sentence face each other, and the symmetry is what makes the statement decisive. Neither party's record can be transferred to the other, and the question of who was right about the past does not alter what the living are answerable for.

**The Repetition Later in the Passage**

The same sentence appears again seven verses later, at the end of a passage about the direction of prayer and the claims of the People of the Book. The repetition brackets the material between the two occurrences, and the reader meets the principle before and after the arguments, so that the whole section is read within its limits.

The Book uses this arrangement when a subject has produced a long exchange of claims. The statement about individual accountability is placed at both ends of the dispute, and the material in between is thereby identified as material the reader should weigh rather than as material that decides the fate of the people being discussed.

**What the Word for Earning Conveys**

The verb used for earning carries the sense of acquiring and, where the object is a deed, of committing it. The Book uses it for the moral proceeds of a person's actions, and the sentence therefore treats deeds as a person's actual property, the only possession that travels with him to the reckoning.

That image appears throughout the Book, which repeatedly describes the Day of Judgment as the point at which every person finds what he has earned present before him. The sūrah has used commercial vocabulary in the same way in its account of the community that traded the Hereafter for this world, and the sentence here applies the vocabulary to the ancestors whose deeds are being used in an argument.

**No Accountability for the Deeds of Others**

The closing clause states that the living will not be questioned about what the earlier community did, and the commentators explained it as a denial of responsibility rather than a denial of interest. The deeds of the ancestors are not the burden of the descendants, and the merit of the ancestors is not their credit.

The Book states the principle in another chapter in the words that no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another, and it adds that every person will be informed of his own differences on the day of return. The sūrah's use of the principle here is aimed at a specific habit: the practice of claiming a position on the strength of a forefather's record rather than on the strength of one's own conduct.

**Why the Correction Was Needed**

The sūrah has been describing communities that made their descent from Abraham and Jacob the ground of their claims, and it has answered with the narrative of what the patriarchs actually did. The verse now removes the premise of the argument altogether. Even if the ancestors were all that the claimants said they were, their standing would not supply the descendants with a position before God.

The Book never denies that the patriarchs were honoured, and the surrounding verses praise them. What the sentence denies is that honour is transferable as a status, since the religion the patriarchs practised consisted of submission and obedience, and those are acts rather than inheritances. A descendant who practises them belongs to the community of the patriarchs, and a descendant who does not has no claim on their record.

**Individual Accountability in the Book**

The Qur'an states this principle in several places, and it does so in the context of communities that relied on lineage. It tells its readers that no one will reap except what he sows, that every soul is held for what it has earned, and that a person's record will be read out to him on the day of judgment. The repetition indicates how important the Book considers the correction.

The sūrah's own treatment of this community follows the same line. The favours granted to the ancestors are recalled so that the descendants may be grateful, not so that they may be confident, and the covenant narrative shows the community's own response to what it received. What is inherited, on the Book's account, is the opportunity and the responsibility rather than the reward.

**The Bracket and the Sūrah's Method**

The two occurrences of this sentence give the reader a technique for handling long arguments about religious history. The Book presents the material, states that the parties are answerable for their own deeds, and returns at the end to the same statement so that the reader does not lose the point in the detail. The method assumes an audience that reads carefully rather than one that needs to be told the conclusion at every step.

The sūrah's later passages use the same approach when they address the Muslims about their own obligations, since the warnings given to the earlier community are turned on the new one in identical terms. What the reader receives from the sentence is a standard that applies to all communities, whatever their record claims for their ancestors.

**What the Verse Asks of Its Reader**

The sentence asks the reader to take up his own case rather than someone else's. A person who has inherited a religious tradition has been given a language, a history, and a set of practices, and the Book treats all of those as provisions for which he is grateful and answerable. What he cannot do is present the record of an earlier generation as a settlement of his own account, and the verse states the reason in a way that leaves no room for negotiation: the two cases are separate, and each will be examined on its own.

**The Tone of the Sentence**

The wording is matter of fact. The Book does not accuse the living of trying to steal the merit of the dead; it states that the accounts are separate and moves on. The effect of that calm is that the principle appears self-evident, which is how the Book often presents its corrections of inherited habits. The reader is left to draw the conclusion, and the following verses continue the argument with the direction of prayer and the claims of the two communities.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:135

> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Invitation Reported**

The verse records an invitation made to the Muslim community by the two communities that possessed scriptures, and the invitation is conditioned on guidance. What is being asked is not that the believers study the Torah or the Gospel but that they adopt the religious identity of the group issuing the invitation.

Commentators explained that the sentence does not describe a joint proposal offering a choice between the two paths. Each community was making the claim for itself, and the verse reports both claims together so that the reader sees the pattern they share. Each believed that guidance passed through its own door, and the answer the sūrah supplies applies to both without distinguishing between them.

**The Answer That Names Abraham**

The response commands the Prophet ﷺ to identify the community with a figure older than both, and the phrase used for faith carries the sense of a path or a way of life. The sūrah has just finished telling the story of that man, and the answer is therefore not a claim but a reference to material the reader has already received.

The Book's method here is to move the discussion to common ground. Both communities honoured Abraham, and both claimed a connection to him, so the sūrah answers the invitation by pointing to him rather than by defending a separate tradition. What the reader is asked to accept is that the religion of Abraham is the one that submission to the final revelation restores.

**The Word Translated as Upright**

The Arabic term rendered here as upright is one of the Book's technical descriptions of Abraham, and it appears in several passages where his faith is contrasted with the paths of the later communities. The word describes a person who turns away from error toward a pure monotheism, and it is used in the Book only of those who hold that position without the distortions the sūrah has been describing.

Commentators noted that the term is not the name of a sect or a group. It describes a state, and the Book uses it in forms that indicate a person is or does something in that condition. The quality belongs to the unspoiled nature God gave to human beings, and the sūrah's later verse about the natural way of God connects the two ideas directly.

**The Range of Meanings Discussed**

The commentators explored the term at length. Al-Ṭabarī understood it as the straight following of Abraham's way, and he rejected narrower readings, such as the identification with pilgrims, which would have included idolaters, or with the circumcised, which would have included the Jews. Others read it as one who is devoted entirely to God, or as a follower of Abraham in the practices he established.

The discussions of the word's origin are less important than its force in the verse. Whatever its etymology, the meaning was clear to the community being addressed, and the sūrah uses it to describe a position defined by what it is not: Abraham was not a polytheist, and the religion being claimed in his name must therefore be free of the associations the sentence excludes.

**Not a Community but a Position**

The Book's use of the term in the plural, describing people who are in that state rather than members of a body, supports the reading that it names a condition rather than an institution. The sūrah's answer to the two communities therefore does not consist of setting up a third community alongside them; it consists of identifying a position that existed before the divisions and that the final revelation restores.

That has consequences for the way the passage should be read. The verse is not an argument that one group's pedigree is better than another's. It is a statement that the religion of Abraham is defined by its content, and the content has been set out in the preceding verses: submission to God, the worship of the House, and the transmission of the same charge to the children.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah**

The sentence follows the reminder that the earlier communities have passed and that each party is answerable for its own deeds, and it precedes the confession of faith that the believers are commanded to make. The three items fit together: individual accountability, the identification of the community with the faith of Abraham, and the statement of what that faith contains.

The sūrah returns to this theme later when it commands the followers of the Prophet ﷺ to follow the way of Abraham and describes him as one who submitted in uprightness and was not a polytheist. The repetition indicates that the identification is central to the passage's argument rather than incidental to it.

**What the Believers Inherit**

The verse gives the community a lineage that is not tribal and a history that is not its own invention. What the believers are told to claim is the position of a man who lived before the scriptures they were invited to adopt, and whose religion the Book describes as pure monotheism. The claim is therefore a responsibility rather than an honour: the community is asserting that it maintains what Abraham established, and the following verses state what that maintenance involves.

**The Tone of the Refusal**

The answer begins with a negation that clears the ground, and then states the alternative in a single clause. The Book does not rebut the two communities at length in this verse, because the material for the answer has already been supplied in the narrative. The reader who has followed the account of the House and the patriarchs knows why the community belongs to Abraham rather than to those who claimed him afterwards, and the sentence trusts that knowledge.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:136

> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Confession Given in the Imperative**

The verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ to state what the believers affirm, and the instruction places the community's creed in a single sentence. The Book often gives its teaching in this form, and the content is arranged so that the reader can recite it as a whole.

The confession begins with God and then lists the revelations, and it ends with a statement about the community's own posture. The structure is important: what the believers affirm is not a set of propositions about themselves but a relation to what God has sent down, and the final clause states the shape of that relation.

**The Revelations Named**

The list moves from the revelation given to the community itself to the revelations given to the patriarchs and then to the prophets of the later line. Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob are named as recipients, and the term for Jacob's descendants covers the twelve tribes that descended from him.

The mention of Moses and Jesus then brings the list down to the two figures whose communities the sūrah has been addressing, and it closes with the prophets in general. By naming the recipients in this order the verse draws a single line of revelation through the whole of sacred history, and it places the community reading it at the end of that line rather than outside it.

**The Descendants of Jacob**

The Book refers to the twelve tribes descended from Jacob in another passage where it describes them being divided and given water in the desert, and the commentators explained the term as referring to Jacob's grandchildren. The mention of the tribes in a confession of faith serves the passage's argument, since the communities that claimed descent from them are being told that their ancestors received revelation as well.

What the verse establishes is a shared history rather than a competition over it. The revelation given to the tribes, to Moses, and to Jesus is affirmed by the believers in the same sentence as the revelation they received, and the Book presents the whole sequence as one provision from a single source.

**No Distinction Between the Messengers**

The middle of the confession states that the community makes no distinction between the messengers, and the sūrah states the same principle again in its closing verses, where the Prophet and the believers affirm their faith in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers without dividing them. The Book's point is that accepting some messengers and rejecting others is not a form of discrimination within belief; it is a rejection of the authority that sent them.

The sūrah has already used this principle to indict the community that believed in part of its scripture and rejected the rest, and the confession here supplies the alternative. What the believers affirm is the whole of the revelation, and the statement is made in the first person plural so that the community recites it together.

**Continuity Across the Scriptures**

The Book states in another chapter that God has ordained for the believers the same religion He decreed for Noah and revealed to Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, commanding that the faith be upheld and not divided. The confession in this verse belongs to the same teaching, and it presents the community's religion as the continuation of a single command rather than as a new departure.

That continuity is what the sūrah's narrative of Abraham has been establishing, and the confession gathers the result into a formula. The believers are told to affirm the revelation given to the patriarchs, the revelation given through Moses and Jesus, and the revelation given to them, and to do so without ranking the recipients in a way that would divide what God sent.

**Submission as the Closing Word**

The sentence ends with the community's submission to God, and the Arabic form places the pronoun before the verb so that the statement reads as a dedication of the community rather than as a description. The word chosen is the same one used of Abraham and Jacob in the preceding verses, and the confession therefore closes by identifying the believers with the religion the passage has been describing.

The verse thus serves double duty in the sūrah's argument. It answers the invitation recorded in the previous sentence by stating what the community holds, and it supplies the content of the faith that the following verses will test against the responses of the two communities.

**The Verse as a Criterion**

The confession is also a criterion. A community that recites it and then treats one part of revelation as acceptable and another as inconvenient has contradicted what it says, and the sūrah's warnings to its own readers make use of the same test. What the verse gives the community is a standard by which its own conduct can be measured, and the Book states it in the language of worship so that the recitation itself becomes the commitment.

The confession works in the sūrah as a rule for weighing claims about the prophets. A claim that assigns one of them to a community formed centuries later is measured against the words the believers recite, and the criterion stays available to any reader who has the verse in front of him. The sūrah does not leave the matter to scholarly arbitration; it supplies a statement both the People of the Book and the believers possess, and it asks them to hold the claims they hear against it.

**Where the Confession Sits**

The sentence stands between the answer given to the two communities and the statement about guidance and schism that follows. The arrangement leads the reader from the claim about Abraham, through the confession of what the community believes, to the consequence of accepting or refusing it, and each step develops the same argument.

The sentence comes after the account of Abraham’s religion and before the passage on the direction of prayer, and it gathers the material that lies between them. Readers have been shown what the ancestors believed, what the two communities claimed about them, and what the believers are told to say; the confession states the position the community holds once those claims have been examined. It is therefore a conclusion placed in the mouth of the community rather than a summary offered by a narrator.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:137

> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Condition and Its Consequence**

The verse sets out the terms on which the two communities would be guided, and it does so without adding requirements beyond the confession the previous sentence has just supplied. What the Book asks of them is what it asks of the believers, and the condition is stated in the form of a comparison between one community's belief and another's.

Commentators explained the phrase so that it would not suggest that the object of belief is somehow duplicated. What is meant is that the two communities should affirm what the believers affirm, and the comparison concerns the content of the confession rather than the existence of two versions of it. Some commentators added that the earlier communities could hold what the believers hold by accepting an undisfigured form of their own scriptures, which would be the same in substance as the revelation given to the Muslims.

**Guidance Attached to Belief**

The sentence makes guidance the consequence of belief, and the Book uses this order consistently. Guidance in the Qur'an is God's gift, and the verse states that it is given to those who accept what He has sent, so that the condition and the gift are held together rather than separated.

That arrangement is important for the argument the sūrah has been conducting. The two communities had claimed guidance as a property of their identity, and the verse states the condition on which it is actually granted, which is the acceptance of the revelation as a whole. What the sentence removes is the assumption that guidance follows from belonging.

**Turning Away as Schism**

The alternative is described as turning away, and the Arabic term for the condition that results carries the sense of a fracture and of opposition. The Book uses the word in other passages for those who split from the truth and set themselves against it, and the term therefore describes more than a difference of opinion.

The choice of word implies that the two communities' refusal would not leave them where they were. The sūrah has described people who recognised the truth and concealed it, and the term used here presents the refusal as a break with the position their own scriptures had assigned them. What they would be opposing is not a community but the truth that had come to them.

**God Will Suffice the Believers**

The sentence then assures the Prophet ﷺ and the community that God will spare them the harm implied by that opposition. The Arabic verb carries the sense of being enough for someone, and the Book uses it in several places where the believers are told that God is sufficient as a protector, a reckoner, or a support.

The expression became one of the community's standing formulas, and the Book records it on the lips of the believers who faced threats and answered that God is sufficient for them and the best protector. The verse in this place supplies the ground of that confidence: the opposition being described does not have the power to determine the outcome, and the One who is enough for the community hears what is said and knows what is intended.

**The Two Names at the End**

The names that close the sentence correspond to the two halves of the situation. God hears what is said against the believers, and He knows what lies behind it, so that the community's position does not depend on its ability to answer every accusation. The Book frequently ends its assurances this way, and the names give the promise its substance.

The two names also appear at the close of a later verse in this sūrah where they follow the promise of divine support in a similar contest. The repetition is characteristic of the sūrah's style, which uses the same closing attributes for situations of the same kind so that the reader learns to recognise the pattern.

**The Tone of the Sentence**

The verse does not celebrate the prospect of division, and it does not threaten the two communities with anything beyond the consequence of their own choice. What it describes is a fork in the road, and the calm wording places the responsibility with the people who must decide.

The Book's treatment of the People of the Book in this passage is consistently of this kind. The sūrah states what they believe, reports what they say, offers the criterion by which the matter can be settled, and then leaves the outcome with them. The instruction to pardon and bear with them appears in the same chapter, and the two passages are read together within the community.

**The Verse as a Summary**

The sentence summarises the argument of the previous verses in a compact form. The confession of faith has been stated, the invitation of the two communities has been reported and answered, and the verse now presents the two outcomes: acceptance, which brings guidance, and refusal, which leaves the refuser in a position of opposition that God will manage on behalf of the believers.

**What the Community Learns**

What the community receives from the verse is a way of conducting itself in a dispute that it cannot settle. The Book does not instruct the believers to secure agreement by argumentative force, and it does not leave them anxious about the results. It states the condition, describes the alternative, and locates the protection where it belongs, and the community's task is to hold to the confession while leaving the outcome to God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:138

> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Word Behind the Translation**

The Arabic term rendered here as the natural way of God is built from a root meaning to dye or to colour, and it carries the image of cloth being plunged into a liquid until it takes on its colour. Several older translations rendered the word as the baptism of God, since immersion is common to both images, and the range of the term is what makes the sentence so suggestive.

Read with that image, the verse describes the believers as having been dipped into something that has changed what they are, so that the religion is not an ornament worn on the surface but the colour of the substance itself. The Book uses physical images for spiritual matters frequently, and this is one of its most memorable.

**The Primordial Nature**

Commentators connected the term with the natural disposition God has instilled in human beings, and the sūrah's later verse about the natural way of God states that this disposition admits no change. The connection gives the sentence its force in the argument of the passage.

The religion being defended is not presented as one tradition among several that a person might adopt by choice. The Book describes it as the original condition of human beings, which the prophets and their scriptures restore, and the image of dyeing fits that claim. A colour that is already in the fabric is not added to it but revealed by it, and the verse presents the religion of Abraham in that light.

**The Range of Readings**

The commentators offered several explanations of the term. One took it as the natural disposition that human beings bear as cloth bears its original colour. Another read it as the way God deals with His creation, since the Book uses the same root for the established pattern of His action that does not change. A third identified it with worship, purification, or the religion itself.

The readings do not compete. God's way, His religion, the purification of the worshipper, and the unspoiled nature of the human being all converge on the same point, which is that the religion taught by the messengers corresponds to what is already written into the human creature and to the pattern by which God deals with His servants.

The differences among the recitations do not change the sense of the sentence, since each of them points to the same idea of an inborn disposition or an appointed pattern. The community’s scholars used the variety to show that the verse concerns something placed in the human being rather than a rule imposed from outside. What the reader takes from the verse is that the religion it names is older than the communities that argue about it.

**The Contrast With a Ritual Claim**

Some commentators noted that the communities addressed in this passage practised a rite of baptism, and they read the verse as asserting that the true dyeing and the true purification come from God rather than from any human ceremony. The sentence would then be answering a claim of the same kind as the claim to guidance in the previous verse.

The point does not depend on that historical reference. What the verse states is that the change of the person belongs to God, and that no community administers it as a rite. The community reciting the sentence affirms that its colouring comes from its Lord, and the image excludes the possibility that it could be applied by any human authority.

**"Who Is Better Than Allah in Ordaining a Way?"**

The middle clause is a rhetorical question of the kind the sūrah uses to close an argument, and it turns the comparison into a statement about authority. If God has given a way, the question of which way is better is settled, and the interrogation simply invites the hearer to acknowledge it.

The Book uses similar questions throughout this passage, and each one reduces a dispute to a point on which the answer is already known. The community is not being asked to weigh competing traditions; it is being asked whether any ordinance could be preferable to the one God has given, and the sentence leaves the conclusion to the reader.

**The Closing Confession**

The sentence ends with a declaration of worship, and the Arabic places the community's devotion before the pronoun in a form that emphasises exclusivity. What the believers say is that they worship Him alone, and the clause matches the confession of Abraham in the surrounding passage, who was described as one who was not a polytheist.

The verse therefore completes the answer given to the two communities in the preceding verses. They invited the believers to adopt their religious identity, and the sūrah answers with a statement about the way God has ordained and about the worship the community offers. The claim being made is not that Islam is one option among several but that it is the way God has given and the relation to God that human beings were made for.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Sequence**

The sentence follows immediately on the assurance that God will spare the believers from the evil of those who oppose them, and it supplies the footing on which the community stands while the dispute continues. What it offers is not a strategy but an identification: this is the way, this is the One who ordained it, and this is the worship the community offers.

The sentence belongs to the group of statements that close the passage on Abraham, and it takes up the vocabulary the sūrah has used from its opening pages onward. The religion is not described here by the name of a community or by the practice of a particular shrine; it is described as a disposition woven into the human constitution by the One who made it. The reader who has followed the sūrah from the account of Adam through the building of the House arrives at a sentence that gathers the whole sequence into a single claim about what people were made for.

**The Image as a Whole**

The image of dyeing is one of the few in the Book that describes the religion as something done to a person rather than something a person does. The two halves of the religion are held together in the sentence: the colouring is God's act, and the worship is the community's response. The verse leaves the reader with both, and the confession of faith in the previous verse supplies the content that the following verses will develop.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:139

> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Put to the Disputants**

The verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ to address the two communities with a question, and the question concerns the ground of a dispute rather than its details. The arguers were contesting a matter that belongs to God, and the sentence asks on what basis they were doing so.

The Book's method here is to expose the assumption beneath the argument. A dispute about God presupposes that one party has a standing to settle what God has decided, and the question in the sentence removes that ground before any particular point is discussed. What the reader receives is a lesson in how the Book handles controversies: it examines the premise rather than the claims.

**Who Was Being Addressed**

Commentators identified the parties as the Jews and the Christians, and some added the idolatrous Arabs, noting that the disputes took different forms. The reports describe objections to a prophet coming from outside the children of Israel, and complaints among the Arabs that a man of higher social standing should have been chosen if a prophet were to be sent.

Both objections have the same structure, which is that they measure the message by the messenger's identity. The verse's answer displaces that criterion by naming what the two sides actually share: the same Lord, the same accountability for deeds, and the same obligation of sincere devotion. The dispute is set inside a relation common to everyone involved.

**"He Is Our Lord and Your Lord"**

The middle of the sentence states a fact that no party to the dispute would deny, and the Book uses this kind of shared premise when it wants to move a controversy onto common ground. God is Lord of all, and the community's relation to Him is not different in kind from that of its opponents, whatever the difference in their response to Him.

The statement also removes a possible reading of the dispute as a contest between two gods or two peoples. The Lord being discussed is one, and the only question left is what He has commanded. The sūrah has made the same point in several ways in the preceding verses, and this sentence states it in its simplest form.

**The Division of Accountability**

The sentence then states that each party is answerable for its own deeds, and the clause repeats the principle stated a few verses earlier about the community that had passed away.
