The Book's method here is to let the creation speak, and the community's scholars saw in the verse an invitation to study the world as a book whose author is the one the previous verse named.

**The Verse as the Ground of the Passage**

The sentence prepares the reader for what follows, where the Book describes those who take rivals beside God despite the signs and describes the love that the believers hold for Him. The evidence has been set out before the contrast is drawn, and the reader receives the account of the two attitudes after having been shown what the creation itself displays.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:165

> Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rivals Taken Beside God**

The verse states that some people take others as equals to God, and the commentators explained the term as describing competitors that are set alongside Him. The Book has already used the same word in the description of those who claim rivals in the creation, and the sentence here applies it to the objects of devotion.

The item that follows identifies the conduct that accompanies the setting up of rivals, which is love, and the verse says that they love them as God should be loved. The charge therefore concerns the direction of a person's love rather than only the correctness of his beliefs, and the reader is shown that the Book treats devotion and affection as belonging to the same subject.

**What It Means to Love Them as God**

The commentators offered several explanations of the comparison. Some read it as describing people who love their idols in the way the believers love God, others as describing obedience offered to leaders as though it were owed to God, and others as describing a love that is divided between God and the rivals.

The variety follows from the wording, which can be understood in more than one way, and the readings converge on the same point. What is being described is a person who gives to something created the attachment that belongs to the creator, whether the object is an idol, a leader, or a habit of the heart. The sentence leaves the reader to examine the direction of his own love, and the Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere supplies the standard.

**The Believers' Love as Greater**

The sentence then states that the believers are stronger in their love of God, and the comparison places the two groups side by side. The community's scholars explained the strength of the believers' love as its being directed undividedly at one object, whereas the love of the idolaters is distributed and is at its strongest only when they are in danger.

The Book's account elsewhere supports the description, since it reports that people call on God with sincerity when they are in a boat on troubled water and then return to their rivals once they reach the shore. The verse's comparison therefore concerns more than intensity; it concerns the constancy with which the love is held, and the community's teachers read the sentence as a description of who the believers are.

**The Love of God in the Book**

The Book uses the language of love in several places, and the community's scholars gathered the passages in which God commands the Prophet to tell people that they should follow him if they love God, in which God describes a people whom He loves and who love Him, and in which the believers are warned that family and property must not be dearer to them than God and His Messenger.

The reports also preserve the words of a man who told the Prophet ﷺ that he had not prepared for the Hour with much prayer or fasting but that he loved God and His Messenger, and the Prophet's answer was that he would be with those he loved. The verse's statement about the believers' love belongs to this body of material, and the community's teachers used it to explain what the love of God consists of in practice.

**What the Wrongdoers Will See**

The verse states that if the wrongdoers could see the punishment they would realise that all power belongs to God and that He is severe in punishment, and the conditional form continues in the next verse, where the scene of the hereafter is described. The sentence tells the reader what the offenders will understand when the matter is no longer hidden from them.

The Book's use of the conditional here gives the statement an unfinished quality that the following verses complete. What the wrongdoers will see is the demonstration of what the previous verse had already declared through the signs, and the reader who has followed the passage from the declaration of God's oneness through the list of signs arrives at a description of the moment when understanding arrives too late.

**The Love That Fear Replaces**

The verse presents the moment of realization as one in which power is seen to belong entirely to God, and the community's scholars noted that this is the knowledge the idolaters lacked in this life. Their failure was not a shortage of information but a refusal to let the information shape their attachment.

What the passage sets before the reader is the difference between knowing that God is one and loving Him as the one, and the verse pairs the two so that the reader can measure his own condition. The believers are described as those whose love is undivided, and the wrongdoers are described as those who will see the truth at the point when it can no longer change them.

**The Verse in the Passage**

The sentence completes the movement that began with the declaration of God's oneness and the list of signs, and it prepares the reader for the account of the hereafter that follows. The Book states the claim, sets out the evidence, and then describes the two responses to it. The reader receives the whole sequence, and the passage leaves him with the question of which of the two loves describes his own.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:166

> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene Described**

The verse describes a moment in the hereafter when those who were followed disown those who followed them, and it states that the punishment will be visible to them. The sentence begins with a word that refers the reader to a time already mentioned, which is the moment of the punishment described in the previous verse.

The Book returns to this scene in several chapters, and the community's teachers read the passages together when they spoke about the accountability of leaders. What the sentence establishes at the outset is that the relationship between a leader and his followers does not survive into the hereafter in the form it had in this life.

**The Leaders and the Followers**

The commentators identified the two groups in several ways. Some took the first to be the leaders of idolatry and the second their adherents, others applied the description to the satans and the human beings who obeyed them, and others read the sentence as a statement about everyone who led or followed in the ways of error.

The readings do not conflict, since the Book's descriptions of the hereafter often apply to a class of people rather than to a single group. What the sentence states is that the relationship of following, whatever form it took, ends in a disavowal, and the reader is shown that the bond between a misleader and his followers is not what either party imagined it to be.

**The Meaning of Recourse Cut Off**

The phrase rendered as recourse comes from a word that means a rope or a means by which something is obtained, and the commentators explained that what will be severed is everything the two groups relied on. Some named the bonds of love and friendship and the ties of kinship that had united them in the world, and others named the deeds on which a person might have hoped to rely.

The image of a rope is used elsewhere in the Book for the means by which a person holds on to safety, and the sentence states that the rope is cut. What the passage establishes is that the relationships and the deeds that people treat as security in this life are not security in the next unless they are of the kind the Book commends, and the reader is left with the question of what he is holding.

**Disavowal in the Book**

The Book describes the disavowal between leaders and followers in other passages, and it states that on the Day of Resurrection the followers and the followed will curse one another. It also reports the words of Satan to those who followed him, in which he admits that the promise he made was empty and tells them that he has no power over them.

The verses in this passage belong to that group, and the community's teachers used them when they warned against following a person without regard for the truth. What the Book presents is a scene in which the authority of a leader evaporates at the moment when it might have been useful, and the reader is shown what the relationship was worth.

**The Isolation of the Individual**

The sentence describes a disavowal that takes place in the presence of the punishment, and the effect is to leave every person alone with his own account. The Book's teaching about the hereafter consistently removes the supports on which a person leans in this world, and this verse removes the support of the group.

The reader is therefore given a picture of the moment when a person discovers that the position he occupied in relation to others no longer helps him. What the sūrah supplies in this passage is not merely a description of the punishment but an account of how the relationships of this life are to be understood, and the verse asks the reader to assess the company he keeps.

The Book’s account of the hereafter repeatedly removes the supports on which people rely in this life, whether they are property, kinship, or the standing that a group confers. The sentence contributes the loss of the group, and the reader is shown a scene in which every person stands with his own record. The community’s teachers read the passage as a description of what awaits those who place their confidence in other human beings, and the verse leaves the reader to examine where his own confidence rests.

**The Verse's Connection to the Previous Sentence**

The verse follows a statement about the wrongdoers seeing that power belongs to God, and it supplies the scene in which that knowledge arrives. The Book has just described what the offenders will understand; the sentence here describes who else will be present and what will happen between them.

The sequence gives the passage its force, and the reader is carried from a general statement about divine authority to a specific account of human relations under its judgment. The community's teachers used the pair of verses when they discussed the responsibility of those who lead others astray, and the passage continues with the words the followers will speak.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes that the bonds of following are severed in the hereafter, that the means on which people rely are cut off, and that the punishment is seen by those it concerns. The reader is given a description that applies to any relationship in which one person leads another away from the truth, and the verse that follows records what the followers say when they see what has happened.

The sentence also supplies the community with a standard for the relationships it forms, since the Book describes the fate of those connections with such clarity. What the verse asks the reader to consider is whether the person he follows will be able to help him when the means of help have been removed. The community’s teachers used the passage in their warnings about those who lead others into error, and the sentence gives their teaching its ground.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:167

> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Words of the Followers**

The verse records what the followers say when they see the outcome, and their words express a wish to return to the world so that they might disown the leaders as the leaders have disowned them. The sentence gives the reader the speech of people whose understanding arrives after the opportunity has passed.

The Book places the words in the mouths of those who had followed, and the statement is symmetrical with the disavowal described in the previous verse. What the followers ask for is the chance to do to their leaders what their leaders have just done to them, and the request reveals what they now understand about the relationship they had entered.

**The Request for Another Turn**

The term rendered as turn refers to the chance to return to the life of this world, and the commentators explained that the request is not granted. The Book's passages about the hereafter frequently record such requests, and the answer they receive is that the time for action has ended.

The community's scholars noted that the wish itself reveals the character of the regret. What the followers want is a chance to act differently, which means that they now know what they should have done, and the verse shows the reader what knowledge is worth when it is no longer connected to the possibility of action. The Book states the same lesson in other places where the people of the Fire ask to be returned so that they might do good.

**The Regret Shown to Them**

The sentence states that God shows them their deeds as a source of regret, and the commentators explained that what the offenders see is the reward they would have received had they acted differently. The Book's image is of a display rather than a reminder, and the wording indicates that the record of what they did is placed before them.

The community's scholars read the phrase as an account of how the hereafter addresses those who failed. What they are shown is not a rhetorical description but the substance of what they chose, and the regret that follows from seeing it is the consequence of the choices they made rather than an additional punishment imposed on them.

**The Comparison With the Reward of the Righteous**

The commentaries describe the moment in terms of a contrast, and they mention reports in which the people of the Fire see the dwellings that the people of the Garden have received and understand what they have forfeited. The wording of the verse concerns the deeds of the offenders, and the community's teachers drew the lesson that a person's actions are what will be presented to him.

The passage's purpose is to give the reader the information in advance, and the Book does so in a form that connects the display of deeds to the choices made in this life. What the reader learns is that the record is being kept, and the verse's account of the regret is placed in the Book so that those who read it may act while the record can still be changed.

**"They Will Never Leave the Fire"**

The sentence closes with a statement that those described will not be brought out of the Fire, and the wording matches the statement of permanence that appeared earlier in the passage. The regret expressed in the verse does not alter the outcome, and the Book states the fact without qualification.

The community's teachers connected the sentence with the previous verse about the cutting off of recourse, and they read the passage as a complete account of the state of those who followed a misleader to the end. What the reader receives is a description of a condition from which there is no exit, and the sentence's placement after the request for a second chance makes the statement's weight clear.

**The Argument With the Earlier Verses of the Sūrah**

The sūrah has already addressed a claim that a certain punishment would last only a limited number of days, and it has asked on what authority the claim rested. The present passage supplies the Book's own account of duration, and the reader who has followed the sūrah's treatment of the subject meets the same statement again.

The repetition is part of the sūrah's method of addressing the expectations that the communities brought to the subject of the hereafter. The Book states its account of the matter repeatedly, and each passage supplies a different aspect, so that the reader receives a settled picture rather than a single assertion.

The earlier passage addressed a claim that the punishment would last for a limited number of days, and the sūrah asked on what authority the claim rested. The present verses supply the Book’s own statement, and the reader who has followed the argument recognises the same subject in a new form. The community’s teachers gathered the passages on the duration of the hereafter, and the sūrah’s treatment of the claim in these verses is part of that collection. What the reader receives is a settled account rather than a single assertion, and the words of the followers are placed within it.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes that the followers will wish for a return, that their deeds will be shown to them, and that the condition they are in will not end. The reader is given the account of the hereafter from the perspective of those who followed, and the passage that follows turns to address humanity with a command about what may be eaten. The transition takes the reader from a scene of judgment to the ordinary conduct of life, and the Book's habit of connecting the two subjects is evident in the movement.

The sentence also shows the reader what the Book’s teaching about the hereafter is for, since the account of a regret that arrives too late is addressed to people who still have the chance to act. The community’s teachers used the passage when they spoke about the difference between knowledge that changes a person and knowledge that arrives at the end. What the verse establishes is that the record of a person’s deeds is presented to him, and that the presentation is the moment when the choices of this life become fully visible.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:168

> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy.

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Address to Humanity**

The verse addresses all people rather than the believers alone, and the call concerns what they may eat from the earth. The Book's address to humanity appears at points where a matter concerns everyone, and the subject of food belongs to that category since the instruction is based on what God has provided for all.

The command follows the description of the hereafter in the preceding verses, and the sequence gives the reader a change of register from the judgment of the next life to the conduct of this one. What the passage establishes is that the response to revelation begins with the ordinary acts of a person's day, and food is the first of them that the sūrah names.

**Lawful and Good**

The sentence pairs two conditions: what is lawful and what is good, and the commentators explained the first as what God has permitted and the second as what is wholesome, pleasant, and free of harm. The Book's usage of the second term elsewhere includes the pure things that the messengers have been given, and the community's teachers understood the pairing to cover both the legal question and the quality of what is eaten.

The two conditions together rule out what is forbidden and what is permitted but harmful, and they also exclude the practice of treating lawful things as though they were prohibited. The verse's phrasing therefore corrects both the people who eat what has been forbidden and those who forbid themselves what God has allowed.

**The Occasion Reported for the Verse**

The commentators report that the verse was revealed in connection with tribes who had made certain animals and crops unlawful for themselves, and the reports name groups that had adopted restrictions of their own devising. The plain import of the sentence is universal, and the community's teachers read it as addressing a practice that was widespread.

The reports show the connection between the verse and the passage that follows, in which the Book describes those who say that they follow what their ancestors practised. What the sūrah establishes is that the standard for what may be eaten is the permission of God rather than the custom of a community, and the sentence states the rule before the following verses describe those who resist it.

**The Footsteps of Satan**

The sentence then forbids following the footsteps of Satan, and the image appears elsewhere in the Book in the context of conduct that leads away from what God has commanded. The commentators explained the phrase as an idiomatic description of yielding to temptation and of adopting a course of action because it has been suggested.

The Book's use of the image gives the reader a way of understanding how a person arrives at a prohibition that God has not made. The footsteps are followed one at a time, and the community's teachers read the phrase as a warning about small steps rather than about a single decisive act. What the verse asks of the reader is that he examine the source of the standards he follows, and the image identifies the source of standards that are not God's.

**A Manifest Enemy**

The closing words state that Satan is a manifest enemy to human beings, and the Book uses the description in a number of chapters. The phrase identifies enmity that is open and known, and the community's teachers understood it as a statement about a danger that has been disclosed rather than concealed.

The reports connect the subject with the verse's occasion, and one report preserved from the Prophet ﷺ describes God stating that He created His servants as people inclined to the truth and that the satans diverted them from their religion and forbade them what God had made lawful. The verse's statement about enmity is therefore supported by a report that describes precisely the practice the sentence is correcting.

**What the Passage Makes of Food**

The verse treats food as a subject that belongs to the religious life rather than to private preference, and the Book's treatment of it elsewhere covers the slaughter of animals, the giving of thanks, and the feeding of others. The command to eat what is lawful and good places the subject in the same category as the commands to worship and to give.

The passage that follows the sentence continues with a statement about what Satan commands, and then with the account of those who refuse the invitation to follow what God has revealed. The reader is shown that the refusal to accept the standard God has set is connected with the conduct the verse corrects, and the whole section deals with the question of whose instruction a person follows.

The community’s scholars drew several principles from the passage, including the rule that what the law has not forbidden remains available to the believer. The sentence in this verse states that the earth and its produce are provided for human beings, and the command to eat from them is therefore a permission as well as an instruction. The reader is shown that the default position of the Book is that the creation has been made for use, and the restrictions that the following verses describe are exceptions to a rule of permissibility.

**The Verse's Place in the Passage**

The sentence opens a teaching about food that occupies several verses and that returns in another chapter where the subject is treated at length. The Book's instructions about what may be eaten are given in the context of its teaching about obedience, and the verse here states the principle before the following verses name the specific prohibitions. The reader is given the general rule and the particular list in the order that lets him understand what the list is for, and the passage continues with a statement about what the enemy of humanity commands.

The sentence opens a section that deals with food and with the standards a community adopts, and it follows the account of the hereafter in the preceding verses. The Book has just described the fate of those who misled others and the regret of those who followed them, and it now turns to the ordinary conduct of the people it addresses. What the passage asks of the reader is that he apply the teaching of the sūrah to the food on his table, and the sentence states the standard before the list of what is forbidden is given.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:169

> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**What the Enemy Commands**

The verse states what Satan commands, and the sentence follows the description of him as a manifest enemy in the previous verse. The Book names three things: evil, indecency, and the attribution to God of what a person does not know.

The structure of the sentence is a contrast with the command that precedes it. The reader has just been told to eat what God has made lawful; he is now told what the enemy of humanity instructs, and the two instructions are presented as the alternatives between which a person chooses.

**Evil and Indecency**

The first two terms describe wrongdoing and shameful conduct, and the Book uses the second frequently for acts that the community would be ashamed to acknowledge. The pairing covers both the harm that a person does and the conduct that degrades him, and the community's teachers read the two as a description of the field in which temptation operates.

The Book states elsewhere that God and the prayer forbid indecency, and the sūrah's later passages repeat the term among the things that the Book commands. The verse's placement of the two terms at the head of the list shows the reader what the command of the enemy leads to, and the community's scholars noted that the wording describes an instruction rather than a suggestion.

The Book uses the first term for the harm that a person commits and the second for acts that shame the one who performs them, and it treats both as things that the community is to avoid without qualification. The community’s teachers noted that the second word appears in the sūrah’s later commands and among the things the Book forbids to the believers, and they read the two terms here as a summary of the field in which a person is tempted. The sentence is therefore general in its scope, and the specific practices that follow in the passage are understood as instances of what the verse has named.

**Speaking About God Without Knowledge**

The third item is the most serious in the sentence, and it concerns statements about God that a person makes without the knowledge to support them. The Book returns to this offence in several places, and the sūrah's following verses describe people who follow the practice of their ancestors and refuse the revelation that has come to them.

The commentators connected this part of the sentence with the prohibitions that communities invented for themselves, since a person who declares something forbidden or permitted on his own authority is claiming a knowledge that belongs to the lawgiver. What the verse establishes is that the offence is not only the act that follows from a false ruling but the assumption of the authority to make the ruling.

**The Occasion in the Following Verses**

The sūrah's next verses deal with people who answer the invitation to follow what God has revealed by saying that they follow what they found their ancestors practising. The commentators connected the passage with the subject of food and with the practices of the tribes that had forbidden certain things, and the present verse's third item names the offence that such practice involves.

The connection explains the placement of the sentence. The Book has just forbidden the following of Satan's footsteps and has described him as an enemy; it now names the content of what he commands. The reader who continues into the next verses sees the practice described in concrete form, and the passage reads as a single argument about the source of a community's standards.

**Al-Ṭabarī's Reading**

The commentators connected the phrase about indecency with the passages in which the Book names the animals that the idolaters had declared forbidden, and they cited the verse in which God states that He has not appointed such categories and that those who disbelieve invent lies about Him.

The reading shows how the community's teachers applied the verse to the practices of their own time. What they drew from it is that a prohibition invented by a community is not a lesser matter than an act of wrongdoing, since it places a human decision in the position that belongs to the law of God, and the sentence treats it accordingly.

**The Command and the Counter-Command**

The passage sets two commands side by side, and the reader is given the authority behind each. One command comes with the provision of what is lawful and good, and the other comes from a being the Book has just identified as an enemy whose enmity is open.

The contrast is the sūrah's method of presenting the choice, and it does not obscure the attractiveness of the second command. What the verse shows is that the guidance of the Book comes with a provision attached, while the instruction of the enemy produces harm and the presumption of knowledge, and the reader is left to compare the two.

The Book’s presentation of the two commands gives the reader the means to judge what is asked of him, since one comes from the Lord of the creation and the other from a being whose enmity has been announced. The community’s teachers drew from the pairing a lesson about the way harmful practices present themselves, since what the verse describes is not offered as evil but as custom. The reader is shown that the source of a practice is what determines its worth, and the passage leaves him with the comparison and with the choice it implies.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the content of the enemy's instruction and the character of the harm it does, and it places the assumption of knowledge about God at the head of the offences it names. The reader is given a standard for judging the practices that a community inherits, and the passage continues with the account of those who appeal to their ancestors. The two verses together address the same practice, and the sūrah uses the pair to show how a community comes to follow a standard that no one has authorised.

The sentence establishes the content of the enmity that the Book has described and names the three things the enemy of humanity wants his hearers to do. The community’s teachers read the list as a picture of how a person is drawn away from obedience, beginning with conduct and ending with statements about God that have no basis. What the reader receives is a description that applies to the practices the following verses describe, and the passage continues with the words of those who answer the invitation to follow the revelation with an appeal to their ancestors.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:170

> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer Reported**

The verse reports what certain people say when they are invited to follow what God has revealed, and their answer appeals to the practice of their ancestors. The Book places the invitation and the reply side by side in a single sentence, so that the reader sees both at once.

The reply is one the Book reports in several chapters, and the community's teachers noted that the wording is nearly identical wherever it appears. What differs is the group being addressed, and the sūrah here leaves the identity general, which allows the reader to apply the description to any community that answers in the same way.

**The Appeal to Ancestral Practice**

The reasoning in the reply rests on the authority of what has been inherited, and the sentence states the position without defending it. What the speakers treat as decisive is that their ancestors did something, and the Book reports the appeal as sufficient in their own estimation.

The commentators noted that the appeal has a history in the Book's accounts of earlier peoples, since the same answer is given by the people of Noah, by the Egyptians who heard Moses, and by the people of Abraham. The repetition shows that the practice of justifying a position by its antiquity is not confined to one community, and the verse's account of it concerns a habit of the human being rather than the error of a particular group.

**The Question Put to the Claim**

The sentence then asks whether the speakers would follow their ancestors even if those ancestors understood nothing and were not rightly guided, and the question exposes what the appeal leaves out. The two conditions named are the absence of understanding and the absence of guidance, so that what is inherited is a practice with nothing behind it.

The Book's use of the question form leaves the reader to supply the answer, and the community's teachers read the sentence as a demonstration that the appeal proves nothing. What the speakers rely on is the fact that something was done before, and the sentence shows that a fact of that kind cannot establish a rule when the ones who did it had neither knowledge nor direction.

**The Parallel in Another Chapter**

The Book reports the same words in another chapter where it describes those who say that what they found their ancestors practising is sufficient for them, and the Book's answer there is the same question. The community's scholars gathered the passages and noted that the Book treats the appeal as a recurring feature of the human response to revelation.

The repetitions give the community its vocabulary for the subject, and they show how the Book's teaching addresses a habit that every generation is tempted to adopt. The reader who is told that a practice is old is invited by these verses to ask what the people who began it knew, and the question becomes the test the passage supplies.

**Guidance and Its Absence**

The verse names guidance as the second thing the ancestors may have lacked, and the sūrah has used the term from its opening verses onward. The Book describes people either as rightly guided or as lacking direction, and the sentence applies the distinction to the generation whose example is being followed.

The community's teachers drew from the verse a warning about the transmission of practice without understanding. What the Book commends is the following of what God has revealed, and the sentence shows the reader that the age of a custom is not what makes it sound. The standard the verse applies is the guidance that the Book itself provides, and the reader is given the means to test what he has inherited.

The term that the verse uses for direction appears throughout the sūrah, from the description of the Book as a guide for the reverent to the request for the straight path that the community recites in its prayer. The community’s teachers noted that the sentence applies the word to a generation whose example was being followed, and that the Book therefore measures ancestral practice by the direction God gives. What the reader receives is a standard by which the customs of a community can be weighed, and the passage continues with the account of those who cannot use the standard because they do not understand what they hear.

**Who Is Addressed**

The commentators connected the verse with the discussion of food in the preceding sentences, and some read it as a statement about the idolaters and the People of the Book, while others took it as a general description. The two readings agree that the verse concerns the practice of justifying conduct by tradition.

The passage around the sentence names the invitation to follow what God has revealed, and the Book's other reports of the same answer show that the reply comes from several communities. The reader is therefore given a description that applies to whoever makes it, and the sūrah leaves the matter open so that the warning is not confined to the people of a particular time.

**The Verse's Place in the Argument**

The sentence follows the account of what the enemy of humanity commands and precedes the parable of the shepherd and the flock. The Book states the instruction, describes the refusal to accept it, and then supplies a comparison that shows the condition of those who turn away.

The movement gives the passage its force, and the reader is carried from an account of the source of a community's practices to a description of what such a community is like. The verse in between supplies the words that explain why the practices are retained, and the passage continues with the image that the Book uses for those who hear the call without understanding it.

The sentence follows the account of the enemy’s instruction and precedes the comparison of those who hear without understanding. The Book states what the enemy commands, reports what the people answer when they are invited to follow the revelation, and then supplies an image for their condition. The reader who follows the sequence from the prohibition of certain foods through the appeal to ancestral practice arrives at the parable with the words of the refusal still in his ear, and the passage continues with the command to the believers to eat what they have been given.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:171

> The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Comparison Introduced**

The verse compares those who disbelieve to a flock that hears the shepherd's calls and cries without comprehending them, and the image is drawn from ordinary experience. What the passage has been describing in words is now presented in a picture, and the reader is shown the condition rather than the argument.

The Book uses comparisons of this kind when a description would be less effective, and the community's scholars noted that the image concerns hearing rather than the message. What the shepherd says is not the subject; what the flock does with the sound is, and the sentence concerns the reception of a summons that is audible but not understood.

**The Shepherd and the Flock**

The picture places the caller in the position of a shepherd and the addressed in the position of animals that respond to the sound of a voice without grasping its meaning. The commentators explained the comparison as describing people who hear the words of the messenger but take from them only the noise.

The image also describes the relation between the caller and the hearers. The shepherd calls because the flock is his responsibility, and the flock's failure to understand does not alter the fact that the call has been made. What the verse establishes is that the fault lies on the side of the hearers, and the picture therefore answers any suggestion that the message was not conveyed.

**Deaf, Mute, and Blind**

The sentence then describes the people in question as deaf, dumb, and blind, and the Book uses the same trio in other passages about those who refuse the revelation. The commentators explained the terms as descriptions of faculties that are present but not used, since the people addressed were able to hear and to speak.

The Book's use of these descriptions elsewhere includes a passage in which the same three words are applied to those whose hearts have been closed to the message. The community's teachers read them as statements about function rather than about the organs, and the reader is shown that the loss described is one that a person brings upon himself by use and habit.

**The Conclusion of the Sentence**

The verse closes by stating that they have no understanding, and the phrase governs the three descriptions that precede it. The Book identifies the root of the condition as the absence of the faculty by which speech is weighed, and the sentence's conclusion therefore explains the images that have been used.

The community's scholars drew a distinction between the person who has not yet heard and the person who has heard and not understood, and the verse concerns the second. What the passage establishes is that the call has reached the people described, and the sentence names the condition in which it was received, which is the condition the Book has been describing in the preceding sentences about those who follow the practice of their ancestors.

**Comparisons of Animals Elsewhere in the Book**

The Book uses animal imagery for those who fail to act on revelation in other chapters as well. It compares those who were entrusted with the Torah and did not carry it to a donkey bearing books, and it compares a person who follows his desires to a dog that pants whether it is driven away or left alone.

The similarity among these passages is in the relation between what is received and what is understood, and the community's teachers gathered them when they spoke about knowledge that does not reach the will. The verse in this place supplies the image that fits its context, since the subject is a call that has been heard and not understood.

**Prophets and Other Warnings**

The comparison also concerns the work of the prophets, and the Book describes the messengers as warners whose task is to deliver the message rather than to compel the response. The verse states what the response of some people will be, and it gives the community a picture of what its own proclamation will meet.

The community's teachers used the passage when they discussed the limits of what a preacher can accomplish. What the Book establishes is that the message reaches the ear of the people addressed, and the sentence describes the condition of those who hear it without the understanding that would change them.

The Book describes the messengers in several passages as warners whose task is to convey the message, and it states that their duty does not extend to compelling the response. The comparison in this verse shows what the delivery of the message may meet, and the community’s teachers read it as a description of the conditions under which the work of proclamation is carried out. What the reader receives is a picture of a call that is audible and of hearers who do not grasp it, and the sentence leaves the outcome with the one who knows what each person will do with what he hears.

**The Verse's Place in the Passage**

The sentence comes after the account of those who prefer the practice of their ancestors to the revelation, and it supplies the image that describes their position. The verses that follow turn to address the believers with a command about the good things they have been provided, and the passage then sets out what has been forbidden.

The reader is carried from a description of refusal to an address to those who accept, and the contrast gives the section its shape. The verse in this place states what the refusal looks like from the outside, and the Book leaves the judgment of the people described to the one who knows what their condition will become.

The sentence stands between the report of the refusal to follow the revelation and the address to the believers about the provision they have been given, and it supplies the image that holds the two together. The Book has described people who answer the invitation with an appeal to their ancestors, and it now compares them to a flock. The reader who continues into the following verses meets the command to the believers to eat what is good and to give thanks, and the contrast between the two responses is what the passage has been building toward.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:172

> O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Address to the Believers**

The verse addresses the believers and commands them to eat from the good things that God has provided, and it joins the command to a call for gratitude. The sentence follows the address to all humanity in the earlier verse, and the difference between the two is instructive.

The first command was issued to humanity as such, on the ground of what God has provided on the earth. The second is issued to the believers, on the ground of what God has provided for them, and the community's scholars noted that the two commands establish the same practice on the same basis. What the reader is shown is that the believers' response to provision is gratitude, and the sentence makes that response the condition of the worship the community offers.

**The Good Things Provided**

The term rendered as good things is the same one used in the earlier address, and the commentators explained it as what is wholesome, pleasant, and free of harm. The wording adds the idea of provision, which the sentence attributes to God, and the community's teachers read the phrase as covering everything that has been given for the use and enjoyment of human beings.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere includes the list of foods that have been forbidden, and the command in this verse occupies the space that the list leaves open. What the sentence establishes is that the believer's default position toward what he has been given is acceptance and gratitude, and that the restrictions are the exceptions rather than the rule.

**Gratitude as the Condition of Worship**

The sentence states that gratitude is to be offered if the community worships God alone, and the conditional form connects the two. The community's scholars explained the connection by noting that a person who acknowledges the giver of what he has received is someone whose worship is directed to the right object.

The Book's frequent pairing of provision with gratitude appears elsewhere in the sūrah, where the children of Israel are reminded of what they were given, and in the appeal to the Quraysh, who are reminded of the security and the provision they enjoy. The verse in this place belongs to that body of teaching, and the sentence makes the recognition of the gift a part of the worship itself.

**The Reports About What God Accepts**

The community's reports attach the same principle to the acceptance of acts of worship. The Prophet ﷺ stated that God is good and accepts only what is good, and the community's teachers used the saying when they discussed the relation between a person's earnings and the acceptance of his prayers and alms.

The report shows how the community applied the verse's command to the question of what a believer brings before God. What the sentence establishes is a link between the material conditions of a person's life and the worship he offers, and the reader is told that gratitude is not a separate act added to the worship but a condition of it.

**The Command in Its Context**

The sentence follows a passage about people who justified their practices by the custom of their ancestors, and it addresses the community that has accepted the revelation. The command to eat what is good is therefore a statement about the freedom that the revelation brings, since the restrictions the earlier communities had invented are not imposed on the believers.

The commentators noted that the passage's discussion of food is connected with the subject of authority. What the Book has established is that the standard for what is permitted belongs to God, and the sentence here draws the practical conclusion for the community that accepts that standard.

The command follows a passage about communities that forbade themselves things God had permitted, and the community’s teachers read the sentence as the correction of that practice. The Book has stated that the standard belongs to God, and the sentence draws the practical conclusion for those who accept it. What the reader receives is a statement about the freedom that the revelation restores, since a community that follows the Book is not bound by the restrictions that other communities have invented, and the sentence places that freedom within the obligation of gratitude.

**Gratitude in the Book's Vocabulary**

The Book's term for gratitude carries the sense of acknowledging a benefit and of acting in a way that shows the acknowledgement, and the community's scholars distinguished it from mere verbal thanks. The same root is used in the Book for what a person owes to his parents and for the failure of a community to recognise what it had been given.

The verse's use of the term gives the reader a task that extends beyond the act of eating, since what the Book asks for is a life that reflects the recognition of the giver. The community's teachers read the sentence as an instruction about the whole of a believer's dealings with what he possesses, and the passage continues with the list of what has been forbidden.

The words rendered as thanks and as ungrateful come from the same root, and the Book uses the pair when it describes how people receive what they are given. The sūrah’s account of the children of Israel includes the command to remember the blessings that were granted to them, and the appeal to the Quraysh reminds them of the provision and the security they enjoy. The community’s teachers read the vocabulary as an indication that the Book treats the recognition of a gift as a duty that accompanies the gift itself, and the sentence in this verse applies that duty to the food the believers have been provided.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes that the believers may eat what God has provided, that the provision is the reason for gratitude, and that the gratitude belongs to the worship the community offers. The reader is given the principle before the list of prohibitions that follows, and the two together form the Book's teaching on the subject in this passage.

The community’s teachers gathered the command in this verse with the address to humanity that precedes it and read the two as a single instruction given to different audiences. What the sentence adds is the connection between what a person eats and the worship he offers, and the community’s practice has preserved the connection in the invocation spoken over food and in the thanks given after it. The reader is given a standard that concerns the ordinary acts of his day, and the passage continues with the list of what has been forbidden and with the concession granted to those who are compelled.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:173

> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity —neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prohibitions Named**

The verse names four things that have been forbidden: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been slaughtered in the name of anything other than God. The list is short and specific, and the community's scholars noted that the Book elsewhere adds to it in a passage that names further categories.

The sentence's opening states that these are the only things forbidden, and the wording stands as a correction to any practice that added restrictions on its own authority. What the reader receives is a statement of what the standard amounts to in practice, and the list follows the command to eat what is lawful and good.

The community’s scholars compared the list in this verse with the longer list in another chapter and concluded that the two together describe the same set of prohibitions in different circumstances. What the sentence supplies here is the standard in brief, and the community’s practice has preserved it in the rulings on what may be eaten and what may be shared with others.

**The Terms of the List**

The commentators explained each item. Carrion is the flesh of an animal that has died without being slaughtered in the manner the law requires, blood is the fluid that is not to be consumed, and the pig is excluded by name. The fourth category covers animals that are slaughtered as an offering to something other than God.

The Book's treatment of the list elsewhere includes additional items, and the community's scholars gathered the passages into a single teaching. The verse in this place states the categories that concern the ordinary circumstances of a community recently addressed on the subject, and the list's brevity reflects the practice of dealing with the matter as it arises.

**The Practice of Slaughter**

The Book's teaching connects the permissibility of meat with the invocation of God's name at the time of slaughter, and the community's practice has preserved the invocation as a part of the act. The reports describe the Prophet ﷺ instructing those who were sent to teach about the proper manner of slaughtering animals.

The rule also bears on the relation between the community and those around it. The commentators noted that the meat of the People of the Book is not included in the prohibition, since the passage concerns what has been offered to something other than God, and the sūrah states that permission elsewhere. The sentence therefore defines the boundary of what the community may share with its neighbours, and the reader is shown that the regulation is practical rather than ceremonial.

**The Permissions of Necessity**

The sentence then states that a person who is compelled by necessity, without desiring what is forbidden and without exceeding what the situation requires, commits no sin. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere states the same permission, and the community's scholars derived from it the rule that preservation of life takes precedence over the ordinary prohibition.

The commentators explained the two qualifications in the sentence. The person must not be pursuing the forbidden thing out of desire, and he must not take more than the necessity requires, and the community's teachers applied the pair to the amount a person may eat and to the length of time over which the concession lasts.

**The Conditions Explained**

The term rendered as one who covets carries the sense of rebellion, and the commentators discussed whether the qualification concerns a person's intention or his conduct. Some explained it as a description of someone who goes beyond the limit, and others applied it to the means by which the food is obtained, including the taking of what is not lawful.

What the community's jurists concluded is that the concession is narrow and that its conditions concern both the internal disposition and the outward act. The sentence therefore does not open a general permission to eat the forbidden; it provides for a person who has no other means of preserving his life, and the community's teachers treated the conditions as part of the ruling.

**The Names at the End of the Sentence**

The sentence closes with the statement that God is forgiving and merciful, and the community's teachers read the pair as the ground of the concession that has been granted. The names appear at the end of rulings elsewhere in the sūrah, and their placement indicates that the legislation is presented as an expression of mercy rather than as an arbitrary restriction.

The reader who has followed the passage from the address to humanity through the address to the believers arrives at a statement about what is not permitted, and the sentence leaves him with the attributes of the one who made the rule. What the verse establishes is that the law's limits and its concessions belong to the same source, and the community has carried both together in its practice.

The community’s teachers noted that the names appear at the close of rulings throughout the sūrah, and that the practice of ending a legal statement with an attribute of God gives the reader the disposition in which the ruling is to be received. The concession described in the sentence is therefore presented as an instance of mercy rather than as an exception to a rule, and the reader is shown that the law and the attributes of the lawgiver belong together. What the verse establishes is that the limits and the permissions of the passage come from the same source, and the community has carried both in its practice.

**The Passage Completed**

The sentence completes the section on food and brings the discussion that began with the address to humanity to its conclusion. The Book has stated the principle, described the practice that it corrects, addressed the believers, and set out the prohibitions along with the concession for necessity. The next verses take up the subject of what is required in return for what has been forbidden and the fairness of the recompense, and the reader is carried from the regulation of a person's table to the account of the one who gives and takes away.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:174

> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Offence Described**

The verse names those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price, and it states what they consume in the process. The sentence returns to a subject the sūrah has already treated, since the charge of hiding the revelation appeared earlier in the passage about the People of the Book.

The new element in the sentence is the commerce, since the concealment is described as a sale. What is being traded is the Book, and what is received is a payment that the verse calls paltry. The reader is shown that the offence the sūrah has been describing has a motive attached to it, and the motive is named as gain.

**Concealment as a Transaction**

The Book uses commercial language for the conduct of the communities that received earlier scriptures in several passages, and the sūrah has already described a group that bought error and error at the price of guidance. The image of a sale makes the choice visible, since a person who sells something receives a price and loses what he gave up.

What the sentence establishes is that the exchange was deliberate. A person who conceals what he has been given and takes something in return has weighed the two and preferred the second, and the verse's description of the payment as paltry states the Book's judgment on the transaction. The community's teachers read the phrase as an indication of the disproportion between what was forfeited and what was received, and the reader is invited to consider what the modern equivalent of such an exchange would be.

**"They Consume Nothing but Fire"**

The second half of the sentence states that those described consume nothing but fire in their bellies, and the image follows from the wealth they have taken. The Book's picture is of people who eat what they have earned, and what they have earned is described in terms of its true nature rather than its appearance.

The commentators connected the phrase with the parallel in another chapter, where those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are described as filling their bellies with fire. The image in both passages makes the same point, which is that what a person consumes in this life may be something other than what he supposes, and the sentence leaves the reader with the picture of an appetite that is fed on what destroys it.

**God's Silence on the Day of Judgment**

The sentence states that God will not speak to them on the Day of Judgment and will not purify them, and the community's scholars discussed how this is to be reconciled with the passages in which God questions people on that day. The Book states elsewhere that He will question all of them concerning what they did, and it also reports an address to the people of the Fire.

Al-Rāzī explained the sentence as describing the withholding of words of welcome rather than the absence of every kind of speech, and he compared it to the treatment of a person who is refused audience by a king. The meaning the commentators settled on is that those described will receive no address of favour, and the community's teachers read the phrase as a statement about the treatment that awaits them rather than about the mechanics of the day.

**Purification Withheld**

The second part of the statement is that God will not purify them, and the commentators explained the verb as covering the praise of a person and the acceptance of his deeds as well as the removal of faults. What the sentence describes is the absence of everything that purification implies, so that the offenders receive neither commendation nor correction.

The Book's use of the term elsewhere includes its own purification of those whom it wills, and the community's scholars noted the contrast between the two statements. What the reader receives is a picture of a condition from which the remedies available in this life have been removed, and the verse's closing words name the punishment that belongs to it.

**The Closing Punishment**

The sentence ends with the statement that a painful punishment awaits those described, and the phrase appears at the close of the sūrah's charges against the communities that mishandled their scriptures. The wording is brief and the reader is left to supply nothing, since the sentence has already described what the punishment consists of in the loss of God's address and of purification.

The community's teachers gathered the passage with the verses that follow, in which the same offenders are described as having bought error at the price of guidance. The two sentences belong to a single account, and the reader is shown the transaction and its consequence in the space of two verses.

**The Passage's Continuing Argument**

The sentence continues the sūrah's treatment of those who possess knowledge of the revelation and deal with it in a way that serves their interest, and it supplies the reason for the warning that follows. The Book has described the concealment of the truth, and it now describes what the concealers have taken in exchange. The reader is given the motive, the act, and the outcome, and the passage continues with a statement of what the offenders have surrendered.

**What the Verse Establishes in the Community**

The sentence establishes a standard for those who hold knowledge of any part of the revelation, and the community's teachers applied it to the scholars of their own time when they warned against teaching for the sake of gain. What the verse describes is not a single act but a disposition toward what has been received, and the reader is left with the question of what he would be willing to exchange for the truth he has been given.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:175

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exchange Restated**

The verse states that those described have purchased error at the price of guidance and punishment at the price of forgiveness, and it repeats the commercial image of the previous sentence in a sharper form. Two items are named, and each of them is the opposite of what the offenders gave up.

The Book's use of this construction gives the reader the measure of the loss in a single line. What was available is named first, and what was taken in its place is named second, so that the exchange is visible without further explanation. The community's teachers read the verse as a summary of the condition that the previous sentence described at length.

**Guidance and Error**

The first exchange concerns direction, and the sūrah has used the term for guidance from its opening verses onward, where the Book is described as a guide for the reverent and the community asks to be shown the straight path. The verse states that those described have taken error instead, and the term for error describes a deliberate straying rather than an innocent mistake.

The choice of words indicates that the people in question had access to the direction and preferred its opposite. The community's scholars noted that the Book's vocabulary for these matters treats the two paths as alternatives that a person selects, and the sentence leaves no room for the suggestion that the offenders were unaware of what they were doing.

**Forgiveness and Punishment**

The second exchange concerns the treatment that follows, and the two terms are again exact opposites. The Book's term for forgiveness describes the covering and the setting aside of a fault, and the punishment named in the sentence is the consequence that the offenders have chosen in its place.

The pairing of the two exchanges in a single clause gives the sentence its force, since the reader is shown that both losses were avoidable. The Book has described the terms on which the concealment could have been repaired in the earlier passage about those who repent and make the matter clear, and the present verse reports the outcome for those who did not.

**The Question at the End**

The sentence closes with the question of how the offenders will endure the Fire, and the commentators explained the wording in several ways. Some read it as a question about what will give them patience in the condition that awaits them, others as a way of saying that nothing will, and others as a general expression of astonishment at the conduct that led them there.

The Book uses questions of this kind where the answer is beyond the reader's ability to supply. The community's teachers read the sentence as a statement about the condition of those who have made such an exchange, and the question leaves the reader to consider what patience would mean in the place described.

The sentence’s question also measures the distance between the two sides of the exchange, since what was taken cannot sustain the person who took it. The community’s teachers used the verse when they spoke of the difference between what a person gains in the world and what he is able to carry with him, and they read the question as the Book’s way of stating that the loss is total. The reader who considers the two commodities named in the sentence is left with a transaction in which nothing remains for the one who made it.

**The Connection to the Preceding Verse**

The verse follows the account of the concealment and the fire that the offenders consume, and it draws out what the exchange consists of. The Book has described the transaction in commercial terms in the earlier sentence, and it now names the two commodities that were traded away.

The sequence gives the passage its shape, and the reader who follows it from the concealment through the exchange to the question at the end has been shown the offence, the motive, and the outcome in three short statements. The community's teachers used the passage when they spoke about the seriousness of trading knowledge for gain.

The two sentences belong to one statement, since the earlier verse describes what the offenders consume and this one names what they surrendered to obtain it. The Book often pairs a description of a condition with an account of how it was reached, and the reader is given the act and the consequence in the space of two lines. The community’s scholars read the pair as a complete account of the offence that the passage has been describing, and the verses that follow explain the ground of the judgment.

**The Vocabulary of Buying and Selling**

The Book uses the language of trade for the conduct of those who deal with the revelation in a number of passages, and the sūrah has already described a community that sold its covenant for a small price. The repetition of the image across the sūrah indicates that the Book treats the matter as a familiar category of offence.

The vocabulary also gives the community a way of describing its own conduct, since the Book applies the language of buying and selling to the exchange of the present life for the next in passages addressed to the believers as well. The verse in this place states the terms of the exchange that the offenders have made, and the reader is left with the question of how he conducts his own.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes that the offenders have surrendered guidance and forgiveness, that the surrender was deliberate, and that the condition they have entered is described in the Book's own terms. The reader is given the account of the transaction, and the passage continues with the statement of the reason for it, which is the treatment of the Book that God sent down in truth.

**The Question's Effect on the Reader**

The closing question does more than describe the offenders. It places the reader in the position of a person who is asked to imagine standing in the condition described, and the Book uses that position when it wants a warning to remain with the hearer. What the sentence leaves behind is not only the information about a group of people but the question of what would sustain a person who had made such a choice, and the community's preachers have used the verse in that way.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:176

> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Given**

The verse states that the punishment described in the preceding sentences follows from the fact that God sent down the Book in truth, and it then describes those who differ concerning it as being in deep opposition. The sentence supplies the reason for the judgment, and the reason concerns the treatment of the revelation.

The Book's method of attaching a cause to a punishment appears throughout the sūrah, and the reader is shown that the outcomes described are not arbitrary. What the offenders did was measured against what they had been given, and the sentence names the gift before it names the offence against it.

**The Book Sent Down in Truth**

The phrase states that the revelation came from God with truth, and the sūrah has used the same form of words at other points in its argument. The statement establishes both the origin and the character of the Book, and the community's teachers read it as the ground of the accountability that the passage describes.

What follows from the phrase is that the concealment of the Book is not a matter of preference among opinions. A person who hides a truth that has come from God is opposing something whose authority is not in question, and the sentence presents the offence in that light before it describes the punishment that belongs to it.

**Those Who Differ Concerning It**

The second half of the sentence describes those who differ concerning the Book as being in deep opposition, and the commentators explained the term as describing a division that has become a standing disagreement. The Book uses the same word in other passages for the conduct of communities that set themselves against the truth.

Some commentators read the reference to the Book as covering the earlier scriptures as well as the final revelation, and others took it as a statement about the disputes among the People of the Book over the meaning of what they had received. Under either reading the sentence concerns disagreement that has become an end in itself, and the community's teachers noted that the term describes a condition of the disputants rather than the subject of their dispute.

**Schism as a Condition**

The Book's word for the condition is connected with the idea of splitting, and the sūrah has described communities that divided their religion into factions. The sentence states that the offenders have arrived at a position in which the truth of the revelation is settled and their opposition nevertheless continues.

The community's scholars read the verse as a warning about the habit of disputing for its own sake, since a person who disagrees after the matter has been established is no longer seeking an answer. What the sentence establishes is that the disagreement itself can be the offence, and the reader is shown that the Book treats a certain kind of controversy as a condition rather than as an activity.

**The Charge Against the Concealers**

The sentence follows the account of those who concealed the Book and sold it for a small price, and it explains what their conduct amounts to in the Book's terms. What began as a transaction ends as a division, and the community's teachers noted the progression in the passage.

The reader is shown that the mishandling of knowledge produces conflict, and the sūrah has already described communities that concealed what they knew and then disputed about the figures of their own history. The verse in this place states the general form of the matter, and it leaves the reader with the connection between the concealment of the truth and the disputes that follow from it.

**The Truth as the Standard**

The phrase about the Book being sent down in truth also supplies the standard by which the disputes are to be judged. The community's teachers used the sentence when they discussed how disagreements among those who possess the revelation are to be resolved, and they pointed to the Book itself as the criterion.

The sūrah has described the revelation as the criterion in an earlier verse, and the present sentence repeats the idea in the context of a dispute. What the reader receives is the reminder that the truth has been given, and the sentence places the responsibility for division on those who have received it and turned aside.

The community’s teachers used the sentence when they discussed how disagreements among those who possess the revelation are to be resolved, and they pointed to the Book itself as the criterion by which the disputants are judged. The sūrah has described the revelation as the standard in an earlier verse, and the present sentence repeats the idea in the context of a division. What the reader receives in the phrase is the assurance that the truth is available and the knowledge that the disputes described in the sentence are disputes about something already given.

**What the Verse Adds to the Passage**

The sentence completes the account of the offenders by naming the ground of their punishment, and it then describes their condition in a single phrase. The Book has stated what they concealed, what they received in exchange, and what they have lost; the present verse names the truth that stood behind all of it. The passage continues with the description of the righteous, and the reader is carried from the account of a failed transaction to a statement of what a life devoted to the truth consists of.

The passage's arrangement is deliberate, since the description of the righteous that follows is meant to be read against the account of those who disputed the Book. What the one group did with the revelation and what the other did with their lives are placed side by side, and the reader is left to weigh the two. The community's teachers noted that the sūrah frequently closes a passage of rebuke with a portrait of the conduct it commends.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:177

> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Correction About Righteousness**

The verse states that righteousness does not consist in turning the face toward the east or the west, and it then describes the person who is righteous in a series of clauses. The opening statement addresses the dispute about the direction of prayer that occupied the earlier part of the sūrah.

The Book's correction does not cancel the direction of prayer, and the commands to face the Sacred Mosque remain in force in the verses that precede this one. What the sentence does is to place the practice within a larger account of what a religious life consists of, and the community's teachers read it as a warning against treating a ritual as the whole of the religion.

**The Occasion Reported**

The commentators report that the verse was revealed after the community came to Madinah, where the Muslims saw the Jewish community praying toward the west and the Christian community toward the east. The sentence addresses that situation directly, and the reports show the Muslims being taught what the comparison between the direction of prayer and the conduct of a life amounts to.

The teaching is therefore placed in the middle of a passage about the direction of prayer, and it does not contradict the commands that surround it. What the Book does is to define the term that the communities were using against one another, and the definition it supplies is a list of the things a righteous person does.

**The Articles of Faith**

The first part of the description names belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets, and the commentators noted that this list is the basis of the community's creed. They also pointed to the report in which the Prophet ﷺ answered a question about faith by naming these items.

The list is short and comprehensive, and the community's scholars used it when they set out what a believer holds. What the sentence establishes is that the righteous person is described first by what he believes, and the order of the clauses shows that the deeds that follow are presented as the fruit of the belief rather than as a substitute for it.

**The Giving of Wealth**

The sentence then describes the righteous as those who give of their wealth despite their attachment to it, and it names the recipients: relatives, orphans, the poor, travellers, beggars, and captives. The commentators explained the phrase about the love of wealth as describing the difficulty of parting with what a person values.

The list covers the people who are close to the giver and those who are not, and the community's scholars drew from it a scheme of obligations and supererogatory giving. The Book's use of the same phrase elsewhere in a passage about feeding the needy shows that the wording is one of the Book's ways of describing generosity, and the sentence places it among the marks of the righteous.

**Prayer, Alms, and Pledges**

The description continues with the establishment of the prayer, the payment of the alms, and the keeping of promises, and these three items cover a person's duties to God and to others.
