## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:229

> Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Limit on Divorce**

The verse states that divorce may be retracted twice, after which the husband must either keep his wife honourably or release her virtuously. The sentence limits the number of times a declaration may be made and revoked, and the community's teachers read the ruling as a measure against the practice of keeping a woman in uncertainty.

The Book's treatment of the subject connects the number of the declarations with the way the marriage ends, and the sentence supplies both the limit and the two courses that follow it. Readers are shown that the legislation provides for the continuation of the marriage and for its conclusion, and the choice is placed within the bounds of honourable conduct.

**The Practice Addressed**

The commentators described the practice that the verse corrected, in which a man would declare divorce and take his wife back before the waiting period ended, repeating the process in order to keep her without giving her either the security of the marriage or the freedom to leave. The sentence's limit closes the arrangement.

The reports also describe the position of the wife within that practice, and the community's teachers noted that the ruling protects her from a situation she could not resolve. Readers are given the account of a measure whose purpose is the protection of the weaker party in the household, and the sentence supplies the rule that the community applied.

**The Prohibition of Taking Back the Dowry**

The sentence forbids the husband to take back any of what he has given his wife, with the exception of the case in which the two fear that they cannot keep within the limits God has set. The community's teachers read the prohibition as a statement about the property that the wife received as part of the marriage contract.

The commentators explained the exception as the arrangement by which a wife obtains a divorce by returning what she has received, and they noted the difference between that arrangement and the case in which the husband initiates the separation. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere supplies the details, and the reader is shown that the property arrangements of the marriage are governed by the same concern for justice that the sentence applies.

**The Compensation for Divorce**

The sentence states that if the two fear they cannot keep within the limits of God there is no blame in what the wife gives to obtain the divorce, and the community's jurists built the procedure of the arranged separation on the clause. The commentators explain that the wife's initiative in this case is met by the return of part or all of what she received.

The arrangement gives the wife a means of ending a marriage that she cannot continue, and the community's teachers read the sentence as a measure of the legislation's attention to both parties. The passage shows that the Book provides for the ending of a marriage at the instance of the wife as well as at that of the husband, and the sentence's wording keeps the matter within the limits that the surrounding verses describe.

**The Limits Named**

The sentence closes with the statement that these are the limits set by God and that whoever transgresses them is among the wrongdoers, and the phrase runs through the verses about the household. The community's scholars read the clause as the warning that accompanies the legislation, and they used it when they set out the seriousness of the arrangements.

The Book's practice of calling its rulings limits appears throughout the sūrah, and the sentence in this place places the rules of divorce within that body of material. The passage shows that the provisions are not a set of options among which the parties may choose freely, and the sentence leaves them with the statement about the boundary they may not cross.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

The sentence stands at the head of the passage on the number of declarations and precedes the rule about the third divorce and the arrangements for the waiting period. The Book has treated the oath of abstention and the first two declarations, and it now supplies the limit that governs the whole procedure.

The section's concern is the concluding of a marriage in an orderly manner, and the community's teachers read the verses as a unit when they taught the subject. The text supplies the rule and its reason together, and the passage continues with the provision that follows the third declaration.

**The Limit That Protects the Woman**

The report behind the sentence describes a woman who came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining about a husband who divorced and then took her back repeatedly, and the answer named the limit that closed the practice. The early community knew marriages in which the wife could neither keep her position nor obtain her freedom, and the ruling removed the arrangement by which that condition was maintained.

The procedure of the arranged separation also grows from the sentence. The wife who returns what she has received in order to obtain her release is named in the clause, and the reports describe the woman who came with the request and the ruling that returned the garden she had been given. The teachers noted that the Book gives the wife a path out of a household she cannot continue, and the jurists built the rules of the practice upon the wording.

The sentence's closing warning about the limits belongs to the whole section and it addresses both parties. What the passage protects is the position of the person whose claim is weaker, and the law of the household rests upon that concern.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the number of the declarations, the two honourable courses that follow them, the prohibition of taking back what the wife has received, the arrangement by which she may obtain a divorce, and the warning that accompanies the limits. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law, and the reader is shown that the Book's legislation protects the woman's position within the household and provides a path out of a marriage that cannot continue.

The verse's provision for the wife's initiative has been read as evidence that the legislation attends to both parties of the marriage, and the community's judges used the clause when the requests came before them. The teachers also noted the prohibition of taking back what was given, since the property of the wife belongs to her and the separation does not reopen the question of what she received.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:230

> So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Divorce**

The verse states that if the husband divorces his wife a third time she is not lawful for him until she has married another man, and it then states that the pair may return to one another if they believe they can keep within the limits of God. The sentence supplies the consequence of the third declaration.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere supplies the details of the procedure, and the community's jurists derived the rule from the sentence and the surrounding verses. Readers are shown that the legislation places a barrier at the end of the process, and the sentence states the conditions under which the marriage may later be renewed.

**The Reason for the Provision**

The commentators explained the rule as the completion of the limit that the previous verse established, and they noted that a man who could divorce and remarry without restriction would be able to keep his wife in a cycle of declarations and waiting periods. The provision removes that possibility.

The community's teachers read the sentence as a measure that protects the woman from an arrangement she could not escape, and they described the effect it has on the seriousness with which a man declares a divorce. Readers are given the account of a ruling whose purpose is the protection of the household, and the sentence's wording places the matter within the framework the preceding verses have built.

**The Intervening Marriage**

The sentence states that the woman must marry another man before the first husband may marry her again, and the community's jurists discussed the character of that marriage and the conditions attached to it. The commentaries record the positions, and most held that the marriage must be a real union rather than a formality.

The discussion reflects the care with which the community handled a provision that could be manipulated, and the reports show the teachers guarding the ruling's purpose. The passage shows that the Book's legislation leaves a door open while preventing the door from becoming a device, and the sentence in this place supplies the condition that the community applied.

**The Return Permitted**

The sentence states that if the second marriage ends the original pair may return to one another if they believe they can keep within the limits of God, and the community's teachers read the clause as the statement of the conditions that govern the renewal. The Book's concern is the observance of the limits rather than the mere resumption of the union.

The wording places the judgment of the parties at the centre of the provision, and the community's scholars noted that the sentence requires an honest assessment from the two who wish to return. The account describes a permission that is bounded by the conditions the passage has described, and the sentence leaves the decision with the parties and the outcome with God.

**The Limits Named**

The sentence closes with the statement that these are the limits that God makes clear to people who know, and the phrase completes the series of rulings that runs through the passage. The community's teachers read the ending as the statement that the legislation is addressed to people who understand what it requires.

The Book's practice of closing a legal passage with a reference to knowledge appears throughout the sūrah, and the sentence in this place supplies the disposition in which the rules are to be received. The passage shows that the provisions about the household belong to the body of guidance the sūrah has been setting out, and the sentence's closing words connect the arrangement with the understanding of those who observe it.

**The Passage's Treatment of the Household**

The verse stands among the rules about the concluding of a marriage, and it follows the passage on the waiting period and the number of declarations. The Book has described the arrangements in sequence, and the community's teachers taught the verses as a single body of instruction.

The section's concern is the orderly conduct of the community's households, and the reader is shown how the legislation addresses each stage of the process. The passage that follows returns to the waiting period and to the treatment of the wife at its end, so that the reader is carried from the limit on the declarations back to the practical conduct of the couple.

**The Barrier and the Door**

The sentence closes the cycle that the earlier verses describe, and the community's teachers read the provision as the measure that made a man consider the weight of his declaration. Reports describe the practice of the formal intervening marriage, and the Prophet ﷺ spoke against the arrangement in which a union is contracted without its conditions, so that the man who is taken back and the one who makes the arrangement were both named in the warning.

The jurists derived the conditions of the intervening marriage from the reports. A genuine union is required, with its own contract and its ordinary consequences, and a marriage designed for the sole purpose of allowing a return does not satisfy the requirement in the view of the schools.

The sentence also leaves the door open, since the pair may return to one another after the second marriage has ended when they believe that they can observe the limits. The closing words address the community's understanding, and the passage's concern is the seriousness of the bond that the couple entered.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the effect of the third declaration, the requirement of an intervening marriage, the possibility of a later return under the conditions named, and the closing statement about the limits. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law of divorce, and the reader is shown that the Book's legislation closes the process at a definite point while leaving room for a renewed marriage undertaken with the observance of the limits.

The teachers used the sentence when they explained why the Book placed a barrier at the end of the process, and they described its purpose as the protection of the marriage from a treatment that would make its declarations idle. The door that remains open shows that the rule is not a punishment, and the conditions attached to the return place the decision with the two who wish to resume their life together.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:231

> When you divorce women and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably. But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺. Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul. Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly. Remember Allah’s favours upon you as well as the Book and wisdom He has sent down for your guidance. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Instruction at the End of the Period**

The verse instructs the community to keep the women honourably or to release them honourably when the waiting period has almost reached its end, and it forbids the retention of the wife for the purpose of harming her. The sentence follows the rules about the number of declarations and returns to the practical conduct of the couple.

The Book's concern is the decision that must be taken once the period has run, and the sentence allows neither of the two courses to be conducted in a manner that injures the other party. Readers are shown that the legislation requires a definite outcome, and the instruction supplies the standard by which the two options are carried out.

**The Harm Forbidden**

The commentators explained the practice that the sentence prohibits, in which a man would take his wife back just before the waiting period ended in order to keep her in the marriage without providing for her, and he would repeat the arrangement as often as he wished. The sentence names the intention as the offence.

The community's teachers read the clause as the measure that closes the possibility the previous verses had left open, and they noted that the Book describes the harm as a wrong done to the man's own soul. Readers are shown that the legislation treats the injury of a spouse as an injury to the one who inflicts it, and the sentence's statement supplies the standard that governs the conclusion of the marriage.

**The Wrong Done to the Self**

The sentence states that whoever acts in that manner wrongs his own soul, and the community's scholars read the phrase as a statement about the condition of the person who inflicts the harm. The Book's use of the language of self-injury appears in its treatment of other offences, and the reader is shown that the offender is not the only party affected.

The wording also removes the possibility that the man might regard the wife as the only injured party, and the community's teachers used the clause when they spoke about the conduct of the household. The account describes a rule whose purpose is the protection of the weaker party and whose warning is addressed to the one who holds the power.

**The Prohibition of Mockery**

The sentence forbids the community to treat God's signs as a jest, and the commentators explained the phrase as a reference to the attitude that treats the rules of marriage and divorce as matters of play. The reports describe the expressions that people used to dismiss a declaration they had made.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere warns against the mocking of its revelations, and the community's scholars connected the passages when they set out the seriousness of the rules. The passage shows that the passage's concern is the weight that the community gives to the arrangements of its households, and the sentence supplies the warning that accompanies the instruction.

**The Reminder of the Blessing**

The sentence instructs the community to remember the blessing of God and the Book and the wisdom that were sent down for its guidance, and the community's teachers read the clause as the reminder that accompanies the legislation. The Book's practice of joining its rulings to the recollection of what the community has received appears throughout the sūrah.

The mention of the Book and the wisdom connects the passage with the sūrah's earlier treatment of what the community was given, and the reader is shown that the rules about the household belong to the guidance that the community has received. The passage closes with the instruction and with the reminder that gives it its setting.

**The Closing Names**

The sentence closes with the command to be mindful of God and the statement that God knows all things, and the community's scholars read the pair as the ground of the whole passage. The attributes accompany the rules about the household as they accompany the sūrah's other instructions.

The Book's practice of ending a legal passage with a description of God gives the reader the disposition in which the rules are received, and the sentence here follows the pattern. The passage shows that the legislation on marriage and divorce belongs to the same body of guidance as the commands about worship and conflict, and the passage continues with the rules about the woman's remarriage.

**The Reckoning of the Household**

The decision that the sentence requires belongs at the end of the waiting period, and the community's jurists built the rules of the return upon it. A man who takes his wife back must do so in a manner that provides for her and treats her as a wife, and the one who releases her leaves her free to marry elsewhere.

The wrong that the sentence forbids has been described by the teachers as the worst of the offences the passage treats, because it is committed by the person who holds the power in the household. The Book names the harm as an injury to the one who inflicts it, so that the offender's own account carries the deed.

The reminder that follows joins the instruction to the recollection of the Book and the wisdom that the community received. The teachers read the clause as the ground of the whole passage, since the rules of the household belong to the guidance that the community had accepted, and the closing attributes place the conduct of its members before the One who knows all things.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the two honourable courses at the end of the waiting period, the prohibition of retaining the wife in order to harm her, the warning about wronging oneself, the prohibition of treating the signs as a jest, and the reminder of what the community has received. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law, and the reader is shown that the Book's legislation on the household joins the protection of the parties with the recollection of the guidance that governs them.

The verse supplied the community with the standard against which a return to the marriage was measured, and the teachers used it when they explained the difference between the reconciliation the Book commends and the retention that it forbids. The passage ends with the mention of the meeting with God, so that the private decisions of the household are placed within the account that every person will meet.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:232

> When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their exhusbands if they come to an honourable agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Instruction Stated**

The verse forbids the community to prevent divorced women from marrying their former husbands when the two have come to an honourable agreement, and it describes the instruction as a counsel for those who believe in God and the Last Day. The sentence closes the treatment of the waiting period and the resumption of the marriage.

The Book's concern is the freedom of the parties to arrange their own affairs within the limits that the passage has set, and the sentence addresses those who stand between them. Readers are shown that the legislation protects the decision of the couple from the interference of relatives and others, and the instruction supplies the rule that the community applied.

**The Occasion Reported**

The commentators connect the sentence with a report in which a man objected to the remarriage of his sister to the husband who had divorced her, and they describe the situation that the verse addressed. The sentence removes the objection by affirming the right of the parties to reach their own agreement.

The report shows the kind of pressure that the ruling addressed, and the community's teachers noted that the sentence protects the woman's position within her family as well as within the marriage. Readers are given the account of an instruction that was given in a particular case and that applies to every similar intervention.

**The Agreement Required**

The sentence states that the permission applies when the parties have come to an honourable agreement, and the community's scholars read the phrase as the condition that governs the remarriage. The Book's practice of attaching its permissions to a standard of conduct appears throughout its legislation.

The wording gives the couple the responsibility for the arrangement while placing it within the framework the passage has described, and the community's teachers used the clause when they discussed the conduct of the families involved. The passage shows that the Book's legislation on the household protects the parties' freedom while requiring that the arrangement be conducted properly.

**The Counsel for the Believers**

The sentence states that this is a counsel for those who believe in God and the Last Day, and the community's scholars read the clause as the description of the audience that the instruction addresses. The Book's practice of connecting its rulings with the faith of the community appears throughout the sūrah.

The phrase places the matter within the obligations that the community has accepted, and the community's teachers used it when they spoke about the treatment of divorced women and of the family arrangements that follow a separation. The passage shows that the instruction is not a private opinion but a part of the guidance that the community has received.

**The Value Stated**

The sentence states that the course it recommends is purer and more dignifying for the community, and the community's teachers read the phrase as the statement of the benefit that follows the instruction. The Book's practice of naming the value of its commands appears at several points in the sūrah.

The wording places the benefit with the community rather than with one of the parties, and the reader is shown that the well-being of the whole body is served by the observance of the rule. The account describes a command whose value is stated in the text, and the sentence supplies the perspective in which the instruction is to be understood.

**The Closing Names**

The sentence closes with the statement that God knows and the community does not, and the community's scholars read the pair as the ground of the instruction that preceded it. The same closing appears at other points in the sūrah where a command runs against the community's assumptions.

The Book's use of the clause gives the reader the assurance that the command's wisdom lies beyond what the community can see, and the community's teachers used it when they explained the rules about the household. The passage closes with the instruction and with the statement about the knowledge that accompanies it, and the passage continues with the rules about the nursing of children.

**The Family and the Woman's Choice**

The report behind the sentence describes a man who refused to let his sister return to the husband who had divorced her, and the revelation removed the objection. The community's teachers read the passage as the statement that the guardianship of the family exists for the protection of the woman rather than for the authority of the guardian over her decision.

The jurists built the rules of the marriage contract upon the balance the verse states. The consent of the woman belongs to the contract, and the guardian's part in it is exercised in her interest and in the manner the law approves. When the parties have agreed on terms that are honourable, the intervention of the relatives becomes the wrong that the sentence forbids.

The clause that describes the instruction as a counsel for those who believe in God and the Last Day places the matter within the obligations the community accepted. The teachers also noted the phrase about what is purer and more dignifying, since the wording places the benefit of the observance with the whole community rather than with one of the parties alone.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the right of the divorced couple to remarry, the condition of an honourable agreement, the standing of the instruction as a counsel for the believers, and the value that attaches to it. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law on the subject, and the reader is shown that the Book's legislation on the household protects the parties' decisions from interference while requiring that they be conducted properly.

The community's teachers used the sentence when they answered families who stood between a divorced couple, and the passage supplied the language of the family's duty as well as the woman's right. The verse also shows that the Book's legislation on the household extends to the relatives of the spouses, so that the household is treated as part of the wider community.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:233

> ˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. And if you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Nursing of the Child**

The verse instructs the mothers to nurse their children for two full years for those who wish to complete the period, and it places the provision of the mother's maintenance and clothing on the father. The sentence follows the rules about divorce and address the care of the children of a marriage that has ended.

The Book's concern is the welfare of the child and the position of the mother who nurses it, and the community's teachers read the sentence as the instruction that governs the period after the separation. Readers are shown that the legislation provides for the consequences of the marriage beyond its conclusion.

**The Two Years**

The sentence names two full years as the period of nursing, and the community's scholars read the figure as the completion of the child's need for the mother's milk. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere connects the period of nursing with the duty of the child toward his parents, and the community's teachers gathered the passages together.

The wording states the period for those who wish to complete it, and the community's jurists noted that the verse allows the parents to agree on a shorter time. Readers are given the account of a ruling that sets the full term while leaving room for the circumstances of the family, and the sentence supplies the framework for the arrangements that follow.

**The Father's Maintenance**

The sentence places the provision of the mother's food and clothing on the father during the period, and the community's teachers read the clause as the continuation of the husband's obligation after the divorce. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere requires support according to the means of the one who provides, and the sentence here applies the standard to the nursing period.

The instruction gives the mother the means to devote herself to the child without the loss of her maintenance, and the community's scholars built the law on the combination of the passages. The passage shows that the Book's legislation on the household continues to bind the parties through the care of their children, and the sentence supplies the rule that governs the period.

**The Limit of Capacity**

The sentence states that no person is charged beyond his capacity, and the community's teachers read the clause as the measure of the obligation that the sentence has imposed. The Book's use of the same statement in other passages about the law shows that the principle is general.

The phrase accompanies the provision of maintenance and the instruction about the parents, and the reader is shown that the legislation takes account of what a person can provide. The account describes a rule whose demand is measured by the ability of the one who bears it, and the community's scholars used the clause when they discussed the obligations that accompany a divorce.

**The Protection of the Parents**

The sentence forbids that either parent be made to suffer on account of the child, and the community's scholars read the clause as the protection of both parties during the period of nursing. The commentators explained the harm that the mother might suffer through the pressure to nurse against her wish and the harm that the father might suffer through the withholding of the child from him.

The clause also extends the same obligation to the father's heir, and the community's jurists discussed the cases the extension covers. The passage shows that the Book's legislation on the subject addresses the position of each party, and the sentence supplies the principle by which the arrangements are to be conducted.

**The Agreement to Wean and the Wet Nurse**

The sentence permits the parents to wean the child by their mutual consent and consultation, and it permits the engagement of a wet nurse with the payment of what is due. The community's teachers read the provisions as the statement of the flexibility that the legislation grants to the family.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere includes the care of the child in the arrangements that follow a separation, and the community's scholars gathered the passages. The passage shows that the Book's concern is the child's welfare within the decisions made by the parents, and the sentence supplies the permission that allows the arrangements to be adapted to the circumstances of the family.

**The Child Between the Parents**

The two years that the sentence names have been read as the full term of the child's need for the milk of its mother, and the jurists measured the rules of nursing and of fosterage upon it. There is no pressure laid upon the mother, whose choice the verse describes as belonging to those who wish to complete the term, and there is no escape for the father from the duty of maintaining her while she performs it.

The provision of food and clothing according to the father's means supplies the practical arrangement, and the verse adds the rule that no one is charged beyond his capacity. The teachers drew from the clause the general principle of the law, that its obligations are measured by what the person is able to bear.

The child's welfare stands at the centre of the section. The parents may agree on the weaning before the term, and they may engage a nurse when the circumstances require it, so that the legislation leaves the arrangements to the family while holding them to the standard the sentence sets.

**The Closing Command**

The sentence closes with the command to be mindful of God and the statement that He sees what the community does, and the community's scholars read the pair as the ground of the instructions the passage has set out. The Book's practice of ending a passage with a description of God appears throughout the sūrah.

The passage closes with the rules about the care of children and with the statement that the conduct of the household is performed before the One who sees it, and the passage continues with the rules about the waiting period and the arrangements of divorce.

The community's jurists referred to the sentence in the rules of fosterage and of maintenance, and the teachers used it when they answered the questions that came to them about the care of children after a separation. The verse's closing command places the arrangements of the family under the awareness of God, since the One who sees what the community does is named at the end of the passage.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:234

> As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Waiting Period for Widows**

The verse instructs those who are left behind by a deceased husband to wait four months and ten days before they may marry again, and it then permits them to dispose of themselves honourably once the term has ended. The sentence follows the rules about the care of children and treats the position of the widow.

The Book's concern is the conclusion of the marriage in an orderly manner and the protection of the woman's position, and the community's teachers read the sentence as the instruction that governs the period after a husband's death. Readers are shown that the legislation provides for the household in every circumstance the community meets.

**The Term and Its Purpose**

The sentence names four months and ten days as the period, and the community's scholars explained the term as a provision by which the parentage of a child is established. The length allows the condition of the womb to become clear in the ordinary case, and the community's jurists built the law on that purpose.

The commentators noted the care with which the term is measured, and they described the practice of the community that the ruling replaced, in which a widow could be bound to a much longer period of seclusion. Readers are given the account of a ruling whose length is determined by the purpose it serves, and the sentence supplies the term that the community observed.

**The Practice Before the Ruling**

The reports describe the customs of the time, in which a widow remained in a state of withdrawal for a year or more, dressed in her worst clothes and confined to a small room. The sentence shortened the period and removed the conditions that had no bearing on the purpose it serves.

The community's teachers read the change as an instance of the legislation's attention to the position of women, and the reports show what the sentence addressed. The passage shows that the Book's treatment of the subject distinguishes between the period required by its purpose and the customs that surrounded it, and the sentence supplies the rule that settled the matter.

**The Reports About the Term**

The commentators discussed the relation between the period named in the sentence and the case of a widow who is found to be pregnant, and the community's jurists concluded that her term lasts until she delivers. The reports also discuss the widow who learns of her husband's death after some time has passed, and the teachers set out the applications.

The material shows the community working through the questions that the sentence leaves open, and the reader is given the account of a ruling that the community applied in its households. The community's scholars noted the concern for the child's parentage that runs through the rules of the waiting period, and the sentence in this place supplies the term from which the applications are drawn.

**The Permission After the Term**

The sentence states that the community commits no wrong in allowing the women to dispose of themselves honourably once the term has ended, and the community's teachers read the clause as the restoration of the woman's freedom to marry. The Book's practice of closing its rules with a permission appears throughout its legislation.

The phrase places the responsibility for the conduct with the woman herself, and the community's scholars noted that the permission is bounded by the standard of honour that the passage names. The passage shows that the Book's legislation on the household leaves the parties with the freedom to arrange their own affairs within the limits it has set, and the sentence supplies the rule.

**The Closing Names**

The sentence closes with the description of God as aware of what the community does, and the community's scholars read the pair as the ground of the instruction the sentence has given. The attributes accompany the rules about the household as they accompany the sūrah's other legislation.

The Book's practice of ending a passage with a description of God gives the reader the disposition in which the rules are received, and the community's teachers used the clause when they spoke about the conduct of the family after a death. The text supplies the assurance that the fulfilment of the instructions is observed by the One who knows.

**The Widow's Term and the Community**

The customs that the sentence replaced were severe, and the reports describe the widow who withdrew from the world for a year, dressed in her oldest clothes, and remained in a small room until the term was complete. The revelation shortened the period and fixed it at four months and ten days, so that her mourning for her husband became a defined observance rather than a condition from which she could not escape.

The jurists derived the rules of the widow's waiting period from the sentence together with the reports that describe the practice of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions. The woman who is pregnant waits until she delivers, and the term runs from the death rather than from the moment she learns of it in the ordinary case.

The purpose the teachers named for the term is the establishment of the child's parentage and the protection of the woman's position. The verse then permits the widow to dispose of herself in an honourable manner once the months have passed, and the community's practice followed the sentence in the marriages that were contracted after its term.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the waiting period of four months and ten days, the purpose that the term serves, the permission to marry once the term ends, and the knowledge of God that accompanies the arrangements. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law on the subject, and the reader is shown that the Book's legislation provides for the widow's position with the same care it gives to the rules of divorce.

The teachers read the change as evidence of the attention the legislation gives to the widow, and the community's law of mourning was built upon the terms the sentence supplies. The verse also states the permission that follows the period, so that the woman's freedom is restored by the same passage that fixes her observance.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:235

> There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Permission to Indicate**

The verse states that the community commits no wrong in making an indication of a proposal of marriage to women who are within their waiting period, or in keeping such an intention to themselves, and it then describes the knowledge of God from which the practice is conducted. The sentence follows the rule that fixed the waiting period and supplies the guidance for the period itself.

The Book's concern is to protect the woman's position while allowing the community to arrange its affairs, and the community's teachers read the sentence as the permission that accompanies the rule. Readers are shown that the legislation separates the proposal from the marriage contract and places the first within the bounds that the passage describes.

**The Distinction Drawn**

The sentence permits the indication but not the contract, and the commentators explained the difference between the speech that suggests a future union and the agreement by which the marriage is concluded. The wording distinguishes the two, and the community's jurists built the law on the distinction.

The instruction also permits the community to keep the intention within itself, and the community's teachers read the clause as the statement that the secret intention is not held against a person. Readers are given the account of a ruling that allows the community to make its arrangements while preserving the period that the previous verse required, and the sentence supplies both permissions together.

**The Knowledge of God Stated**

The sentence states that God knows what the community holds within itself and instructs them to be mindful of Him, and the community's scholars read the clause as the ground of the permission. The Book's practice of attaching the reference to God's knowledge to its permissions appears throughout the sūrah.

The wording places the arrangement before the One who knows the intention, and the community's teachers used the clause when they set out the ethics of the proposal. The passage shows that the permission is bounded by the awareness that the intention is seen, and the sentence supplies the reminder that accompanies the instruction.

**The Prohibition of the Secret Contract**

The sentence forbids the community to make a secret agreement to marry and requires that the speech be honourable, and the commentators explained the phrase as the statement of the purpose to marry rather than a hidden contract. The community's jurists read the clause as the prohibition of the arrangement that would bypass the waiting period.

The wording also forbids the community to resolve on the contract before the term has ended, and the reports show the cases to which the prohibition applied. The account describes a rule that keeps the community's arrangements open while preventing the abuse of the period, and the sentence supplies the standard by which the speech is judged.

**The Reports and Applications**

The commentaries record the questions the community put to the Prophet ﷺ about the proposals made during the waiting period, and they describe the guidance that was given. The reports show the community applying the sentence to its own circumstances.

The material also describes the differences among the teachers about the phrases that may be used, and the community's jurists recorded the positions. The passage shows that the Book's legislation on the subject attends to the manner of the speech as well as to its content, and the sentence supplies the principle from which the applications were drawn.

**The Closing Name**

The sentence closes with the description of God as forgiving and forbearing, and the community's scholars read the pair as the ground of the permission that the sentence has granted. The attributes accompany the ruling as they accompany the other provisions about the household.

The Book's treatment of the subject connects the leniency of the law with the knowledge of the one who made it, and the reader is shown that the instruction leaves room for the community's weakness while requiring the observance of the period. The passage continues with the rules about the divorce that follows a betrothal.

**The Speech Before the Contract**

The distinction the sentence draws between the indication and the agreement belongs to the law of the marriage contract, and the jurists described the two forms of speech in detail. A man may tell the woman, in a manner that does not constitute a request for the contract, that he wishes to marry her, and the schools set out the phrases that they placed within the permission and those that they placed outside it.

The clause that permits the intention to be kept within the heart has been read as a statement about the mercy of the legislation, since the community could not be answerable for what it considered silently. The teachers noted the difference between that permission and the secret agreement, which the sentence forbids because it closes the matter before the term has ended.

The closing attributes accompany the instruction, and the community's practice followed the distinction the sentence draws. The reports record the proposals that the companions made during the waiting periods of those they wished to marry, and the judges of the early community applied the wording to the cases before them.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the permission to indicate a proposal during the waiting period, the permission to keep the intention secret, the prohibition of the secret contract, the requirement that the speech be honourable, and the attributes of God that accompany the ruling. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law on the subject, and the reader is shown that the Book's legislation on the household joins the protection of the period with the freedom of the community to make its arrangements.

The sentence set the standard for the speech of the community in a matter where the feelings of the woman and the rights of the former husband meet. The teachers used the passage when they explained that the Book protects the period while allowing the community to plan its affairs, and the attributes at the close place the hidden intention before God.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:236

> There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Case Described**

The verse addresses the case of a divorce that occurs before the marriage has been consummated and before a dowry has been fixed, and it states that the community commits no wrong in such a separation. The sentence follows the rules about the waiting period and the proposal, and it supplies the provision for a marriage that ends at its beginning.

The Book's concern is that the dissolution of an arrangement that has not been completed should not leave either party in difficulty, and the community's teachers read the sentence as the statement that the separation itself is permitted. Readers are shown that the legislation addresses the situations that arise at every stage of the marriage contract.

**The Provision Required**

The sentence instructs the husband to provide for the woman in such a case, and the community's scholars read the clause as the obligation that accompanies the separation. The commentators explained the provision as a gift given according to the means of the one who provides.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere requires the payment according to what is reasonable, and the community's jurists connected the passages when they set out the law. Readers are given the account of a ruling that attends to the position of the woman who has entered a betrothal and then been released from it, and the sentence supplies the obligation that the community applied.

**The Measure of the Provision**

The sentence states that the provision is to be made according to the means of the one who has the wealth and according to his circumstances, and the community's teachers read the clause as the standard by which the amount is set. The wording distinguishes between the person of ample means and the one of limited means.

The Book's practice of measuring its obligations by the capacity of the one who bears them appears in the passages about the household and elsewhere, and the community's scholars applied the principle to the provision required by the sentence. The passage shows that the Book's legislation attends to the position of both parties, and the sentence supplies the rule that governs the amount.

**The Rightful Duty**

The sentence describes the provision as a duty upon those who do what is right, and the community's teachers read the phrase as the statement of the obligation that the separation creates. The Book's language of the honourable appears throughout the rules about the household.

The wording places the provision within the standard of conduct that the passage has described, and the community's scholars used the clause when they discussed the difference between the gift that is required and the one that is recommended. The account describes a ruling whose force rests on the community's sense of what is fitting as well as on its obligation.

**The Reports and Applications**

The commentaries describe the cases in which the companions divorced before the consummation and before the fixing of a dowry, and the reports record the provision they made. The material shows the community applying the sentence to its circumstances.

The community's jurists also discussed the relation between the sentence and the rules about the dowry that follow it, and they set out the cases in which half of the dowry is due. The passage shows that the passage treats the arrangements of the marriage as a connected body of law, and the sentence in this place supplies the provision for the case it names.

**The Place of the Verse**

The sentence stands between the rules about the waiting period and the proposal and the verse that treats the divorce after a dowry has been fixed, and it supplies the provision for the case that comes between them. The Book has addressed the stages of the arrangement in order, and the reader is shown how the legislation covers each.

The community's teachers read the verses as a unit when they taught the law of the household, and the passage's concern is the protection of the parties in the arrangements that conclude a marriage. The passage closes with the instruction about the provision, and the verse that follows supplies the rule for the case in which the dowry has already been named.

**The Marriage Released Early**

The case the sentence describes concerns a contract that was concluded and then dissolved before the couple had come together and before the amount of the dowry had been named. The Book removes the blame from the separation itself and places the duty of the gift upon the husband, so that the woman who had waited for the marriage is not sent away with nothing.

The jurists measured the gift by the circumstances of the man and by the practice of the community, and they distinguished the case of the woman whose marriage had been consummated from the case of the one who had not been touched. **The Place in the Sūrah**

The sentence stands before the verse of the Pedestal and after the passage about the messengers and the earlier communities, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the preparation for the material that follows. The Book has set out the guidance and the obligations and now calls the community to act on what it has received.

The wording connects the appeals of the sūrah with its instruction about the nature of God, and the reader is shown how the passage moves from the command to the description of the One who gave it. The community's scholars noted that the following verse supplies the ground of the whole appeal, and the sentence in this place supplies the call that precedes it.

**The Day Without Bargaining**

The day the sentence describes has been named in the community's teaching by what it lacks, and the three absences remove every expectation of help. The bargain that a person might offer is not accepted, the friendship of the world does not carry a claim, and no intercessor stands except with the permission that the Book names elsewhere.

The teachers drew from the description the urgency of the command, since the wealth that is stored is of no use once the account begins. The community's practice of charitable giving was built on the verse together with the passages that promise the reward, and the jurists repeated the sentence when they spoke about the obligations of property.

The closing statement about the disbelievers has been read as the description of those who refuse the duty after the Book has made it clear. The passage's turn to the verse that follows is deliberate, since the description of God that comes next supplies the ground of the appeal that the community has just received.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the obligation of spending from what the community has been given, the absence of bargaining and friendship and intercession on the day it describes, and the standing of those who refuse the command. The community's teachers used the verse when they encouraged generosity and when they set out the obligations of property, and the reader is shown that the sūrah calls the community to act while the opportunity remains.

The community's teachers repeated the sentence when they exhorted the believers to give from what they held, and the passage supplied the reminder that the opportunity belongs to the present life. The verse also prepares the reader for the description of God that follows, so that the appeal and the account of its source are read together.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:255

> Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the EverLiving, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse Named**

The verse is known in the community by the name of the Pedestal Verse, and it occupies a place of its own among the passages of the Book. The sentence opens with the declaration of the oneness of God and proceeds through a series of statements about His attributes, and the community's teachers read it as the passage that describes the One to whom the whole sūrah is addressed.

The Book's concern is the knowledge of God that stands behind its instructions, and the community's teachers read the sentence as the ground of everything the sūrah has set out. Readers are shown that the legislation and the narratives of the earlier passages depend on the description given here, and the verse supplies the statement that orders the whole.

**The Opening Declaration**

The sentence opens with the name of God and the statement that there is no god but He, and the commentators noted that the declaration comes before the attributes that follow. The wording then names the Living and the Self-Subsisting, and the community's scholars explained the two as the description of the life that belongs to God and the standing by which all else stands.

The Book's use of the two names elsewhere connects them with the reliance of the creation on its Lord, and the community's teachers gathered the instances. Readers are given the account of a passage that begins with the statement of unity and proceeds to describe the one who is named.

**The Freedom From Slumber**

The sentence states that neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him, and the commentators explained the clause as the statement that God's care of the creation is never interrupted. The wording places before the community the assurance that the affairs of the world are attended to at every moment.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere connects the knowledge of God with the order of the creation, and the community's scholars read the clause as the ground of the trust that the sūrah asks of the community. The passage shows that the verse's concern is the constancy of the divine care, and the sentence supplies the clause that answers the anxiety of those who are reminded of their dependence.

**The Dominion Named**

The sentence states that everything in the heavens and everything on the earth belongs to God, and the commentators explained the clause as the statement about the range of the dominion. The wording places the affairs of the creation within a single ownership.

The Book's practice of asserting the dominion of God appears throughout the sūrah, and the community's teachers used the clause when they spoke about the property that the community holds. The account describes a statement that governs the instruction about spending in the verse before, and the sentence supplies the ground of the obligation that the community has received.

**The Intercession**

The sentence asks who may intercede with God except by His permission, and the commentators explained the clause as the statement that no one approaches the authority of God without what He grants. The community's scholars discussed the intercession that the Book names elsewhere and the conditions attached to it.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere describes the day on which no intercession avails without the leave of God, and the community's teachers connected the passages. The passage shows that the verse's answer to its own question is the permission of God, and the sentence supplies the statement about the sole authority that governs the matter.

**The Knowledge and the Pedestal**

The sentence states that God knows what is before the creation and what is behind it, that they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills, and that His pedestal embraces the heavens and the earth, and it closes with the statement that the guarding of them does not tire Him and that He is the Most High and the Most Great. The community's scholars explained the clauses in turn, and they discussed the meaning of the pedestal at length.

The passage's closing describes the care that sustains the whole creation, and the community's teachers read the last clauses as the completion of the description. The wording places the knowledge and the power together, and the reader is shown that the verse describes the One who orders the whole of the creation and the revelation.

**The Ground of the Whole Passage**

The placement of the verse within the sūrah has been noticed by the community's teachers, and they read it as the ground of the instructions that surround it. The appeal to spend in the preceding verse rests on the ownership and the knowledge that this sentence describes, and the legislation of the sūrah as a whole is presented as the guidance of the One who is named here.

The reports describe the place the passage holds in the devotion of the community, and its memorisation was encouraged and its recitation was granted a standing of its own. The teachers connected the practice with the description of the divine care that the verses set out, so that the words are recited as the statement of confidence in the One who guards the creation.

The scholars discussed the clauses in detail across the centuries, and their commentaries record the discussions of the intercession, the pedestal, and the knowledge that encompasses the created order. The passage closes the section with the names that belong to God alone, so that the reader leaves the instructions of the sūrah with the description of the One who gave them.

**The Standing in the Community**

The verse is among the most widely memorised passages of the Book, and the community's teachers read it on many occasions, including the setting out on a journey and the seeking of protection. The reports describe the place that the passage holds in the community's devotion and teaching.

The material shows that the verse has been given a standing of its own among the passages of the Book, and the community's scholars recorded the sayings that were transmitted about it. The passage closes with the description of God that the sūrah places before its community, and the verses that follow treat the obligations that accompany the knowledge the passage supplies.

The community's teachers placed the verse at the head of the material about the divine attributes, and its recitation has remained part of the practice of the believers in their private and public devotions. The passage also supplies the foundation on which the surrounding commands rest, since the appeal that precedes it and the obligations that follow both depend on the description given here.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:256

> Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Rule Against Compulsion**

Lā ikrāha fī al-dīn — the sentence is a legal principle stated in four words, and it follows the description of God in the verse of the Pedestal, which supplies its ground: the One who owns the heavens and the earth does not require a servant's assent to be forced, because the assent is worthless if forced. Al-Ṭabarī records the occasions that the early authorities attached to it, and none of them changes the rule; they show the situations the rule settled.

The principle is not a concession to weakness. The messengers argue, warn, and invite (16:125), and the Book never presents the invitation as a contest of power. What the sentence removes is a specific expectation: that the community's authority over a city could be used to convert its households, when the earlier verses had already required the community to live among people of other faiths.

**"Sound Judgment Has Become Clear from Error"**

The second clause gives the reason: al-rushd — mature judgement, the capacity to see where a road leads — has become distinct from al-ghayy, the ruinous course. The Book's pairing of these two words recurs (49:7, where God "has made faith beloved to you and beautified it in your hearts"). The reasoning of the sentence is that compulsion is unnecessary where the difference is visible: a case must be argued, not enforced, and if it is argued then the hearer keeps the decision.

This is where the verse's theology and its law meet. The Qur'an's most frequent objection to the deniers is not that they are outvoted but that they refuse to look — "have they not considered" runs through the sūrah's arguments. The clarity assumed here is the clarity of evidence, and the sentence protects the process by which evidence does its work.

**The Handhold That Never Breaks**

The sentence then describes the person who renounces the false objects of worship and believes in God as one who has grasped al-ʿurwa al-wuthqā — the firmest handhold, the handgrip that does not give way. The Qur'an uses the same image again in 31:22, where "whoever submits his face to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold." The metaphor is physical and unglamorous: a person hangs, and the question is whether the thing above him holds.

The order of the two clauses matters. Renunciation comes before affirmation — the empty hand must let go before it can close on the grip. The jurists read the pair as the rejection of tāghūt and the acceptance of God, which is the whole content of the faith; the verse does not mention anything else the person must do to be secure, and that silence has been read by the commentators as the emphasis the sentence intends.

**What the Reports Say About the Occasion**

Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr transmit three occasions from the generation of the companions. The best known concerns households of the Anṣār in Madinah whose children, by vows taken before Islam, had been placed with Jewish families; when the Naḍīr were expelled from the city, the parents asked whether the children should be compelled to return to the Muslim community. A second report tells of a man whose two sons had become Christians and left for Syria; a third of believers who had been nursed among Jewish households and wished to depart with them.

The reports give the verse its setting: it was revealed into mixed families, not into a theory of tolerance. The scholars graded the transmissions differently, but the rule they were used to illustrate was agreed, and the verse's wording is general enough to govern every analogous case.

**The People of the Book and the Jizyah**

A further discussion belongs to the jurists: how the sentence relates to 9:29, where the People of the Book are to pay the jizyah and be subject to the community's authority. Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī record the readings — that the prohibition of compulsion concerned the People of the Book and those who paid the jizyah, or that it states the general principle while the sword applied to the idolaters of Arabia who had broken their treaties. The community's practice favored the first reading, and the law of the protected communities developed from it.

**Hearing and Knowing**

The verse closes with samīʿ and ʿalīm — Hearing and Knowing. The two names answer the two parties of every conversion dispute: the argument as it was spoken is heard, and the belief that a person keeps quiet about is known. Force can produce words; the attributes secure the point that only words can be produced. The sentence therefore ends where the conscience is examined.

**Parallels Across the Book**

The rule of the sentence is not isolated. Sūrah Yūnus puts the same point as a question addressed to the messenger: had your Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed together, and then — "would you compel people until they believe?" (10:99). Al-Kahf states the principle as a permission: "So whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). Al-Ghāshiyah closes the matter: the messenger is a reminder, not a controller over people (88:21–22), and the Book repeats the formula in 76:3, where the path is shown and the choice left open.

Al-Ṭabarī draws the legal consequence that the community's part in the matter is bayān — the clear delivery of the message — and that the outcome belongs to God. Ibn Kathīr adds that the verse does not forbid calling people to the faith; it forbids the assumption that the call can be completed by force. The two positions together are the community's settled reading, and the sūrah's own command to argue with the People of the Book "in the best manner" (16:125) belongs to the same instruction.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence is the charter of the community's manner of invitation: no coercion, a case made clear, a handhold offered rather than imposed, and an account kept by God rather than by the community's enforcers. The verses that follow turn immediately to the guardian of the believers, so that the reader moves from the rule of the invitation to the One who guides.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:257

> Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Guardian Named**

Walī is a word with a range of duties inside it: ally, protector, the one who manages the affairs of another. In the Qur'an it is used for kinship, for patrons, and for God, and the jurists distinguished walāya (the bond that carries protection) from wikāla (the delegation of a task). When the sentence says that God is the walī of those who believe, it is claiming for Him what the tribes of Arabia paid their patrons to provide: defence, management, and a place to belong.

The Qur'an warns the community about the opposite mistaken allegiance in 3:28 and 4:88–90, where the taking of disbelievers as awliyāʾ is discussed; the same root carries the concept of loyalty that a city of mixed alliances could not afford to keep vague. The sentence answers an ordinary question from the community's early years: whose protection does a believer actually live under?

**From Darkness into Light**

The second clause gives the guardian's work: He "brings them out of the darkness into the light." The plural is used because the Qur'an's idiom prefers it — the variety of errors is many, and the truth is one; the image recurs in 5:16, 14:1, 33:43, 57:9, and 65:11, where leaving the darkness is always God's act done through revelation. The light is named with the definite article because there is one.

Al-Ṭabarī reads light and darkness here as guidance and error. Ibn Kathīr adds the observation the image invites: darkness is not one thing but a condition in which direction is impossible, and light is similarly not a doctrine but the ability to see where one is going. The verse describes a change of condition rather than an instruction set.

**The Idols as Guardians**

The sentence then draws its negative pole: "As for those who disbelieve, their guardians are false gods (ṭāghūt) who lead them out of light and into darkness." The symmetry is deliberate and is one of the few places in the Book where the movement runs backwards in the same image. The things they trust cannot bear the weight, and the path bends downward.

The commentators note that the ṭāghūt here is plural in meaning even where the form is singular: every object of reliance that takes God's place — an idol, a chieftain, a market, a habit — can serve as the patron of a life. Al-Rāzī observes that the sentence denies the disbelievers even a false benefit: their guardians do not merely fail to help, they actively lead.

**The Residents of the Fire**

"The residents of the Fire; they will abide therein forever." The Qur'an states the permanence in the present tense, a device the grammarians call the certain future. The word khālidūn is used of the people of the Garden as well, and the verse's symmetry keeps the two destinies paired in the reader's mind, as v. 39 and v. 81 of the same sūrah do.

The sentence is not simply a threat appended to a pastoral image. In the passage's argument, the destination is the outcome of the direction: a life that has been conducted on the path away from the light arrives where that road ends.

**The Pastoral Image Underneath**

Both halves of the verse describe people being led. The Qur'an's anthropology is not that of the self-made man; the question it presses is who is managing the affair. In 2:286 the community is taught to say "You are our Master (mawlānā)" — the same vocabulary from the other side of the relationship. The verse in this place is the affirmation that the community has chosen its guardian deliberately.

**The Motif Through the Book**

The image of this verse is one of the Book's most persistent. Al-Nūr calls God the Light of the heavens and the earth (24:35); al-Māʾidah says the Book guides by it "those who follow His good pleasure to the ways of peace, bringing them out of darkness into light" (5:16); Ibrāhīm's mission is described with the same words (14:1), and the prayer of the angels for the believers in 33:43 and 57:9 repeats them. Al-Ṭabarī concludes from the consistency that the singular "light" of this verse is the guidance itself, and that the plural "darknesses" of the Book's idiom corresponds to the many ways of losing it.

The community's allegiances were the practical question underneath. Madinah's population included Jewish clans, pagan tribes, and the emigrants, and the Book addresses the matter in 3:28 (a warning against taking disbelievers as patrons over believers), 4:88–90 (the hesitation of the hypocrites in the affair), and 60:8–9, which distinguishes those who fight the community from those who do not. Al-Qurṭubī gathers these under walāya: the bond that carries protection must be given to God first, and the ordinary dealings of neighbourhood and trade remain open to everyone. The verse's contrast is therefore a statement about ultimate reliance, not a prohibition of civility, and the sūrah's later verses on marriage, oaths, and debt assume exactly that openness.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The verse is a statement about patronage, movement, and destination, in that order: God as walī, the movement from darkness to light, the counterpart movement of those who take false patrons, and the two ends. It supplies the creedal frame for everything the sūrah says about obedience, and the following verses introduce the disputant who thought his kingship made him a rival of God — the next portrait of a life being led by the wrong patron.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:258

> Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship? ˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death.” He argued, “I too have the power to give life and cause death.” Abraham challenged ˹him˺, “Allah causes the sun to rise from the east. So make it rise from the west.” And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Dispute with the King**

The verse opens with the messenger addressed — a-lam tara ilā alladhī ḥājja Ibrāhīma fī rabbihi — and introduces a ruler who argued with Abraham about his Lord, "because God had given him kingship." The clause is placed at the front, as the Qur'an habitually places the cause of a fault: the man's authority is named before his argument, because the authority is what the argument rested on.

Al-Ṭabarī and the later commentators identify him with Nimrod, but the identification comes from the narrative traditions of the earlier communities (isrāʾīliyyāt) and not from the ḥadīth. The Qur'an leaves him unnamed, and the verse's force does not depend on the name. What is stated is the type: a person whose power over other people's lives persuaded him that he had power over their being.

**"My Lord Gives Life and Causes Death"**

Ibrahim's first move is theological in the plainest terms: the One I call upon disposes of life and death. The answer, "I give life and cause death," is the report of the king's boast, and al-Ṭabarī preserves what was said to have happened next: he brought two prisoners, killed one and spared the other, and called the sparing a granting of life. The early commentators record the anecdote as illustration of the pretence, not as part of the verse.

The exchange exposes a distinction the Arabic preserves cleanly: the king's power was over people already alive. The Qur'anic claim is about iḥyāʾ and imāta as the giving and taking of existence — a claim about creation that no magistrate can imitate. The verse reports his answer without comment, letting the reader see it.

**The Sun from the East**

Ibrahim then changes the terms of the argument: "God brings the sun from the east; bring it from the west." The move is characteristic of the Qur'anic argument from nature, which is the same method 6:78 uses when Abraham watches the rising sun: the sign is not a proposition but the standing order of the world, and no king administers it.

Al-Rāzī observes that the second argument is not a harder version of the first; it is a different kind of argument, chosen because the first could be met with a performance and the second could not. The verse says the man was "confounded" (fa-buhita) — the dictionary sense is a stunned silence impossible to answer, and the Qur'an stops there instead of supplying the reply.

**The Confounded King**

The narrative ends without a conversion. The silence is part of the Qur'an's method: it presents the encounter as a demonstration for the reader's benefit rather than as a story with a satisfying ending. The same ruler-type appears again in 79:24 with Pharaoh's "I am your lord most high," and in both cases the Book's interest is in the internal logic of power claims.

The verse closes with "God does not guide the wrongdoing people," a formula that is often misread as arbitrary. In al-Ṭabarī's reading the clause states a consequence: the one who has bent the truth to his own authority is not in a position to receive the guidance that requires honesty about evidence, and the obstruction precedes the deprivation.

**The Argument from the Order of Nature**

Al-Rāzī stresses that the second argument is a different kind of proof, not a stronger one. The king could stage an execution and call it the granting of life; nobody can stage a sunrise. The Book returns to this order repeatedly: the alternation of night and day is a sign for people who listen (10:67), the sun runs to its appointed course (36:38), and Abraham's own reflection on the rising sun stands in Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:78). The argument is available to every hearer, which is why the Qur'an treats it as the common ground of the discussion with the deniers.

The power claim itself belongs to a theme the sūrah develops elsewhere. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states that God gives sovereignty to whom He wills and takes it from whom He wills (3:26); 2:247 says the same in the matter of Talut; and 4:54 notes that Abraham's own descendants were given a mighty sovereignty. The point of those verses is that authority is a grant rather than a personal property — which is precisely what the ruler of this verse forgot. The verse's closing formula about guidance belongs to the same diagnosis: the person who uses the truth as an instrument of his own standing has put himself where guidance does not reach. The passage then turns to the ruined town, where a different question is asked and answered.
