**What the Verse Establishes**

The verse establishes the pattern by which the sūrah considers power: a claim to kingship, an argument about the divine prerogatives, a sign drawn from the order of creation, and a silence. Al-Rāzī's comment on the whole passage is worth noting: Abraham's argument relied on what everyone could see, and the Qur'an's use of the scene is aimed at the reader — who is invited to choose between the two patrons the previous verse described. The narrative that follows turns from the ruler who could not raise the sun to the man who asked how a ruined city could be raised.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:259

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink— they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A City Fallen on Its Roofs**

The verse opens with a second observation: a man passing by a town "khāwiyah ʿalā ʿurūshihā." Khāwiyah carries both ruin and emptiness — the roofs have come down onto the walls, and nothing stands. The word choice appears in the poetry of the pre-Islamic Arabs for abandoned campsites, and the verse uses it to present a place from which every sign of life has gone.

The commentators name the man variously: Ezra (ʿUzayr), Ezekiel, or al-Khiḍr, with some holding he was no prophet at all but a man shown the demonstration. The Qur'an leaves the identity open, and the scholars of the community recorded the positions without coming to agreement. The lesson hangs on the question he asks, not on his identity.

**The Question and the Answer**

The question asks how a place in that condition could ever be restored, and it concerns possibility, and it is answered by an event rather than by reasoning, since the account states that the man was made to die for a century and then brought back to life. The man who asked how resurrection could work becomes the demonstration of it.

Al-Rāzī reads the sequence as part of the sūrah's method of teaching by sign. The question was not treated as an offence, and the commentators compared it with Abraham's "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead" in the following verse. In both cases the request comes from a desire for the evidence of the eyes rather than a wager of the mind.

**The Food That Did Not Spoil**

"Look at your food and your drink — they have not spoiled." The instruction has the quality of a laboratory demonstration: God could have raised the man in a different place, but the verse puts him back beside his own provisions, unspoiled after a century, so the miracle is something he can inspect with his hands.

The commentators noted further that the preservation of the food answers a subsidiary question the man had not asked: whether the identity of a body survives the decomposition of the grave. His provisions had done so. The verse then moves to the more difficult case.

**The Bones and the Flesh**

"Look at your donkey" — and the verse describes the bones set up and clothed with flesh. The scholars discussed the referent of the phrase; most read it as the animal's restoration, some as the man's own body. The donkey is mentioned because it was the property whose loss he could measure.

The Qur'an elsewhere describes the first clothing of bones with flesh as the creator's own work (23:14), and the verse's vivid language here serves the visual argument. When the man sees it, the account records his verdict that he now knows God has power over everything

**A Sign for Mankind**

One clause explains the purpose of the whole event: "that We may make you a sign for mankind." The same word, āya, is used for the verses of the Book and for the wonders shown to the earlier communities. The Qur'an uses Pharaoh with the same expression in 10:92 — "so that you may be a sign" — where the sign is negative, a warning rather than a proof.

The community's scholars drew the point that the sign is intended to circulate: it happened to one man so that many could hear the report. The sūrah's use of narrative follows this logic throughout, and the verse's coda — the man's own confession — is the form the report takes.

**The Question Asked Three Times**

The question "how long have you tarried?" occurs in three places in the Book, and the community's commentators read them together. The sleepers of the cave give the same estimate when they wake (18:19), and in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn the resurrected reply in the same terms, having lost the ability to measure the interval (23:112–114). The three accounts agree that the span of the grave is experienced as almost nothing.

Al-Ṭabarī draws from the sequence the point that the demonstration was for the man's own certainty; the raising of the donkey was an argument addressed to his eyes, since his question had been about the possibility of the deed. Some of the early authorities also read the verse as a statement that the man was made a prophet, while others pointed to 10:92, where Pharaoh is called a sign for those who come after — a warning rather than a proof. The disagreement turns on the function of the sign, not on its reality, and the confession at the verse's end — "I know that God has power over all things" — is the fruit the account intends.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The verse establishes the demonstration of resurrection by means of a witness who lived it: ruin, the question, death, the hundred years, the unspoiled provisions, the reconstituted animal, the sign, and the confession. Al-Ṭabarī records that the phrase "and look at the bones, how We set them up" was read by some of the companions with a different subject, and the variation shows how closely the early community attended to the scene. The passage then turns to Abraham's request, so that the reader meets two kinds of question in succession: the doubter's and the prophet's.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:260

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you not believe?” Abraham replied, “Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured.” Allah said, “Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet's Request**

"And when Abraham said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.'" The request follows the scene of the ruined city, and the sūrah pairs the two so that the reader compares the question of the passerby with the petition of the prophet. The answer opens with a question of its own: "Do you not believe?" — which the commentators read as an affirmation rather than a rebuke, on the pattern of a teacher confirming what a student already holds.

Al-Ṭabarī collects the occasions the early authorities offered: that Abraham had seen carrion contested by creatures of sea, land, and air and wondered how the parts could be reassembled; that he wanted a sign to strengthen his argument with the ruler of v. 258; that the question belonged to his exchange about the sacrifice of his son. The reports do not fix the occasion, and the verse itself supplies none.

**"So That My Heart May Be at Peace"**

The crucial clause is Abraham's answer: "Yes, but so that my heart may be at peace (li-yaṭmaʾinna qalbī)." The Qur'an uses the same root in 13:28 — "surely in the remembrance of God hearts find rest" — and in 89:27 for the serene soul. The word describes a settled state, not the absence of proof.

The scholars of the community took care with this. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said, in the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, "We have more right to doubt than Abraham" — a statement the commentators explain as a rhetorical argument: if doubt were possible for a prophet, the Prophet ﷺ would have more occasion for it than Abraham, and since he has none, neither had Abraham. The ḥadīth's purpose is to defend Abraham's rank against a misreading of the verse, not to report a doubt.

Al-Rāzī adds that knowledge has degrees: assent of the mind, and the tranquillity of the heart that comes with witnessing. The request asks for the second while the first is already present.

**The Four Birds and the Command**

"Take four birds and incline them to you" — the command begins with training, since the sign will end with a summons the birds must obey. The commentators explain that Abraham was to make them familiar with him, then cut them into pieces, scatter the parts on the hills, and call them back.

The detail matters to the argument. Resurrection here is presented as a gathering (jamʿ) rather than a raw creation: the parts exist, and they are assembled. The Qur'an makes the same distinction in 17:49–51 and 75:3–4, where the question is whether scattered bones can be collected. The verse answers in the mode of demonstration.

Al-Ṭabarī records that the birds were made so familiar with Abraham that they came at his word before the demonstration, and the commentators read the training as part of the sign: the summons at the end of the sequence is answered because the summons was the same voice that had called them from the first. The scattering on separate hills removes any natural explanation, since no ordinary cause gathers cut flesh from distant slopes; what answers is the call itself.

**The Call Answered**

The command's conclusion is stated in advance: "they will come to you in haste." The obedience of the created order to the call of the One who gave the command runs through the sūrah — the same motif appears in 41:11 with the heavens and the earth answering "we come willingly." The sign is not finally about birds; it is about the relation between the summons and the response.

The scholars also noted that the demonstration used Abraham's own hands and voice. The prophet is not a spectator of his own proof; he trains the birds, scatters them, calls, and watches them return.

The Qur'an describes the response of the created order to the divine command in the same terms elsewhere, as when the heavens and the earth answer that they come willingly (41:11) and when the angels do what they are commanded without hesitation (16:50). The scholars of the community read the birds' return in this verse as a recorded event rather than as a figure of speech, and the conclusion of the sequence — Abraham calling and the parts reassembling and flying to him — is the demonstration that his petition had asked to see.

**"Mighty, Wise"**

The verse closes with ʿazīz and ḥakīm — Mighty and Wise. The first name answers the doubt about power, the second the question about how: the arrangement of the demonstration was not random but ordered, a visible sign in which the pieces are cut, separated, and then rejoined. The whole narrative of the verse is designed to show that the "how" is precisely what the viewer is allowed to see.

**Knowledge That Grows**

The Book commands the Prophet ﷺ to pray for increase of knowledge — "My Lord, increase me in knowledge" (20:114) — a request that would be meaningless if the knowledge of a prophet were a fixed quantity. Al-Rāzī reads the clause as the key to Abraham's petition: what the friend of God asked for was not the belief he already held but a further degree of it, which is why the answer began with "Do you not believe?"

The ḥadīth transmitted by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, in which the Prophet ﷺ says, "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," has been read by the commentators as a defence of Abraham's rank rather than an admission of doubt in either man: if any prophet could have wavered, the Prophet ﷺ would be the more likely, and since he did not, Abraham's request is shown to be obedience seeking evidence. The Sufi reading recorded by al-Rāzī follows the same line — the request was for witnessing, not for proof — and 13:28, where hearts find rest in the remembrance of God, shows what the desired tranquillity is. The verses that follow turn to the seed and the harvest, where the same God who restores birds to life multiplies a grain.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The verse is the sūrah's most detailed account of the resurrection, and its teaching is delivered through a request made by a prophet and answered by a demonstration he performed. The next verses take up wealth and the multiplying of reward, so that the reader moves from the multiplication of broken birds into life to the multiplication of a grain into a harvest — the same God, the same arithmetic of restoration.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:261

> The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains. And Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Parable Opened**

The sentence presents the spending of wealth in the cause of God under the figure of a seed that produces seven ears of grain, and the community's teachers read the image as the answer to the anxiety that accompanies the loss of property. The Book has been addressing the obligations of charity through the passage, and the parable here supplies the account of what the giver receives.

The choice of a grain as the object of the image has been noticed by the commentators, since the seed is the smallest part of the harvest and the multiplication belongs to the order that God has established in the earth. The teachers drew the lesson that the reward of charity follows the pattern of the creation rather than the measure of the gift.

The sentence opens with the comparison of those who spend, so that the parable describes their condition rather than the nature of the wealth they part with. The giver is named first, and the harvest follows.

**The Seven Ears**

The commentators discussed the number of the ears and the grains that each of them contains, and they described the abundance that the figure presents. The image was explained as the account of a reward that exceeds the act many times over, and the interpreters noted that the Book's promises regularly use the language of multiplication.

The teachers also observed the consideration that the figure gives to the sower, since the seed is not consumed but planted, and the wealth that is given for the sake of God is described as remaining in the hand of its owner in a better form. The community's preachers used the image when they answered the argument that charity reduces a person's property.

The passage's earlier verses have named the reward of those who spend, and the parable here supplies the figure by which the community pictured it. The two statements belong together in the sūrah's treatment of the subject.

**The Multiplication Stated**

The sentence adds that God multiplies for whom He wills, and the community's scholars read the clause as the statement that the increase belongs to the divine decision rather than to the measure of the act. The teachers noted that the same wording appears in the descriptions of the provision that God grants, so that the reward of the giver is placed within the general bounty of the Creator.

The reports of the community describe sayings of the Prophet ﷺ about the measure of the reward, and one of them states that a good deed is written tenfold or up to seven hundredfold, with the exception of the fast, which the Book reserves for its own reward. The teachers gathered the material when they explained the sentence.

The clause also serves the community's understanding of generosity, since the person who gives does not calculate the return himself. The multiplication is left to God, and the sentence supplies the assurance that the calculation is in better hands.

**The Reports About the Reward**

The reports of the community preserve the sayings that describe the reward of charity in concrete images, and the teachers used them when they taught the subject. One report describes a man who brought an animal to the Prophet ﷺ and declared that he gave it in the way of God, and the answer described the reward that the giver would receive in the like of what he had offered many times over.

The material shows the manner in which the community received the promise of the sentence. The parables of the Book were explained through the images of the daily life of the people, and the teachers regarded the two forms of statement as the confirmation of one another.

The commentators also noted the difference between the reward that the Book promises and the increase that belongs to the dealings of the world. The first is granted by the decision of God, and the second follows the measures that He has placed in the creation.

**The Name All-Encompassing**

The verse closes with the description of God as bountiful and knowing, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the ground of the promise. The first name, which is also rendered as all-encompassing, carries the sense of a generosity that no measure limits, and the second concerns the knowledge of every act and every intention.

The teachers noted that the two names answer the two doubts that a giver may hold. The fear that the gift is too small for a reward is answered by the bounty that has no limit, and the fear that the act will be forgotten is answered by the knowledge that records it.

The Book uses the pair in the passages that treat the provision of the creatures, and the community's scholars gathered the instances when they explained the attributes. The verse therefore ends with the statement about the One who receives the gift.

**The Parable in the Sūrah**

The sentence belongs to the long passage on charity that runs through the middle of the sūrah, and the teachers read the parables of that section as a series that presents the subject from several sides. One image describes the reward of the giver, another describes the charity that is ruined by the reminder of it, and a third describes the giver who has lost his harvest at the end of his life.

The arrangement of the material gives the community a complete treatment of the subject. The sentence in this place supplies the encouragement that answers the reluctance of the giver, and the verses that follow supply the warnings that protect the act from what destroys it.

The teachers of the community drew the lesson that the passage addresses the intention as well as the act, since the reward of the gift depends on the state of the person who gives it. The parable of the grain is therefore read with the verses about the manner of giving.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the figure of the seed and the harvest, the multiplication of the reward by the decision of God, the generosity that no measure limits, and the knowledge that records the act. The community's teachers used the verse to encourage the believers in their giving, and the sūrah's later verses were read with it when the community examined the conditions of the charity that God accepts.

The clause about the will of God also supplies the answer to those who called the promise into question after their own experience of the world. The harvest of the giver belongs to the life to come, and the sentence places the whole matter within the bounty of the One who gives it.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:262

> Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words—they will get their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Condition Stated**

The sentence names the reward of those who spend their wealth in the cause of God and then do not follow what they have given with reminders of their generosity or with words that wound. The verse supplies the condition that accompanies the act, and the community's teachers read it as the statement that the manner of the giving belongs to the giving itself.

The sūrah has already treated the spending that is offered for the sake of God, and the sentence here describes the quality that preserves it. The Book's method in the passage is to present the act and then to name what protects it, so that the community learns to attend to the whole of the matter.

The wording places the reminder and the injury after the gift, and the teachers noted the choice. The harm of the two is done to a person who has already received the help, and the sentence names the offence that follows the benefit.

**The Two Faults Named**

The commentators explained the first fault as the reminder that a giver delivers to the one who received from him, whether it is spoken openly or conveyed by the manner of his conduct. The second is the word or the act that causes pain to the person who was given to, and the teachers described the shame that such conduct produces in someone whose need has been exposed.

The community's scholars noted that the sentence joins the two, since the reminder of the gift and the injury that accompanies it belong to the same disposition. A person who regards his gift as a favour to be acknowledged has already treated the one who received it as his debtor.

The Book elsewhere warns against the conduct that breaks the heart of the poor, and the passages that treat the subject were gathered by the commentators when they explained the sentence. The duty of the giver therefore includes the protection of the dignity of the one who receives.

**The Reward Named**

The sentence states that those who give in the manner it describes will have their reward with their Lord, and the community's teachers read the phrase as the assurance that the promise is kept for them. The wording places the reward in the keeping of God rather than in the hands of the recipients, so that the giver does not look to people for the requital of his gift.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere promises the increase of what is spent, and the sentence here states the outcome for the givers whose conduct has preserved the act. The two statements were read together by the community's scholars, so that the promise of the increase and the promise of the reward were understood as one.

The teachers also drew attention to the order of the sentence, since the reward is named for those who have completed the giving with the manner the verse requires. The condition is not an addition to the act; it is part of what makes the act what it is.

**The Fear Removed**

The sentence continues with the statement that no fear will come upon them and that they will not grieve, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the promise that accompanies the people of the Garden throughout the Book. The wording appears in the descriptions of the reward elsewhere, and the teachers regarded the repetition as the confirmation of the giver's standing.

The first clause concerns what lies ahead, and the second concerns what has passed, so that the two together describe a condition that is complete. The community's preachers used the formula when they spoke about the state of the believers in the life to come.

The phrase also answers the anxiety that the giver may feel about the property he has parted with. The fear that poverty follows the gift and the grief over what has been spent are both removed, and the sentence leaves the community with the assurance that accompanies the act.

**The Teaching of the Passage**

The sentence supplies the standard that the verses that follow develop, and the community's teachers read the whole passage as a single instruction on the manner of charity. The reminders of the gift, the injury, and the display of generosity are treated in the verses that come after, so that the sentence here states the principle in advance of the details.

The scholars of the community drew from the passage the rule that the acceptance of a gift is injured by the conduct of the giver as much as by the gift itself. The poor who are given what they need and then reminded of it have been harmed, and the Book does not treat the act as a benefit to its giver.

The teachers also observed that the passage is addressed to a community whose giving was part of its shared life, so that the warning concerns the relations of its members rather than a practice of the wealthy alone. The sentence therefore taught the manners of the community as well as the law of its charity.

**The Teachers' Use of the Sentence**

The preachers of the community returned to the sentence when they described the conduct that destroys the reward of a gift, and the reports describe their attention to the manner of the giver. The material shows the care with which the early community treated the feelings of those who lived in need.

The community's teachers also used the verse when they set out the duties of the wealthy toward those who served them, since the reminder of a favour is the temptation that accompanies the possession of property. The sentence supplied them with the reminder that the words of the giver are written.

The instruction in the passage that follows takes the same subject further with a comparison, and the community's scholars read the two together. The sentence in this place therefore stands at the head of the treatment of the manner of giving, and the verses that follow supply its illustration.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the reward of those who give without the reminder of their generosity and without the word that wounds, the assurance that accompanies them, and the standard by which the manner of the giving is judged. The community's teachers used the verse when they taught the conduct of charity, and the scholars of the community placed it among the instructions that protect the dignity of the poor.

The passage continues with the comparison that treats the same subject under another figure, so that the reader is given the promise of the reward and the warning of what destroys it in the verses that follow one another.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:263

> Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Comparison Stated**

The sentence states that a word of kindness and an act of forgiveness are better than a charity that is followed by an injury, and the community's teachers read the comparison as the statement of the Book's scale of values. The verse follows the instruction about the reminder and the hurtful word, and it supplies the alternative that the passage recommends.

The comparison has been explained by the commentators in the light of the passage's concern for the poor. A gift that is accompanied by a reproach leaves the recipient with a wound, while a kind word gives him something without cost to the giver, and the sentence rates the second above the first.

The wording does not diminish the duty of charity. It states that the value of a given act is measured by the whole of what the recipient receives, and the community's scholars drew from the sentence the rule that the manner belongs to the act.

**The Kind Word**

The commentators explained the phrase as the speech that soothes the person who is in need, and they included the greeting, the encouragement, and the prayer offered on his behalf. The teachers noted that such a word can come from a person who has nothing to give, so that the sentence opens a door of goodness to everyone.

The Book's treatment of speech elsewhere commends the words that mend a relationship, and the community's scholars gathered the instances when they explained the phrase. The sentence therefore places the tongue beside the hand among the means by which the community serves its members.

The teachers also observed the order of the sentence, since the kind word is named before the forgiveness that follows it. The two belong to the same disposition, and the community's preachers used the phrase when they described the manners that accompany the withholding of a gift that cannot be given.

**The Forgiveness Named**

The second element of the comparison is the forgiveness that a person extends to a request that troubles him, and the commentators explained the phrase as the overlooking of the manner of the one who asks. The teachers described the case of a poor person whose approach is rough or whose asking is importunate, and they read the sentence as the instruction to answer him with pardon rather than with reproach.

The community's scholars connected the phrase with the passages about patience and about the pardon that the Book commends, and they used the material when they taught the conduct of the giver and the one who has nothing to give.

The wording places the forgiveness among the goods that the sentence rates above the spoiled gift. The person who pardons the fault of the needy has given him something, and the community's teachers counted the act among the goods that the Book rewards.

**The Attributes Named**

The verse closes with the description of God as self-sufficient and forbearing, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the ground of the comparison the sentence has drawn. The first name states that God has no need of the property that the community offers, and the second describes the patience with which He bears the faults of His servants.

The teachers drew from the attributes the lesson that the honour of the giver is not increased by the gift itself, so that the reminder of a favour reveals an error about the source of what a person owns. The Book's teaching about property elsewhere describes it as a trust, and the community's scholars gathered the passages when they spoke about the subject.

The two names also answer the state of the giver who fears that the withholding of a gift will be held against him. The One who is self-sufficient does not require the gift, and the person who has nothing to give may still earn the reward by the manner he keeps.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence stands between the instruction about the spoiled charity and the comparison of the two givers in the verses that follow, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the development of a single subject. The passage has treated the reward of the giver, the fault that destroys it, and the modest good that the Book rates above the harmed gift.

The teachers of the community drew the lesson that the passage attends to the condition of the poor as much as to the virtue of the rich. The Book's concern runs through the whole section, and the sentence in this place supplies the statement that a person who has nothing is not left outside the service of his community.

The following verses carry the argument to its illustration, and the community's scholars read the whole passage as a unit when they taught the law of charity. The sentence therefore supplies the principle, and the parables that follow supply the demonstration of it.

**The Teaching Drawn**

The community's preachers used the sentence when they answered those who excused themselves from giving because they owned little. The verse supplied the reminder that the kind word and the pardon are within the reach of every person, and the material shows the formula repeated in the exhortations of the early teachers.

The scholars of the community also noted that the sentence protects the dignity of the poor in the very passage that calls for generosity, since the Book does not treat the recipient as an object of pity. The wording places him among the persons to whom a service is owed and from whom a fault may be pardoned.

The passage's instruction therefore covers the whole of the relationship between the giver and the one who receives. The sentence in this place supplies the standard by which both are measured, and the verses that follow develop the same theme with the figures of the rock and the garden.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the superiority of the kind word and the pardon over the charity that is followed by an injury, the standing of the modest goods within the community's service, and the attributes of God that supply the ground of the comparison. The community's teachers used the verse when they taught the conduct of the giver and the consolation of the one who had nothing to give, and the sūrah's treatment of charity continues with the comparisons that follow in the next verses.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:264

> O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Their example is that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain— leaving it just a bare stone. Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity. Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Annulment Forbidden**

The sentence addresses the believers and forbids them to annul their charity through reminders of generosity and through injury, and the community's teachers read the instruction as the statement that an act of goodness can be destroyed by the conduct that follows it. The Book has named the reward of the givers who preserve their gifts, and the sentence here states what removes it.

The wording is addressed to the givers themselves, so that the danger the passage describes lies in their own conduct rather than in the conduct of those who receive. The community's scholars noted the point, since the poor who are given and then reproached have no part in the loss that the sentence describes.

The instruction also implies that the act and its manner belong together. What the Book calls the annulment is the destruction of the value of the gift, and the teachers described the affair in terms of a person who works and then dismantles what he has built.

**The Show-off Named**

The sentence compares the conduct of the one who annuls his charity with the conduct of a person who spends his wealth to be seen by people and who does not believe in God or the Last Day. The commentators noted the pairing, since the display of a gift places its purpose in the eyes of the community rather than in the pleasure of God.

The teachers explained the phrase about the belief as the statement about the root from which the conduct grows. The person who looks for the praise of his neighbours has taken them as the audience of his act, and the Book's description places him outside the company of those who give for its sake.

The community's scholars also noted that the sentence does not describe the scale of the gift but the state of the giver. A small gift given in the manner the passage commends is preserved, while a large gift offered for display has nothing behind it.

**The Parable of the Rock**

The sentence presents the figure of a smooth rock with a thin layer of soil upon it, and a downpour that strikes it and leaves it bare. The commentators explained the image as the description of an act that appears to be productive and is found to be empty, since the rain washes away the soil on which a crop might have grown.

The teachers connected the meaning of the figure with the subject of the passage. The thin layer of dust stands for the charitable act, and the downpour stands for the reminder and the injury that remove it, so that the giver is left with nothing at the time he needs it most.

The image also describes the condition of the surface, since the rock offers nothing for the seed to take hold of. The community's scholars read the detail as the statement about the heart in which the act was not rooted in the intention that the Book requires.

**The Rain and the Bare Stone**

The commentators drew the comparison with the parable that follows, where the same rain falls on a fertile garden and produces a double harvest. The two figures share the water and differ in the ground, so that the sentence's teaching concerns the condition of the person who receives the heavenly gift rather than the gift itself.

The community's teachers read the pair as the Book's method of presenting two ends of the same act. The rainfall of the world's opportunities reaches both kinds of people, and what they produce depends on what they have made of their hearts.

The material also shows the care with which the community's scholars handled the figures of the Book, since they identified each element of the parables and then drew the whole together. The reading they transmitted presents the section as a single instruction about the intention of the giver.

**The Closing Statement**

The sentence closes with the statement that these people have no power over anything of what they earned, and the community's scholars read the clause as the account of the loss that the parable describes. The teachers noted the form of the phrase, since it does not deny that the gift was made but states that its value has passed.

The Book's use of the language of earning for the spiritual result appears in the passages that treat the account of the Hereafter, and the community's scholars gathered the instances when they explained the sentence. The reward of an act is described as a possession that a person carries, and the verse states that the person in question holds nothing.

The final clause states that God does not guide the disbelieving people, and the teachers read it as the statement about the condition of those whose conduct has replaced the purpose of the act. The sentence in this place therefore ends where the previous passage ended, with the guidance that the Book grants to those who seek it.

**The Passage's Concern**

The verse stands within the long treatment of charity in the sūrah, and the community's teachers read the parables of the section as a series of instructions about the manner of giving. The sentence in this place supplies the warning that accompanies the promise of the earlier verse, and the passage then supplies the comparison of the good giver.

The section's concern is the honesty of the act before God, since the community's giving was visible to its members and the temptation to seek their approval was near. The Book's answer is the account of the two grounds and the two harvests, and the sentence here supplies the first of them.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the prohibition of annulling charity through reminders and injury, the description of the giver who acts for display, the parable of the rock and the rain, the loss that follows for such a giver, and the statement about the guidance that the unbelieving people do not receive. The community's teachers used the verse when they warned the wealthy about the manner of their giving, and the sūrah's next verse supplies the corresponding account of the giver whose act is rooted in the pleasure of God.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:265

> And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah’s pleasure and believing the reward is certain, is that of a garden on a fertile hill: when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Parable**

The sentence presents the second of the two comparisons and describes those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and out of a confirmation within their own souls. The community's teachers read the figure as the counterpart of the rock in the verse before, so that the same rain is shown falling on two kinds of ground.

The wording names two conditions in the giver, the purpose of the act and the certainty that accompanies it. The commentators explained the second as the assurance of the heart that the promise of God is true, so that the person gives without the fear that the matter is uncertain.

The verse therefore describes the inner state of the giver before it describes the harvest. The Book's concern in the passage runs through the intention as well as the act, and the sentence supplies the statement of the intention that the earlier verses have commended.

**The Garden on the Height**

The image the sentence uses is that of a garden situated on elevated ground, and the commentators discussed the placement of the garden at length. Some explained that such a spot is reached only by the rain and not by the streams of the valley, so that the garden depends on the bounty that comes from above.

Others related the term to the growth that the ground produces, so that the phrase describes a fertile rise from which the crops come forth. The teachers set out the readings and noted that both of them serve the sentence's purpose, since the garden in either case yields its fruit by the gift that the sky supplies.

The community's scholars also observed the contrast with the bare rock of the previous verse. The one surface keeps nothing, and the other holds what it receives and returns it many times over.

**The Double Harvest**

The sentence states that when a heavy rain falls the garden yields twice its ordinary produce, and the community's teachers read the phrase as the description of the reward that accompanies the act of the giver. The Book's earlier parable has promised the harvest of seven hundred grains, and the two figures were read together by the community's scholars.

The word rendered as twice has been explained as the statement of a full and repeated return, and the commentators noted that the figure describes the reward of the life to come rather than the property of this one. The teachers used the sentence when they spoke about the abundance that the Book promises to those who spend.

The clause also places the harvest within the order that God has established in the earth, since the rain and the ground work together. The community's preachers drew from the image the lesson that the act of the giver is the seed and the reward is the fruit that follows it.

**The Soft Rain**

The sentence adds that if no heavy rain falls, a light rain is sufficient, and the commentators explained the clause as the statement that the garden is never left without its yield. The teachers read the detail as the account of the giver whose opportunities are modest, since his act also produces its fruit although the measure of the rain differs.

The wording gives the community the assurance that the scale of the gift does not determine whether it is accepted. What the sentence requires is the character of the giver, and the rain that reaches the garden, whether heavy or light, is enough for its fruit.

The community's scholars also noted the consolation that the clause supplies to the believer who owns little. The Book's promises in the passage are addressed to all who give in the manner the verses describe, and the sentence here includes the small measure within the promise.

**The Certainty Named**

The sentence names the confirmation within the souls of the givers, and the commentators explained the phrase as the certainty that their gift is received and their reward is kept. The Book's description of the believers elsewhere includes the assurance that accompanies their deeds, and the teachers gathered the passages on the subject.

The phrase also supplies the answer to the fear that the previous passage addressed, since a person who knows that his gift is not lost gives without the anxiety that spoils the act. The community's scholars read the sentence as the account of the disposition with which the believers spend.

The wording places the confirmation within the person rather than in the circumstances, so that the state of the giver does not depend on the response of those who receive. The teachers used the sentence when they answered the community's questions about the acceptance of the gifts that were given to people who did not acknowledge them.

**The Attribute at the Close**

The verse closes with the statement that God sees what the community does, and the community's scholars read the clause as the ground of the whole passage. The attribute places the acts of the givers and the hidden conditions of their hearts before the One who observes them.

The teachers drew from the closing the lesson that the manner of a gift is as visible to God as the gift itself. The person who gives in the way the sentence describes is seen, and the person whose act is spoiled by the conduct that follows it is seen as well, so that the two parables rest on the same knowledge.

The sentence therefore ends with the assurance that accompanies the reward. The community's preachers used the clause when they spoke about sincerity, and the passage's treatment of charity reaches its conclusion with the statement about the divine sight.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the description of the givers who seek the pleasure of God with certainty in their hearts, the image of the garden on the height, the double harvest that the rain brings, the sufficiency of the light rain, and the attribute of sight that closes the passage. The community's teachers used the verse when they encouraged the believers whose means were small, and the sūrah's next verses turn to the parable of the garden that is destroyed at the end of a life, so that the whole section presents the harvest and its loss together.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:266

> Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines, and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up? This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Put**

The sentence asks whether any of the community would wish for the situation it describes, and the community's teachers read the question as the Book's method of bringing a matter home to the hearer. The passage has presented the two harvests, and the question here presents the loss that a person may meet at the very end of his life.

The form of the address has been noticed by the commentators, since the sentence does not describe a stranger but places the hearer within the scene. The Book's use of the question in its parables appears elsewhere, and the teachers gathered the instances when they explained the passage.

The wording also names the garden as the possession of the person addressed, so that the wish is presented as the natural desire of any owner. The loss that follows is therefore measured against what the person had valued most.

**The Garden Described**

The sentence describes a garden of date palms and vines with rivers flowing beneath it and every kind of fruit within it, and the commentators identified the scene as the image of the abundance that the Book uses for the reward of the believers.

The teachers noted the elements of the description and the order in which they are named. The palms and the vines supply the produce of the settled land, the rivers supply the water on which the garden depends, and the fruits of every kind complete the account of a possession that leaves nothing to be wished for.

The community's scholars observed the connection between the figure and the earlier verses about the harvest of the giver. The garden of the parable stands for the wealth and the good deeds of a lifetime, and the sentence describes the condition of the person who has gathered them.

**The Old Age and the Children**

The sentence adds that the owner has grown old and that his children are weak, and the commentators explained the clause as the account of the moment at which the loss is least bearable. The person described has no strength to build again and no children who could take up the work that he has left.

The teachers drew attention to the detail of the children, since the Book's image of the household's continuation is present in the scene. The hope of the owner was placed in the generation that follows him, and the sentence describes it as unable to help.

The wording thus completes the picture of a person whose resources have been gathered into one place. The community's scholars read the passage as the description of the situation in which every support has been removed, and the question that opens the sentence applies to it.

**The Fiery Whirlwind**

The sentence then describes the whirlwind that contains fire and consumes the garden, and the community's teachers read the image as the statement about the event that destroys what the person had built. The figure gathers the elements of a storm and of a burning, so that nothing of the garden remains.

The commentators connected the whirlwind with the conduct that the previous verses have described, since the reminder of the gift and the injury that follows it are the wind that removes the harvest. The teachers explained the sentence as the picture of a person who stands before the account of his life with nothing left of the acts in which he had trusted.

The reading was preserved in the community's teaching of the passage, and the scholars drew from it the lesson that the value of a deed is not secure until the end of the life in which it was performed.

**The Application to the Givers**

The commentators applied the parable to those who spend their wealth and then ruin the act by their conduct, and they described the account of such a person in the life to come. The Book's earlier verses have compared the gift to a seed and to a garden, and the sentence here presents the loss of the whole harvest.

The teachers also drew a wider application from the passage, since the person described in the sentence is one whose deeds are gathered into a single store that an event removes. The community's scholars used the figure when they spoke about the need to protect good works from the faults that destroy them.

The sentence therefore supplies the counterpart of the parables that precede it. The two earlier figures have compared the grounds on which the rain falls, and the figure here describes what becomes of the garden when the last day of a life brings the storm.

**The Other Reading**

The commentators preserved a further explanation of the sentence, transmitted from one of the early authorities, which applies it to the person who performs good works and then turns to evil ones so that his earlier deeds are wasted. The teachers set out the reading beside the first and noted the subject they share.

The material shows the care with which the community's scholars handled the parables of the Book, since they gathered the explanations and did not confine the passage to one application. The verse's concern in each case is the end of a person's work, so that the readings serve the same lesson.

The wording of the sentence supports the wider application, since the garden may stand for the deeds of a lifetime rather than for a gift alone. The community's scholars used the passage when they warned the believers against the conduct that follows a good act.

**The Closing Invitation**

The sentence closes with the statement that God makes His revelations clear so that the community may reflect, and the community's teachers read the clause as the statement of the purpose that accompanies the parables. The figures have been presented in order for the hearer to consider what they require of him.

The Book's habit of attaching the invitation to reflect to its parables appears throughout the sūrah, and the community's scholars gathered the instances when they explained the passage. The sentence in this place therefore ends with the call that makes the image a matter for the hearer's own account.

The teachers drew the lesson that the community is expected to read its own life in the figure. The garden, the old age, the children, and the storm belong to the experience of the hearer, and the sentence leaves him to consider which of the two harvests he is preparing.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the parable of the garden that is consumed at the end of a life, the condition of the owner whose strength and children have failed him, the destruction that removes the whole harvest, the application of the figure to the acts that are ruined by what follows them, and the invitation to reflect that closes the passage. The community's teachers used the verse when they spoke about the security of deeds at the end of life, and the sūrah then returns to the instruction about the wealth that is spent, so that the parable and the command stand beside one another.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:267

> O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth. Do not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command to Spend Well**

The sentence addresses the believers and instructs them to give from the good things that they have earned and from what God has brought forth from the earth, and the community's teachers read the command as the statement about the quality of what is offered. The passage has treated the manner of the giving, and the sentence here adds the standard that applies to the gift itself.

The wording joins two sources of wealth, the trade of the community and the produce of the land, so that the instruction covers the whole of what its members owned. The teachers noted the breadth of the phrase, since the command applies to the merchant and the farmer alike.

The Book's treatment of generosity elsewhere states that the believers will not attain the piety the passage describes until they spend from what they love, and the community's scholars read the two verses together when they taught the subject. The sentence in this place supplies the standard by which the gift is measured.

**The Good Things Named**

The commentators explained the phrase as the wealth that is wholesome and lawfully acquired, and they discussed whether the wording concerns the value of the property or its standing in the law. The two readings were set out and combined, since the community's teachers held that the Book requires the gift to be both lawful and good.

The teachers drew attention to the person who gives what he would not accept himself, since the sentence names the practice and answers it with the reminder that the giver is a person like the one who receives. The Book's teaching about the community's shared life runs through the passage, and the sentence supplies one of its clearest statements.

The phrase also implies the obligation that accompanies the acquisition of property, since the wealth that is earned is described as the material from which the community's service is drawn. The scholars of the community used the sentence when they set out the duties that attach to possession.

**The Bad Excluded**

The sentence forbids the choice of the worthless things for donation and describes the giver who would accept such a thing only with his eyes closed, and the community's teachers read the phrase as the statement about the knowledge that the giver himself possesses. The person who offers what he would not take has testified against his own gift.

The commentators explained the image of the closed eyes as the description of the reluctance with which a person receives a thing of no value, so that the sentence measures the gift by the standard of the giver's own judgment. The Book's argument in the passage rests on the plain sense of fairness among its members.

The teachers also noted that the prohibition concerns the intention with which the worthless thing is chosen. The community's scholars explained that the command does not forbid the gift of a small amount, and that what it forbids is the search for the dregs of a person's property in order to preserve the rest.

**The Reports About the Practice**

The commentators connected the sentence with the practice of those who hung the bunches of dates in the mosque for the poor of the community, and they transmitted the report that a group brought inferior dates after the good ones had been given. The teachers read the report as the occasion for the instruction, and the sentence answered the practice it described.

The material shows the manner in which the community's charity was conducted in its first years, since the gifts were placed where those in need could take from them. The reports describe the care of the Prophet ﷺ in the conduct of the community's giving, and the teachers used them when they explained the passage.

The community's scholars drew from the reports the lesson that the Book's requirement concerns the gift and the intention together. The sentence does not forbid the small gift; it forbids the gift that the giver himself would not wish to receive.

**The Attributes Named**

The verse closes with the description of God as self-sufficient and praiseworthy, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the ground of the command. The first name states that God has no need of the gift, and the second places the praise with the One from whom the wealth and the ability to give it have come.

The teachers drew from the attributes the lesson that the instruction of the sentence is given for the benefit of the giver rather than for the need of the receiver. The community's preachers used the clause when they answered those who imagined that their gifts conferred an obligation on God.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere describes the wealth of the community as a trust that was lent to it, and the community's scholars gathered the passages when they spoke about property. The two names at the close of the sentence supply the disposition in which the instruction is received.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence stands within the long treatment of charity that occupies the middle of the sūrah, and the community's teachers read it as the instruction about the material of the gift after the verses that treated its manner. The passage has dealt with the reminder of the gift and the injury that follows it, and the sentence here turns to the thing that is offered.

The teachers also noted the connection with the command that follows, where the community is warned against the threat of poverty that discourages the gift. The passage's arrangement presents the standard of the gift, the obstacle that stands before it, and the promise that answers the obstacle.

The community's scholars read the whole section as a body of instruction about the conduct of the wealthy, and the sentence in this place supplies the rule by which the community's judges assessed the gifts that were brought before them.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the command to give from the good things that the community has earned and from the produce of the earth, the prohibition of the worthless gift, the standard that the giver's own judgment supplies, and the attributes of God that close the instruction. The teachers used the verse when they taught the conduct of charity, and the sūrah's following verses treat the fear of poverty that discourages the act, so that the standard and its obstacle are presented in order.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:268

> The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Promises**

The sentence sets the threat of Satan beside the promise of God, and the community's teachers read the pairing as the description of the two voices that speak to the person who considers a gift. The passage has just required the good thing to be given, and the verse here identifies the fear that rises against the command.

The wording speaks of what Satan threatens and of what God promises, so that the two parties are named and the two expectations are set out. The community's scholars noted the form of the sentence, since it presents the matter as a choice between two accounts of what the future holds.

The Book's treatment of the human condition elsewhere describes the suggestions that reach the heart, and the teachers gathered the passages when they explained the subject. The sentence in this place supplies the clearest account of the manner in which the reluctance to give takes shape in the mind of the believer.

**The Threat of Poverty**

The commentators explained the first clause as the description of the fear that the person feels for the property he has earned, since the thought of what may be lost accompanies the decision to give. The teachers described the way the threat works, because the fear is presented as a certainty about the future while the outcome remains in the hand of God.

The community's scholars read the clause in the light of the Book's other passages about provision, which state that the wealth of a person is written for him and that nothing reaches him except what has been appointed. The sentence therefore exposes the argument of the fear as the invention of the one who proposes it.

The reports of the teachers describe the experience of the early community in the same terms, and the material shows the fear named as the obstacle that the passage addresses. The command to give from the good things is thus protected by the reminder of the One who supplies them.

**The Command to Indecency**

The second element of the first clause describes the command toward indecency, and the commentators explained the phrase as the statement that the same suggestion leads a person from the withholding of charity to the commission of other offences. The teachers described the progress of the matter in the soul, since the habit of refusal grows into the loss of the good and then into the deed itself.

The teachers of the community observed the connection between the two parts of the sentence. The fear of poverty is placed beside the invitation to indecency, so that the reluctance in the matter of wealth is presented as the beginning of a course rather than as a single decision.

The Book's treatment of the soul elsewhere describes the stages by which a person is drawn away from the good, and the teachers used the passage when they spoke about the tendencies that the believer is required to resist. The sentence in this place supplies the description of the influence that the community's preachers named.

**The Promise of Forgiveness and Bounty**

The sentence then names what God promises, which is forgiveness and a bounty from Him, and the community's scholars read the clause as the answer to the threat that precedes it. The first term provides for the faults of the person who gives, and the second supplies the abundance that the fear had placed in doubt.

The teachers drew attention to the order of the two promises. The forgiveness comes before the bounty, so that the community's anxiety about the faults of its own conduct is addressed together with the fear about its property.

The wording places the bounty as coming from God, so that the increase of the giver is not drawn from a hidden source but from the hand of the One who has promised it. The jurists of the community used the clause when they encouraged the believers whose means were modest, and the passage's earlier parables of the harvest were read with it.

**The Reports About the Two Inspirations**

The reports of the community preserve a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that describes the suggestions that reach the heart of a person, and the material states that the angel brings the promise of the good while the other brings the invitation to evil. The teachers used the saying when they explained the sentence, and the community received it as the account of the struggle that the verse describes.

The commentators built their explanation of the passage on the two movements that the report names, so that the person is presented as the place in which two accounts of the future are offered. Scholars of the community drew from the material the lesson that the decision belongs to the person to whom both are addressed.

The report's instruction was preserved in the community's teaching of the passage, and the teachers repeated it in their exhortations to the believers. The sentence in this place supplies the Book's own statement of the matter that the saying describes.

**The Attributes Named**

The verse closes with the description of God as bountiful and knowing, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the ground of the promise that the sentence has stated. The first name, which also carries the sense of a generosity that no measure limits, answers the fear of poverty, and the second answers the anxiety about the intention with which the gift is given.

The teachers noted that the two names belong to the attributes that the earlier verses of the passage have named, so that the same description closes the instruction about the gift and the account of the promise that accompanies it. The early teachers of the community read the repetition as the confirmation of the subject.

The attributes also complete the answer to the threat. The poverty that the fear describes is measured against the bounty of God, and the hidden condition of the heart is placed before the One who knows it. The sentence therefore leaves the community with the promise rather than the fear.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the threat that Satan presents, the command toward indecency that accompanies it, the promise of forgiveness and bounty from God, and the attributes that close the verse. The community's teachers used the passage when they answered the reluctance of the believers and when they described the two suggestions that contend in the heart, and the sūrah's next verse names the wisdom that God grants, so that the gift of understanding follows the promise of the bounty.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:269

> Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills. And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege. But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Gift of Wisdom**

The sentence states that God grants wisdom to whom He wills, and the community's teachers read the verse as the statement about the gift that orders the whole of a person's conduct. The passage has treated the gift of wealth and the fear that surrounds it, and the sentence here names the understanding that governs both.

The wording places the granting of wisdom with the decision of God, so that the gift is described as a bestowal rather than an attainment. The community's scholars noted the form of the phrase, since the sentence names the One who gives before the description of those who receive.

The Book's use of the term covers the understanding of the revelation and the conduct that follows from it, and the teachers gathered the passages in which the word appears. The sentence in this place supplies the statement of its value.

**The Interpretations**

The commentators explained the wisdom named in the sentence in several ways. Some held that it is the knowledge of the Book, including its clear and its figurative passages and its rules, while others described it as the reverent awareness of God which the reports present as the beginning of the matter.

The teachers also recorded the reading which connects the term with the ability to judge and to understand the affairs of the community, and a further discussion among the scholars concerned the relation between wisdom and the office of prophethood. The positions were set out and examined, and the community preserved the discussion in its books of commentary.

The readings share the sense that the gift concerns the understanding of what the Book has revealed and the use of that understanding in the conduct of life. The community's scholars drew the two together, so that the wise person is described as one who knows and who acts upon what he knows.

**The Much Good**

The sentence adds that the one who has been given wisdom has been given a great good, and the community's teachers read the clause as the evaluation that the verse places upon the gift. The Book's choice of the phrase has been noticed, since the sentence does not describe the amount of the good but its kind.

The commentators explained the clause as the statement that the gift exceeds what a person can measure, since the wisdom of a servant orders his dealings in this life and prepares his account for the next. The community's preachers used the phrase when they encouraged the believers to seek understanding in the Book.

The wording also places the term of the good at the side of the loan and the harvest that the passage has described. The wealth of the community is described in the earlier verses as a means, and the sentence here names the possession that governs the use of the means.

**The People of Reason**

The sentence closes with the statement that none takes the reminder except those who possess understanding, and the community's scholars read the clause as the description of those who receive the instruction of the passage. The Book uses the same phrase in the verses that call its community to consider the signs.

The teachers drew from the clause the lesson that the attention of the hearer is itself a gift, so that the perception of the good named in the sentence depends on the mind that God has opened. The community's scholars read the passage as the statement that the reason of a person is honored by the Book's address.

The phrase also supplies the ground of the community's study of the revelation, since the Book expects its readers to bring their understanding to its verses. The teachers of the community built their method on the sentence.

**The Reports About Wisdom**

The reports of the community preserve a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that names the two things for which envy is permitted, the wealth that is spent in the way of truth and the wisdom by which a person judges and teaches. The material shows the value that the community attached to the gift, and the teachers used the saying when they explained the sentence.

The commentators also discussed the relation of the verse to the passage in which the community is commanded to spend, and they read the two as parts of a single instruction. The fear that the earlier verse describes is answered by the promise, and the promise is completed by the gift of the understanding that directs it.

The teaching of the community preserved the connection between the two subjects, so that the pursuit of wisdom and the discipline of property were presented as parts of one conduct. The sentence in this place supplies the link between them.

**The Place in the Passage**

The verse stands between the instruction about the threat of poverty and the statement about the wealth that is given, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the sequence of the passage's teaching. The community is commanded to give, the obstacle to the gift is named, the promise that answers it is stated, and the gift of understanding is described.

The teachers of the community drew the lesson that the passage presents the whole of the matter, from the command to the disposition that sustains it. The sentence in this place supplies the gift by which the community's members read the instruction and act upon it.

The verses that follow return to the subject of the gift and the account that is kept of it, so that the section continues its treatment of charity. The sentence therefore stands within the passage as the statement of the understanding that the rest of the instruction requires.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes that wisdom is a gift of God to whom He wills, the identification of the wisdom with the understanding of the Book and the conduct that follows it, the greatness of the good that it brings, and the reception of the reminder by those who possess understanding. The community's teachers used the verse when they encouraged the study of the revelation, and the sūrah's next verses return to the obligations of the community in the matter of its wealth.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:270

> Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Statement of Knowledge**

The sentence states that whatever charities the community gives and whatever vows it makes are known to God, and the community's teachers read the clause as the confirmation that accompanies the instructions of the passage. The Book has described the reward of the givers and the gifts that are accepted, and the sentence here names the knowledge that keeps the account.

The wording places the two kinds of offering together, the free gift and the undertaking that a person binds upon himself, so that the instruction covers the whole of what the community offers. The scholars noted the breadth of the phrase, since the vow was a practice of the community and the sentence treats it within the same statement.

The clause also supplies the assurance that the intention behind the gift is perceived. The community's teachers drew from the sentence the lesson that the secret and the open belong to the same record, and the passage's earlier treatment of the hidden and the shown gift was read with it.

**The Vow Named**

The sentence names the vow beside the charity, and the community's commentators explained the practice that the word describes. A vow in the community's usage is a person's undertaking to perform an act of worship or to give something if a matter he desires comes to pass, and the Book treats the fulfilment of such undertakings among the obligations of the believer.

The teachers noted that the sentence joins the two offerings although their causes differ, since the charity is given from the person's property and the vow binds his conduct. The Book's instruction elsewhere commends the fulfilment of what is vowed, and the passages on the subject were gathered by the commentators when they explained the verse.

The wording also places the vow within the knowledge of God, so that the undertaking is described as an act that the person presents rather than as a matter between him and the people who hear his promise. The community's scholars used the clause when they taught the seriousness of the vow.

**The Account Kept**

The commentators explained the phrase as the statement that God keeps the account of what the community gives and intends, so that nothing of it is lost. The teachers described the knowledge of God in the terms that the Book uses elsewhere, where every act and every intention is recorded.

The clause supplies the answer to the anxiety that accompanies a gift that receives no acknowledgement from the people. The community's scholars read the sentence as the assurance that the value of the act does not depend on the notice it receives, and they used it when they encouraged the believers whose giving was unknown to their neighbours.

The wording also implies the judgment that follows the account, so that the knowledge named in the sentence belongs to the passage's treatment of the reward and the loss. The community's teachers connected the clause with the verses that describe the two harvests.

**The Wrongdoers Stated**

The sentence closes with the statement that the wrongdoers have no helpers, and the community's scholars explained the term as the description of those whose conduct in the matter of charity has placed them outside the help they expected. The commentators connected the phrase with the earlier passage about the giver who acts for display, since the persons described in that verse are the ones whose giving was ruined.

The teachers drew attention to the word rendered as helpers, since the sentence denies the assistance of every party on whom a person might rely in the account of his deeds. The community's preachers used the clause when they spoke about the day on which no intercession avails without the permission of God.

The reading preserved in the community connects the phrase with the verse that precedes it in the passage, where the wrongdoers were described. The sentence in this place therefore completes the treatment of the subject with the statement about those whose offerings bring them no benefit.

**The Relation to the Passage**

The sentence stands among the verses about charity that occupy the middle of the sūrah, and it follows the sentence about the gift of wisdom. The teachers read the order as the passage's movement from the promise to the account, since the bounty that has been described is kept in the knowledge of God.

The commentators also connected the verse with the instructions that follow, where the community is told of the charity that may be given openly and that which is given in secret. The sentence supplies the ground of both, since the record of God stands behind the act whether the community sees it or not.

The whole section therefore presents the wealth of the community as material for the account, and the sentence in this place states the knowledge that conducts it. The community's scholars read the passage as a unit when they taught the obligations of property.

**The Teachers' Use of the Sentence**

The community's preachers returned to the sentence when they addressed the wealthy among the believers, and the reports describe their use of the clause about the vow when they taught the seriousness of a promise made to God. The material shows the passage applied to the circumstances of the community's own life.

The teachers also drew from the sentence the lesson about the gifts that are given without notice. The knowledge that the verse names supplied the community with the assurance that the act of a person who cannot show his giving is preserved, and the preachers repeated the clause in their exhortations.

The passage's concern runs through the whole of the community's conduct, and the sentence supplies the statement that nothing of it is hidden. The teachers of the community built their teaching of the passage upon that ground.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the knowledge of God over the charities and the vows of the community, the standing of the vow among the offerings that the Book treats, the account that keeps what a person gives and intends, and the statement about the wrongdoers who have no helpers. The community's teachers used the verse when they encouraged the believers in their giving, and the sūrah's next verse turns to the manner in which the gift may be given, so that the account and the conduct stand together in the passage.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:271

> To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Ways Stated**
