The sentence permits the charity that is given openly and rates the gift that is given in secret to the poor above it, and the community's teachers read the pair as the statement that the Book judges the act by the intention behind it. The passage has named the display that ruins a gift, and the sentence here sets out the two manners that the community may choose.

The wording places both acts within the good, so that the public gift is not condemned. The scholars noted the point, since the sentence protects the community's visible giving while preferring the manner that is hidden from it.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere commends the concealment of the gift, and the community's teachers gathered the passages when they set out the subject. The sentence in this place supplies the comparison that the community applied.

**The Open Gift**

The commentators explained the first clause as the statement that the community's visible charity serves the life of the city, since the poor learn where help may be found and the wealthy are reminded of their duty. The teachers described the encouragement that such giving provides to those who see it.

The community's scholars also noted the offices that the Book has established among the believers, where the public collection and distribution of alms belongs to the conduct of the community. The sentence's permission covers the appointed charity as well as the free gift.

The reading preserved in the community connects the clause with the report that ranks the open performance of the obligatory alms above the same act done in secret, and the teachers set out the measure when they explained the subject. The sentence in this place states the general principle, and the reports supply the application.

**The Secret Gift**

The second clause rates the gift that is hidden and given to the poor as better for the giver, and the commentators explained the preference in the light of the danger that the public act carries. The teachers described the temptation that accompanies the visible gift, since the giver may come to value the notice of his neighbours above the acceptance of the act.

The community's scholars drew attention to the phrase about the poor, since the sentence describes the gift that reaches the person in need without the embarrassment of the encounter. The Book's concern for the dignity of the recipient runs through the passage, and the hidden gift preserves it.

The teachers also described the practice of the early community, where the giver placed his gift in the hand of a person who did not know its source. The material shows the manner in which the sentence was applied, and the community preserved the accounts of those who gave in that way.

**The Expiations Named**

The sentence states that the secret gift absolves the giver of some of his evil deeds, and the community's scholars explained the clause as the statement that the good acts remove the faults of the person who performs them. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere states that good deeds take away those that are evil, and the passages were read together by the commentators.

The teachers noted that the sentence places the removal of the faults among the benefits of the hidden gift, so that the act serves the person's own account as well as the need of the recipient. The community's preachers used the clause when they encouraged those whose past conduct troubled them.

The reports of the community describe the saying that a good deed should follow an evil one so that the fault may be erased, and the teachers gathered the material when they explained the sentence. The clause in this place supplies the Book's own statement of the matter.

**The Reports and the Ranking**

The reports preserve the explanation transmitted from one of the early authorities, which distinguishes the obligatory alms given openly from the free gift given in secret and rates each according to its kind. The teachers used the ranking when they answered the community's questions about the two manners, and the material shows the care with which the subject was handled.

The commentators also connected the sentence with the passages about sincerity that appear in the Book, and they drew from the whole the principle that the intention of the giver determines the value of the act. The community's scholars built their teaching of charity upon that ground.

The saying that the left hand should not know what the right hand gives was repeated in the community's instruction, and the teachers used it when they explained the preference of the sentence. The material shows the manner in which the Book's comparisons were received.

**The Attribute at the Close**

The verse closes with the statement that God is aware of what the community does, and the community's scholars read the clause as the ground of the comparison the sentence has drawn. The attribute places the public gift and the hidden one within the same knowledge, so that nothing of the matter escapes the record.

The teachers drew from the closing the lesson that the difference between the two manners lies in the state of the giver rather than in the perception of God. The community's preachers used the clause when they spoke about the display that ruins the act, since the One who sees is not impressed by what the neighbours observe.

The Book's practice of ending its instructions with a description of God appears throughout the passage, and the community's scholars read the arrangement as the statement that the whole of the community's conduct belongs to the record. The sentence therefore leaves the community with the comparison and with the knowledge that accompanies it.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the goodness of the open gift, the preference of the gift that is given in secret to the poor, the removal of the faults that accompanies it, and the awareness of God that closes the instruction. The community's teachers used the verse when they taught the manners of charity and when they ranked the practices of the wealthy, and the sūrah's next verses turn to the guidance that belongs to God, so that the treatment of the gift continues with the statement about the One who accepts it.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:272

> You are not responsible for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills. Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Address to the Messenger**

The sentence addresses the Prophet ﷺ and states that he is not charged with the guidance of the people he calls, and the community's teachers read the clause as the comfort given to a messenger whose care for his people was known. The Book has described the disputes and the refusals of the earlier verses, and the sentence here relieves the messenger of a burden that belongs to God.

The wording places the guidance with God, so that the task of the messenger is described as the conveyance of the message. The community's scholars noted the point, since the passage's concern is the manner of the call rather than the response to it.

The sentence also belongs to the passage that treats the community's charity, and the teachers read the two subjects together. The messenger is released from the responsibility for the faith of those who receive, and the community is instructed about the gift that it gives and the account that belongs to it.

**The Guidance Stated**

The commentators explained the clause as the statement that the acceptance of the faith rests with the decision of God, and they connected it with the passages in which the Book declares that the messenger cannot guide the person he loves. The community's scholars gathered the verses on the subject when they set out the limits of the prophetic office.

The teachers drew from the sentence the lesson that the community's duty is the invitation, while the outcome belongs to the One who knows the hearts. The passage's treatment of the disputes with the people of the Book was read in that light, so that the messenger's part in the matter was understood as the clear delivery of what he received.

The wording also protects the messenger from the reproach of those who refused, since the Book states that the responsibility for the refusal rests with the person who made the choice. The community's preachers used the clause when they answered those who measured the message by its reception.

**The Occasions Reported**

The commentators connected the sentence with several occasions in the community's early life, and the reports describe believers who withheld their charity from relatives who had not accepted the faith. One account names a woman who asked about her grandparents among those who associated partners with God, and others describe the families whose connections reached into the tribes that had not entered the community.

The material also records the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, who gave to those who asked of him without regard to their religion. The teachers read the sentence and the reports together, since the instruction answered the scruples of the believers and confirmed the practice of their messenger.

The teachers of the community discussed the occasions at length, and the positions they transmitted show the care with which the passage was applied to the circumstances of the city. The sentence in this place supplies the rule that settled the matter.

**The Charity for All**

The sentence states that whatever good the community spends is for its own benefit, and the community's teachers read the clause as the statement that the gift serves the giver whatever the faith of the person who receives it. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere describes the act of the righteous as a benefit for the soul that performs it, and the passages were gathered by the commentators.

The wording also removes the expectation of the return from the person who is given to, so that the community's gift is placed in the hand of God. The teachers drew from the clause the lesson that the charity which is offered for the sake of the Lord does not depend on the character or the response of the recipient.

The jurists of the community used the sentence when they set out the scope of the charity that the believers may offer, so that the rule reached the households of the city whatever their religion. The passage therefore presents the gift as a service that the community owes to the need it meets.

**The Face of God**

The sentence adds the condition that the community seeks the Face of God in what it gives, and the commentators explained the phrase as the statement about the purpose of the act. The Book uses the figure of the Face for the pleasure of God, and the passages that speak of those who give for it were gathered by the teachers.

The wording also completes the clause about the benefit, since the act that is performed for the sake of the Lord is the one that returns to the giver. Scholars of the community read the two together, so that the gift becomes an investment in the account of the person who offers it.

The teachers drew attention to the phrase when they taught the intention of the giver, and the reports of the community show the formula used in its exhortations. The sentence in this place supplies the Book's own statement of the purpose that the passage requires.

**The Repayment**

The sentence promises that what the community spends will be paid back in full and that the community will not be wronged, and the community's teachers read the clause as the assurance that accompanies the instruction. The Book's earlier verses have compared the gift to a seed and to a garden, and the sentence here states the account in the language of a debt that is settled.

The reports of the community include the account of a man whose charity was given in the night to persons he did not know, and the teachers used the material to illustrate the manner in which the account is kept. The community's preachers repeated the clause when they encouraged the believers whose giving had brought them no acknowledgement from the people.

The promise of the full repayment also places the reward beyond the measure of the gift. The early teachers of the community read the sentence with the verses that describe the multiplication of the reward, so that the three statements were understood as one assurance given in different figures.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the release of the messenger from the responsibility for the guidance of his people, the benefit that the giver draws from his own gift, the purpose of the act in the pleasure of God, and the promise of the full repayment that will not be withheld. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the scope of charity and the duty of the call, and the sūrah's next verses describe the poor who are the proper recipients of the gift, so that the instruction continues with the account of those for whom it is intended.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:273

> ˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg. You can recognize them by their appearance. They do not beg people persistently. Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Recipients Named**

The sentence names the poor who are constrained in the way of God and who cannot move about the land, and the community's teachers read the passage as the description of those for whom the charity of the believers is intended. The Book has spoken of the gift that is given for the sake of God, and the sentence here identifies the persons who are in need of it.

The wording places the constraint at the centre of the description, since the inability of the person is presented as the reason for his poverty. The community's scholars noted the phrase, because the Book does not describe the poor as idle but as unable to work.

The teachers drew from the sentence the lesson that the community's gift is directed to the persons whose condition is known rather than to those who make the loudest claim. The passage's concern for the dignity of the recipient was read with the instruction.

**The Constraint Explained**

The commentators explained the phrase as the description of a person who is held back from travelling for work, whether by the service of the community or by the circumstances of his situation. The teachers discussed the cases that the phrase covers, including those who are engaged in learning or in the defence of the community.

The wording also implies the poverty that follows the constraint, since the person who cannot work has no means of his own. The community's scholars described the condition of such a person as hidden from the view of his neighbours, and they read the sentence as the instruction that reaches him.

The reports of the community describe the circumstances of the city in which these verses were revealed, where the poor who served the community lived without the means to provide for themselves. The sentence in this place supplies the rule for their support.

**The People of the Veranda**

The commentators connected the sentence with the group of the poor who lived in the sheltered part of the mosque in Madinah, and the reports describe their devotion, their study, and their lack of means. The teachers named them among those for whom the passage was intended, and the material supplied the community with its example.

The reports also describe the manner in which the Prophet ﷺ provided for them and the way their needs were met from the gifts of the believers. The teachers of the community read the accounts together with the sentence, so that the instruction and its application were presented as one subject.

The material shows the place that the poorest members of the community held in its life, since the mosque itself sheltered them. The teachers drew from the passage the lesson that the community's worship and its care for its poor belong to the same order.

**The Restraint**

The sentence states that those who do not know the condition of such a person suppose him to be wealthy because of the restraint he observes, and the community's teachers read the clause as the description of a poverty that does not show itself. The wording places the restraint as the reason for the mistake of the observer.

The commentators explained the restraint as the dignity that keeps the person from asking and from displaying his need. The teachers described the state of the person who bears his condition without complaint, and they read the sentence as the Book's recognition of that conduct.

The jurists of the community drew from the clause the lesson that the visible condition of a person is not the measure of his need. The passage's instruction therefore requires of the believers an attention that passes beyond appearances.

**The Mark**

The sentence states that the community knows such people by the mark they bear, and the commentators discussed the signs by which their condition appears. The reports describe the pallor of hunger and the effects of the hardships that the person has met, and other explanations concern the humility that the face of a believer shows.

The teachers gathered the readings and noted the point on which they agree, that the sign is perceived by those who look with care. Scholars of the community connected the sentence with the reports about the insight that the Book grants to the believers, and they used the passage when they spoke about the attention that the community owes to its poor.

The wording also supplies the assurance that the persons described are known to God, and the sentence closes with the statement that the community will be repaid for whatever good it spends. The account of the poor and the promise to the giver stand together in the passage.

**The Reports About Asking**

The reports of the community preserve a saying of the Prophet ﷺ in which he described the poor person who restrains himself from asking, and the teachers used the material when they explained the sentence. The early teachers of the community also discussed the measure of the wealth that makes a person's asking improper, and they transmitted the positions that were worked out in the early generations.

The passage's instruction was applied by the community's judges when the gifts of the believers were distributed, and the reports describe the care with which the persons named in the sentence were identified. The material shows the manner in which the Book's teaching entered the practice of the city.

The commentators drew from the sentence the lesson that the community is to seek its poor rather than wait for their requests. The teachers repeated the instruction in their exhortations, and the passage supplied the community with the rule for the distribution of its charity.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the identification of the poor who are constrained in the way of God, the restraint by which their condition is concealed, the mark by which the community recognizes them, the statement that they do not press their requests upon people, and the knowledge of God over whatever is given. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the recipients of charity and when they urged the believers to seek those whose need was hidden, and the sūrah's next verse names those who spend by night and by day, so that the description of the recipients is followed by the account of the givers.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:274

> Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Description Stated**

The sentence describes those who spend their wealth by night and by day, in secret and in the open, and the community's teachers read the four phrases as the statement that the giving of such persons is not confined to an hour or a manner. The passage has treated the recipients of charity, and the sentence here returns to the givers with the description of a conduct that continues.

The wording uses the pairs of opposite times and opposite manners, so that the whole of a person's life is included within the description. The community's scholars noted the completeness of the phrase, since no part of the day or of the conduct is left outside it.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere commends the giving that is concealed, and the sentence includes it beside the gift that the community observes. The teachers read the four phrases together as the statement that the value of the act lies in what it seeks rather than in the manner it takes.

**The Four Manners**

The commentators explained the first pair as the description of the times in which a person gives, since the night and the day cover the whole of the life of the giver. The teachers noted the mention of the night first, when the act is hidden from the community and unknown to the neighbours.

The second pair describes the two manners that the Book has already examined, and the sentence includes both of them within the conduct it praises. The community's scholars drew from the wording the lesson that the gift which is offered for the sake of God is accepted whatever its manner, provided the intention is sound.

The four phrases were also read as a description of the different circumstances in which the believers gave in the community's early years, when the poverty of the immigrants was met from the property of those who had settled in the city. The sentence in this place supplies the account of the conduct that answered that need.

**The Reports About the Occasion**

The commentators transmitted the reports that connect the sentence with particular members of the early community, and the material names two of the most prominent believers who are said to have distributed a portion of their wealth in the four manners the verse describes. The teachers recorded the reports and read them as the illustration of the sentence.

The community's scholars noted that the sentence states the matter in general terms, so that the reports describe instances of the conduct rather than the limits of the verse. The passage's teaching belongs to every giver who meets its description.

The accounts also show the manner in which the community's early generosity was received and the attention that was given to the needs of the poor. The teachers used the material when they spoke about the conduct of the companions, and the sentence supplied the standard by which their giving was described.

**The Reward Named**

The sentence states that the reward of such givers is with their Lord, and the community's teachers read the clause as the assurance that their acts are kept. The same promise appears in the earlier verse about those who spend without following their gift with reminders of it, and the repetition supplies the confirmation of the subject.

The wording places the reward with God rather than in the hands of the community, so that the giver looks beyond the notice of his neighbours. The community's scholars drew from the phrase the lesson that the act of giving is directed to the One who receives it.

The clause also answers the anxiety that accompanies the gift that no one observes. The teachers used the sentence when they encouraged the believers whose giving was hidden, and the passage's earlier verses about the secret gift were read with it.

**The Promise Completed**

The sentence closes with the statement that no fear will come upon them and that they will not grieve, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the description of the condition of the believers in the life to come. The wording appears in the earlier verses of the passage and in the Book's descriptions of the reward, and the teachers regarded the repetition as the confirmation of the promise.

The first clause concerns what lies ahead, and the second concerns what has passed, so that the pair describes a state from which the anxieties of both directions have been removed. The community's preachers used the formula when they spoke about the standing of the givers.

The sentence therefore completes the description of the givers with the assurance that belongs to them. The teachers drew from the two clauses the lesson that the wealth given for the sake of God is exchanged for a security that does not end.

**The Section Closed**

The sentence is the last of the passage that treats the giving of charity, and the community's teachers read the section as a body of instruction that includes the command, the manner, the material, the recipients, and the promise. The verses have examined the act from every side, and the sentence here gathers the conduct of the givers under a single description.

The scholars of the community observed that the passage begins with the parable of the seed and closes with the account of those who give at all times and in every manner. The arrangement presents the harvest of the act and the conduct of the person who performs it.

The following verse turns to the practice of interest, which the Book sets beside the charity that has been described. The community's teachers read the two subjects together, so that the passage's treatment of the wealth of the community continues into the verses that follow.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the description of those who give at every time and in every manner, the reward that is kept for them with their Lord, and the removal of fear and grief that accompanies them. The community's teachers used the verse when they encouraged the believers in the giving that the passage requires, and the section that treats charity reaches its conclusion with the promise stated here, so that the reader is carried from the conduct of the givers to the account of the practice that the Book forbids.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:275

> Those who consume interest will stand ˹on Judgment Day˺ like those driven to madness by Satan’s touch. That is because they say, “Trade is no different than interest.” But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest. Whoever refrains—after having received warning from their Lord —may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah. As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Practice Addressed**

The sentence describes those who consume interest and states that they will not rise except as a person whom Satan has touched with madness, and the community's teachers read the account as the Book's treatment of a practice that belonged to the dealings of the city. The passage has completed its instruction about charity, and the sentence here turns to the gain that is acquired without an exchange.

The image at the beginning has been explained by the commentators as the description of the state of such a person on the day of the rising, when the disorder of his condition appears to those who see him. The community's scholars noted the figure and read it as the picture of an account that has been disordered in its foundation.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere describes the practice among the evils that the community is forbidden, and the teachers gathered the passages when they set out the law. The sentence in this place supplies the first of the verses that treat the matter at length.

**The Term Ribā**

The community's scholars examined the term that is rendered as interest, and they explained that it denotes an increase or a gain that the practice adds without a corresponding exchange. The teachers noted that the term covers more than the modern usage of the word that translates it.

The commentators described the two forms that the reports identify, one connected with the deferment of a debt and the other with an unequal exchange of goods of the same kind. The scholars of the community built the law upon the distinction, and the discussions of the jurists over the centuries supplied the details.

The sentence in this place states the prohibition of the practice, and the verses that follow describe the conduct of those who persist in it. The community's teachers read the passage as the treatment of the subject that completes the instruction about the wealth of the believers.

**The Two Kinds**

The reports describe the first kind of the practice as the fee that was charged when a debt came due, since the creditor would offer the debtor the choice between payment and an increase in the amount for a further term. The community's scholars explained that such an arrangement could double the principal in a year and redouble it in the years that followed.

The second kind concerns the exchange of the same kind of goods in unequal measures, and the reports describe the practice as it was conducted in the market of the city. The teachers noted the two forms together, since the Book's prohibition covers the gain that is taken without the exchange that the law requires.

The Qur'an mentions the doubling that the practice produced in another passage that addresses the believers, and the community's commentators connected the two verses when they set out the subject. The sentence in this place supplies the general statement of the prohibition.

**The Report of the Early Practice**

The community's books preserve the description transmitted from the earliest generation of the teachers, and the report explains the custom of the pre-Islamic period in which a creditor would demand payment or an increase at the time the debt became due. The material shows the practice that the passage addressed and the manner in which the community understood it.

The scholars of the community drew from the report the account of the principal that the debtor would lose if the deferment continued, and they used it when they explained the severity of the prohibition. The passage's language about the practice was read with the description that the report supplies.

The teachers also noted that the Book contrasts the practice with trade, since the sentence records the claim of those who make no distinction between the two. The material supplied the community with the framework of its law on the subject.

**The Claim Answered**

The sentence records the claim that trade and interest are alike, and the community's teachers read the statement as the account of the argument that the Book answers. The two practices belong to different orders, since one is an exchange that the parties conduct with the risk and the labor that the law approves while the other is a gain that is taken for the deferment alone.

The commentators explained the answer that the sentence supplies, which is the statement that God has permitted trade and forbidden the practice. The community's scholars drew from the clause the lesson that the difference is established by the command rather than by the reasoning of the parties.

The wording also shows the manner in which the Book responds to the community's arguments, since it states the claim and then supplies the rule. The teachers used the passage when they set out the method of the law, and the sentence supplied the principle for the subject.

**The Rule for the Past**

The sentence states that the person who desists after the warning of his Lord may keep what is past and that his affair belongs to God, and the community's scholars explained the clause as the mercy that accompanies the instruction. The past dealings were not to be reclaimed, and the account of them was left with God.

The teachers noted the phrase about the warning, since the ruling is connected with the person's knowledge of the prohibition. The community's judges applied the clause to the cases that came before them in the early years, and the reports describe the manner in which the transactions of the new believers were treated.

Those who return to the practice after the instruction are described at the end of the sentence as the inhabitants of the Fire who remain in it, and the community's teachers read the threat as the statement of the seriousness of the subject. The sentence supplies the rule, the mercy, and the warning together.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the description of those who consume interest, the claim that they make about trade, the ruling that separates the two practices, the permission for the past dealings of those who desist, and the threat that is addressed to those who return to the practice. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law of the subject, and the sūrah's following verses continue the treatment with the instruction about the debts that remain, so that the passage closes its account of the wealth of the community with a subject on which the community's law rests.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:276

> Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful. And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Outcomes**

The sentence states that God destroys interest and causes charity to grow, and the community's teachers read the pair as the account of the two paths that the passage has set out. The verse follows the prohibition of the practice and supplies the statement about the outcome that belongs to each of the two dealings.

The wording places the acts together, since the gain that is taken without an exchange and the gift that is offered for the sake of God are presented as two ways of seeking an increase. The Book's answer is that the increase comes from God in the one case and is removed by Him in the other, whatever the appearance of the accounts may be.

The community's scholars noted the connection with the earlier parable of the seed and the harvest, where the same figure of growth is used for the reward of the giver. The passage's treatment of wealth has placed the two subjects beside one another throughout, and the sentence here gathers them into a single statement.

**The Term Used**

The commentators drew attention to the word that the sentence uses for the growth of charity, since it belongs to the same root as the term for the practice that the passage prohibits. The Book sets the two against one another by the vocabulary itself, so that the increase that comes from the law is contrasted with the increase that the practice produces.

The teachers read the choice as one of the passage's deliberate arrangements, and they used it when they explained the subject. The community's scholars described the two forms of increase in their books, so that the difference between the gain of the transaction and the gain of the gift was preserved in the community's teaching.

The sentence in this place therefore explains what the passage has already shown in its parables. The Lord who brings the harvest from the seed is the One who blights the practice, and the two acts of the sentence belong to the same authority.

**The Blighting Stated**

The first clause has been explained by the community's commentators as the statement that the practice removes the blessing from the wealth that is acquired by it. The teachers described the manner in which the loss appears, whether in the property itself, in the affairs of the person, or in the account that is kept for the life to come.

The reports of the community preserve sayings about the practice that describe its outcome, and one of them states that the person who engages in it meets a loss whatever the increase that the accounts of the world show. The teachers used the material when they explained the sentence.

The wording also answers the argument of those who measured the matter by the returns that the practice produced. The Book presents the outcome as the decision of the One who owns the wealth, so that the apparent gain of the practice is not the measure of its result.

**The Growth of Charity**

The second clause states that God causes the charity to grow, and the community's scholars explained the phrase as the description of the reward that is kept for the giver. The earlier passage has compared the gift to the seed that produces seven ears and to the garden that yields its fruit twice over, and the sentence here supplies the summary of those figures.

The teachers drew from the clause the lesson that the increase of the gift belongs to the act that the law approves, so that the community's generosity is not a loss but an investment in the account of the person who gives. The community's preachers used the phrase when they encouraged the believers whose means were modest.

The wording also places the growth in the hand of God, so that the person who gives does not look to the people for the return. The sentence in this place completes the account of the two dealings, and the passage's instruction about the wealth of the community continues with the verses that follow.

**The Attribute at the Close**

The sentence closes with the statement that God does not love any sinful ingrate, and the community's teachers read the pair of descriptions as the account of the disposition that the practice produces. The word rendered as ungrateful carries the sense of a person who denies the favour he has received.

The teachers drew attention to the connection between the practice and the denial of the One who owns the wealth, since the person who takes the gain for the deferment alone has placed his dealings outside the instructions of the law. The community's scholars used the clause when they spoke about the conduct that the passage corrects.

The wording also supplies the answer to the claim that the two practices are alike, since the sentence describes the outcome of each and names the character that belongs to the first. The Book's method of joining its rulings to the description of the persons addressed appears throughout the passage.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence stands at the head of the verses that complete the treatment of the practice, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the passage's summary before its instructions. The Book has set out the judgment in the previous verse, and the sentence here states the two outcomes and the character of the persons who are addressed.

The community's scholars observed that the passage on charity has closed with the description of the givers and that the passage on the practice opens with the account of its result. The two sections were read together when the community taught the subject of wealth.

The verses that follow continue the treatment by commanding the believers to give up what remains of the practice, so that the sentence and the command belong to a single instruction. The community's teachers read them as one body of material about the community's dealings.

**The Teaching Drawn**

The community's teachers drew from the sentence the lesson that the wealth of a person is not measured by the increase it shows in the accounts of the world. The material shows the formula repeated in their exhortations, since the practice was woven into the dealings of the city and the prohibition required a change in the habits of its people.

The scholars of the community also used the sentence when they explained the difference between the increase that the law approves and the increase it forbids. The two words of the verse supplied them with the distinction, and the community's preachers returned to it in their teaching of the passage.

The sentence therefore supplies the principle that the community applied to the transactions of its members, and the passages that follow supply the commands that the principle required. The reader is given the two outcomes and the character of the persons whom the sentence names.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the blighting of the practice and the growth of charity, the contrast that the vocabulary of the two clauses carries, the outcome that belongs to each kind of dealing, and the standing of the sinful ingrate before God. The community's teachers used the verse when they taught the dealings of the believers, and the sūrah's following verses command the community to give up what remains of the practice, so that the sentence stands as the statement of the two outcomes that the commands complete.

---
## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:277

> Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Description Stated**

The sentence names the believers who perform the righteous deeds, establish the prayer, and give the alms, and it states that their reward is with their Lord. The verse follows the sentence about the blighting of the practice, so that the community is shown the conduct that stands beside the dealings the passage forbids.

The four elements of the description belong to the Book's account of the faith, and the community's teachers read them as the marks by which the believers are known. The sentence in this place joins the belief of the heart, the work of the hands, the worship of the body, and the gift of the property in a single description.

The Book has used the same combination in the verses about the people of the Book, and the community's scholars gathered the passages when they set out the subject of the faith. The sentence in this place supplies the account of what the community's profession requires.

**The Faith and the Deeds**

The first two elements of the sentence place the belief beside the righteous conduct, and the community's teachers read the order as the statement that the faith of a person produces the acts by which it is known. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere describes the believers by their conduct, and the passages were gathered by the commentators.

The scholars of the community drew from the pairing the lesson that the profession of the tongue is not separated from the work of the person in the teaching of the Book. The sentence therefore presents the faith and the deeds as one matter rather than as two.

The wording also names the deeds in general terms before the two particular practices that follow, so that the sentence covers the whole of the good that a person performs. The community's teachers used the clause when they spoke about the breadth of the righteous conduct that the Book commends.

**The Prayer Established**

The third element names the prayer, and the community's scholars explained the phrase as the account of the worship that orders the day of the believer. The Book has treated the prayer in the passage about the middle prayer, and the community's teachers read the two passages together.

The wording describes the practice as established rather than as performed, and the commentators noted the sense of the phrase. The prayer that the sentence names is the practice that a person maintains with its conditions and its times, so that the community's law of worship was built upon the clause.

The sentence therefore places the worship of God beside the service of the poor, and the community's scholars drew from the order the lesson that the two belong to the same conduct. The passage's treatment of wealth and its instructions about devotion were read as one body of material.

**The Alms Given**

The fourth element names the alms, and the community's teachers explained the practice as the obligation that the law places upon the property of the believers. The sentence stands at the end of the passage about charity, and the clause here supplies the account of the institutional practice that the Book treats.

The commentators noted the contrast with the practice that the previous verses prohibit, since the alms are the means by which the wealth of the community circulates among its poor. The two subjects were set beside one another in the passage, so that the community learned the difference between the gain that the law approves and the gain that it forbids.

The scholars of the community drew from the clause the lesson that the property of the believers carries a claim upon it, and they built the law of the alms upon the sentence and the passages that accompany it. The clause in this place belongs to the community's practice from its earliest years.

**The Reward Named**

The sentence states that those whom it describes have their reward with their Lord, and the community's teachers read the clause as the assurance that accompanies the conduct. The phrase appears in the earlier verses about the givers, and the community's scholars noted the repetition as the confirmation of the promise.

The wording places the reward in the keeping of God, so that the believers do not look to the community for the requital of their conduct. The teachers used the clause when they encouraged the members of the community whose acts were unknown to their neighbours.

The promise also answers the anxiety that the instruction about the practice had produced among the believers, since those who had engaged in the dealings had to abandon what remained of them. The sentence supplies the assurance that the conduct the Book requires is not a loss.

**The Fear and the Grief**

The sentence closes with the statement that no fear will come upon the persons it describes and that they will not grieve, and the community's scholars explained the pair as the description of the condition of the believers in the life to come. The closing appears in the earlier verses of the passage, and the teachers regarded the repetition as the confirmation of the standing of those described.

The first clause concerns what lies ahead and the second concerns what has passed, so that the pair describes a condition from which the anxieties of both directions have been removed. The community's preachers used the formula when they spoke about the state of the believers.

The sentence in this place therefore completes the passage's account of the conduct that the Book commends with the promise that belongs to it. The teachers drew the lesson that the community's dealings and its worship are joined in the reward that the verse names.

**The Passage's Concern**

The sentence stands among the verses that complete the treatment of the practice, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the passage's presentation of the two conducts. The verses before it describe the blighting of the practice and the growth of charity, and the sentence here supplies the description of the persons who perform the conduct that the Book approves.

The community's scholars also connected the sentence with the passage about the changing of the direction of prayer, since the same combination of belief and conduct appears there in the Book's account of the community. The teachers read the two passages together in their teaching.

The verses that follow command the community to give up what remains of the practice, so that the sentence and the command belong to one instruction. The passage therefore presents the conduct that is required together with the practice that is forbidden.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the description of the believers by their faith and their deeds, the establishment of the prayer, the payment of the alms, the reward that is kept for them, and the removal of fear and grief that accompanies them. The community's teachers used the verse when they taught the marks of the believers and when they set out the obligations of the community, and the sūrah's following verses address the community directly with the command to complete what the passage requires of it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:278

> O believers! Fear Allah, and give up outstanding interest if you are ˹true˺ believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command Stated**

The sentence addresses the believers and instructs them to be mindful of God and to give up what remains of the practice that the passage has treated, and the community's teachers read the command as the completion of the prohibition. The Book has described the two outcomes and the conduct of those whom it commends, and the sentence here turns to the community with the instruction that the matter required.

The wording names what remains of the practice, so that the believers who had entered the community were required to abandon the gains that were still due to them. The teachers noted the phrase, since the command concerned the outstanding claims rather than the acts that had already been completed.

The sentence closes with the condition that the persons addressed are believers, and the community's scholars read the phrase as the statement that the conduct belongs to the faith that the community professed. The Book's method of joining its commands to the description of those addressed appears throughout the passage.

**The Mindfulness Named**

The first clause of the sentence instructs the community to be mindful of God, and the community's teachers explained the phrase as the description of the awareness that governs the whole of a person's conduct. The Book uses the term throughout its instructions, and the community's scholars gathered the passages when they set out the subject.

The teachers noted the order of the sentence, since the mindfulness of God is named before the command to give up the practice. The community's scholars read the arrangement as the statement about the disposition from which the obedience of the law proceeds.

The wording also places the command within the community's relationship with its Lord, so that the dealings of its members are presented as a part of the service that the Book requires. The sentence in this place therefore belongs to the passages that treat the community's conduct as a whole.

**The Remainder Named**

The commentators explained the phrase about what remains as the reference to the increases that a creditor could still claim from the debts that were outstanding at the time of the instruction. The community's scholars discussed the cases that the phrase covers, and they described the manner in which the dealings of the city were settled after the command.

The teachers also noted that the phrase did not require the abandonment of the principal, since the passage that follows states the rule about the return of what was lent. The sentence in this place concerns the addition that the practice had placed upon the debt.

The community's jurists built the law of the subject upon the combination of the verses, so that the principal of a loan remained the right of the lender while the addition was removed. The passage's treatment of the matter was read as a single body of instruction.

**The Condition of Faith**

The sentence closes with the statement that the command applies to the persons who are believers, and the community's scholars read the clause as the statement about the connection between the conduct and the profession. The teachers described the phrase as the reminder of what the community had accepted when it entered the faith.

The wording also serves the instruction that follows, since the passage then addresses those who do not comply with a warning whose severity belongs to the subject. The teachers of the community read the two verses together, and they drew from the pair the lesson about the seriousness of the matter in the community's law.

The commentators noted that the phrase does not describe a doubt about the persons addressed but states the condition on which the command rests. The Book's use of the same formula elsewhere appears in its instructions, and the community's teachers gathered the instances.

**The Reports About the Practice**

The reports of the community describe the circumstances in which the instruction was received, and the material shows the practice as it was conducted in the city and the changes that the command required. The teachers used the accounts when they explained the passage.

The commentators also transmitted the reports about the manner in which the community's authorities dealt with the outstanding claims, and the material shows the care with which the matter was settled. The jurists of the community drew from the reports the lesson that the instruction was applied to the cases that existed rather than to the persons alone.

The passage's treatment of the subject was studied by the community's jurists, and the books of law record the discussions that grew from the verses. The sentence in this place supplies the command from which the discussions begin.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence stands between the account of the two outcomes and the warning that addresses those who persist in the practice, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the passage's movement from the description to the instruction. The Book has stated what the practice does and what the charity achieves, and the sentence here requires the community to act upon what it has been told.

Scholars of the community observed that the command is addressed to the community as a body, so that the subject belongs to the conduct of its members and to the order of its dealings. The passage's material on wealth therefore treats the individual and the community together.

The verses that follow state the warning and the rule about the principal, so that the sentence and the following verses form one instruction. The community's teachers read them as a unit when they taught the law of the subject.

**The Teaching Drawn**

The community's preachers drew from the sentence the lesson that the change required of the believers reached the claims that they held as well as the dealings they conducted. The material shows the formula repeated in the exhortations, since the practice was established in the habits of the city and the instruction required the community to examine its accounts.

The scholars of the community used the sentence when they explained the relation between the command and the faith that the community professed. The condition at the close of the verse supplied the ground on which the instruction was urged.

The passage therefore presents the command together with the reason for it, and the sentence in this place supplies the community with the disposition that the obedience of the law requires. The reader is given the instruction and the standing of those who receive it.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the command to be mindful of God, the requirement to give up what remains of the practice, and the condition of the faith under which the instruction is given. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law of the subject and when they urged the believers to complete the change that the passage required, and the sūrah's next verse states the warning that belongs to those who do not comply, so that the command and its consequence are presented in order.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:279

> If you do not, then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger! But if you repent, you may retain your principal—neither inflicting nor suffering harm.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning Stated**

The sentence addresses those who do not comply with the command and warns them of a war from God and His Messenger, and the community's teachers read the clause as the most severe warning that the Book addresses to the community on any matter of property. The passage has required the believers to give up what remains of the practice, and the sentence here states the consequence of the refusal.

The wording places the matter within the relations of war, so that the person who persists is described as one whom the community's authority may confront. The community's scholars noted the form of the phrase, since the instruction concerns the conduct of the community as a body rather than the private fault of an individual.

The verse then states the rule for those who turn back, which is the retention of the principal without the addition, and the sentence closes with the statement about the wrong that is neither inflicted nor suffered. The community's teachers read the two clauses together as the account of the outcome for those who return.

**The Reports About the Phrase**

The commentators transmitted the explanations of the early teachers about the warning, and one of them described the state of the person who consumes the practice on the day of the rising. The material shows the severity that the community attached to the subject, and the teachers used the reports when they explained the verse.

The community's scholars also discussed the meaning of the phrase as the statement that the person has placed himself in the position of an enemy of God and His Messenger. The reading supplies the sense of the warning without the need for a further act.

The teachers of the community drew from the reports the lesson that the matter belonged to the gravest of the offences that the Book treats, since the passage names the two sources of authority in its warning. The sentence in this place supplies the statement from which the community's law on the subject was built.

**The Authority and the Practice**

The community's jurists discussed the application of the warning, and some of them held that the authority of the community is charged with compelling those who persist in the practice to give up their gains, and with fighting them if they refuse. The material shows the manner in which the passage was understood by the judges of the community.

The scholars also noted that the warning belongs to the dealings that the community conducts among its members, so that the instruction has a public as well as a private dimension. The Book's treatment of the matters of property elsewhere places them within the responsibilities of the community's order.

The teachers drew from the passage the lesson that the wealth of the community is governed by rules that its authority may enforce. The sentence in this place supplies the ground on which the community's practice rested.

**The Principal Retained**

The sentence states that those who turn back may keep the principal of their wealth, and the community's teachers read the clause as the mercy that accompanies the warning. The commentators explained that the addition that the debt had carried was removed while the amount that had been lent remained the right of the lender.

The scholars of the community noted the balance that the clause preserves, since the debtor is released from the increase and the creditor is not deprived of the property that was his. The passage's treatment of the subject was read by the jurists as a body of instruction that attends to both parties.

The wording also supplied the community with the framework of its law about the debts that had been contracted under the earlier practice, and the judges of the community applied the clause to the cases that came before them. The sentence therefore completes the instruction with the rule that settled the accounts of the city.

**The Wrong Named**

The sentence closes with the statement about the wronging and the wronged, and the community's teachers explained the phrase as the description of the relation that the rule establishes between the two parties. The creditor who demands the addition wrongs the debtor, and the debtor who withholds the principal wrongs the creditor.

The community's scholars read the clause as the standard by which the dealings of the believers are measured, so that neither party is permitted to exceed the right that the law has established. The Book's concern for fairness in the matters of property runs through the passage, and the sentence supplies its statement.

The teachers also noted the placement of the clause at the close of the instruction, since the rule is presented together with the reason for it. The community's preachers used the phrase when they spoke about the dealings of the believers with one another.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence stands between the command to give up the practice and the instruction about the debtors who are in difficulty, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the passage's movement from the warning to the mercy. The Book has required the community to abandon the practice and has named the consequence of the refusal, and the verses that follow treat the cases of those who cannot pay.

The community's scholars observed that the passage treats the subject of wealth from the side of the creditor and the debtor in turn, so that the whole of the relationship is addressed. The sentence in this place supplies the rule for the claims that the earlier dealings had created.

The verses that follow commend the creditor who grants the respite and who releases the debt, so that the passage closes with the generosity that the Book has been recommending throughout. The sentence and the verses together form the community's law on the subject.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the warning addressed to those who persist in the practice, the severity that the phrase carries, the retention of the principal by those who turn back, and the statement about the wrong that is neither inflicted nor suffered. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law of the practice and when they described the responsibilities of the community's authority, and the sūrah's next verse turns to the debtor who is in difficulty, so that the warning is followed by the instruction that completes the treatment of the subject.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:280

> If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Instruction Stated**

The sentence instructs the creditor to grant the debtor who is in difficulty a respite until the time of ease, and it states that the release of the debt as charity is better for him. The verse follows the rule about the principal and supplies the instruction that governs the cases in which the debtor cannot pay.

The Book has treated the claims of the creditor in the previous verses, and the sentence here places the claim within the circumstances of the person who owes. The community's teachers read the two passages together, so that the law of the debt and the duty of mercy were presented as one subject.

The wording addresses the creditor with the voice of the instruction, and the community's scholars noted the form of the phrase. The passage does not require the release of the debt; it commends the respite and then names the gift that exceeds the duty.

**The Case of Difficulty**

The commentators explained the phrase as the description of the debtor whose circumstances prevent him from paying, and they discussed the state that the term covers. The community's jurists built the law of the insolvent debtor upon the sentence and the reports, and they set out the manner in which the case is established.

The teachers noted the kindness of the instruction, since the passage does not treat the inability to pay as a fault to be punished. The Book's teaching about the community's shared life runs through the passage, and the sentence here supplies the rule that protects the weaker party of the contract.

The community's scholars also observed the difference between the person who cannot pay and the person who refuses, since the sentence concerns the first. The judges of the community applied the distinction when the disputes over debts came before them.

**The Respite Named**

The sentence instructs the creditor to wait until the time of ease, and the community's teachers explained the phrase as the statement that the term of the debt is extended to the point at which the debtor is able to pay. The wording gives the creditor the duty of patience and the debtor the time that his circumstances require.

The commentators noted that the instruction is addressed to the person who holds the claim, so that the passage attends to the conduct of the one who has the power in the contract. The Book's method of naming the party whose restraint is required appears in its other instructions about dealings.

The community's scholars drew from the clause the lesson that the wealth of the creditor does not entitle him to press a person who cannot pay. The passage's concern for fairness, which the previous verse named, is carried forward in the instruction of the sentence.

**The Gift Commended**

The sentence adds that the release of the debt as charity is better for the creditor, and the community's teachers read the clause as the invitation to an act that exceeds the obligation. The Book's treatment of charity in the earlier passage supplies the framework of the statement, since the gift that is given for the sake of God is described there as a loan that is repaid.

The scholars of the community noted the phrase about the better course, since the sentence places the remission of the debt among the goods that the Book commends while leaving the claim of the creditor in place. The wording therefore presents the release as a choice rather than as a requirement.

The teachers also drew from the clause the distinction between the respite and the remission, so that the community's law preserved the right of the creditor while the gift remained with the person who chose it. The passage's instruction was applied by the judges with attention to the two matters.

**The Reports About the Duty**

The reports of the community preserve a saying of the Prophet ﷺ about the creditor who grants the delay to the person in difficulty, and the material describes the reward that is recorded for each day of the respite. The teachers used the saying when they explained the sentence and when they encouraged the believers in the conduct that the verse commends.

The community's scholars gathered the material about the conduct of the early believers in the matters of debt, and the accounts describe the generosity with which the claims were settled among them. The passage's teaching was received as a part of the community's conduct rather than as a rule for the courts alone.

The commentators also noted the connection between the sentence and the passage about charity that precedes it, since the release of a debt is presented in the Book as one of the forms that the gift takes. The two subjects were read together by the community's teachers.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence stands between the rule about the principal and the reminder of the day of the return, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the passage's movement from the law to the account. The verses have treated the practice that is forbidden, the warning that accompanies it, and the claims that remain, and the sentence here supplies the conduct that the Book requires of the creditor.

The community's scholars observed that the passage attends to the person who owes as well as to the person who lends, so that the teaching of the section covers the two parties of the contract. The sentence in this place supplies the rule for the weaker of them.

The verse that follows names the day on which every soul is paid for what it has earned, and the community's teachers read the reminder as the ground of the instruction. The passage therefore closes its treatment of the dealings with the account that belongs to the life to come.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the duty of the respite for the debtor in difficulty, the commending of the release of the debt as a gift, and the difference between the obligation of the creditor and the generosity that exceeds it. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law of debts and when they urged the wealthy among the believers to the conduct that the passage commends, and the sūrah's next verse names the day of the return, so that the instruction is followed by the reminder that accompanies it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:281

> Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reminder Stated**

The sentence instructs the community to be mindful of the day on which it will be returned to God and states that every soul will then be paid in full for what it has earned. The verse closes the passage on the practice and places the dealings of the community within the account of the life to come.

The passage has treated the wealth of the believers through many verses, and the sentence here supplies the reminder that accompanies the whole. The community's teachers read the clause as the ground of the instructions that the section has set out, since the law of the dealings rests on the return that the sentence names.

The wording addresses the community with the command of mindfulness, so that the reminder is given as an instruction rather than as information alone. The Book's method of attaching its teachings to the awareness of God appears throughout the sūrah, and the sentence in this place applies it to the matters of property.

**The Day Named**

The commentators explained the phrase as the description of the return to God at the end of the present life, and they gathered the passages that treat the subject. The community's teachers read the sentence with the verses about the account, so that the dealings of the believers were understood to belong to the material that the day will examine.

The wording places the return in the future and describes it as certain, and the community's scholars noted the form of the phrase. The Book's teaching about the last things supplies the framework in which the sentence stands, and the sūrah's other passages on the subject were read with it.

The scholars of the community also observed the position of the verse at the end of the passage on the practice, since the reminder is given after the instructions have been completed. The arrangement presents the law and the account together, so that the community received the two as one teaching.

**The Payment in Full**

The sentence states that every soul will be paid in full for what it has earned, and the community's teachers read the clause as the assurance that the account of the day will be exact. The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere uses the same language of the payment that is completed, and the passages were gathered by the commentators.

The wording places the payment before the statement about the wrong, so that the sentence presents the outcome of the account as a matter of justice rather than of loss. The community's scholars read the two clauses together, and they drew from the pair the lesson that no one will be deprived of what his deeds have earned.

The teachers also noted the connection with the previous sentence about the debtor and the creditor, since the wealth of the community is described in the Book as a matter for the account. The passage's treatment of the dealings is completed by the reminder that the payment of the day is exact.

**The Wrong Named**

The sentence closes with the statement that no one will be wronged, and the community's teachers read the clause as the assurance that the account of the day is free of the faults that attend the dealings of the world. The Book uses the phrase in the passages that describe the justice of God, and the community's scholars gathered the instances.

The wording also supplies the answer to the anxiety of the person who has been treated unjustly in the matters of wealth. The teachers drew from the clause the lesson that the claims that the courts of the world fail to settle belong to the account that the sentence describes.

The scholars of the community used the phrase when they spoke about the consolation of the poor and the warning to those who hold the property of others. The passage's treatment of the subject ends with the statement that the account of the day is free of error.

**The Place in the Passage**

The sentence closes the passage that treats the practice and the dealings of the community, and the community's teachers read the arrangement as the passage's final word on the subject. The verses have stated the prohibition, the warning, the rule about the principal, the respite for the debtor, and the generosity that exceeds the duty, and the sentence here supplies the reminder that gathers them.

The community's scholars observed that the reminder of the return appears at the close of several of the sūrah's passages, so that each body of instruction ends with the account. The teachers used the arrangement when they taught the sūrah as a whole.

The verses that follow turn to the writing of the contracts, so that the treatment of the dealings continues with the practical instruction. The sentence in this place therefore completes the account of the practice before the passage takes up the arrangements of the community's agreements.

**The Teaching Drawn**

The community's preachers drew from the sentence the lesson that the wealth of the world is held under the account that the verse names. The material shows the reminder repeated in their teaching of the passage, and the community's conduct in the matters of property was formed by the instruction.

The scholars of the community also connected the sentence with the passages that describe the justice of God, so that the community's understanding of the account was built on the Book's own statements. The clause about the wrong supplied the ground of the community's confidence in the fairness of the judgment.

The passage therefore ends its treatment of the dealings with the statement that gathers the law, the mercy, and the account. The reader is given the instruction and the reminder together, and the community's teachers read the two as one teaching about the wealth of the believers.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The sentence establishes the command to be mindful of the day of the return, the certainty that every soul will be paid in full for what it has earned, and the assurance that no person will be wronged in the account. The community's teachers used the verse when they set out the law of the dealings and when they encouraged the believers to attend to the account of their property, and the sūrah's following verses turn to the writing of the contracts, so that the reminder and the practical instruction stand beside one another.
